Welcome to our translation of Sixty Verses on the Logic for Proving Emptiness, certainly one of the greatest works in the history of Asia, and the world.  It was composed almost 2,000 years ago by Arya Nagarjuna, who is one of the most wonderful thinkers of all time.  It is a difficult book, since emptiness itself is a difficult subject, but as with so many difficult things in the world, the rewards of happily attacking the difficulty are substantial.

We have prepared for you not just a translation, but one can say an entire manual for getting the most out of Master Nagarjuna’s classic.  This wisdom manual can be broken down into nine different sections:

Here in the introduction, we offer you first some information about our three authors: Arya Nagarjuna (c. 200ad); Je Tsongkapa, Lobsang Drakpa (1357-1419); and his disciple Gyaltsab Je, Darma Rinchen (1364-1432).  Details of the lives of ancient thinkers are almost always scarce; but we believe that the information available can illuminate the writings of these authors, and is worth the effort of digging out—and so we have.  We have also completed a detailed analysis of our authors’ works, and a statistical “impact study” of how their compositions have affected our world.  The latter is possible only now that we have searchable input of all the relevant works, due to the efforts of the Asian Legacy Library (ALL).
2) Root text, plus commentary by Gyaltsab Je

The major part of the current volume is the commentary by Gyaltsab Je upon Arya Nagarjuna’s Sixty Verses.  We offer you first the original Sanskrit of the root text, which unfortunately has not yet been recovered in full.  Next comes the Tibetan translation of the root text along with the Tibetan for Gyaltsab Je’s commentary, accompanied by its modern English translation.
3) Notes to Je Tsongkapa’s lectures on the Sixty Verses

Gyaltsab Je’s illustrious teacher, Je Tsongkapa, once delivered an oral teaching on the Sixty Verses, with Gyaltsab Je taking careful notes.  These notes were published as a separate work, and provide valuable insight into the thinking of both Nagarjuna and Gyaltsab Je.  We here provide the entire transcript, with the Tibetan original; accompanying root text; and English translation.
4) Unique features of the Consequence Group

Gyaltsab Je’s commentary discusses some of the unique features of this highest historical school of Buddhism, but they are difficult and can use some additional clarification for modern readers.  Thus we have added, in Appendix A, a thorough study of these features drawn from major thinkers of the historical lineage.

It is a custom of Tibetan philosophical commentators to descry an outline in the original ancient writings, to better organize our understanding of them.  In a way, such outlines actually constitute a profound commentary in themselves.  It’s easy to get lost in the many outline levels as we go through the explanation; so we have not only included them in the commentary, but also listed them separately, here in Appendix B.  We encourage you to spend some good time to study this outline, to get a more wholistic view of the original work—which is written in more amorphous poetry.

Although Arya Nagarjuna’s root text is distributed throughout the commentary even in the original carving of the latter, it is tremendously useful to be able to read this original work through on its own, in its own flow.  And so, in Appendix C we offer you the entire root text in an easily readable form.
In Appendix C we offer a complete listing of Arya Nagarjuna’s 141 total writings, by topic; and then in Appendix D the same for Gyaltsab Je.

We include four separate bibliographies of relevant source and reference works, for texts originally written in Sanskrit; Chinese; Tibetan; and then modern languages, primarily English.  The ancient writings here are most often accompanied by the corresponding ALL catalog number; with which you can easily obtain searchable versions on the ALL website, free of charge.
Finally, at the end of this volume, you will find a description of the different components of the Diamond Cutter Classics Series of great books, currently numbering 120 works.
A topical summary of the Sixty Verses

It’s a tremendous advantage—as we delve into the work—to have at hand a short list of the important concepts presented in the flow of one of these ancient classics of Asian literature.  It’s also necessary for the next section of this introduction, where we examine the intended and actual impact of the mother work, the Sixty Verses.

The customary obeisance at the very beginning of the Sixty Verses stresses the theme of the entire work: the essential bond between the concepts of emptiness, and the way in which all things exist in a dependent relationship.
Arya Nagarjuna jumps immediately into a difficult examination of the ideas of existence & non-existence—both in their traditional meaning, and their deeper meaning.
The distinction of infants vs. aryas

Next we are introduced to the idea that there are two kinds of people in the world: those who actually know what’s going on, and those who never did.  The latter are referred to as “infants” or—as modern, colloquial, and disparaging English might put it—“two-year-olds.”  The former are known as “aryas,” or “those with a higher understanding” of emptiness; and Nagarjuna himself is considered foremost among all of these, in the history of this world.
Living in the world of pain,

The indisputable procession of every human life—for each & every one of us—is a traumatic and painful birth followed by growing & learning through our younger years; a sometimes stable middle age; and then the inevitable pain & terror of descending into old age and the unknown of death.  Nagarjuna leads us into the idea that really understanding the world of pain is to escape it.

Nagarjuna then begins to explore the idea that the world is like a magic trick or illusion—not what it appears to be, when the magician makes something impossible happen.  The Arya especially asserts that when something stops—when we stop the pain of life, for example—what’s happening is not at all what it seems.
Nagarjuna delves into the state of mind that sees the reality behind the illusion; can it even perceive, at all, the false appearance of the illusion?
The Arya explores the famous ancient expression for reaching our spiritual goals—“I have done what I had to do.”  Maybe it’s not what we thought?
If it’s the case that endings are not what we thought they were, then how can beginnings be what we thought they were?  And can that understanding help us reach the end of pain?

If we totally misunderstand the endings & the beginnings of things, then won’t we be swamped in misunderstanding for those very things between these beginnings & endings of theirs?  And won’t that distort our daily behavior & feelings?

We begin to delve into the idea that—if things start & stop somehow through a process of dependence—then they cannot be starting & stopping as we thought they did; which misimpression has caused us all of our problems, to date!

The wearing out of things and relationships and human bodies is one of the greatest pains in our life; this too has its causes—perhaps they can be stopped, if we can identify them correctly.  And thus stop our pain.

Yes, the historical Buddha did describe a starting & a stopping; and certain facts of life: the parts to all persons; their senses; the categories of all existing things.  But he didn’t ever intend for us to take these as literal descriptions of how things start & stop.
Those who understand the deeper interpretation of Lord Buddha’s teaching can then free themselves from all pain.
There is a path in, and a path out
Not understanding this deeper interpretation of truth is a true path to a continued life of suffering.  The world becomes a grand and macabre, illusory trap.

Teaching a sincere student can properly begin with some apparent overstatement, which is then wisely corrected when they are ready.  It’s important for a teacher to be able to recognize these personality types—then dangerous for the student if they fail, and wondrous when they succeed.
How it feels when we do break through to the deeper intent of our teacher’s teachings; and the considerable trouble if we are slow doing so.
It is not impossible that a major part of the world as a normal person experiences it is a product of their own unrecognized imagination.  How then could they proceed through this world accurately?
What types of people should we actually expect to misunderstand how much of their world is a mental creation?  What types of more perceptive people should be ashamed of this continued failure?

At the very start of the book, we were misunderstanding existence & non-existence; and starting & stopping.  Which has brought us here, to believing—by inference—that the world has stopped entirely, or else could never change an iota.
What it feels like to continue in our blindness,

We approach the shore of a quiet lake in the middle of the night, and are shocked to see that the moon has fallen out of the sky and is floating atop the water.  Sooner or later we will catch our own mistake.

Conflict between all human beings (including between those who understand what the Buddha really meant, and those who do not) is an added tragedy to the already toxic mix of our natural sufferings.  And this conflict always comes from grabbing at lake moons.  Its resolution is obvious.
There is a place between seeing a lake moon and realizing it was never there.  Most of us live in this inbetween place.  Every time we go to that place, we are vulnerable to the viper of unhappiness.
Sooner or later we will figure out what’s going on with the reflection of the moon in the lake.
Let us avoid—as we become aware that there are two moons here—taking the real one as being “real” in the way we used to think.
Do it for a higher purpose

Any time we do something wonderful in this life—whether it’s finishing an important, ultimately helpful book, or any other good deed—let us dedicate it to the higher purpose of seeing all living kind freed from their self-imposed suffering.
for the last 2,000 years or so
The pioneering work of searchable meta-databases such as the Asian Legacy Library now makes it possible for us to propose an accurate answer for an intriguing question:

Alright, we’ve seen that list of topics that Arya Nagarjuna wanted his Sixty Verses to convey to readers; and a sensitive reading even of the English translation (and of The Arya’s other available writings) can indicate which themes were particularly important to him.  That is, we can with fair accuracy say which ideas Nagarjuna was especially hoping his readers would grasp; and use.

And because we can now, on ALL, do a data search through some three million pages of two millennia of ancient texts within a few seconds, we can actually assess: Did Nagarjuna’s message get through to his readers, the way he wanted it to?  Because that’s exactly what he himself is exploring in his Sixty Verses, for the messages that Lord Buddha himself placed in his bottles & threw out into the sea of history.

If all the bottles were collected and deciphered by readers in the centuries following Nagarjuna, we can relax and simply pass our bottles on, in a selection of modern languages, and our work is done.

But perhaps our statistical research will reveal that some bottles are still floating around in the ocean of ancient libraries.  In that case, we can do the world a great service by gathering them in, and pointing out—in this introduction—their contents.

The way we have accomplished our impact study here is to analyze which particular lines of the Sixty Verses have most often been quoted and explained, in the 18 centuries since Nagarjuna.  This was possible because in modern times we have two representative bodies of literature derived from the earliest works—such as those by The Arya.

First we have the Tengyur Collection of ancient Buddhist writings translated into Tibetan over a significant period ending about 600 years ago.  These are commentaries to the original teachings of Lord Buddha which were almost all composed in Sanskrit; and they themselves date from about 450bc up to about 1000ad.  They include about 3400 different titles, in 210 volumes that average roughly 600 pages each.

ALL has digitalized, in searchable format, the entire contents of the woodblock edition of this collection created in Derge, Tibet, in about 1730.  This collection (considered the most authoritative of its genre) would include almost all of the works written by Arya Nagarjuna which reached Tibet and were translated into Tibetan; but it would also include all of the instances where writers after Nagarjuna quoted his Sixty Verses—thus demonstrating the impact of his verses on roughly 40 generations of Buddhist thinkers and, most significantly, which verses and concepts these writers gravitated towards.
That is, how close did The Arya come to conveying the wisdom he wanted to convey, to these first 40 generations, over the first 800 years?

And then for the almost exactly 1,000 years since the teachings of the Tengyur reached Tibet, we have another collection of writings which we refer to as the Sungbum, or authoritative collected writings of the Tibetan sages.  One of the earliest catalogs of this body of literature was completed at Tohoku University in Japan in the late 1930’s, and includes about 2,000 different works.   ALL has cataloged several hundred thousand Tibetan writings in libraries all over the world, and has input and properly subject-indexed over 15,000 of the selected, most authoritative of these works.

What this means is that we can “search” the thousand years since Buddhism ended in India, and then continued on and thrived, in its most authentic form, inside Tibet.  We can find out which ideas within the Sixty Verses thrived, and affected real people, and which very special ideas were—perhaps—largely overlooked.  And when we identify those ideas, we can ourselves try to “correct” the impact of the Sixty, highlighting the “overlooked” ideas and restoring the balance of ideas that The Arya was seeking.

We should note here the necessary limitations of our exercise.  First, it could be many decades before we complete the task of creating accurate, searchable, digital copies of the tens of thousands of native Tibetan works ahead of us.  And so we have captured only a representative sample of later references to the Sixty, although we can say that the native Tibetan works input already by ALL represent the indisputable cream of authoritative philosophical commentaries.

Secondly, we have restricted our search to citations where the native author—whether very ancient Indian or less ancient Tibetan—has identified in situ the Sixty Verses as the source of their quotation.  It is possible to take the individual lines of the Tibetan translation of Nagarjuna’s work and search for them separately to see where & when they were quoted—in both the Sungbum and the older, translated Tengyur—but we felt it would be too time-consuming, especially since we note (especially in the Tengyur) that there are different Tibetan translations for the same original verses.

That is—as we might expect, going through the same translation process as we ourselves in our own times—there were different translations circulating, and the process of finalizing one particularly authoritative version took centuries.  We may search the database for specific lines in the standard translation, but we will necessarily then miss the same lines in an alternate translation; and thus misjudge the impact of those lines upon Nagarjuna’s future generations.

There is another note we should make here, that spellings of the Tibetan translation of the title of the Sixty Verses can differ; specifically, where we wrongly see rig-pa (“mind”) for rigs-pa (“logic” for proving emptiness).  We checked both spellings in our search, in order to bypass this error.

So now that our task is defined, let’s get to it.  Which ideas from the Sixty Verses—from among all those we have listed in our brief study of major topics above—most affected people in the last 2,000 years or so?  And which were perhaps not understood or appreciated fully?
Which concepts would Arya Nagarjuna want us to pay more attention to, for our own benefit?

Digging through the ideas from the Sixty Verses that did make it into the collective consciousness of the later wisdom lineage, we can first make some general observations, and then drill down to specific verses and the concepts they convey.  There are 16 subject categories of the Derge Tengyur—again, these are works from ancient India that could be quoting our Sixty Verses—and we find specific citations in ten of the works there (not counting the Verses and its commentary themselves).

These ten are divided among three subject categories on the philosophical school of the higher Middle Way (here known as Madhyamika); the secret teachings (or Tantra); and what are known as Miscellaneous Topics—in this case, upon how to develop the deep meditation on emptiness known as “special insight,” or vipashyana.  This is partly because of the primacy of the concept of emptiness in the thinking and practices of these three crucial areas.

Secondly, the schools of ancient India (such as parts of the Abhidharma, or Higher Knowledge movement) which The Arya is correcting—either directly or indirectly—would not have been expected to quote him.  And other schools, such as Pramana (Logic & Perceptual Theory) or Svatantrika (lower Middle Way) would have risen to prominence only centuries after he wrote (even given the tradition that he himself lived for centuries).

As for the works in the Middle Way section, we should note that there is an entire major work of 30 full folios (well over 200 pages, if translated into English) devoted exclusively to the Sixty Verses; and this is the commentary to it composed by the 7th-century savant Chandrakirti.  This author is best known for his masterwork, Entering the Middle Way, a commentary to Arya Nagarjuna’s most famous writing of all time, entitled simply (and tellingly) Wisdom.

Together, these two books can be considered the foundation of all the greatest emptiness teachings upon this planet.  And so we can easily assert that the core idea of all of The Arya’s works has indeed been captured and passed on over the two millennia since he wrote.
Now for the meat of the matter: Which specific thoughts from the Sixty made it, first of all, into the collective consciousness of the first 800 years after The Arya?
Let’s look first at the most referenced ideas from the Sixty Verses in the Tengyur collection.  One of the “winners” here is verse 50 of the 60, which reads—

The core concept here is that one about all conflict in the world flowing from the habit we all have, of taking a reflection of the moon upon still lake water as being the real moon.  To put it in common terms, the entire world around us—and we ourselves—are flowing from seeds in our own mind: seeds that were planted when we were kind or not so kind to others.

Most of us though have never realized that the world is this way (why would we, without learning how it works?); and so when we meet another person who takes a completely different position from us (about almost anything), there is the potential for conflict.

The lesson here though is that neither your position nor my position ever came from anything but me myself, from my seeds.  Thus we can’t even say that there is a “my position” or a “your position”: we take no position.

The point then is not at all that it’s somehow wrong ever to take a position; in fact, we are taking a position on positions already here.  Unfortunately though there appear to have been a great number of people who took this verse to mean that a gentleperson never asserted their own ideas—even when they were correct.
Another winner in the quoted verse competition for the ancient Indian writings is the following—

This seems a fairly straightforward verse about teaching the idea of emptiness only to those who have been properly prepared for it—and the need to do so has forever been enshrined within the traditional vows for bodhisattvas.  Those who approach emptiness too early, and misunderstand it, bluntly, “ruin their life.”

On a deeper level, though, let us recall our context.  As we will learn from Je Tsongkapa below in this introduction, Arya Nagarjuna’s intention in writing the Sixty Verses in the first place was to correct Buddhist schools of thought that had sprung up and thrived during the six or seven centuries between him and Lord Buddha.

These schools had accepted the apparent import of the first turning of the Wheel of the Dharma—those teachings granted by the Buddha during the first of the three major periods of his teaching career here on this earth—as being literal, and his final word.  And this apparent import had left no room for the proper idea of emptiness, as we have just described it with lake moons.

In Nagarjuna’s scheme of things, then, Lord Buddha in his basic, expository teachings on the parts of the person; the doors of sense; and the divisions of existent entities was simply laying the groundwork for his later teachings in the second turning of the Wheel—in talks such as the Heart Sutra, or the Diamond Cutter Sutra.
This in turn set the stage for both of these Turnings to be explained as but figurative, in the third turning of the wheel; set the stage for what we now know as the Mind Only School.

If you really think about it, then, The Arya is making the astounding assertion that the lower way of Buddhism (the Hinayana) is actually just the beginning of the higher way (the Mahayana).  He was not just designing a new system that was later bitterly criticized by the old; he was telling those of the old system that they were the opening stages of the new.

These thoughts—first described by Lord Buddha himself in the sutra called What I Really Meant (the Sandhi Nirmochana)—were only perfectly delved by our second author in this volume, Je Tsongkapa, in his Essence of Eloquence, on the art of interpreting the teachings of Lord Buddha.  And certainly Arya Nagarjuna is pushing us there, with this section where he describes how certain instructions are only meant to soften the mind for deeper ones.

A third verse that makes it several times into the Tengyur is the very first of the sixty (again, counting the preface verse as zero).  Instinct tells us that Arya Nagarjuna is very likely to use this opening verse to express one of the guiding thoughts of his entire work—
Those whose minds have gone beyond
The idea that things could exist or not,
And who no longer dwell there,
Understand that the meaning of a cause
That there is nothing at all to see.

The idea that the world, and especially our suffering within this world, is the product of the interaction of causes & results—what is famously called “dependence,” or more clunkily “dependent origination”—is perhaps the defining concept of the earlier schools whom The Arya is addressing in his Sixty Verses.  In this verse, he is making again an astounding claim: That the very meaning of dependence is emptiness.

In simple terms, we can see this as the impossibility of the final, indivisible moment of one entity causing or triggering the birth of another—as when a seed gives rise to the sprout for a tree.  We must agree that the seed exists in time, and that it ages.  In a sense then there is an “earlier” portion of the seed—a “front end”—and there is a “later” portion of the seed: a “back end.”

For there to be a cause-and-effect relationship between the seed and the tree which springs from it, two entities must be present.  This is simply because, in every case, a “relationship” requires that two things are present, in the same time, to enjoy that relationship.  In theory then the back end of the seed must be making contact with and engendering the front end of the tree.
The problem is, that the front end of the tree doesn’t exist until the seed has disappeared—having caused the tree.

In short, there is an emptiness of our normal concept of seed+tree even at the root of dependent origination: dependence itself exists only in the context of emptiness.  Which makes it especially silly to say that we accept dependence, but not emptiness.

By the way, the punchline here is that those seeds in our mind lay down a seed; and then lay down a sprout popping out of the seed; and then lay down a tree that grew out of the sprout.  The seed and the sprout and the tree are connected then not to each other—they are dependent, not on each other—but rather upon the real seeds that created each of them individually: mental seeds.

And this fact should never be repeated without adding the words…“seeds, which were planted in our mind by treating others with kindness, or not.”  Which ties dependence & emptiness to an ethical way of life.

It is again one of Nagarjuna’s most ardent fans—Je Tsongkapa—who stands as evidence that this particular concept from the Sixty Verses survived the test of time (despite being imperiled, like most great ideas, during selected generations).  Some 13 centuries after The Arya, Tsongkapa composes a concise masterpiece entitled A Praise of Lord Buddha, for Teaching the Concept of Dependence.  Here and elsewhere he forever bonds together the two guiding principles of dependence & emptiness; demonstrating in fact their own dependence.

Let’s take a look now at the verses from the Sixty that appear most often in authoritative works of the literary tradition in Tibet during the millennium from the substantial introduction of Buddhism into that land, up to the present time.

We can say first of all that there are five or six times more references than we see in that first, Indian millennium: Nagarjuna is catching on!  And we can say as well that it is different concepts catching on, than in the first thousand years.  Let’s look at just the top five of the many examples.
Verse 20 of the Sixty is perhaps the biggest winner, with over 20 references.  Here is how it reads:
Through any nature of its own

Conventional wisdom in the Eastern classics tells us that a cessation or stopping of, for example, an undesirable human quality is the simple absence of that quality, and thus represents an unchanging thing—since you can’t be more or less absent, when you’re absent.

Remember though that this verse appeared, in our topical summary above, inbetween a clarification of dependence, and a demonstration that the Buddha’s earliest descriptions of this principle were spoken with a grander scheme in mind: to bring the student further on towards the sacred space of emptiness.

As such, the absence referred to here involves two very different vacancies.  First, the absence of any stopping of a changing entity which has not resulted from the wearing out of its causes.  We have only to look at a worn-out shoe; or a sock with a hole in it; or an uncooperative, aging automobile to appreciate this particular kind of emptiness.

Second, all absences—like all presences, in fact—reflect the “causes” of an ultimate stopping, which is the non-presence in every entity in the universe of existing from its own side, rather than from the seeds in our mind.

Here—at the juncture between the old school’s dear principle of dependence, and the new school’s cherished emptiness—the existential stopping in all entities allows the stopping of everything negative in life, and all suffering.  Once we understand that everything and everybody we ever meet is flowing from our own mental seeds, it becomes pointless ever to blame anyone, or hurt anyone.
And when there’s no longer any point to hurting anyone, we never again plant a negative seed.  Without its seeds, suffering itself ceases in our world.
Another particularly persistent verse from the Sixty is the 35th, which describes what this ceasing of suffering is like; in other words, which informs us of nirvana—
As the only thing which is true;
What person could there ever be
Were not things which were wrong?

In our topical summary earlier on, we saw that this verse lies within what we called “the feeling of discovery,” or the sensation of finally understanding what the Teacher meant for us to learn all along, even when she or he was skirting the pith of the matter until they felt we were truly ready for it.

The question of just what nirvana is has stood starkly inbetween the old and new ways of Buddhism.  The main thrust of thinking before Nagarjuna said that—when a person achieves this particular freedom from the suffering world—it is because their physical form and mental processes have simply shut down, forever.  It sort of feels like cutting off your whole arm, to cure an open cut on your palm.

Nagarjuna and his ilk rejected this description of nirvana, and instead asserted that in its simpler form, nirvana was the end of negative thoughts brought about by realizing how there is nothing in our life that is not coming from our own mental seeds: which is not my own fault.  Again, how can I strive against another person’s behavior towards me, when I realize that this behavior is coming from myself?

In its deeper form—as we sense reflected in the opening lines of this verse—nirvana as freedom from unwanted baggage does not require us to disappear physically and mentally from the world.  When we stand in the presence of highest truth during the direct perception of reality, we stand without any perception of anything which is not totally real.  And it is in this sense that we have shed the suffering world.
Another bestselling verse that strongly survived the test of time during this last millennium follows closely after that last one about nirvana—
Why then would it ever be

When we read ancient texts that talk about the world we live in as being a figment of our imagination, then naturally this can invite feelings of nihilism: What’s the point of being alive, if my whole life is just an unreal dream?
A careful reading of this particular verse corrects that overly extreme interpretation.  When we say that the world is a “product of our imagination,” we have one of two things in mind.

One, we are living in a world created by our own mind, but only in the sense that seeds planted within our mind by past moral or immoral behavior towards others are ripening and organizing the raw data around us into correspondingly pleasant or unpleasant objects.  Which is, of course, why some people say a song is fantastic when the same song sounds like a train wreck to someone else, possessed of different seeds.

Please note: In this case the world around me is a result, in a way, of my imagination; but that absolutely doesn’t make it anything less than real.  If you think it does, go out on a highway and stand in front of a speeding car and see if the steel bumper that crushes your knee is real or not.

On a deeper level, we live in a world of sheer imagination when we fail to recognize this other sense of imagination, this world created by my own mental seeds.  This is a different kind of imagination, where we think something is there that could never be there.  A mirage in the desert—and nothing there to drink.
It takes one to know one
Our next popular survivor of the centuries appears early on in the Sixty Verses—
Things and the absence of things.

According to our topical outline above, these lines are part of a section of our text where we learn that there are two—and only two—types of people in the universe.  Some have come to see, directly, that there is nothing at all out there which is not flowing from the seeds in our own mind; and thus they have undergone the ultimately precious direct perception of emptiness.  Throughout this section, Nagarjuna refers to these people as “great beings,” using the Sanskrit word mahatma, as it was rightfully used with Mahatma Gandhi.

Then there are people who have yet to see that life and the world are flowing from their own mental seeds; and throughout our texts here they are referred to as “infants,” in the sense of a very young child who simply doesn’t understand what is going on around them.  The kind of child who makes faces at the other baby in the mirror; as you and I do when, for example, “another” person criticizes us.

Great beings have seen that nothing that is not coming from my own mental seeds was ever there; and they have seen that whatever they do see is coming from their seeds.  Throughout the ancient literature, such beings are referred to with the Sanskrit word arya—which, despite its profane use historically by the Nazi political party of the Second World War—does indeed refer to a “higher person,” but only in the sense of one who has seen emptiness directly; and thus seen for example the ultimate and correct self-interest of in fact refusing ever to harm another person.

It takes one to know one, and throughout the 20 or so centuries after Nagarjuna lived, he has been known by the moniker of “The Arya,” implying correctly that he was perhaps the greatest of all people in history to directly see and then teach, to all of us, emptiness.
The greatest hit of all time
By a huge amount, the most quoted lines, of all the lines, in the Sixty Verses are those of the final, sixtieth verse—
Of what I have just done,

As noted above in our topical summary, these are the “do it for a higher purpose” lines.  Arya Nagarjuna knew—even before the impact study numbers came out—that he had done a great goodness for the world, for centuries to come, by writing his Sixty Verses.  As with everything else he ever owned (including his own head, as we shall see), he decided to share this extraordinary act of good karma with everyone in the world around him, to help them become fully Enlightened Beings.

And so thus, even today, it is a custom in Buddhist monasteries throughout Tibet to repeat this last verse at the end of each & every virtuous activity—especially that of attending a Buddhist lesson with our own Teacher.  Are you curious, with us, how this custom may have started?  Let’s go on a side trip there, and then return to see if there are any absolutely vital verses or concepts that may not have survived the last 20 centuries so robustly.

Who started—and who passed on—the custom of using the final verse of the Sixty Verses as an all-purpose dedication of any good karma we ever perform?  You may be interested to know that a part of this verse was likely taken verbatim—either consciously or subconsciously—by Arya Nagarjuna from one of several works in the Kangyur collection.
This is in the earlier portion of the verse, which reads—

We see this piece in seven different variations among the thousand-odd works of this collection of the speech of the Buddhas themselves.  The first four are in a work from the secret teachings entitled The Ascertainment of Suchness: Heart of All Secrets, where it mentions for example both “the crystal palace of your vast compassion, born from completing the collections of merit & wisdom,” as well as “completing the collection of merit & wisdom, as the pledge of the host of the secret world.”
Next, in another secret work entitled Lines of Auspiciousness, for All Three Jewels, we see—
In a similar work entitled That Mighty Secret Teaching of the Play of the Supreme Horse; the Matchless Intent of Each & Every One Gone Thus, we read:
Finally, in an open teaching named Calling to Witness with a Hundred Prostrations, we see this variation for the final lines—
Of the negative seeds within us,
May it come then that we bless

We also see the exact same lines as for our full 60th verse—whether they are the source of Arya Nagarjuna’s verse, or copied from it, is unknown—within the Tengyur Collection, in a secret work relating to Manjushri (the Angel of Wisdom) entitled A Ritual for Raising the Wish for Enlightenment.  Another, partial reference to a common variation of the verse may be found in a secret work of the Mahamudra, or Great Seal, entitled The Song of the Diamond.

Next let’s go forward in time to the Sungbum collection of native Tibetan works.  Leaving Gyaltsab Je and Je Tsongkapa’s works directly commenting on the Sixty, we analyzed 18 occurrences of Arya Nagarjuna’s full dedication verse, in the writings of 10 of Tibet’s most authoritative authors, over a period of more than five centuries.

Je Tsongkapa himself, writing circa 1400, uses the verse twice to discuss unique beliefs of the Middle Way school about achieving enlightenment.  His other leading disciple, Kedrup Je, employs the lines around 1420 for the same purposes.

Just about the same time, the Mongolian sage Hortun Namka Pel references the verse—for the first time we have located—to specifically discuss the practice of dedicating good karma, in a well-known work of the lojong genre, dedicated to developing the Wish for enlightenment.

Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen, the great textbook writer of Sera Jey Monastery—part of Tibet’s “Big Three”—uses the lines, around 1500, no less than four times, primarily in discussions on the components of an Enlightened Being.  Kedrup Tenpa Dargye, the Jetsun’s counterpart at Sera Mey Monastery (and apparently one of his closest disciples), utilizes the verse thrice for similar purposes in the decades following.

About 150 years later, his Holiness the Fifth Dalai Lama—Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso—again quotes the entire verse in a discussion of the makeup of a Buddha.  And then finally, somewhere near 1700, the great Jamyang Shepa specifically uses the verse within a ritual for offering a special torma cake, as a prayer.  By 1740 or so then we have the famed Keutsang Lama Lobsang Jamyang Munlam using the verse as a dedication.

Within a few decades later, His Holiness the Third Panchen Lama, Pelden Yeshe, returns to the verse in a presentation on the bodies of a Buddha.  And then to close our discussion, the great Pabongka Rinpoche, Dechen Nyingpo, writing in the early 20th century, references the verse twice in philosophical discussions; and then once as a final dedication prayer, in his explanation of the famed Crown of Knives.

In conclusion then it would seem—from our research—that the current custom of using Arya Nagarjuna’s final verse as a closing dedication prayer in each & every sort of daily monastic activity has developed within those same great monastic institutions, themselves.

Having taken our quick look at verses that particularly stand out in the test of time in the two thousand years since The Arya, let us review the numbers one more time to discover if there are any particular ideas that may have been overlooked over the generations.

As anyone who has spent any time, for example, in the 25-year course of a geshe or Master of Buddhism can tell you, circumstances just seem to “gang up” on certain concepts or sections of scripture over decades and centuries in any institution, and with any teacher or lineage of teachers.  It might be that a major instructor has to leave the monastery for a few weeks to care for an ailing parent; it may be that lectures by a visiting monastic leader prevent a topic from being covered properly in the regular curriculum.  And then there is no one in the institution to pass those particular verses on to the next generation, and they fall into disuse.
That is, some ideas that deserve to live instead just fade away.

Reviewing the personal history of each of the 60 verses here—as we did for the closing verse—would be too much.  A more practical approach might be to highlight the verses that we believe (and this is an admittedly subjective evaluation) The Arya would have felt were most important.  And then we trace how healthy these verses remained over the millennia.
Inevitably, this exercise will lead each of us, in our own journey, to do our best to appreciate and reinvigorate these particular concepts.

We made an executive decision to stick to a Top Ten, partly because The Arya seems to have favored multiples of ten—witness not just his Sixty Verses, but also his Seventy Verses on Emptiness, or (if it is his) the Fifty Verses on Novice Monks.
Those whose minds have gone beyond
The idea that things could exist or not,
And who no longer dwell there,
Understand that the meaning of a cause
That there is nothing at all to see.

The first winner of our Top Ten Verses award is, not surprisingly, the very first verse (again, not counting the preface verse).  We’ve already seen that this verse—and its core message, that emptiness and dependence are themselves interdependent—did survive the test of time.
It also means that we have
Done what we had to do.

This particular verse has had an anemic history over the centuries; it was almost never cited—in fact, only by Arya Nagarjuna’s disciple, Master Aryadeva.  And then somehow it seems to have been overlooked, along with its tremendous core idea: that if what is truly real is only that which we see in the direct perception of emptiness, then the rest (including everything in a normal person’s whole life) is somehow not even there.
And so how then could we ever lead a successful life?

As evidence, The Arya points to the perfect homogeneity of what we see in the direct perception, as opposed to the kaleidoscope of a single normal day.  Gyaltsab Je takes pains here to debunk the idea that emptiness refers to common nothingness, and the nearly countless ridiculous schools in history that have tried to practice it this way.  As we will see, this is one of several topics he decides to expand on spontaneously, within his commentary to the Sixty.
Each one of us can contribute to the revival of this verse by focusing on this really crucial topic in our teaching and personal practice, as did Gyaltsab Je.

Get this: nobody quotes this verse, in the last two thousand years, except for the commentators to the Sixty Verses who have to (i.e., Master Chandrakirti, and our own Gyaltsab Je).  But what this is, is a direct reference to dependence in the form of the Wheel of Life: the ultimate representation—and by Lord Buddha himself, on at least three occasions—of the downward cycle that defines our normal human existence.

That is, what The Arya here calls the “wheel of dependence” contains the famous twelve links in the chain reaction that represents all of our suffering.  If we take just the first two links in this chain, we can look at how misunderstanding the world triggers the situation where we react for example to the positions that others (seem to) take, in a negative way.

This Wheel of Life has been, by the way, an especially favorite topic with Buddhists throughout the 25 centuries since Lord Buddha himself.  These Buddhists have included, prominently, those who denied the concept of emptiness.  But what The Arya is astoundingly pointing out here is that the twelve links of this famous chain reaction cannot actually be triggering each other—since, like the seed and the tree we discussed above, they can never make contact; because not even the slightest part of the two can exist at the same time, and for contact between two things you need…two things!
Even those things that cause the starting & ending of all things have no…starting or ending of their own!
To put it simply, the fundamental concept of cause & effect, or dependence, or dependent origination, cannot exist independent of emptiness.

We could throw in here the priceless idea of the twelve links or components of the process of suffering not just as a circle—and a downward circle at that—but as just one more set in an endless chain of whole interlocking circles.  The wheel of dependence does not just turn, impossibly, once; it links into countless other such wheels, before we were born and after we die.
Hey!  Let’s all try to revive this invaluable verse as well!  To do so, we have to explain it; and to explain it, we have to chew on it ourselves!
We’re going to give the #4 Award to another verse that we believe The Arya would have put there, himself.
Through any nature of its own

We have to say that, in this case, history got it right—and this verse is cited all over the place.  Still, if it’s in the Top Ten, it is probably not given the full appreciation it deserves.  Our human tendency, in terms of examining why we hurt, is to focus on why something bad started happening to us.  But—as we can all agree—it would probably be worth nearly equal time to examine why something good stopped happening to us.  And the answer is in there, hiding.

As far as being cited, this verse lays somewhere solidly below the top performers.  Aside from reiterating some of the ideas we’ve already talked about here, though, it represents an astounding reference to the entire centuries-old issue of Lord Buddha—or any other teacher in the history of Buddhism—tailoring their message to fit people of only novice thinking capacity, as a means of giving them a start towards higher versions of the ideas.

And what is the status of this “lower” presentation?  Is it a lie, if it’s technically untrue?  Is learning addition a lie, relative to the algebra it’s headed towards?  Or is it a genuine stepping stone in one entire, truly functioning staircase?  Again, we would say that it’s Je Tsongkapa himself who wants to draw our attention to these questions as deserving a lot more discussion than the literary tradition has afforded them.
This verse and the previous one have performed, over the ages, at a similar level—not too exciting.  But as a strategy, the lines are extremely exciting.

It’s all tied up, similar to what we have described already, in the emptiness of starting & stopping.  Again, since maybe the #1 suffering of life is (as Lord Buddha himself noted) impermanence, then it would seem to be the most exciting thing in the world to have a verse that really tears it apart, for us to deal with in a new & successful manner.
And who are free of attachment,

This verse lays almost exactly in the same mediocre citation percentile as our last two.  But not only does it reiterate the concept of certain teachings as a “means to an end,” it goes further in describing what later became known as a “proper vessel”: candidates for deeper teachings.  Even calling people “candidates” in the context of emptiness instruction is earth-shattering.  And the expression, “sheer absence” as what we hold back, and then grant!  These lines are a grand lesson plan for the universe!
If it’s as we’ve described it,
This poor verse is very close to being never quoted, in the entire lineage (only once).  It contains though an extremely valuable concept within the Sixty Verses, which is of a “viper” or “demon.”

A huge part of human suffering has nothing to do with physical misery; rather, it’s the turmoil within our minds created by our own negative thoughts, minute-to-minute.  A big theme of Nagarjuna’s here in the Sixty is that there are certain states of misunderstanding that are particularly fertile ground for the arisal and maintenance of unhappy thoughts.

Misunderstanding is seen here as an opportunity or opening for emotions like anger, greed, jealousy, improper desire.  It makes the mind a “playground for the very demons.”  If we were more aware of that—and if we had studied books like the Sixty Verses and understood misunderstanding well—we could stop leaving openings for the demons.  And that would be well on our way to constant happiness.

As we’ve noted above, this particular verse has been a darling of people’s over the course of history—unfortunately, often in discussions of why it doesn’t mean that those of us who back the idea of emptiness don’t or shouldn’t define & stick to that position.  And so although we don’t need to launch a campaign to bring back awareness of these lines, we do have to be vigilant that they are read & used accurately.
Of what I have just done,

The final verse of the 60, as we have well documented, has a well-deserved place within the many thousands of wisdom books and oral wisdom teachings over the centuries.  The idea that we are dedicating our study of a book that the author himself dedicated the writing of to countless beings is particularly sweet.

If we want to go deeper here, we need to turn (as we mentioned above) to working with the philosophical references to the verse—understand more clearly just what merit & wisdom are; and understand their specific results apropos the two resulting bodies of an Enlightened Being.  A starting point here is an appreciation of the first three of the six perfections of a bodhisattva as method; the last two as wisdom; and the fourth as a bridge between the two.  Let’s do our homework!
A final comment on the Top Ten

It is said, correctly, that a person who has seen emptiness directly also enjoys an uncommon, direct perception of upcoming events for—say—the coming five centuries, relative to the times in which they themselves live.

Which begs an interesting question here: Is it possible that Arya Nagarjuna could foresee that certain verses of his Sixty would get lost in the shuffle; or ignored; or grossly misinterpreted?  Could it be…that he was quite consciously setting up one of those “means to an end” teaching situations, where he poses us a riddle (or even pre-poses an imperfect answer to the riddle) and then allows us our own personal moment of discovery, when we solve the riddle on our own?
Was this all meant to be this way?
Let’s go to The Arya’s life

When you’re writing an introduction to a vitally important book like this, it’s a good strategy to get your important philosophical points in early; and then turn for example to the historical information, just in case people don’t make it very far into these first few pages.  So why don’t we relax now, and enjoy a little review of The Arya’s own life, and other such topics?

First, we are pleased to share with you that we have included an unusually detailed biography of Arya Nagarjuna in the pages following this introduction.  There is a typical problem with people who lived, like Nagarjuna, thousands of years ago (think Jesus, or Confucius) that we have little real information about their personal development and life, beyond vague or overly complimentary generalities.

We are fortunate then that we have a fascinating biographical picture of The Arya assembled from native sources by a native master, Khen Rinpoche Geshe Lobsang Tharchin, a very high geshe and former abbot of Sera Mey Monastery who lived 1921-2004.  With the permission of his translator and collaborator Dr. Artemus Engle, we include here the biography which was prepared for their publication, Nagarjuna’s Letter—a great translation of Nagarjuna’s personal letter of instruction to the ancient Indian king Udayibhadra, and the commentary upon this letter composed by Je Tsongkapa’s teacher and student, Jetsun Rendawa, Shunnu Lodru (1348-1412)—who was also a major influence upon Gyaltsab Je, our main author here.  And so we invite you to turn to those pages now; enjoy the biography; and then return here to the introduction.
We can add a few details about The Arya as well.  First of all, some description of what kind of arya he was: what manner of person among those who have seen emptiness directly.

In general terms, the process of even passing through the necessary preparation to see emptiness directly is said to require millions of years; and so it’s no surprise that credible reports (really based upon their writings and deeds) of people who have attained the rank of an arya in our world average about one per five hundred years.

The native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur Collection of the entire body of Buddhist commentaries from ancient India surviving in Tibetan translation is itself one of the greatest pieces of bibliographical science ever written; it dates, as we have noted, from about 1730.  This work specifically mentions that Arya Nagarjuna had attained the first bodhisattva level, which is known as Perfect Happiness; and this is repeated elsewhere throughout the ancient tradition.

That is, in general there are two kinds of aryas: two types of people who see emptiness directly.  One is a bodhisattva, meaning a person who is dedicated to becoming enlightened so that they can serve countless living beings living upon countless worlds.  The other is yet to reach this motivation, but has undergone that ultimate insight into how things work.
When we see emptiness directly on the bodhisattva track, we have simultaneously reached that first bodhisattva level, Perfect Happiness; and this then is the kind of arya that The Arya was.

Beyond that, certain qualities stand out to us even as we just read what he wrote, 20 centuries ago.  First, we can say that he valued brevity: Nagarjuna always says what he wants to say, in the clearest and briefest words possible, and then moves on.  He can write flowerly things, but he chooses not to.  He wants to respect our time; and that in itself is a high kind of morality.

Secondly—but perhaps primarily—Nagarjuna has a keen sense of the irony of life.  He is willing to laugh at himself, and at the mess of mortality that we have all put ourselves into.  He is funny, on a deep and meaningful level.  But at the same time we can feel a deep sense of compassion: he has obviously devoted his entire life to the labor of pulling us all out of that mortality.

Nagarjuna is courageous.  Very much like the Tibetan spiritual hero Je Tsongkapa, he is not afraid to approach and master any topic or idea, regardless of how very difficult it may prove to crack.  This pair are also persistent, and they will both continue digging into a concept until they are fully satisfied that they grasp it fully.

They both love books—the ancient classics.  Nagarjuna, as we can see from his biography, took the trouble to travel essentially to a foreign planet (of the nagas) to recover ancienter classics that were missing in this world; and we know from Master Xuanzang’s personal notes in the 7th century that he had organized a major library of philosophical treasures.  And who can forget the image of Je Tsongkapa digging around the hundreds of manuscripts in one of the first attempts at a Buddhist canon, at the monastery of Tsel, circa 1387?

They can both write; which is no small thing!  The Arya, much more than Je Tsongkapa, enjoys writing in lines of poetry, and seems to have a sensitive—almost musical—ear, which comes out even after his Sanskrit is translated into Tibetan.  It almost seems as though “hearing” the faint and exquisite “sound” of emptiness has tuned his senses.

Just a quick note, in case you weren’t aware; the name “Nagarjuna” itself means something like “Master of the Dragons.”  As you will see from his biography, Nagarjuna was intent on recovering some important books that had been taken off by the dragons, who—as everybody knows, especially from Smaug in The Hobbit—love to steal & horde shiny & valuable things.

The Arya used his powers of persuasion to bring the dragons (or nagas, which is like an ancient Indian water dragon) under his thrall, mastering them so strongly that they would even take forms like cobras to gather over his shaved monk’s head and shade him from the sun.  This is how we see him in the traditional carving here, which by the way notes in the writing below that “he was an arya, who had laid his holy eyes upon the true nature of reality.”

The second half of Nagarjuna’s name seems to have come from the name of perhaps the greatest hero of many thousands of years of Indian mythology: the ultimate archer, and moral genius, Arjuna, from the Bhagavad Gita—which predates The Arya by about 500 years.  There is something of a story behind this name Arjuna in itself.

Nearly all Sanskrit words are built from a verbal root, and there is one which is pronounced irj, technically represented as  ṛj.  This has a base meaning, according to the great father of American Sanskrit studies, William Dwight Whitney (1827-1894), of “to direct, stretch, or attain.”  It came into the Sanskrit word raja—meaning “king,” or literally “the one who directs everybody”—and thence to the Latin rex, with the same meaning (Tyrannosaurus Rex, “King of the Tyrant Lizards”).  This then morphed into our English regal, and royal.

We also have another root from Indo-European, a mother language of the Western world linked with Sanskrit.  Here,  arg has a base meaning of shining, or brilliant, and bright white.  We even see this root in the English verb to argue, which originally meant “to make lucid, or clear.”

We also see arg in the word argent—Latin and then English for “silver,” along with Argentina, “Land of Silver.”  It is even conceivable that argent in this sense is related to arya—with a base meaning of “gone higher,” or “gone beyond”—through a very fundamental root ṛ or ṛch, meaning “to go, to send.”  We see then the white & shining silver as a “noble” metal, or high among metals.

This would tie into the ancient use of arya and Aryan to refer to the lighter-skinned invaders of north India, who some 4,000 years ago pushed the darker, indigenous Dravidian peoples down to the south, where they still live today.  This became the unfortunate, ignorant foundation for the caste system of historical India—where arya came to refer to higher-caste, more-white.

Thus in traditional Sansksrit/Tibetan glossaries we also see arjuna defined a leader, or one who asserts authority (Tib: srid sgrub), in the way that Nagarjuna asserted his authority over the nagas.  This is reflected in how the great Tibetan historian, Buton Rinpoche, Rinchen Drup (1290-1364)—who as we’ve mentioned was as well prominent in assembling the Tengyur Collection—explains The Arya’s name:

The naga in the name Nagarjuna refers to those water dragons called nagas.  He was referred to as this “dragon” first of all because he refused to remain on the dry land between the two extremes, the two shorelines, of things never changing, or stopping altogether; rather, he had been reborn within the vast reaches of the way of all things.
Like those acquisitive creatures, Nagarjuna was lord over a hoard of the jewel treasures of the scriptures; and like a dragon he could incinerate and clarify things, with the light of his eyes alone.

The arjuna part of his name refers to a person who holds authority over others; for Nagarjuna was one who held reign over the kingdom of the teachings, and kept authority over the armies of the enemy of negative qualities, subduing them entirely.
And thus we combine naga and arjuna into Nagarjuna.  The text of Clarifying the Verses puts it this way:
Of staying in the two extremes,
Of the treasure hoard of the Dharma,
Of his teachings on the wisdom
Here in the world of his disciples
Of all three realms, with the gods.
Thus do I bow to Nagarjuna,
Of our enemy, this suffering life.

We might finally note, in closing, the use of the word arjuna to refer to the Indian trees Myrobalan Arjuna or Terminalia Arjuna, due to the shining white color of the inner bark, which is incidentally used as a medicine to improve the heart.  The former is of course the source of the medicinal arura fruit, beloved substance of the Medicine Buddha, filling his bowl.  Thus in the early Chinese translations we see The Arya’s name rendered either as “he with power or authority over the nagas” (龙猛 Long Meng) or as “tree of the nagas” 龙树 Long Shu).

Finally, in the ancient books we sometimes see The Arya’s name listed as Nagarjuna Garbha.  The Tibetans translated the latter part as “heart,” or “essence,” so we can render the whole as “Essence of the Dragon Master.”  The point is that his one obsession is trying to get us to understand the concept of emptiness, at the very heart of all things.  And it’s no coincidence that this same word often refers to “Buddha nature,” or the “womb of the coming Buddha” which lies within each of us, woman or man.

Any time we look into the life of a great Buddhist teacher, it helps to geoposition them between their major teachers & major disciples.  The first, of course, to see what may have been the major influences on their own development; the second to determine somewhat of their own personality, to see what kind of person they attracted—and how successfully they mentored them.  And both, of course, to gather further insight into their primary philosophical interests.

Of Arya Nagarjuna’s own teachers, common monastic tradition points to one main person: the tantric sage Saraha (seen at left), known primarily for his spiritual songs, or doha—many of which still survive in the Tengyur Collection, especially in a work entitled The Treasure Chest of Spiritual Songs (Doha Kosha).  A favorite topic of these songs was the Great Seal, or Mahamudra, which we mentioned earlier in conjunction with the final verse.

Mahamudra, in its correct interpretation, refers to the practice of getting at the subject of emptiness—the ultimate nature of things—by carefully observing and thinking about how our own mind thinks, and the principle of dependence as revealed therein.  And this obviously deeply affected the student, Nagarjuna.

Saraha is also known to have written a number of brief pieces on the secret practices of Avalokiteshvara, or Loving Eyes—as well as a number of esoteric lineages such as that of the Secret Collection, or Guhya Samaja.  All of these, tradition says, were passed down to Nagarjuna himself; and this is reflected in the latter’s known writings—which we will soon discuss.

Finally, we see in the Blue Annals Saraha’s own teacher listed as the king Visukalpa, which is sometimes rendered in Tibetan as Visukawa (Bi-su-ka-wa).  And Pabongka Rinpoche in a lineage tree states that in the earlier part of his life, Saraha was known as “the Brahmin Rahula.”

As for his own disciples, there is one that he was so close to that they are referred to as “the Father & the Son,” a sometimes appellation for an extremely close master/disciple relationship which is also applied to Je Tsongkapa and his two closest disciples, Gyaltsab Je and Kedrup Je.  The son in this case is the sage Aryadeva, who is best known to us for his 400 Verses, in explanation of emptiness.

There is also a tradition—which we see repeated in the Blue Annals—that Arya Nagarjuna had a group of four close disciples: Sakyamitra, Aryadeva, Nagabodhi, and Chandrakirti himself.  Listings like this have no doubt contributed to the tradition that The Arya lived for centuries, since some of the four are separated—as far as we know now—by almost 500 years.
Arya Nagarjuna’s works from the Tengyur:

There is a tradition in the great Tsongkapian monasteries of Tibet which says that we learn about a sage’s life not from their biography, but from their writings.  We have done a thorough study of compositions attributed to Arya Nagarjuna in the afore-mentioned catalog to the Derge edition Tengyur Collection of Buddhist works from ancient India which survive in Tibetan translation.  We have as well made some additional comments based upon the native catalog to the Sertri or “Golden Calligraphy” edition.  We here present to you our results, as a deeper look into the character of our primary author in the present volume.

To summarize, the Derge catalog attributes some 120 works to The Arya which survive in that edition, in Tibetan translation.  This count does not include three works (mentioned below) which the author of the catalog (the “Great Editor” Tsultrim Rinchen, 1697-1774) says that they were aware of, but which had not yet reached Tibet.  The count further does not include two works sometimes attributed to The Arya but which our editor (and we would agree; listed below) doubts were actually written by him.

Let’s take a statistical snapshot of the content of The Arya’s works, and then list the works themselves individually in the appendices, since they are so very important to the entire Buddhism.  We count the total folios here (two pages each, front & back) as 614, which in our Diamond Cutter Classics format would work out quite close to 5,000 pages of English.  The average folios for each work are 5; or the equivalent of 40 English pages.  A great number of works (brief poems or eulogies) are but a single folio; while the longest compositions run around 70 folios (just over 500 English pages).

The Sertri Catalog lists about 15 additional works, some of which may be works in the Derge under an alternate name or translation.  It should be noted that this catalog is also missing a significant number of the works by The Arya reported in the Derge catalog.

As for subject matter, we can divide the topics of Nagarjuna’s works broadly into four categories: praises (eulogies) and related pieces; formal works on the Diamond Way (Vajrayana, or secret Buddhism); philosophical works; and secular works.

The section on praises includes 21 works for a total of 32 folios, which represents 18% of The Arya’s writings, and 5% of the page quantity—which is to say, Nagarjuna was indeed fond of this vehicle: of presenting even deep philosophical concepts disguised as a heartfelt ode either to a person or to an idea.

The writings on the Diamond Way include 53 works, amounting to 44% of The Arya’s total title output, in 35% of the page quantity.  We ascertain here 18 different categories of the secret teachings, listed as follows—which again is itself a tribute to Nagarjuna’s primary teacher, the sage Saraha.

We have added an asterisk where the category seems to have received relatively more attention from The Arya.  And it’s worthwhile to note here that an entire section of the many secret titles in the Tengyur is actually named from him; this is the Klu-sgrub lugs or “Nagarjuna System” category within the tantras of the “unsurpassed” class devoted to the Secret Collection.  It is also noteworthy that Nagarjuna felt that a proper practitioner of the deep secret teachings should at the same time have a strong footing in the bodhisattva pledges and vows; and so important works on this topic have been included among his tantric writings within the various catalogs—as noted following.
4) Vajradhara, the Keeper of the Diamond
6) Krodhadeva Pancha, the Five Fierce Angels
8) Mudras (including Mahamudra), the Seals, or Partners
9) Bodhisattva Practice in the secret teachings
the Perfection of Wisdom as a secret teaching

As for philosophical works, The Arya has composed 39 titles in 333 folios, which amounts to exactly a third of his total works in 54% of his folios.  These are the titles that are most well known in present times, including for example Wisdom (his greatest work); the String of Precious Jewels; the Letter to a Friend; and of course the current Sixty Verses.    We can broadly divide this category into original philosophical compositions; commentaries upon the ancient sutras; and then epistles, advices, and prayers.  It should be noted that the epistles are essentially as pithy and crucial as the formal philosophical works.

The final category of The Arya’s writings, the secular section, subsumes seven different works accounting for only about 5% of his total writings, and folios.  Included here are five compositions on the topic of classical medicine.
For interested readers, we have included in Appendix C a summary, by topic, of all the separate works of Nagarjuna generally reported in the Tibetan Tengyur catalogs mentioned above.
Six Books on the Logic of Emptiness

A favorite topic on the philosophical writings of The Arya is a group of them known as “The Collection of Works on Logic” (Tib: Rigs-tsogs), which very importantly more clearly translated refers to “The Collection of Works on Proving Emptiness” (i.e. sTong-nyid rigs-pas bsgrub-pa’i tsogs).  This type of expression is reflected even in the title of our present work, Yukti Shashtika, where the shashtika means “sixty” and the yukti is a standard logic term for a syllogism.

The latter word is interestingly derived from the Sanskrit root  yuj, which means “to join,” as reflected in the sometimes Tibetan translation as jorwa (sbyor-ba), meaning a syllogism which properly joins together the required components that actually define a correct syllogism (tsul-gsum).  We see this same root for example in words like yoga (a practice joining body & mind through the medium of the inner winds, or prana); yoke (joining two animals together on a plow), and jugular (the vein joining head and neck).

Most often, this Collection of Works on Proving Emptiness is listed as having six members; but there are opinions!  We thought our readers would get a deeper insight into The Arya’s works as a body, by reading three short pieces on the topic here.  The first appears in that famous history of Buddhism by Buton Rinpoche, writing in the 14th century—

The books that state the heart of the matter outright—or, we can say, the essential meaning—are those of the “The Collection of Six Works on the Logic of the Middle Way.”  First there is (1) Seventy Verses on Emptiness, which demonstrates that every existing entity is empty of any nature of its own, and consists of dependence free of the elaborations of the two extremes [of either existing from its own side or—barring that—not existing at all].

Then there is (2) The Root Text on Wisdom, which serves to deny ideas like saying that things which grow from other things could do so in any real way.  These two compositions can be considered the foundation or core of the Collection.

Next we have (3) the Sixty Verses on Reasoning, which employs reasoning to prove these points.  Then there is (4) Ending All Argument, which serves to disprove the attempted criticisms of other parties on those first works.  (5) Crushing to a Fine Dust discusses the way in which these other parties frame their logic and arguments.

Finally we have (6) A Proof of Words, which demonstrates that—even though ultimately they have no nature of their own—the words used in the everyday world are, on a deceptive level at least, still perfectly correct and real.  With this then, it is said, we have the six works of the Collection.
The esteemed Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen, mentioned above, analyzes the same Collection in the following words:

And so we have the Collection of Works on Logic—the Root Text on Wisdom and the rest—which in general combine two topics: (1) proving the object of perception (that is, the subtle form of emptiness) with logical reasoning; and (2) demonstrating how the subject state of mind which comes to a realization of this particular object is in fact the very root of both freedom from the world of pain, and the attainment of omniscience itself.

As for the first of the two, (1) the Root Text on Wisdom takes as its primary task denying that what is to be proven could exist through any nature of its own.  (2) Crushing to a Fine Dust then then denies the sixteen forms of logical expression which could act to do the proving.

Our next task is to describe how—despite the fact that things have no nature of their own—the way in which everything does what it does is still perfectly valid.  First here there is (3) the Seventy Verses on Emptiness, which elaborates upon the seventh chapter of The Root Text on Wisdom to demonstrate how—in general—the working of things in the universe is all valid.
Next is (4) Ending All Argument—elaborating on the first chapter of Wisdom and demonstrating how, in particular, the way things work in the world is valid with disproving and with proving ideas.

Once we have utilized these works to establish the object of emptiness (in its subtle form) with logical reasoning, we turn to (5) the Sixty Verses, which demonstrates that the subject state of mind here—the view which realizes this particular object—is the very root for attaining just freedom from pain.
And then finally we have (6) the String of Precious Jewels, which shows that this same view is as well the root of the attainment of omniscience.

So there we have two slightly different takes on the Six Books, with a different opinion on what work will be the sixth.  Let’s turn finally to the matchless Je Tsongkapa, and see what he thinks on this issue—
Let us describe how that great being, Nagarjuna, wrote on these two great denials, undertaking to prove that actual truth of all things; and using logical means to accomplish the proving.
First there were four works, beginning with (1) the Root Text on the Middle Way, where The Arya disproved the positions of other groups, and certain of our own Buddhist groups, together.
Next was (2) Ending All Argument, which is an expansion of ideas presented in the first chapter of the Root Text, itself entitled “An Examination of Factors.”
Then there was (3) Seventy Verses on Emptiness, which expands upon ideas found in the seventh chapter of the Root Text, entitled “An Examination of Starting, Staying, & Stopping.”
And then we have (4) The Sixty Verses on Reasoning, in which The Arya denies certain ideas of our own Buddhist groups, in particular.
We then add a fifth work, (5) Crushing to a Fine Dust, in which Nagarjuna disproves the proofs of the sixteen expressions of logic.

Some then add A Proof of Words, or else the String of Precious Jewels, or else Fear for Nothing At All and say that the collection of works by The Arya which present the proofs is fixed at six.  Still others say that the Seventy Verses on Emptiness is the work which is the main body, and that the Root Verses on Wisdom is itself the expansion.  You should understand that these two positions are mistaken.

We might point out that Arya Nagarjuna’s works are a special point of focus for our present Diamond Cutter Classics translation effort.  Aside from the present work, we are also mostly through a translation of Wisdom, with an excellent commentary by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675-1748) based upon the explanation of Je Tsongkapa himself and thus entitled A Ship on the Sea of Emptiness: The Wisdom of Nagarjuna.  This will run about 800 pages in the English.

We also have a good start on Gyaltsab Je’s own commentary to the String of Precious Jewels, itself entitled A Clarification of the Essential Meaning of the “String of Precious Jewels,” on the Middle Way—a work that in English translation should run about 600 pages.  A translation of The Arya’s Essence of Dependence may be found in an appendix to our already-completed, 500-page translation of Stopping the Circle of Sadness, The Buddhist Teaching of the Wheel of Life, by the above-mentioned Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568).

The Master’s Stages of Meditation is found in full in our publication, Emptiness Meditations, a masterwork of these meditations by Choney Lama which comprises 450 pages.  As a separate document we have translated Nagarjuna’s Ceremony for Committing to the Wish for Enlightenment, in 25 pages.  And then of course we can add the early translation of the famed Letter to a Friend by Khen Rinpoche Geshe Lobsang Tharchin and Dr. Artemus Engle, which in 160 pages includes the wonderful commentary by Jetsun Rendawa (1348-1412).
And so—including the present work—our ambitious readers have about three thousand pages of Arya-related material to enjoy!

Sometimes we learn things about an ancient writer by looking at what she or he didn’t write about.  As we can see from the many headings in the excellent subject catalog structure to the literature by the Asian Legacy Library—and its precursors in the subject structure of the various editions of the Kangyur and Tengyur collections—a standard range of topics has evolved, over the centuries.

Gyaltsab Je, as we will see, displays a great degree of “range” between these topics in his writings; and almost no one has matched the range displayed by his teacher, Je Tsongkapa.  But which of these topics do we not find covered by The Arya, and what conclusions might we draw from that?
The Kangyur collection of works by Lord Buddha and other fully enlightened beings has twelve traditional subject categories:
2) The perfection of wisdom in 100,000 lines (12 volumes)
3) The perfection of wisdom in 25,000 lines (3 volumes)
4) The perfection of wisdom in 8,000 lines (1 volume)
5) The perfection of wisdom in 18,000 lines (2.5 volumes)
6) The perfection of wisdom in 10,000 lines (1.5 volumes)
7) Other teachings on the perfection of wisdom (1 volume)
9) The “majority” (a further collection of sutras) (6 volumes)
11) Nirvana (one massive work on the topic) (2 volumes)

Broadly, we can say that The Arya displays great range in these topics.  His 39 philosophical works cover—better than anyone, really—the emptiness teachings that comprise the perfection of wisdom here.  His four commentaries on sutra help treat those categories, and his 53 separate writings on the secret teachings neatly complete that picture.

What we don’t see from The Arya is a major effort to cover the only remaining subject category here: vowed morality, or vinaya.  What conclusions can we draw from this lacuna?  Nagarjuna did devote writings to the vows of the bodhisattva, dropping those among his secret teachings in a statement of its own about how to properly undertake those practices.

Perhaps he felt that the legalistic subject matter of the traditional monastic vows had already been treated as deeply as the topic allowed, by the Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma) writers who had held reign in the centuries before him?  Perhaps he saw the bodhisattva vows as the ultimate monastic code?  Perhaps he was focused on people rather than monks—as we see in his unsurpassed epistles to secular rulers of his day.

Alright, a quick look at the subject matter of the Tengyur, or the writings of Arya Nagarjuna’s “contemporaries”—the great human writers of Buddhist India, although he stands near the very front of that line historically.  The Tengyur collection contains 16 different subject categories; basically, we can consider this a list of everything that was worth knowing, to these greatest thinkers ever upon this planet:
9) Stories of past lives of the Buddhas (4.5 volumes)
12) Study of the Sanskrit language (4 volumes)

There is some ambivalence in this subject listing between topic and format; for example, dividing the Middle Way school into higher Middle Way (“Middle Way”) and lower middle way (“Perfection of Wisdom”) because of fine philosophical differences; and then separating epistles from these two for example just because they were written as letters to people, and not treatises.

Within the context of this ambivalence, we can say that The Arya has obviously covered songs of praise, with his 19 works in the genre.  Again, he has 53 works on the secret teachings.  He is the very father of the middle way genre mentioned here, with all of his 39 philosophical pieces; and we have the four direct commentaries to sutra.

Nagarjuna is perhaps the greatest epistle writer of all of Buddhism; and he does treat both the theory and specifics of language in several works.  He is a master of treatises on medicine; and has formally written on secular knowledge.

What subjects has he chosen not to cover, in this Tengyur context?  He does not write on the perfection of wisdom in the context of the lower Middle Way school, because it simply did not exist until people started arguing—centuries later—about what he himself had written.  And at any rate he would not support their defining concepts, such as the self-existence of the efficacy of logic.

The Mind Only school in its formal cast as well only defined itself with the sage brothers Arya Asanga and Master Vasubandhu, several centuries after our Arya.
