Higher Knowledge, or Abhidharma, is the very group that Nagarjuna is correcting here in the Sixty, and we have no formal presentations by him on their tenets—especially from their point of view, as we do with Vasubandhu.  We have already mentioned why The Arya, on the topic of vowed morality, might leapfrog to the bodhisattva and secret moral codes.

Although Nagarjuna weaves the principles of formal logic throughout every inch of his thinking, he does not treat logic & perceptual theory (Pramana) in the formally organized manner pioneered by Masters Dignaga and Dharmakirti more than three centuries after his time.

Again, he does treat language, but not primarily in the Tengyur genre of formal Sanskrit language study.  And finally, he is an early pioneer of the monastic tradition of largely ignoring any formal investigation of the theory of the fine arts.

This tradition would state, incidentally, that life is too short to expand our curiosity beyond the specific topics immediately required to stop the cycle of pain & death itself.  And that in itself, with no further comment, explains succinctly those of the 170 subject categories of the Sungbum collection of native Tibetan writings not covered among his personal pursuits already noted.

As noted at the outset, we have included within the appendices the combined root text of the Sixty Verses.  For the verses available, we add the Sanskrit based on the version of Li Xuezhu and Ye Shaoyong, as listed in the bibliography.

For the Tibetan, we have used the straight Derge Tengyur version in the combined root text found in this volume after the commentary and notes.  We would guess that a later party has inserted sometimes slightly differing full Tibetan verses into Gyaltsab Je’s commentary, but knowing that it may be of historical interest—giving the paucity of competing versions of the early Tibetan translations still available after the standardization of the Tengyurs—we have included items of interest there.
In concluding the portion of our introduction devoted to the root text, let’s quickly look at how it was passed down through the ages.

Formal commentaries on the Sixty Verses are few & far between.  We have mentioned that by the great master Chandrakirti, around 650ad, entitled simply A Commentary to the Sixty Verses on Reasoning (Yukti Ṣaṣṭika Vṛtti).  And of course there is the missing autocommentary by The Arya himself.  But we have not found any other full explanation of the text from ancient India.

Buton Rinpoche mentions “a short piece drawn from the Sixty Verses and explained in brief,” written by Acharya Vairochana, but we have not found a copy in the Derge Tengyur.  On the following page the Rinpoche mentions a version of the root text in six folio sections, and then apparently a rough explanation of the work in but one.

As for major Tibetan commentaries, we have of course the current work by Gyaltsab Je; and the included lecture notes for Je Tsongkapa.  In the massive St Petersburg Catalog of the Asian Legacy Library we see a single reference to A Jewel for Nagarjuna’s True Intent, a commentary of 25 folios to the Sixty written by “the monk Lobsang Tendzin,” who identifies himself as a disciple of the great Changkya Rolpay Dorje (1717-1786).  We have not found any other copy of this work, nor have we yet been able to look at this one.

We know of course—from the lecture notes to be discussed below—that Je Tsongkapa felt that the Sixty Verses was important enough to give a public teaching on it attended by Gyaltsab Je, who then composed the lecture notes.  Interestingly, we have a record that Je Tsongkapa heard the text himself from his and Gyaltsab Je’s teacher, the Sakya master Jetsun Rendawa.  This occurs in a biography of Je Rinpoche entitled The String of Incredible Jewels—

The father and his spiritual son [Jetsun Rendawa & Je Tsongkapa] then made their holy way to Radreng Monastery, leading a massive group of the ordained who were themselves keepers of the baskets of scripture.  They kept their winter retreat there, where the great Rendawa—that holy lama—gave Dharma teachings on topics such as the Sixty Verses on Reasoning, and the 25 topics of the Secret Collection.

We see in the biographies of Tsongkapa that this was about the year 1400ad.  And so it was one of those times in a lineage when a particular ancient classic called to teachers & disciples for the period of several generations.

An interesting feature of such lineages is that later monastic fans of a work who have heard it from their own teacher will try to piece together a lineage for the oral blessing of the title back to its original author—even if that author happens to be many centuries removed.

To be honest, some details of these oral lineages seem to a modern scholar to have been reconstructions rather than records; but still in our case they help us appreciate how the explanation of Nagarjuna’s book reached our own authors, and thence to us ourselves.

And so here is the traditional oral lineage for the Sixty Verses.  The majority of the list we offer as reported by the great historian and bibliographer Longdol Lama Ngawang Lobsang (1719-1794); please note that he has included two additional ways of tracing the lineage down to him.

From Longdol Lama we have filled in the lineage up to Pabongka Rinpoche Dechen Nyingpo (1878-1941) as reported by the latter in his own record of teachings received; and then we’ve completed the line up to the modern day, through his students.

Which brings us in this introduction, finally, to the work on Nagarjuna’s Sixty Verses by the great Tibetan thinker Gyaltsab Je—which comprises the great majority of the present volume.

The title of Gyaltsab Je’s own commentary to Nagarjuna’s work—as we normally see it carved on the initial heading page—is simply A Commentary to the “Sixty Verses on Reasoning.”  In the colophon though Gyaltsab Je reveals a more lavish and telling title: Crushing the Words of the Impudent, a Commentary upon the “Sixty Verses” of That Great Being, Nagarjuna—The Arya.

In general then we can note, first of all, that the work often drops into faux debate style—meaning that our author creates an antagonist who comes to make a claim about the content of The Arya’s work; and Gyaltsab Je then gets to destroy this claim (with gusto), all in the formal logic format.

Secondly, Gyaltsab Je—in keeping with many great writers of the Tsongkapian lineage—has included a (complex) topical outline on the verses, to help us appreciate the flow and true intent of each verse within that flow.  Again, we have added this outline as a separate document in Appendix B below, and we encourage the serious reader to spend some time with it, to unlock Arya Nagarjuna’s actual intent for every part of his work.

This outline is admittedly imposed by our commentator, but after all that’s his job.  It’s interesting, if you have time, to compare this outline to the one that Je Tsongkapa himself gives orally, in the lecture notes.  We’ve already noted how the root text verses for the commentary seem to have been added later by another party, with sometimes slightly different versions of the lines.  As a representative example, see our footnote to verse 59 in Gyaltsab Je.

If we follow Gyaltsab Je’s commentary and outline carefully, we detect that he has added three major discussions of his own, for topics that he felt were important to expand upon.  These are some of the most valuable sections of this entire book.  Let’s track them, using the Tibetan folio numbers inserted in our translation, since those won’t change with succeeding publications.

The first discussion occurs at f. 5a, and it relates to an extremely important topic of our book, where Arya Nagarjuna asserts that—if any particular object is any way misleading or illusory—then it cannot make its appearance to any mind which is in the direct perception of ultimate truth, or emptiness.  We can even say that this is a test of whether an object is completely real or not.

The objection then comes that—if that assertion is correct—then the very state of mind which confirms this fact cannot itself exist, since it cannot appear to the mind in that state either.  This then would seem to throw the entire presentation into question.  Gyaltsab Je at this point jumps up and declares, “It would be silly for me to even waste my time here destroying certain wrong ideas; but I would love to discuss this one!”

At f. 17a, Gyaltsab Je starts an additional, very helpful discussion of the two realities: ultimate reality and deceptive reality.  His comments here on the concept of a “correct” deceptive reality and a “mistaken” deceptive reality are very valuable, and in fact he seems to have gone on to compose an entire major work devoted to this topic, of the two realities.  We’ll be seeing that in his list of writings below; it is entitled A Presentation on the Two Realities, along with Instructions on Correct View, entitled “A String of Precious Jewels.”  In the colophon to his summary of Master Chandrakirti’s great Entering the Middle Way, our author even identifies himself as “someone who has attained some little mental illumination on the theory of the two realities.”

Our author also offers an expansion, at ff. 28a-29b, on the tricky concept of not taking any philosophical positions at all; without careful clarification, this discussion has led many a junior thinker astray.  And so we can say, in summary, that Gyaltsab Je is the perfect commentator, clarifying these difficult ancient verses, and guiding us through them and their potential pitfalls.

We can well imagine that Gyaltsab Je’s own interest in the Sixty Verses sprang from the teachings that his two teachers—Je Tsongkapa and Jetsun Rendawa—gave upon the work.  We have a surviving collection of lecture notes that Gyaltsab Je took during Tsongkapa’s teaching, and as translators we felt that our readers would very much enjoy this extra bonus—and so we add them in this volume, in their entirety.  By quantity, they represent only about a third of the length of Gyaltsab Je’s formal commentary.

As noted, this lecture record is largely written in debate format, and it’s fascinating to imagine one of the greatest Buddhist teachers of all time presenting nearly all the material from a teaching throne in an animated argument, sort of a re-creation of original debates, but two millennia later.  Again, this entire work is formed around the bones of an outline, and our reader can learn a lot by comparing the two outlines.

We should point out here that there is a distinct roughness to the notes: they are literally rough notes.  Anyone who has been around a lot of Buddhist teachings knows how often this can happen: a major disciple, already a very busy person, takes on the job of being a human recorder (in a time many centuries before electronic recordings), and perhaps never again has time to polish their notes.  And so we see various small textual problems, which though have no impact upon the meaning; the wording around the title and colophon seems to imply that the notes were readied for publication by others, later.

We should note here, by the way, that the printing of the Tibetan used for the main commentary here, by Gyaltsab Je himself, was quite “dirty,” and that the translators had to make over a hundred obvious corrections to the text.  Not-so-obvious corrections or debatable corrections we have left in the format {%} for dedicated scholars to think about themselves.

Those who have attended many teachings also know very well how a famous and already very busy Buddhist teacher may start out a subject covering it in great detail, only to find that other demands on their time prevent them from maintaining this detail all the way through to the end of the teaching sessions, if they hope to finish explaining the whole book.  In monastic parlance this style of teaching—accelerating in speed through the subject matter as the lectures continue—is so common that it even has its own name: it’s called a tabgyu (rta-rgyug), or “horse race.”

We should note here that—although we are careful in the present volume to supply our readers with quite some biographical detail for Arya Nagarjuna and Gyaltsab Je, we will not do so for our third author, Je Tsongkapa.  This is because our translation team has already produced the most detailed biography of this master available, again entitled King of the Dharma: The Illustrated Life of Je Tsongkapa.  This volume is accompanied by reproductions of numerous paintings from a very rare, original set; and we encourage our serious reader to acquire even just the e-book version and dig in.

Finally, for the translators ourselves, we found the lecture notes to be a great chance to review Arya Nagarjuna’s work after we had labored through the commentary: our reader can treat it as sort of a self-test on the relevant concepts.

Gyaltsab Je’s personal name has some considerable mystery; let’s delve in!  The first things we can say is the obvious: that the word gyaltsab (rgyal-tsab) in Tibetan literally means “substitute (tsab) for the king (gyal-po)” which is the Tibetan word for a “regent”: someone who comes and substitutes for the king if they are ill or deceased, or too young yet to serve.  In this sense it has come to mean the person who assumes the leadership role in a spiritual lineage, after the passing of the original founder of that line.

As such, Gyaltsab Je derives his name from the fact that he became the head of Je Tsongkapa’s lineage, after the Master passed away.  We may point out that any historical document or book which refers to him with this name was necessarily written after that passing, which occurred in 1419.

The Tibetan word je (rje), by the way, connotes “lord,” as in the “lord of the land.”  There are metaphoric uses where for example the diamond is called, in Tibetan, dorje (rdo-rje), or “lord (je) of all stones (do),” with the head letter r anomalously pronounced between, in this term.  The title is also added to the names of certain very special lamas, such as Je Tsongkapa or his other closest disciple, Kedrup Je (1493-1568).

We actually have a snapshot taken at the moment in which Gyaltsab Je became Gyaltsab Je.  The year again is 1419, and here is how the author of an ancient, illustrated biography of Je Rinpoche—named Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648-1721) describes the scene:

Je Tsongkapa walks then to his room, where he feigns now serious illness.  On the following day, with Duldzin, Gyaltsab Je, and others in attendance, Gyaltsab Je begs the Lord, “Please grant us something in the way of advice.”  The Lord takes the folding sage’s cap from his head, and tosses it into Gyaltsab Je’s lap.  He hands him his monk’s cloak as well.  And then he says to them, “Understand what I mean when I do this; now go and perfect the Wish to become enlightened for others.”  He is, in effect, appointing his successor as throneholder.

Here we see the actual, miniature scene on a much larger scroll painting.  If you look carefully, you can see the Founder’s Hat being passed from Je Tsongkapa to Gyaltsab Je, kneeling.  There is a small tear in the scroll painting crossing Je Tsongkapa’s head, which always seemed significant to us in a depiction of his final hours in this world.

There is something deeper going on in the transfer of leadership which creates the name “Gyaltsab Je.”  This same biography details the founding of the great Ganden Monastery near Lhasa, Tibet, by Je Rinpoche and his close disciples, in the year 1409—ten years before the transfer.  The two disciples who are said to have taken primary responsibility for this difficult task were Duldzin Drakpa Gyeltsen (1374-1434) and Gyaltsab Je himself.  Ganden becomes the headquarters for Je Tsongkapa and his close disciples for the rest of their lives.

The name “Ganden” is itself a Tibetan translation of the Sanskrit word Tushita, drawn from the verbal root  tush (tuṣ), meaning “to be content, or happy.”  This is the name of the Heaven of Bliss, a Buddha paradise where good Tibetan Buddhists hope to be reborn.

This paradise is ruled over by the coming Buddha, Maitreya, fifth of the thousand Buddhas of this eon (our Buddha, Shakyamuni, is the fourth).  Maitreya is poised to come to this earth from Tushita Paradise, and is often referred to as the yuvaraja or “young king” or regent of Tushita—because our Buddha handed this paradise over to Maitreya when he came to this earth.  Maitreya is then, literally, the Gyaltsab of Tushita.

Gyaltsab Je held the throne of Ganden for 13 years after his teacher’s passing.  And so he too was, literally, the Gyaltsab of Tushita.  He has as well during this time written one of the first great monastic textbooks of Tibet, a study of an ancient text called The Jewel of Realizations.  It was taught to the Indian master Arya Asanga around 350ad, by Lord Maitreya, during this master’s visit to Tushita Paradise.
It’s not difficult to picture, then, a mirror-image of the divine Tushita reflected here upon our earth, and one Gyaltsab reflecting another, and sitting there in reign.

The lineage of the throneholder of Ganden, by the way, has continued down to the present day—with Je Tsongkapa counted as the first one, and Gyaltsab Je as the second.  The position is known as the Ganden Tripa, literally “Throneholder of Ganden.”  The current holder is the 104th; and Kedrup Tenpa Dargye, the 16th-century textbook writer who offers us a piece in our appendices on details of the two Middle Way schools of emptiness, was the 22nd.  While His Holiness the Dalai Lama is generally considered a leader of all Tibetan Buddhism, the Ganden Tripa is the formal head of the Gelukpa—one of the four Buddhist traditions of Tibet.

Is there similar significance to Gyaltsab Je’s monk name, “Darma Rinchen”?  In his biography (which we will cover soon), we see that he was granted this name in 1373 when—at the age of 10—he took his vows for leaving the home life, and becoming a novice monk.  The name was granted by the two monks who oversaw the ordination ceremony: Rinchen Gyeltsen, and Draktokpa Shunnu Tsultrim.

The “Rinchen” then would have been taken from his preceptor’s name, as is monastic tradition.  The “Darma” is a bit of a mystery.  We can say, first of all, that it is not the Sanskrit word dharma, for “Buddhist teachings,” although his name has been misspelled that way even by some Tibetans of the lineage; and dharma’s have on occasion been mis-rendered as darma as well.

Darma in Tibetan by itself means “becoming grown up” (and thus still young) or also “fully grown up” from having been a child before.  As we will see in Nagarjuna’s text, to go from being an “infant” to an arya (someone who has seen emptiness directly) is one of the few most important goals of Buddhist practice.  We can distantly imagine Gyaltsab Je’s second preceptor, Shunnu Tsultrim, wanting to give him the “grown up” name rather than his own “youth” name, which is the meaning of shunnu.

We see darma by the way in the age connotation used in the name of the evil Tibetan king Lang Darma (Glang dar-ma), who around 900ad nearly destroyed all Tibetan Buddhism.  The name is explained as being a derogatory one applied by the common people of the time connoting a “youthful (dar-ma) ox (glang), stupid and deceitful.”

There is a custom of referring to someone with their home place name first; and there are several place names darma or close to that, for example near Tsomey Dzong, southeast of Lhasa—but none of them seems to relate particularly to our author’s birthplace, and there would normally be a four-syllable monastic name after the place name.

The Tibetan verb darwa means to spread the teachings, and we should note that when Gyaltsab Je introduces himself in the colophon of a work, he very often includes this word to express his intent that his writing spread and help people.

But the most likely intent of the name Darma, in our opinion, is as we see it in the ancient Tibetan term tsa darma (tsa dar-ma), which connotes “a warrior of exceptional bravery.”  This kind of word is often found in personal names of monks, to refer to being a spiritual warrior, as we also often see in the word pawo (dpa’-bo), closely related to the Tibetan word for “bodhisattva.”

Any Tibetan Buddhist monk who has taken an initiation into the Diamond Way, or secret teachings, will also have received a secret name.  We see one colophon—to Gyaltsab Je’s lecture notes to The Inner Drop of Spring, mentioned below—where he seems to give us that name, for himself: Mikyu Dorje, for the original Sanskrit Akshobhya Vajra, or “Unmoving Diamond.”

There is, finally, a fascinating gloss of Gyaltsab Je’s ordination name in the Great Biography of Tsongkapa, already mentioned above.  The author, the esteemed philosopher Gyalwang Lobsang Trinley Namgyal, pulls lines out of the root tantra of Manjushri—the Angel of Wisdom—to prove that both Je Rinpoche and Gyaltsab Je were predicted by the Buddha, thousands of years before they were born.  Here is the relevant section—
We also see the following lines in the biography entitled A Thousand Rays of Light, Emanating from the Lotus Garden of the Fortunate:

Some have stated that these lines were intended to foretell the coming of that greatest of sages, Vasubandhu.  Now it is true that “the first letter is famously known to be ba” would apply equally here, [since ba is used in Tibetan for the Sanskrit va]; but then we have “know that he will keep the fame”—and we don’t see the word “fame” anywhere in Master Vasubandhu’s name.

As such, we can say without question that this is, rather, a prediction of the coming of the Lord himself, [since Je Tsongkapa’s personal name, “Lobsang Drakpa,” does include the word for “fame”—drakpa].

Now we also see the line that talks about “the letter ba, famed for effort in keeping their vows”; and we can consider it along with that “famously first letter ba.”  The fact is that ba happens to be the base letter in the Tibetan syllable lo (spelled blo), which forms the first part of Lobsang Drakpa, the personal name of our omniscient Lord.  Thus the lines are clearly referring to him, given the drakpa or “fame” mentioned here as well.

Then we also see those lines about “the ra which is the other initial letter,” and “the intelligent one, with the first letter ma.”  These two are a prediction of the coming of Gyaltsab Darma Rinchen, for they reflect that ancient custom of keeping a reference mysterious by flipping around earlier & later letters.

How does that apply here?  The latter reference, about “the intelligent one, with the first letter ma,” is actually an allusion to the ma in the first half of Gyaltsab Je’s personal name, Darma.  And then the former reference, about “the ra which is the other initial letter,” is an allusion to the opening ra in the second half of his name: Rinchen.

Yes, we know that to a westerner, the lengths to which they go here to connect our author to an ancient scripture seem artificial; but if it really is true that the original author here was an Enlightened Being, then it doesn’t stretch the imagination at all to see him sending us a quiet message of joy about two very special people to come.

We’ll here begin a brief biographical sketch of Gyaltsab Je’s life; it is largely drawn from his entry in the famed Biographies of the Lamas of the Tradition of the Steps of the Path, composed by the great Tsechok Ling, Yongdzin Yeshe Gyeltsen (1713-1793).

Current oral tradition in the great Tsongkapian seats of learning includes some enlightening accounts of Gyaltsab Je’s personal behavior, and we have whet your appetite with a few sprinkled in here.  They are excerpted from our presentation and translation of Jamyang Shepa’s biography of Je Rinpoche in King of the Dharma: The Illustrated Life of Je Tsongkapa.

The sources agree that Gyaltsab Je was born in 1364, which makes him only seven years junior to his root lama, Je Tsongkapa—and he lived 13 years longer.  This is an unusual difference in age, because the sheer number of years it takes to become a real master of the tradition means that an age difference of 25 to 30 years is rather the norm in these relationships.  Add to this the fact that Gyaltsab Je was already a very famous figure in Tibet even before he met Je Rinpoche; which means that if he submitted himself at a comparatively late age as an understudy of a generational peer, that peer must have been a truly extraordinary person.

The first thing that Yongdzin Yeshe Gyeltsen says about Gyaltsab Je’s life is that he had become a bodhisattva long before he was born into this life; and that he came into this world by the force of his own prayers to help spread Je Rinpoche’s teachings here.

He was born in the “blessed area” of Nyangtu in the Tibetan state of Tsang, which is to the west of the capital city, Lhasa.  The district was Rinang, “Among the Mountains,” and the locality called Dzochey—which we can place about 150 miles southwest of Lhasa, towards the city of Shigatse.

Gyaltsab Je’s father was a member of the nobility, and named Tapunpa; his mother was Jomo Sherab.  His birth year—1364, a wood dragon year (shades of Dragon Master)—was the same year that Buton Rinpoche passed on; which is to say, Gyaltsab Je arrived at the perfect time to utilize the thousands of translations of the Indian classics organized by Buton.

As we alluded to above, he took his first ordination vows (meaning the general vow to leave the home life, followed by his novice monk vows) at the age of ten—in a water ox year, 1373—from the preceptors listed earlier, at the monastery of Ne-nying, which is just to the south of Gyangtse, a town about 165 miles southwest of Lhasa.

Again it was here that he was given the personal name of Darma Rinchen; and our biographer notes that he “protected his vows carefully and instinctively, the way that a normal person would protect their own eyes, from something headed to harm them.”

Beginning the task of learning to read & write was an important moment in medieval times in Asia; normally the only way to do so—in the typical complete absence of public educational institutions—would be to sit at the feet of a willing master.  In this case that master’s name was Pel Gunpa.

Gyaltsab Je then studied the two greatest classics of logic & perceptual theory (pramana)—in the form of A Compendium on Accurate Perception by the Indian sage Dignaga (c. 440ad), and A Commentary on Accurate Perception by Master Dharmakirti (c. 650ad)—along with similar topics, under the tutelage Kunga Pel (1285-1379), who also served as the head of Jonang Monastery, about 25 miles west of Shigatse.  This lama was also a teacher of both Jetsun Rendawa and Je Rinpoche.

Our author then studied the perfection of wisdom (prajna paramita, which by this point referred primarily to the tenets of the Independent branch of the Middle Way school), under Rinchen Dorje of Rinang.  He then learned higher knowledge (abhidharma) under Chujey Dundrup Rinchen of Nyangtu (who our biographer points out is not the same Dundrup Rinchen, 1309-1385, who instructed Je Tsongkapa at an early age; had dreams about his coming birth; and granted his own novice vows).

Gyaltsab Je then studied vowed morality (vinaya) under the master Lodru Sangpo, who is also known as Kashipa Losel.  He was further instructed by the great translator of Sanskrit, Kyabchok Pelsang; and Shangpa Kunkyenpa, Sherab Pelsang.

The greatest influence during these training years though was Jetsun Rendawa, Shunnu Lodru (1348-1412), who imparted to Gyaltsab Je deeper detail on the topics of the perfection of wisdom; logic & perceptual theory; higher knowledge; and middle way in the open teachings—as well as secret teachings, most prominently those of the Secret Collection, or Guhya Samaja.
In time, Gyaltsab Je became the main disciple of Jetsun Rendawa, and was recognized as one of a group of the seven greatest teachers of his generation.

It was a custom in those days—when a person had completed their basic studies—to take a tour of the major monasteries of their entire region, and participate in the daily debates there; both as an examination of one’s own understanding so far, and to gather new knowledge in these hotbeds of wisdom.  Je Tsongkapa’s own “debate tour” was a defining time in his life; we even have scenes painted of many of the sessions—they too end at Jetsun Rendawa’s feet.

This custom is still followed in the great Tsongkapian monasteries, where the best of the student monks will participate in the annual Jang Gunchu public debates, which rotate among the major seats of learning; and at the end of their studies be required to defend their grasp of the classics in open debate at each major college, if they are hoping to acquire a higher geshe (Master of Buddhism) degree.

And so Gyaltsab Je’s debate tour around the state of his residence (Tsang) took him to the great monasteries of Sakya; Sangpu; and Tsetang.  As a result of his efforts, he was in the end declared a Master of the Ten Books (Kachupa)—composed of the five Indian classics still studied for the geshe degree, along with a major commentary to each.

When he is 25 years old (in an earth dragon year, 1388) Gyaltsab Je takes his full monk’s vows with Chujey Kunga Pel serving as the vowmaster, and Jetsun Rendawa himself as the master of ceremonies—the two principal roles in a monastic vow ceremony.  Our biographer says that “he then honored his vows as well as Upali”—referring to a devoted disciple, of the Buddha himself, who was also an arya.

Gyaltsab Je then went on another debate tour, this time to the great monasteries of the central Tibetan state of Uw.  He had heard (as we will see below) of the popular new teacher from east Tibet—Je Tsongkapa—and purposely went to see him teach at Radrong town in the area of upper Tu, about 200 miles southeast of Lhasa.

We share the scene below, idealized, again in the detail of a painting in the Tsongka Gyechu set from The King of the Dharma; Je Rinpoche in these renderings always wears the yellow pandit’s hat, and we see him speaking with Gyaltsab Je.  The year, according to our research, is most likely 1397; Gyaltsab Je is 33 years old and already entering his prime; Tsongkapa is 40.  Here’s how Jamyang Shepa describes the event—

Je Tsongkapa then spends the summer at Radrong in Nyeltu.  It is at this time that the greatest of his spiritual sons—Gyaltsab Rinpoche, Lord of Reasoning, and an emanation of Kulika Pundarika himself—first meets the Master.  He comes to a teaching on the subject of Je Rinpoche’s Presentation of the Path of the “Commentary on Valid Perception,” and as a result immense faith springs up in his heart.  Gyaltsab Je makes a prostration to the Lord, and racked with sobs begs his permission to serve at his feet, and never be separated from him for a moment, for as long as they both might live.  The Lord then grants this permission.

Gyaltsab Je was stunned by the moral and scriptural brilliance of this new teacher, and followed him for life as his main personal attendant, or shabdrung (zhabs-drung).  He drank in deeper teachings on subjects he had already been taught, and added new topics and private instructions for which Je Tsongkapa was the consummate master: the steps on the path (lam rim), and the Diamond Way in the form of the two-fold teaching on the Secret Collection (Guhya Samaja); the three-fold teaching on the Crimson Lord of Death, the Ebony Lord of Death, and the Frightener (Rakta Yamari, Kirshna Yamari, Bhairava); the instructions for the triad of Highest Bliss, the Diamond of Pleasure, and the Wheel of Time (Sanvara, Hevajra, Kalachakra); the two levels of yogic practice; and comparative teachings on the secret levels of creation & completion.

One of Gyaltsab Je’s own colophons—written to his commentary on The Higher Line, one of the five great Books of Maitreya—pretty much summarizes how he himself would describe his relationship to his two greatest influences:

I have written on this topic after learning it directly from the holy lips of Kumara Mati, the high & holy Rendawa; and then later learning it—imparted, in its magnificent completeness—from the one that I have sat before for many years now, in the dust at his holy feet; learned, in unparalleled kindness, from the holy lips of Je Rinpoche, the All-Knowing Lobsang Drakpa, Shining One, One of Goodness, Who Has No Equal Upon the Surface of This Entire Planet.
There are a number of defining moments in Gyaltsab Je’s subsequent service of his teacher; one occurred we believe in 1403, and is again described by Jamyang Shepa:

On the Holiday of Miracles, Je Rinpoche makes powerful prayers, and in particular grants extensive teachings on the Jewel of Realizations, linking his explanation to the original sutra.  When these teachings are completed, he instructs his disciples to perform extensive offerings.

The disciples go to make butter lamps, and by the time Gyaltsab Je comes to take a butter-lamp cup, all the cups have already been carried off by others.  And so Gyaltsab Je goes and gets a huge basin; places some clarified butter in the bottom; inserts a great many cotton wicks; and offers it to the Lord.

Je Rinpoche gazes out over all the butter lamps, and then says to the assembly: “Let the butter of all the lamps be poured into the basin.”  Then he gives his approval for Gyaltsab Je to undertake a special task: “I want the Master of the Ten Great Books here to write up a record of what we taught, and compose a commentary based on these notes.”
In actuality, what Je Tsongkapa is saying at this moment is “I hereby empower Gyaltsab Je as my successor, my regent.”

The light of a butter lamp is a powerful image across the entire length of the Asian wisdom tradition for the light of understanding; and so it would appear that Je Rinpoche is so sure of the selection of his successor that he makes this decision more than 15 years before his passing.  This sensitivity to prepare his succession well ahead of time is another of countless indications of his mastery not just as a teacher, but as the leader of a lineage of wisdom.

Aside from massive tasks such as undertaking the construction of Ganden Monastery itself at his master’s behest—six years later, in 1409—some of the most important acts of service that Gyaltsab Je ever accomplished were the many records he made (such as the one translated in this volume) at teachings which Je Tsongkapa gave during the 22 years after their first meeting.

Reading the colophons of first carvings of Je Rinpoche’s works, we constantly see Gyaltsab Je’s name mentioned as the scribe who took down the notes, and labored to turn them into polished philosophical works of their own.  One of our favorites among these transcripts is the extraordinary record of teachings granted by Tsongkapa on the topic of vowed morality, at the temple of Namtseb Teng, in 1401.  We can almost feel the festival atmosphere of the Master doing a team-teaching event along with Jetsun Rendawa and the master translator Kyabchok Pel Sangpo.
And then we see Gyaltsab Je’s guiding hand again for example in the record of Je Tsongkapa’s important secret teachings at the location of Sera Monastery, on the Inner Drop of Spring, in 1407.

Again, Ganden was founded only two years later; and in the colophons to Gyaltsab Je’s own works—although he rarely mentions the exact year—we do see that it was during his 13 years as abbot here that he did much of his greatest work.  Our biographer notes that Gyaltsab Je was particularly mindful of the ancient monastic rules in helping to design and construct Ganden; and also played a prominent role during ordination ceremonies granted by Je Tsongkapa.

Gyaltsab Je was 56 years of age when he assumed leadership of the lineage at Ganden; and aside from teaching tours to places like Ne-nying, where he often offered his advice and material support for the monasteries (and also trained Kedrup Je in these tasks), he largely remained in house and teaching until the close of his life.

At the age of 68, in an iron pig year of 1431, he formally turns the lineage over to his younger Dharma brother Kedrup Je, Gelek Pel Sangpo—and passes on in the following year, 1432.  This occurred on the Potala Hill, where the Potala Palace of the Dalai Lamas would be built a few hundred years later.  Tradition says that there was a rain of jewels & flowers upon the occasion, and that it went on for a full three weeks.

Before we move on to analyzing Gyaltsab Je’s philosophical interests, we might pause and make a note about his personality, which to today is a topic of discussion in the great monasteries.  As we’ve mentioned, he was already a noted—and frankly cocky—scholar before he met Je Rinpoche.  Here in a scene from King of the Dharma we see the “real story” of him going into that meeting!

As is not always immediately evident in cheerful later accounts, Je Tsongkapa’s earth-shattering arrival into central Tibet—and into the history of Buddhism itself, as well as now the entire world—was not some placid event.  The following account is very typical of his reception; remember that, as we shall see in the paintings, Gyaltsab Je was his favorite disciple of all—his right-hand man (literally always to Je Tsongkapas’s own right in scroll paintings)—and the one to whom he bequeathed his dharma throne (“Gyaltsab” literally meaning the “regent who holds the throne”).

I heard this story first from Sermey Gisur Gyalrong Geshe Lobsang Thardo, the irrepressible nephew of Khen Rinpoche Lobsang Tharchin (1921-2004, abbot of Sera Mey Monastery).   Geshe Lothar, as he is commonly known, is the former giku—vice-abbot and debate master—of Sera Mey, as well as for many years the head of Gyalrong College and director of the Sera Mey Food Fund, which Khen Rinpoche founded to keep the refugee monks fed.

Geshe Lothar is a remarkable and remarkably kind man who saved Rinpoche’s life on several occasions during the flight from Tibet, and who for many decades has shepherded countless young monks—myself included—through their life and geshe studies at the monastery.  Nobody tells these things better than Geshe Lothar:

“Je Tsongkapa you see rolls into the Lhasa area from his home in east Tibet and right away starts to make a name for himself teaching in the temples and monasteries around town.  People are flocking to hear him, which of course stirs a bit of jealousy among some of the other monks.

“One of these is Gyaltsab Je (who was of course at that time known by his original name, Darma Rinchen).  Gyaltsab Je’s already probably the most famous logician in all of central Tibet by this time, and he starts to get irritated that everyone’s talking about this new guy instead.

“One day Gyaltsab Je hears that Je Tsongkapa’s going to be giving a teaching at a temple not far from his home.  So he puts on his fanciest robes and highest pandit’s hat (a wizardish pointed cap reserved for the greatest thinkers).  He’s running a little late, so he decides to cut across some fields to get there quicker.

“Then something weird happens, this kind of shift in the world that happens around high Lamas, and Gyaltsab Je suddenly finds himself lost amongst a bunch of rolling, grass-covered hills that all look the same.  To his relief, a herd of milk cows crests one of the hills, and behind it comes a decidedly shabby shepherd girl, who smells much like her mooing charges.

“So Gyaltsab Je walks up to the girl and demands, ‘You there! I need some help here! I’ve heard that that new guy, Big Nose From the East, is giving a teaching somewhere around here today.  If you know which way I need to go to get there, tell me now, and make it snappy!’
“The girl looks him shyly up and down, in all his monastic grandeur, then replies, ‘And may I ask, esteemed sir, who you yourself may be?’
“Gyaltsab Je puffs up his chest and declares, ‘I am the master Darma Rinchen, quite probably the greatest logician ever seen in the entire Land of Snows!’

“The girl looks down demurely and says softly, ‘Oh my!  How wonderful for a wretch like me to meet your esteemed self!  In fact I have dreamed of this day for years, because I have a burning philosophical question that I have longed to ask a sage the likes of you.’
“Gyaltsab Je beams and gives her a condescending look of pleasure.  ‘Of course, my child, you may ask any question you please, however difficult it may be.’
“The shepherd girl looks around for a moment, then points over to one of the cows.  ‘There! That one! Look, right now!’

“Gyaltsab Je turns to see a huge, brown, doe-eyed momma cow slowly lift her tail up high in the air.  And you know what that means.  Her bunghole comes up straight to the sky, and out squeezes a big turd, which (respecting the laws of gravity) then does that sort of a back-flip and falls to the ground in a huge flat pile—foof!
“‘What I wanted to ask,’ smiles the young maiden as she flutters her tender eyelids, ‘is this.
“‘We can see that, when the cowpie is actually coming out of the cow, then for a short time the cowpie’s bottom becomes its top.  Do you follow me?’
“Gyaltsab Je nods, concentrating fiercely.  ‘But then,’ she says, ‘when it topples over and plops on the grass, the top—as it were—changes into the bottom.  Do you see?’
“Gyaltsab Je nods instantly.  His genius is rising.
“‘And so,’ she concludes cutely, ‘I was wondering if you could tell me—which is the top of the cowpie, and which its bottom?’

“Gyaltsab Je takes a step back, glances into her eyes, looks over at the innocent, inquisitive face of the cow, and then leans over the cowpie to inspect it.  And in that moment, for the first time in his life, his mind goes utterly blank.  No assertion, no major premise, no minor premise, no analogies, no valid reason, and no…logical conclusion.  He looks back up at the girl, blankly.
“‘Well I…well I…well I don’t know,’ he stutters.  ‘I can’t really say.’

“The girl nods once, and when her eyes rise again to meet Gyaltsab Je’s they hold the fury of the fire that ends this very world: suddenly she is the Angel of Death herself, wrapped in hellfire blazing crimson like the sun.

“She turns around and drops to her knees.  Suddenly there is a bouquet of burning incense sticks in her hands; she throws herself flat on the ground, points the sticks in her clasped palms to the east, and cries out, ‘I don’t know about anybody by the name of Big Nose From the East.  But if you seek the Great One, Our Matchless Lord and Savior, that Incomparable Light of Wisdom for Our Entire Planet and The Very Cosmos Itself, well then, sir, you must walk on in the direction that I pay my unworthy obeisance.’

“Gyaltsab Je is blinded by the light for a moment and, by the time his eyes recover, the girl and her cows are way off behind him, halfway up the next hill.  He shakes his skull to clear it, hitches up his robes, and marches straight ahead, too bull-headed and proud to be dissuaded.

“Now I wanna say it was the other great disciple—Kedrup Je—but that’s a bit early so I think it was Tsako Wonpo, or somebody like that, who was already at the temple helping to get the place ready for the teachings.  He has clairvoyance and can read people’s minds; he sees Gyaltsab Je coming and knows he has an act of arrogance planned: he will enter the temple and refuse to doff his pandit’s hat to Je Tsongkapa.

“You gotta realize what a huge breach of etiquette this is in Tibet—sort of like showing up in a church for a talk by His Holiness the Pope wearing nothing but your underwear, and fire-red underwear at that.

“So Tsako Wonpo climbs up on the roof of the temple, right over the front door.  Gyaltsab Je is late—everyone’s already seated, and when he steps up to the temple doors everybody turns around, awed to witness the arrival of the Great Logician.

“At this moment, Tsako Wonpo lowers a thread with a fishhook tied to it.  He snares Gyaltsab Je’s pandit hat and it falls off into Gyaltsab Je’s hands.  A murmur passes through the crowd: If even the great Gyaltsab Je removes his hat to him, then this new teacher has got to be something special!

“Now this galls our Gyaltsab Je even worse.  He gets his cap back on and—as Je Tsongkapa mounts the teaching throne up in the front of the temple—he angrily pushes his way through the crowd.  He steps up on the stage and then actually sits down on the throne next to Je Tsongkapa himself!

(At this point Geshe Lothar’s eyes are big as pumpkins.  I nod.  Now this is like being in your red undies when His Holiness the Pope speaks to 60,000 people at Giants’ Stadium, and walking up to stand next to him at the pulpit.)

“Je Tsongkapa though he’s cool, he doesn’t blink an eye.  He calmly starts to give his teaching [which in fact was on logic, as we see in the extended caption to the actual scene from the paintings].  About ten minutes into the talk, Gyaltsab Je—absolutely spellbound—respectfully removes his cap.

“Two minutes later he gets off the throne and sits down on the stage.  And two minutes later Gyaltsab Je bursts out crying for the beauty of the most magnificent words he has ever heard.  He throws himself at the Master’s feet, and begs permission to stay at Je Tsongkapa’s side for the rest of his life and lives.  And the rest,” concludes Geshe Lothar with that endemic twinkle in his eyes, “and the rest, my boy, is history.”

Here in monastic oral tradition we see a hint of how Gyaltsab Je’s personality might have been.  And do you remember that debate tour around 1388 that also took him to the great Sakya Monastery?  It is said that here he met and debated two of the greatest scholars of the Sakya tradition of Tibet: Yaktun Sangye Pel (1350-1414) and his teacher, Rongtun Sheja Kunrik (1367-1449).

Both masters are known for their extensive writings; Yaktun composed a famous commentary upon the Perfection of Wisdom in 8 volumes, of over 5,000 pages.  Gyaltsab Je’s comment to him after their debate?  Monastic tradition says it was:
Well, the whole problem of your
poor performance is that you haven’t
devoted any serious time to studying the classics!
Even in our own text here we see side comments from Gyaltsab Je like—
That idea of yours reflects a fundamental ignorance…and as such should be discarded.
I have to take my hat off to you “followers of the highest school” who make no distinction at all between what the path puts a stop to, and what the ultimate reasoning puts a stop to.
It seems evident that Gyaltsab Je’s acerbic style infected his younger Dharma brother Kedrup Je.  Witness a few comments from his famed Interlude on Emptiness:

There are a few people who, unfortunately, haven’t had much training; and they claim that The Compendium was written in keeping with the books of the Collection of Logic Works of the Middle Way.  These are folks that just blurt out anything that comes to mind, even if it doesn’t make any sense at all.

There are people who say that the very heart of a Buddha, unchanging and unmoving, represents the foundation consciousness presented in those works; or that the sutra called What I Really Meant was intended to be taken literally.  We would proclaim to the skies though that these thinkers are just blabbing anything that pops into their head, without having lain their eyes on a single letter of those texts.
If anybody ever shows up who’d be willing to rely on this fellow’s words, I’d have to tear my hair out and cry to the skies, Are you…nuts??
And who else but Gyaltsab Je would tuck away, at the very bottom of his book, the optional title, Crushing the Words of the Impudent?

Our reader might be scratching their head, and wondering how the man who edited one of the greatest moral teachings in thousands of years—that lecture by Je Rinpoche at Namtseb Teng—could even think to engage in a gross form of the sixth of the top ten negative karmas of all time: harsh words towards another.  Remember though that Lord Buddha himself was one of the fiercest debaters of his time, and that if the motivation is sheer kindness for another, many things are goodness.

Again, we learn a lot from a master’s masters, and their disciples.  Among Gyaltsab Je’s teachers we see listed Kenchen Kashipa; Rinchen Gyeltsen of Ne-nying; and Kashipa Rinchen Dorje.  In the colophon to his massive commentary to the Compendium of Higher Knowledge, he credits Kedrup Dundrup Rinchen (1309-1385), also a teacher of Je Rinpoche.  In the colophon to a brief work on logic, and again in his massive Sunlight, he further mentions Kunga Pel (1285-1379), a throneholder of Jonang, although he would have been quite young even in this lama’s final years.

But of course the greatest influences were Jetsun Rendawa and Je Tsongkapa; and it’s worth noting that the two were Nagarjuna fans themselves.  For example, Jetsun Rendawa’s commentary to The Arya’s Letter to a Friend is a true classic; and Je Rinpoche’s explanation of Wisdom (entitled The Ocean of Reasoning) and his masterpiece on Chandrakirti’s commentary to it (entitled An Illumination of the True Thought) are some of the greatest emptiness treatises ever penned.

Our biographer notes that Duldzin Drakpa Gyeltsen—who as mentioned above took responsibility, with Gyaltsab Je, for building Ganden Monastery—was his “principal Dharma son.”  And of course there was Kedrup Je, as well as the young Gendun Drup (1391-1474), who would later be recognized as the first Dalai Lama.  We also see the following listed as his students:
Chen-nga Lodru Gyeltsen (1402-1472), a great scholar
and master of the lojong tradition for training to
Drachungpa Yunten Gyatso, a throneholder of Tashi Hlunpo
Jamyang Chujey Tashi Pelden (1379-1449), who wrote some
Lodru Tenpa, the 7th Ganden Tripa, also an abbot of Ganden
Takpu Pelden Dundrup (1383-1450), who held the abbot’s seats

In the end of course, Gyaltsab Je succeeded wildly in his assignment as the regent of the lineage, and the tradition he helped start became one of the largest and most celebrated in the history of Buddhism in this world.  This line, in part because of his example, has been known for six centuries as highly accurate and insightful in its many thousands of scriptural presentations—one of the largest bodies of high-quality philosophical literature ever to occur upon this planet.
A study of Gyaltsab Je’s writings

As we did for Arya Nagarjuna—and for Je Tsongkapa, by referring our reader to the listing of his works in The King of the Dharma—let’s do a statistical study of Gyaltsab Je’s extraordinary writings, and then focus on a few of the most impactful.  We’ll include a complete list of his works in Appendix D.

In general, our author’s body of work is most often considered as a component of the Collected Works of the Father & Son (Yab-sras gsung-‘bum), which is the traditional collection that is carved onto woodblocks together, for the works of the “Father” Je Tsongkapa and the sons Gyaltsab Je & Kedrup Je.  This comprises 263 works in 38 volumes: 162 works in 18 volumes for Je Tsongkapa; 35 works in 8 volumes for Gyaltsab Je; and 66 works in 12 volumes for Kedrup Je.  If all of this output were translated into English, it would require something over 100,000 pages; Gyaltsab Je by himself has written some 3,014 folios (6,028 pages), or the equivalent of over 24,000 English pages.  And there is no fluff here—quite the opposite, as anyone who has spent any substantial time with these three gentlemen can tell you.
Here is a breakdown of the subject matter for Gyaltsab Je’s works:
1) Secret teachings: 7 titles in 157 folios (20% of total titles,
2) General rituals: 2 titles in 36ff (6% of titles, 1% of folios)
3) Middle way (higher Madhyamika): 9 titles in 509ff (26% of titles,
4) Perfection of wisdom (lower Madhyamika): 4 titles in 446ff
5) Mind only (Chittamatra, or Yogacara): 2 titles in 445ff

There are some general notes we can make here.  First of all, as a Master of the Ten Books, or early equivalent of a geshe, we would have expected at least some coverage of the categories of vowed morality (vinaya) and higher knowledge (abhidharma); but here Gyaltsab Je seems to be following Arya Nagarjuna’s own example, focusing his time and efforts on crucial, difficult subjects relating to emptiness as the core of the method for leading beings out of the suffering world.

Secondly, we can see that he is heavily favoring the category of logic & perceptual theory—we know from his biography above that in his own study this was his first exposure to the classics; that he loved polemic both in his writings and on the monastic debate ground; that he was publicly known as a logician and even met his Root Lama at a logic lecture.  And of course he has set many of his writings on other topics in debate format, as here in his commentary to the Sixty Verses.

We might also note that in many of his colophons, the full name that Gyaltsab Je prefers to us for himself is Rikpa Mawa Darma Rinchen (Rigs-pa smra-ba Dar-ma Rin-chen): Darma Rinchen, Logic Whisperer.

Third, there is an almost odd absence of anything but major works here.  In Je Tsongkapa’s collected writings, for example, we have one “work” listed which is actually 135 brief pieces.  These include personal letters and brief poems or eulogies or the like.  However, we cannot call them “minor works,” as some have been wont to do—for they include pieces like the Three Principal Paths that have become recognized as great spiritual classics in their own right.  Gyaltsab Je though has nothing but hundreds-of-pages monsters.

At any rate, we can say about Gyaltsab Je that his habit was to take major topics—major classics—and write major commentaries about them.  He fearlessly tackled the most difficult subjects; in the inter-monastic competitions at the annual winter debates between the cream of geshe candidates from the Great Three monasteries of the Tsongkapian tradition, the standard text used is Gyaltsab Je’s Sunlight on the Path to Freedom—his extraordinary explanation of Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Accurate Perception.  In a month of all-day public debate, sometimes going all night as well, it is rare to cover more than the first few pages of this deep commentary—which we may consider the greatest of all his works.
If we were to list a “Top Ten” of Gyaltsab Je’s works then, it might look like this:
1) Sunlight on the Path to Freedom, equivalent to about 3,500 English pages, in complete explanation of the Commentary on Accurate Perception of Master Dharmakirti (650ad).
2) Illumination of the True Thought, equivalent to about 4,500 English pages, massive commentary in two huge volumes to the Ascertainment of Accurate Perception, also by Master Dharmakirti.
3) An Explanation of the “Sutra on Accurate Perception,” equal to 1,000 English pages, in commentary upon the Compendium on Accurate Perception by Master Dignaga (440ad).

4) The Point of Entry for Bodhisattvas, equal to 1,300 English pages, one of the few major commentaries written in Tibet upon the indispensable Guide to a Bodhisattva’s Way of Life, by Master Shantideva (750ad).
5) A Commentary to “The Higher Line,” equal to 1,800 English pages, in commentary to an essential motherwork of the Mind Only school by Lord Maitreya & Arya Asanga (350ad).

6) The Essence of the Very Eloquence of the Ocean of Higher Knowledge, equal to 1,700 English pages, in explanation of the Compendium on Higher Knowledge of Arya Asanga—again a mother book of the Mind Only school.

7) The Essence of Excellent Explanation, equal to 1,000 English pages, on the 400 Verses of Master Aryadeva (230ad), root disciple of Arya Nagarjuna.  A really essential early explanation of emptiness.

8) An Illumination of the Essential Meaning, equal to 1,800 English pages, on the String of Precious Jewels of Arya Nagarjuna—a letter to a king which reads just like a work on the steps to the path (lam-rim) on emptiness steroids.

9) The Jewel of the Essence of the Explication, equal to 2,800 English pages, in commentary upon Master Haribhadra (775ad) in commentary upon the most famous work of Lord Maitreya & Arya Asanga, the Jewel of Realizations.  In a way this work could be considered one of the first works of an entire genre of yikcha (yig-cha) or extremely important monastic textbooks which continued in the major Tsongkapian monasteries for six centuries following.

10) A Swift Entry to the Path of Great Bliss, along with two other, briefer works—for a total equal to 500 English pages, in famed explanation of the secret teaching of the Wheel of Time (Kalachakra).

In the absence of detail about Gyaltsab Je’s movements in his life, there are some conclusions we can draw from where he was living when he wrote some of his major works, as he almost always records his location—although not the year—in his colophons.  Let’s take a look then at those Top Ten works.

Sunlight on the Path to Freedom was written in retreat it seems at Ne-nying, southwest of Lhasa, where he had taken his first monastic vows, and which we know he would visit late in his life.  At this same location he composed the commentary to The Higher Line.  Major works require major time—and major time in private; we can imagine that he may have taken off to Ne-nying to write, when things got too busy at Ganden Monastery.

With the exception of his explanations of the secret teaching of the Wheel of Time (where the colophons give no place of composition), Gyaltsab Je’s seven other major works were all written at Ganden, which was still so new that it was also being referred to as “that cloister up on Nomad’s Hill” (‘Brog ri-bo che dge-ldan).  It was surely the case that commentarial works were needed at the new monastery, during the 13 years of Gyaltsab Je’s abbacy.

There is, finally, a note in one composition—the massive commentary upon Dharmakirti’s Ascertainment of Accurate Perception—which mentions that the writing was begun at Ganden but finished in a mountain retreat spot favored by a master from the earliest days of Tibetan Buddhism named Kou Yeshe Jungney.  This also appears to be a spot where our author and his companions could get away from the business of the monastery and get some quiet, focused time.

Here at the Diamond Cutter Classics project, we often refer to the process of translating a new book as “snow on the mountain,” meaning that the entire process of putting out a new work closely resembles the way in which snow falls upon a high mountain peak; gradually melts; and then wends its way down the mountain to the valleys—and from there inevitably to feed the ocean.
Our thanks to all the people whose hard work to make our translations possible follows the same pattern.

First, at the peak of the mountain, is the snow-treasure of the Asian Legacy Library’s free online database of ancient Asian books.  Millions of pages have been scanned or input in searchable form, under the leadership of executive director John Brady, over the last 35 years.  He is assisted by—just to name a few—Emma Lewis, Christine Vimala Sperber, Christina Kasica, Joel Crawford, Arina Garcia, Osiris Luciano, Ben Ghalmi, Ven. Phil Baker, and Alona Stoliarchuk.

The massive labor of inputting all of the Tibetan works in the database over all of these years has been completed by the ALL Input Operator Team, headed now for many years by Ms. Sonam Lhamo.  At the National Library of Mongolia, the catalog team has been led by the Library Director, Ms. Bayarkhuu Ichinkhorloo; and the Project Manager, Dr. Sainbileg Byambadorj.  The new cataloging project at Gandantegchinlen Library is led by Ven. Munkhbaatar Batchuluun.

ALL’s Sanskrit materials are input at the Varanasi ALL Input Center, under the direction of Dr. Santosh Dwivedi; the Kathmandu ALL Input Center, directed by Drs. Miroj & Milan Shakya; and the Kerala ALL Input Center, directed by Dr. N.V. Ramachandran.  Thank you all for your endless work!

We are very grateful for Aisha Nguyen, who tirelessly searches every corner of the web for any and all Sanskrit materials that we may need input; as well as David and Nancy Reigle, for helping to define and provide us with the most accurate, high-quality editions possible of any work in the Sanskrit language.

The cataloging and input work cannot be accessed without the priceless subject cataloging by the Diamond Cutter Classics team dedicated to this 35-year effort, now led by Nicholas Lashaw and Geshe Michael Roach—the translators of the present volume—and Ben Kramer.  Nick & Ben also manage the DCC translator team, including all our fellow translators, and we would like to share deep gratitude with every one of them—you keep us going!
We are also infinitely indebted to all those who support the work of DCC, around the world; including our tireless and deeply dedicated sponsors.

We rely heavily upon the fine work of the Buddhist Digital Resource Center (BDRC) for obtaining original scans of the many source works our translations require.  The Head Librarian, Karma Gongde, has offered us years of wonderful service and advice; and BDRC Executive Director Dr. Jann Ronis and Chief Technology Officer Élie Roux continue to give all of us really excellent support.

The next step in translation is the manuscript editing, which for technical books like this one is always a massive effort.  We would especially like to thank Bets Greer, Nick Lashaw, Anatole Nguyen, and all the other editors contributing their time.  We are in awe of the work by the Diamond Cutter Press staff, who get all these translations out into the world—especially in the new ebook formats.  Thank you Rosa van Grieken, Ven. Elizabeth van der Pas, and Katey Fetch.

Finally, our entire translation team would have no central place to meet and conduct the many hundreds of translation sessions that books like this require, without the offices in Sedona, Arizona, supplied through years of effort by John Brady; Connie O’Brien; Tim Lowenhaupt; and Gail Deutsch.

Our grateful thanks to all of you, and to everyone else who has contributed to our work.  Your trust in us is a big part of the reason why we can complete projects—like the present volume—which require quite nearly a decade each.

As a kid, Nicholas Lashaw had an ear for music.  As a young adult he traveled extensively in Latin America, and picked up Spanish and Portuguese pretty easily; and so he realized that he also had an ear for languages.  At some point, and for some unknown reason, he decided to pursue a degree in Mechanical Engineering, and graduated with honors.

Shortly after, Nicholas got very interested in transcending, or at least improving, this human experience; met some very special teachers; and undertook extensive studies in Buddhist philosophy & yoga.

Very soon he was fortunate enough to have the opportunity to marry his passions for language and Buddhist philosophy, and began to learn to translate Tibetan.  As his studies blossomed, he helped his teacher to found the Diamond Cutter Classics non-profit organization—which he still helps to run today.

Also passionate about sharing the ideas that he learns about in the old books, Nick teaches with the Diamond Cutter Institute and is a Professor at the Sedona College of International Management; both of these being organizations which make these ancient philosophical concepts relatable and applicable to modern people in the modern world.

Somewhere in the stream of his life Nicholas also started and helped run a garden design company; built a yoga studio; built retreat cabins; played in rock bands, and helped to create a beautiful baby daughter.  He currently resides somewhere near the ocean with his wife and daughter and their sheepdog, where he is happily preserving and translating the Buddhist books, surfing, meditating, and recording music in his free time.

Geshe Michael Roach was born in Los Angeles and grew up in Phoenix, Arizona.  He graduated with honors from Princeton University, and is a recipient of the Presidential Scholar medallion from the President of the United States at the White House.  He has also received the McConnell Scholarship Prize from the Princeton School of Public and International Affairs, as well as an honorary doctorate in the Congress of Mexico from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM).

Michael is the first foreigner in the 600-year history of Tibet’s Sera Mey Monastery to receive the title of Geshe (Master of Buddhism), after 25 years of study.  After graduation, he founded the Asian Classics Institute (ACI), translating over 20,000 pages of the geshe course and designing 36 courses of studies in English, for modern people of all walks of life.

At his teacher’s directive, Michael—in order to confirm that the principles of the ancient texts could be used in modern life—helped in 1981 to found the Andin International Corporation, which became one of the largest diamond jewelry companies in the world, and was purchased by super-investor Warren Buffett in 2009.  Michael used the majority of his income from the business to found and run the Asian Classics Input Project (now called ALL, or Asian Legacy Library), starting in 1987.  This is the largest free, online searchable database of ancient Asian literature in the world.

Michael also helped found the Three Jewels Outreach Center of New York; DCI Global; the Sedona College of International Management; the Yoga Studies Institute; Green Stretch Pen; Diamond Mountain Retreat Center; The Knowledge Base; Diamond Cutter Press; and the Diamond Cutter Classics translation center.  Each of these institutions helps preserve and make available the precious wisdom of ancient Asia, in the modern world.

Michael is the author of some 100 books and major translations.  His most popular works include The Diamond Cutter: The Buddha on Managing Your Business & Your Life; and How Yoga Works.  He lives in the small town of Rimrock, Arizona, with his wife Veronica, whom he first met some 50 years ago.  Together they enjoy gardening, charitable work, yoga & gym trips, and running their small Peach Tree Café, for local cowboys & cowgirls.
by Khen Rinpoche Geshe Lobsang Tharchin

Arya Nagarjuna, as is widely known, founded the Middle Way tradition of Buddhism.  His appearance was prophesied in numerous scriptures, among them the Journey to Langka; the Great Realization of Gentle Voice; the Great Cloud; and the Great Drum.

Four hundred years after the final nirvana of the Buddha Shakyamuni, there was living in Southern India—in a land called Vidarbha (literally, the “Land of Palms”)—a prosperous Brahmin who had no sons.  A sign appeared to him in a dream, indicating that he would receive a son if he paid homage to a hundred Brahmins.  He did so, praying earnestly that his deeply-held wish might be fulfilled; and ten months later a son was born.

The newly-born child was taken to a soothsayer, who said that although the infant did indeed have the signs of an exceptional person, he would live only seven days.  The anxious parents asked whether something couldn’t be done to avert the fate.  The soothsayer replied that if they gave food to a hundred persons, the boy would live for seven days and that—if they made offerings to a hundred monks—he would live for seven years.  Nothing beyond that could be done.

The parents completed the second of the suggested offerings.  As the end of the seven years approached they sent the young boy, in the company of several attendants, on an excursion—for they would not be able to bear the sight of their son’s corpse.

While travelling, the boy experienced a vision of the god Khasarpana (a particular manifestation of Loving Eyes).  Soon afterwards, the party reached the great monastery of Nalanda.  While they were standing near the dwelling of a Brahmin named Saraha, the boy uttered several verses of poetry.

The Brahmin heard the lines, and invited the party inside.  He asked them of their journey and about how they had come to reach Nalanda.  One of the attendants related the boy’s story and told of his imminent death.

Saraha replied to this that—if the boy were to abandon the worldly life by taking a vow of renunciation—there was a way to avoid the plight.  The boy agreed to do so, and was first initiated into the “Mandala of Limitless Light which Conquers the Lord of Death.”  Afterwards he was instructed to recite special mantras.  On the eve of his seventh birthday in particular he recited them throughout the night, and thus overcame this encounter with the Lord of Death.

Upon reaching the age of eight, the boy took the vow of renunciation and began studies of the traditional sciences.  He studied as well scriptural texts of each of the major schools of Buddhist thought.

Some time afterwards he again met his parents, and later requested the very same Brahmin Saraha to instruct him in the esoteric teachings of the glorious Secret Collection.  He was taught the appropriate secret books, together with their complete oral instruction.

Next, after submitting a formal request to the monastery’s abbot, the boy took the full ordination of a monk and became known as Bhikshu Shrimanta.  Being one of those who is watched over by Manjushri in all their lives, the monk found opportunities for hearing, in its entirety, the Dharma of both the open & secret teachings from the bodhisattva teacher Ratna Mati—who was a manifestation of Gentle Voice in his “divine youth” aspect.  In this way Shrimanta came to be a consummate master of the Dharma.

At a later time a great famine arose, leaving the monastic community of Nalanda with no means of subsistence.  The abbot, Sthavira Rahula Bhadra, appointed Bhikshu Shrimanta as the steward of the community.

Although the famine lasted twelve years and greatly reduced the population of the surrounding land of Magadha, the young monk was able to sustain the community by utilizing his knowledge of the alchemical science.  He had acquired this knowledge from a Brahmin priest who was well versed in it, in the following way.

The monk first prepared two sandalwood leaves as charms for the miraculous skill known as “swift-footedness.”  Carrying one leaf in his hand and the other concealed in the sole of his shoe, he then proceeded to the distant island where the Brahmin lived, and asked to be given instruction into the elixir which transforms common metals to gold.

The Brahmin thought to himself that the stranger must be carrying some special charm which had allowed him to travel to the isle.  Desirous of acquiring it, he said to the monk: “Knowledge must be exchanged for knowledge, or compensated in gold.”

“Well then,” replied Bhikshu Shrimanta, “we must exchange knowledge”—and he gave the Brahmin the charm he had been carrying in his hand.  Thinking that the visitor could no longer leave the island, the priest gave him the instruction.  Using the leaf he had kept in the sole of his shoe, the monk then returned to Magadha.  He was thus able to provide Nalanda’s monastic community amply with all their essential needs, through transmuting great quantities of iron to gold with the alchemical elixir.

Some time after this, Bhikshu Shrimanta served as the abbot of Nalanda.  He paid great tribute to those members of the community who observed the three trainings properly, and expelled those full and novice monks who were morally corrupt.  He is reputed to have banished as many as 8,000 monks.

It was during this period as well that one Bhikshu Shankara composed a scripture entitled the Ornament of Knowledge.  It was written in 12,000 verses and represented an attempt to discredit the doctrine of the greater way.  By means of logic, Bhikshu Shrimanta was able to refute the argument completely.  He also disproved many other scriptures denying the validity of this higher way.  On one occasion, in a place called Jata Sanghata, he defeated 500 masters of other schools in debate, and brought them into the inner system by overcoming their false views.

During that time when The Arya was teaching the Dharma of the three baskets widely to many followers, two youths who were actually emanations from the water-dragon beings, or nagas, came to him seeking the Dharma.  With their presence, the entire area became filled with the fragrance of sandalwood.  Upon their departure, it disappeared; and when they returned, the delightful scent reappeared as well.

The Arya asked them the reason for this, and the youths replied that they were sons of the dragon king Taksaka.  They had anointed themselves with essence of sandalwood as immunization against human impurities.

The Arya then asked them to give him some of the sandalwood to fashion an image of Tara, and to assist him in constructing temples as well.  The two youths answered that they would have to ask their father, and then left.

The pair returned after two days to tell The Arya that only if he himself came to the Land of the Dragons could they do as he bade.  Aware of the benefit to all beings which would result from his going, The Arya did indeed journey to this land, where King Taksaka and other righteous water dragons presented him with innumerable offerings.

The great being preached the Dharma to the dragons in compliance with their every supplication, bringing them so much satisfaction that they entreated him to remain among them permanently.  He answered: “Because I have come here for the purpose of securing the sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 verses and ‘dragon clay’—which is needed for the construction of temples and offering shrines—I have no opportunity now to stay.  I shall perhaps be able to return in the future.”

When he had acquired the expanded version of the Mother of the Victors; several shorter texts of the Perfection of Wisdom; and great quantities of dragon clay, The Arya prepared to return to our world: the continent of Jambu.  It is said that in order to ensure The Arya’s return to their land, the water dragons kept from him a small portion at the end of the 100,000 Verses.  The missing portion—the last two chapters of the unabridged sutra on the Perfection of Wisdom—was therefore replaced by the corresponding chapters of the Perfection of Wisdom sutra in 8,000 verses.  This is why the final two chapters of each sutra are identical.

After securing these sutras, The Arya greatly advanced the influence of the tradition of the greater way.  When he preached the Dharma in the monastery park, the dragons performed acts of reverence, such as six of them forming a parasol to shade him from the sun.

Having thus become the Lord of the Dragons, or Nagas, The Arya was named “The Naga.”  Because his skill at spreading the Dharma of the greater way resembled the shooting speed and mastery of the famed archer Arjuna, of ancient India, he became known as well as “The Arjuna.”  It is otherwise explained that he was called “Nagarjuna” because, by practicing the rituals for reaching the goddess Kurukulla, he gained authority over such naga dragons as King Taksaka, and others.

Nagarjuna later travelled to the area of Pundra Vardhana where—utilizing the practice of alchemy—he performed many acts of great generosity.  In particular, he bestowed great quantities of gold upon an elderly Brahmin couple and thus instilled them with great faith.  The Brahmin elder served Nagarjuna and listened to the Dharma from him; after his death, he was reborn as the Master Bodhinaga.

Nagarjuna also constructed many temples.  Once, when he was preparing to transform a large, bell-shaped boulder into gold, an emanation of Tara with the form of an old woman appeared and said to him: “Instead of doing this, you should go to the Mountain of Splendor and practice the Dharma.”  Later he did go there, to perform the practices for reaching Tara.
On another occasion, when he had accomplished the rites for invoking the goddess Chandika, the goddess herself carried The Arya into the sky and attempted to take him to the celestial realms.

“I have not exerted myself in order to travel to the celestial realms,” he said to her.  “I have, rather, invoked you in order to provide support for the community of those who practice the greater way, for as long as the Buddha’s teaching remains in this world.”

And so they returned to this world, and the goddess established herself to the near west of Nalanda, manifesting herself in the form of a noblewoman of the royal caste.  Nagarjuna instructed her, saying: “A great stake of khadira wood, so large that a man can barely lift it, has been driven into the wall of a stone temple dedicated to Manjushri, the Gentle Voice.  Until that stake turns to ashes, you must provide subsistence for the temple’s spiritual community.”

With articles of every sort, the lady made offerings to the spiritual community for twelve years.  During this time the steward of the monastery, a novice monk of evil nature, made continual promiscuous advances to her.  The noblewoman made no replies, until one day she finally said: “If the khadira-wood stake ever turned to ashes, we could be united.”  The wicked one therefore set the stake afire.  When it had become ashes, the goddess herself vanished.

There was another time when a number of elephants were threatening to damage the Bodhi tree at Vajrasana, the “Seat of the Diamond” (present-day Bodhgaya).  Nagarjuna erected two stone columns behind the sacred tree, which provided protection for many years.

When the elephants later returned, The Arya erected two images of Mahakala astride a lion, wielding a club.  This was also effective, but the danger nonetheless reappeared and a stone fence was built around the tree.  Outside the enclosure, The Arya constructed 108 offering shrines.  These stupas were huge, and each one was crowned by a smaller shrine containing sacred bone-relics of the Buddha.

The Arya further constructed many temples and stupas in the six major cities of Magadha—Shravasta, Saketa, Champaka, Varanasi, Rajagirha, and Vaishali.  He also provided teachers of the Dharma with all their needs.

Above all, Nagarjuna knew that virtually no one understood the true meaning of the scriptures on the Perfection of Wisdom.  He also knew that, without having realized this meaning unerringly, there was no means for achieving liberation.

He thus widely proclaimed the Middle Path, which asserts that emptiness (the essential meaning of dependent origination, that all things are totally void of a self-existent nature) is totally consistent with principles expressing an infallible relation between “black” and “white” karma and its consequences.

By means of his five-part collection of works on logic The Arya clearly expounded the ultimate meaning of the Buddha’s Wisdom.  This collection consists of the major treatise, the Root Text on the Middle Way, and its four limbs: the Sixty Verses on the Reasoning of the Middle Way; the Seventy Verses on Emptiness; Smashing Argument to Dust; and Defeating All Dispute.

After this period, Arya Nagarjuna stayed for six months on Mount Ushira, to the north.  He was accompanied by a thousand disciples and sustained each one with a daily tablet of a quicksilver rasayana, or elixir, that he had prepared.

One day a disciple, Siddha Singkhi, respectfully touched the pill to his head but did not eat it.  The Arya asked why, and his follower answered: “I have no need of the pill.  If it pleases you, Arya, please prepare a number of vessels by filling them with water.”  Thus a thousand large containers were filled with water and placed there, in the forest.
