The siddha, or accomplished master, then added a drop of urine to each of the vessels, which transformed all the liquid into the “elixir of gold.”  The Arya took all the vessels and concealed them in a secluded, inaccessible cave, uttering a prayer that they might serve to benefit beings of the future.

This Siddha Singkhi had not always been so adept.  When he first met The Arya, he was so dull-witted that he could not learn even a single verse over a period of many days.  The Arya then told him, in a jesting tone, to meditate that a horn had grown on top of his head.

The disciple did so, maintaining his object of meditation so sharply that he achieved the tangible and visible sign of having grown a horn.  He was therefore unable to leave the cave in which he was meditating, for the horn got caught on the sides of the entrance.  The siddha was then instructed to meditate that the horn was no longer present, and it subsequently disappeared.

Realizing that his disciple’s mental faculties had now become sharply developed, The Arya taught him several profound meanings of the secret mantras.  Nagarjuna then instructed him to meditate once more, and the follower ultimately attained the Siddhi of the Mahamudra: the Great Seal of Emptiness.

Later The Arya travelled to the northern continent of Kurava.  Along the way, in a city named Salamana, he encountered several children playing in the road.  Nagarjuna read the palm of one of them, a boy named Jetaka, and prophesied that he would become King.  On the return journey, following the accomplishment of his goal in Kurava, The Arya met the former youth, who had since become King.

For three years Nagarjuna remained with the King, who bestowed upon The Arya many precious jewels.  In return, he composed for the King a jewel of the Dharma: namely, the text named A String of Precious Jewels.

It was then that Nagarjuna travelled south, as the emanation of Tara had advised him to do, in order to practice meditation at the Mountain of Splendor.  Here Nagarjuna also turned the Wheel of the Dharma, that of both the open and the secret teachings, extensively—and it was at this time that he composed, in particular, the scripture entitled A Praise of the Realm of All Things.
In general, The Arya’s compositions are divided into three collections:

The Collection of Discourses, which includes such works as the String of Precious Jewels; the Letter to a Friend; the Hundred Verses on Wisdom; the Tree Trunk of Wisdom, and A Drop of Elixir for Healing All Beings.
The Collection of Tributes, including A Praise of the Realm of All Things; A Praise of Going Beyond the World; A Praise of the Inconceivable, and A Praise of the Ultimate.
The Collection of Logic Writings—the afore-mentioned Root Text on the Middle Way and associated works.

In addition to these, Arya Nagarjuna composed other important treatises in explanation of both the open and secret teachings and—indeed—performed activities as though the Buddha himself had returned to this world.

It is said that Nagarjuna made three “great proclamations of the Dharma.”  The first was his upholding the ethical discipline at Nalanda Monastery, as previously explained.  This was like the first turning of the Wheel of the Dharma by the victorious Buddha.

The second proclamation was his clear exposition of the Pure Middle View, through the composition of the collection of logic treatises and others.  This was similar to the Buddha’s second turning of the Wheel.

The third great proclamation was constituted by The Arya’s activities upon the Mountain of Splendor in the south, where he composed such works as the Praise of the Realm of All Things.  This was akin to the final turning of the Wheel of the Dharma by Lord Buddha.

Such extensive labors on behalf of the Dharma and living beings aroused great displeasure in the demoness Mara and the forces of evil.  A boy, Kumara Shaktiman, had earlier been born to the queen of King Udayibhadra.
Years later, the mother was presenting her son with a rare, fine garment when the boy told her: “Put this away for me.  I shall wear it when it is time for me to rule the kingdom.”
“You shall never rule,” replied his mother, “for Arya Nagarjuna has made it happen that your father and he are of a single life.  Your father will not die unless The Arya does.”

The boy was so overcome with grief that his mother continued: “Don’t cry so! The Arya is a bodhisattva, and if you ask him for his head he will not refuse.  With that, your father will also die—and you shall acquire the kingdom.”
The child followed his mother’s suggestion and Nagarjuna did indeed agree to give his head.  Yet however much effort the boy used, his sword could not cut Nagarjuna’s neck.

The Arya then told the boy: “Long ago, while cutting some grass, I happened to kill an insect.  The force of that misdeed remains with me still, and you can thus sever my head by using a blade of kusha grass.”

This the boy did, and so was able to cut off Nagarjuna’s head.  The blood which flowed from the wound turned to milk, and the following words issued from the dismembered head: “From here I depart to Sukhavati, the Heaven of Happiness.  In the future, I shall enter this body again.”

The wicked prince cast the head away at several leagues’ distance, fearing that it would once more join the body.  Since The Arya had attained the practice of rasayana, however, his head and body became stone-hard.  The two are said to be coming nearer and nearer, one to the other, every year; in the end to be joined once more.  Nagarjuna will then again perform great works for the benefit of the Teaching and all living beings.
As it is written in the Great Realization of Gentle Voice, Arya Nagarjuna lived for a total of six hundred years:
After I, the Tathagata, have passed away
And four hundred years have elapsed,
A full monk named “The Naga” shall appear,
Of great faith and benefit to the Teaching.
He shall achieve the stage of Great Joy
And for six hundred years remain alive.
Nothing Is the Way It Seems:
,RIGS PA DRUG CU PA’I t’IKKA BZHUGS SO,
Herein lies A Commentary to the “Sixty Verses on Reasoning.”

,DE LA ‘DIR BDAG NYID CHEN PO ‘PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS MDZAD PA’I RIGS PA [f. 2a] DRUG CU PA NI GANG BSHAD PAR BYA BA’I CHOS SO,,
The work that I will be commenting upon in this text is the Sixty Verses on Reasoning, composed by that great being, the Realized One, Nagarjuna.

DE YANG SPYIR BKA’ THAMS CAD KYI DGONGS PA MTHAR THUG DBU MA CHEN PO’I DON CAN DU BSTAN PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, KHYAD PAR NYAN THOS SDE PA SKYE ‘JIG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR ‘DOD PA DAG GI LOG RTOG DGAG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DE DAG LA YANG GRAGS PA’I NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD KYI LUNG DON RIGS PAS GTAN LA ‘BEBS PAR BYED PA YIN NO,,

Our first, general goal is to demonstrate that the ultimate intent of everything which Lord Buddha ever taught was to express the ideas of the magnificent Middle Way.  More specifically, we will use logic to establish the meaning of the scriptures of the listener group—something that even they recognize—in order to refute their mistaken position that things could start or stop on their own.
‘DI LA, RTZOM PA’I SNGON ‘GRO MCHOD BRJOD DANG, BRTZAMS PAR BYA BA’I GZHUNG DNGOS, BRTZAMS PA’I DGE BA BSNGO BA’O,,

To meet these goals, we will proceed in three steps: explaining the offering of praise which Arya Nagarjuna makes as a preliminary to composing his text; the actual text that he has composed; and his dedication of the virtue created by this composition.
DANG PO LA, DGOS PA’I DON, BSDUS DON, TSIG DON GSUM GYIS ‘CHAD PA NI,

There are three parts to the first of these: establishing the purpose of the offering; a summary of its content; and a discussion of the meaning of each word.  We begin then with the first verse of Arya Nagarjuna’s text:
I bow down to that Lord of the Able Ones,
The one who said that things occur in dependence;
Who with this method rid himself of the idea
That anything could start or stop.
DE LA DGOS PA NI, RANG NYID YA RABS DAM PA’I SPYOD PA DANG MTHUN PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR DANG,
What is the purpose of this verse of praise?  It is to demonstrate that Nagarjuna himself is acting in accordance with the holy actions of the honorable ones.
BSTAN BCOS RTZOM PA’I BYA BA MTHAR PHYIN PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR YIN NO,,
It is also for the purpose of ensuring that he completes the composition of the work.
PA TSAB KYI ZHAL NAS, ‘PHAGS PA YAB SRAS MCHOD BRJOD LA DGOS PA MI BZHED DE, DGOS PA ‘GA’ ZHIG LA DMIGS NAS, DE BLO YUL DU BYAS [f. 2b] NAS MCHOD BRJOD BYED PA MA YIN NO,,

Pa-tsab says that he doesn’t accept the idea that the Realized One and his spiritual son had any particular goal in mind when they made their offerings of praise.  They didn’t consider a number of possible goals, and then bring some particular one to mind at that point.

‘O NA JI ZHE NA, YUL KHYAD PAR CAN LA DAD PA DRAG PO SKYES NAS DAD PA KHA SHOR GYI PHYAG MDZAD PA YIN TE, DPER NA, DAD LDAN ‘GA’ ZHIG DGOS PA LA RTOG DPYOD MI BYED PAR GANG DU SKYABS ‘GRO THOL BYUNG DU ‘BYUNG BA BZHIN ZHES GSUNG SKAD,

And suppose you were to ask Pa-tsab, “Well then, why did the Master offer this prostration?”  He would reply, “It was because he was suddenly overcome by fierce feelings of faith toward an extraordinary object of virtue, and spontaneously threw himself on the ground.  It’s like, for example, when someone with a lot of faith suddenly decides to go for refuge, without considering any specific goal.”
GTZANG PA SA RBOS NA RE, DE LTAR DGOS PA MI BZHED DE, BZHED NA ‘PHAGS PA YAB SRAS CHOS CAN, GANG ZAG DAM PA MA YIN PAR THAL,
Neither does Sabu of Tsang accept that Nagarjuna had any particular goal in mind here.  And if you were to assert that he did have such a goal, Sabu would reply with this argument:
Consider the Realized One and his spiritual son.
Are you saying that they aren’t holy people?
DGOS PA’I LAN LA RE BA DANG BCAS PA’I PHYIR, DPER NA TSONG PA BZHIN ZHES ‘KHOR GSUM KHAS BLANGS DANG DAM BCA’ LA LUNG DANG GRAGS PAS BSAL BA’I THAL ‘GYUR ‘GOD LA,

And if you replied, “Why do you say that?” he would answer you with the following sarcastic statement, meant to show how what you accept denies the very thing you seek to prove; and how your position contradicts both scripture and common knowledge:
Because, according to you, they are hoping for some reward for themselves, by performing this prostration.
They thus become, for example, nothing more than traders.

RMA BYA BYANG YES NA RE, DE LTAR DGOS PA MI BZHED DE, SA LA GNAS PA’I CHAGS BRAL GYI GNAS SKABS YIN PAS, BLANG DOR GYI DMIGS PA THAMS CAD BCOM NAS DGOS PA RTZIR MED PA’I PHYIR CES GZHAN LA GRAGS KYI GTAN TSIGS ‘GOD LA,

Jangchub Yeshe of Maja doesn’t agree either that there is any special reason for Nagarjuna to bow down here.  In support of this he uses the type of logical reason which is based on the opponent’s common knowledge, saying that by this point The Arya had already reached the level of a bodhisattva, and rid himself of desire.  He had as well destroyed all appearances that some things should be taken up and some things should be avoided.  As such, says Jangchub Yeshe, there is no use trying to determine what Nagarjuna’s goals might have been.
ZHANG THANG SAG PAS KYANG, RIGS PA DRUG CU PA’I t’IKKAR DE DAG DANG MTHUN PAR BKOD MOD,
Shang Tangsakpa, in his own commentary to the Sixty Verses, has as well put forth arguments that are in keeping with those of the three teachers mentioned above.
All of these arguments, however, are incorrect.

DE LA RE SHIG PHYOGS DANG PO MI RIGS TE, THAR PA DON GNYER GYI BLO BCOS MA MA YIN PA BSKYED PA’I GANG ZAG DGOS PA LA MI BLTOS PAR ‘GYUR TE, DANG BA SKYES NAS CHOS BYED PA’I PHYIR, RIN PHRENG DU, DAD CAN NYID PHYIR CHOS LA BRTEN ZHES GSUNGS SO,,
Let’s take a brief look at how the first position is wrong:

According to Pa-tsab’s view, a person who has reached an uncontrived aspiration for freedom would have never to be acting for the purpose of reaching some goal, since they would be undertaking their practice solely out of intense feelings of faith.  As the String of Jewels says, “They follow their practice for faith itself.”
GNYIS PA’ANG MI RIGS TE, DAM PA BYA BA GANG BYED KYANG GZHAN DON LA ‘JUG PAR MTHONG BA’I PHYIR,
The second argument is wrong as well.  We can see for ourselves that whatever holy people do, they do it for the sake of benefiting others.
GSUM PA’ANG MI RIGS TE, MNYAM GZHAG TU BCOM PA’I PHYIR ZER NA, KHYAB PA MA NGES SHING, RJES THOB TU BCOM PA MI ‘GRUB STE, BLANG BYA LEN ZHING DOR BYA ‘DOR BA’I PHYIR,

The third idea is also mistaken.  If Jangchub Yeshe is saying that it’s during a state of deep meditation that one has destroyed all appearances, and thus Nagarjuna has no goal in mind, then we would say that it’s not necessarily the case.  If he’s saying that these appearances have been destroyed during the aftermath period, following such a meditation, then we would say he is simply wrong—since we do at this point undertake certain actions and avoid others.
DES NA ‘PHAGS PA YAB SRAS CHOS CAN, RTOGS LDAN MIN PAR THAL, DGOS MED KYI BYA BA LA ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR, GANG ZAG RMONGS PA BZHIN,
Therefore I can offer the following debate:
Consider the Realized One and his spiritual son.
Are you saying that they are not people of great understanding?
Because they perform actions that have no purpose.
They are, for example, like people who are very confused.
THAL BA KHAS BLANGS DANG BSAL BA [f. 3a] STON TSUL ‘OG TU ‘CHAD PAS MA SPROS SO,,
You would accept the necessity of the conclusion here.  As for how it is mistaken, I will not expand on that here, as we will be covering it below.
BSDUS PA’I DON NI, BSTOD PHYAG GNYIS BSTOD PA LA RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA DANG, SKYE ‘JIG SPANGS PA DANG, DE TSUL JI LTAR SPANGS PA RNAMS KYIS BSTAN TO,,

As for our summary of this section, the praise (from among the praise & the prostration) is expressed by saying that Lord Buddha gave the teachings on dependence and that he rid himself of the belief that things could start or stop; and by describing the way in which he overcame that belief.
TSIG DON LA DNGOS DANG, RTZOD SPANG GNYIS SO, DANG PO LA, PHYED PHYI MA’I TSIG DON NI, PHYAG ‘TSAL LO,

Our discussion of the meaning of the words of praise will have two parts: first, the actual meaning of these words; and second, a defense against several objections that people might raise.  Let’s begin by looking at the meaning of the first half-line of the verse, which says, “I bow down.”
GANG LA NA, RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA KHO NAS THUB DBANG DU BZHAG CING, RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA’I THUB DBANG DE LA’O,,

And who is it that Nagarjuna is bowing down to?  There is a being whom we establish as being the Lord of the Able Ones, for no more reason than that he taught the concept of dependence; and it is to this one—the Lord of the Able who spoke dependence—that Nagarjuna bows.
THUB DBANG NYID KYANG RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA’I ‘JOG BYED KYI RGYU YIN TE, GZHAN LA NUS PA MED PA’I PHYIR,
Deciding whether or not someone is the Lord of the Able Ones depends on whether or not that person has taught dependence.  This is because no one else has that kind of ability.
NYAN THOS DANG, RANG SANGS RGYAS DANG, BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’ RNAMS KYANG THUB PA’I DBANG POS BSTAN PA NYID LAS RTOGS NUS PA YIN GYI, RANG DBANG DU NUS PA MED DO,,
Listeners, self-made buddhas, and bodhisattvas are able to understand dependence from the teachings of the Lord of the Able Ones, but they don’t have the capacity to do so on their own.
DE LTA NA THUB DBANG DU ‘GRUB PA RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA NGES PA LA BLTOS, DE YANG THUB DBANG DU NGES PA LA BLTOS PAS PHAN TSUN BLTOS PA’I PHYIR, GNYIS KA MI ‘GRUB BO ZHE NA,
Someone may come and raise the following objection—

Based on what you’ve said, deciding whether or not someone is a Lord of the Able Ones depends on determining whether or not they are teaching dependence.  But that in itself depends on determining whether or not they are indeed a Lord of the Able Ones.  Since proving one depends upon proving the other, neither can be proved!
PHAN TSUN BLTOS PAS NGO BO NYID KYIS MI ‘GRUB PA ‘DOD LA, SPYIR MI ‘GRUB PAR THAL NA NI KHYAB PA MED DO,,

We can agree that the two depend upon each other, and so neither is proven in and by itself.  To say though that it is therefore the case that they cannot, in general, be proven is not a necessary conclusion.
YON TAN GZHAN GYIS MI BSTOD PAR RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BA KHO NAS BSTOD PA CI ZHE NA,
Another question someone may ask is: “Why is it that Lord Buddha is being praised only because he has taught dependence?  Why can we not praise him for his other good qualities?”
BSTOD PA PO’I RANG BZHIN DANG, BSTOD PA’I RNAM PA DANG, BSTOD PA’I RGYU’O,,
In reply we can talk about the nature of the one who has made the praise; the form that the praise takes; and the reason for the praise.
DANG PO NI, SLOB DPON RANG NYID DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAS DGYES PA’I KHYAD PAR BRNYES PA DANG, RTEN ‘BREL RTOGS PAS YON TAN THAMS CAD KYI ‘BYUNG GNAS SU GZIGS PA’O,,
First, the Master has himself reached a certain kind of joy caused by perceiving suchness; and he has seen that understanding dependence is the source of all good qualities.
GNYIS PA NI, GSUNG BYA RTEN ‘BYUNG RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES PAS, MTHAR LTA’I DRI MA THAMS CAD DANG BRAL BA DE STON BYED DU GYUR PAS YON TAN GYI DBANG PHYUG TU GYUR PA’O,,

Second, the dependence which was taught didn’t start on its own.  That is, it too is free of each & every stain of extreme views.  The one who teaches this dependence, then, is the lord of every good quality.
GSUM PA NI, SLOB DPON RTEN ‘BYUNG ‘CHAD PAR BZHED PA DANG, DE STON [f. 3b] PA PO DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA LA GUS PA BSKYED PA’O,,
Third, the Master intends to teach dependence in his own work, so it is proper that he should show respect to the one who first taught it—to the One Gone Thus.
PHYED PHYI MA’I TSIG DON NI, GANG GIS RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA TSUL ‘DI YIS SPANGS PAR GYUR PA’I THUB DBANG DE LA PHYAG ‘TSAL LO,

Now for the meaning of the rest of the verse: “I bow down to the Lord of the Able Ones, who was able to rid himself of the idea that things could start or stop through some nature of their own; and he did so by employing this method of understanding the meaning of dependence.”
THUB PA NI LUS NGAG YID GSUM THUB PA’O,,
The literal meaning of “Able One” is that this person has been able to perfect the three of what they do; what they say; and what they think.
DBANG LA PHYUG PA DANG, DBANG CHE BA GNYIS TE, TSOGS GNYIS BSAGS PA DANG NYAN THOS SOGS LA MNGA’ BSGYUR BAS SO,,

Our Buddha is the “lord” (Tib: wangpo) of these Able Ones in the sense that he is both rich in power (wang), and also possesses greater power (wang).  This is because he has completed the two collections, and also because he holds dominion over the listeners and the rest.

TSUL ‘DIS ZHES PA LA BSHAD TSUL BZHI STE, RGYU ‘BRAS PHAN TSUN BLTOS PA DANG, SNGA MA LA BRTEN NAS PHYI MA RIM BZHIN DU ‘BYUNG BA DANG, DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS TSUL GYI RIM PA DANG, ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA’I RIGS PA’I TSUL LO,,

The expression “with this method” can be explained in four different ways: (1) through understanding that causes & effects exhibit a mutual dependence; (2) through understanding that later effects occur, in succession, depending on earlier causes; (3) through the various stages of the method for perceiving suchness; and (4) through the method of logical reasoning which will be explained here.
DE’I DBANG GIS GANG GIS LA YANG BZHI STE, RGYU GANG GIS DANG, GSUNG BA PO GANG GIS DANG, THUB DBANG DU ‘JOG PA’I RGYU GANG GIS DANG, ‘THAD PA GANG GIS ZHES SO,,

Four methods imply four factors: causes acting as factors; a teacher acting as a factor; the reason for deciding that someone is a Lord of the Able Ones, acting as a factor; and the veracity of an argument acting as a factor.
RTEN ‘BYUNG GSUNG BAS THUB DBANG YIN PAR MA ZAD KYI, DNGOS PO RNAMS KYI RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA BKAG PA’I PHYIR YANG THUB DBANG NGO,,

Teaching dependence is not the only thing that can make one a Lord of the Able: we also give this name to someone who has denied that things which do something could either start or stop through some nature of their own.
GANG GIS SPANGS NA, RGYU ‘BRAS PHAN TSUN BLTOS PA’I TSUL ‘DI YIS SO,,
What is it that enables us to rid ourselves of that wrong idea?  It is the method where we realize that causes & effects exhibit a mutual dependence.
‘BRAS BU ‘BRAS BUR ‘JOG PA RGYUS BSKYED PA DANG, RGYU RGYUR ‘JOG PA YANG ‘BRAS BU SKYE BA LA BLTOS PAS SO,,
This is because we can only say that a result is a result when a cause has produced it; and because we can only say that a cause is a cause once its result has grown.
YANG SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA DAG SPANGS SO,
We can also say that one is a Lord of the Able when they have employed the method of ridding themselves of the idea of starting & stopping.
GSUNG BA PO GANG GIS TSUL JI LTAR NA, SNGA MA LA BRTEN NAS PHYI MA ‘BYUNG BA’I TSUL ‘DI YIS SO,,
What kind of method is involved when this someone teaches others?  Here, it is where what comes later occurs in dependence upon what comes earlier.
YANG RGYU GANG GIS SPANGS NA SKYE BA SHES PAS ‘JIG PA SHES ZHES PA’I RTOGS TSUL LAM STON TSUL GYI RIM PA’I TSUL ‘DI YIS SO,,

And what cause helps us to give up these wrong beliefs?  It is a method which involves steps—a method of teaching the path which relates to a method of realization: “If you understand starting, then you will understand stopping.”
DE LTAR BSTAN PA LA DGOS PA CI YOD CE NA, RIM PA ‘DIS GDUL BYA LA PHAN GDAGS PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR RO,,
“What’s the purpose of teaching it this way?” one may ask.  Because doing it in steps like this is meant to help the student.
YANG SLOB DPON RANG NYID KYIS ‘OG NAS ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA’I GSUNG RAB LAS GSUNGS PA’I [f. 4a] RIGS PA’I TSUL ‘DI YIS SPANGS PAR GYUR PA’O,,
We can also say that we get rid of these things by using the method of the reasoning spoken in the Buddha’s teachings, as will be explained by the Master himself further on.
GNYIS PA RTZOD SPANGS NI STONG NYID BDUN CU PA DANG, RTZOD LDOG LA BSTOD PA MA MDZAD PAR ‘DI LA MDZAD PA CI ZHE NA,

Secondly, let’s address objections.  Someone may come and ask: “Why did Nagarjuna include an offering of praise in this book, without having included one in the Seventy Verses on Emptiness, or Putting an End to All Argument?”
RTZA BA SHES RAB DANG ‘DI NI THOG MA NYID NAS RTEN ‘BREL CI TZAM LAS BRTZAMS NAS GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA RANG DBANG BA’I BSTAN BCOS YIN PAS MCHOD BRJOD MDZAD LA,

The Root Text on Wisdom and this book start off from the very beginning by presenting a touch of dependence; they are works which stand on their own, and therefore Arya Nagarjuna added an offering of praise to them.
GNYIS PO NI RTZA BA’I ‘PHROS DON TZAM YIN GYI, LOGS SHIG TU BRJOD BYA RANG DBANG BA MED PAS MA MDZAD DO,,

The other two works mentioned are just an extension of the ideas expressed in the Root Text—they don’t have a separate, independent subject matter; and so the Master did not include in them an offering of praise.
GANG LA ‘PHROS PA NI ‘GREL PA LTAR RO,,
If you’re wondering what parts of the Root Text they are extensions of, this information is found in the commentary.
GNYIS PA BRTZAMS PAR BYA BA’I GZHUNG DNGOS LA, RTEN ‘BREL MTHA’ BRAL DU BSTAN PA DANG, PHUNG SOGS GSUNGS PA DRANG DON DU BSGRUB PA DANG, PHUNG POR ZHEN PA’I NYES DMIGS DANG, THAR PA’I PHAN YON NO,,

Secondly, I will cover the following topics in the actual text to be composed: demonstrating that dependence is freedom from extreme positions; establishing that statements about the parts of a person and so on were figurative; problems of attachment to the parts of a person; and the benefits of freedom.
is freedom from the two extremes
DANG PO LA, YOD MTHA’ DGAG ,MTHA’ GNYIS KYI SGRUB BYED DGAG ,MTHA’ GNYIS KYI NGO BO DGAG PA’O,,
The first topic has three parts: refuting the extreme view that things exist; refuting arguments in favor of the two extreme views; and refuting the substance of the two extreme views.
Refuting the extreme view that things exist
DANG PO LA, RTEN ‘BYUNG SPROS BRAL DU GANG GIS RTOGS PA DANG, YOD MTHA’ ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA’O,,

The first of these parts has two divisions of its own: who it is that realizes that dependence is the absence of elaboration; and the reasoning which we use to refute the extreme view that things could exist.
DANG PO LA DNGOS DANG, ZAB MO BSTEN PAR GDAMS PA’O,,
The first division has two steps: the actual explanation, followed by advice that we rely on an understanding of the profound.
on who it is that realizes
DANG PO NI, BU MA SKYES PA DE BU SKYES SO ZHES PA’I SGRA’I DON DU ‘GAL BA LTAR SKYE ‘GAG MED PA YANG RTEN ‘BREL GYI SGRA’I DON DU ‘GAL LO ZHE NA,
Here is the first.  Someone may come and make the following assertion:

It’s a contradiction of terms to say that a woman who has never given birth has had a baby; just so, it is a contradiction of terms to say that the meaning of dependence is that nothing starts or stops.
BYIS PA’I BLO LA BLTOS NAS ‘GAL BAR RTOG NA NI RTOGS SHIG ,KHO BO LA NYES PA MED DE,
If you’re going to use that infant’s mind of yours to imagine that there is some kind of contradiction here, then go ahead.  For us, there’s no such problem.

BYIS PA RNAMS KYIS RTEN ‘BREL GYI MING NYID LAS RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PA ZHEN PA’I PHYIR ‘PHAGS PA’I GZIGS PA LA BLTOS NAS NI RTEN ‘BYUNG RANG BZHIN MED PAR CHES GSAL BAR KHONG DU CHUD NUS SO ZHES BSTAN PA’I PHYIR,

As soon as infants only hear the word “dependence,” they immediately hold on to the idea that it possesses some sort of self-nature.  And so we can ourselves conclude with absolute clarity that—relative to the way a realized being sees things—dependence has no nature of its own.  In order to convey this thought, Master Nagarjuna gives us the next verse of the root text.
Asti nāsti vyatikrāntā buddhir yeṣāṃ nirāśrayā,
Asti nasti vyatikranta buddhir yeshan nirashraya,
,GANG DAG GI BLO YOD MED LAS,
,DE DAG GIS NI RKYEN GYI DON,
,ZAB MO [f. 4b] DMIGS MED RNAM PAR RTOGS,
Those whose minds have gone beyond
The idea that things could exist or not,
And who no longer dwell there,
Understand that the meaning of a cause
That there is nothing at all to see.
RKANG PA PHYED DANG GSUM GYIS RTOGS BYED DANG, PHYED DANG GNYIS KYIS RTOGS BYA BSTAN TO,,
The first two and a half lines [of the Tibetan] tell us who it is that realizes; the last line and a half tell us what it is that is realized.

DE LA TSE ‘DIR STONG PA NYID LA GOMS PA RLABS CAN MED KYANG, SNGON ‘DAS PA’I SKYE BAR GOMS STOBS DANG LDAN PA ‘PHAGS PA SH’A RI’I BU LA SOGS PA GANG DAG GI BLO DE DAG GIS NI RNAM PAR RTOGS TE, YE SHES KYIS MNGON SUM DU BYED CES PA’I DON TO,,

On the subject of who it is that realizes, there are those—such as the high being Shariputra—who had not familiarized themselves in a very powerful way with emptiness during their present lifetime, but who had nonetheless become very acquainted with it in past lives.  Those are minds which understand emptiness; which is to say that they do so directly, by means of wisdom.
,JI LTAR ‘JIG RTEN LAS DANG NYON MONGS
RGYUR BCAS BYED RGYUR LDAN ‘BYUNG DANG,
,LAS DANG NYON MONGS PA DAG LDOG RGYU
DE YANG ‘DREN PAS RAB TU GSUNGS,
,GANG NA SKYE DANG RGA DANG RGUD PA’I
SDUG BSNGAL NGES PAR MI GNAS PA,
,THAR PA’I MCHOG DE SMRA BA’I KHYU MCHOG
DE YIS RANG GIS MKHYEN TE GSUNGS,
ZHES PA’I TSIGS BCAD ‘PHAGS PA SH’A RI’I BUS ‘PHAGS PA RTA THUL LAS THOS PA TZAM GYIS DE KHO NA NYID KHONG DU CHUD PAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
The high being Shariputra mastered the true meaning of suchness merely from hearing the following lines of verse from the realized one, Ashvajit:
It has been spoken by our Guide
That the world has come about through causes.
And those causes that created it
He is the leader of all those
He has come to know himself;
For he is without question beyond
The suffering of birth, aging, & despair.
BLO JI LTA BU ZHE NA, YOD PA DANG MED PA’I MTHA’ GNYIS SU MTHONG BA LAS RNAM PAR ‘DAS SHING DE GNYIS LAS GZHAN PA’I DBUS MED PA’I PHYIR, DE LA’ANG MNGON ZHEN GYIS MI GNAS PA’O,,

Someone may ask just what kind of mind it is that is able to do this.  It is the kind that has gone completely beyond seeing the two extremes of existence and non-existence, or some other between these two.  And thus this mind no longer dwells in the belief that these are real.
GANG RTOGS NA RKYEN RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I DON TO,,
What does this mind realize?  It realizes the meaning of dependence, causes.

DE YANG BYIS PA RNAMS SKRAG PAR BYED PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE RNAMS KYIS GTING DPAG PAR MI NUS PA’I PHYIR ZAB MO RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES PA NYID KYIS YOD PA DANG MED PA DANG DBUS YONGS SU RTOGS {%RTOG?} PA’I BLO PHYIN CI LOG GI YUL DU DMIGS MI NUS PAS DMIGS SU MED PA’O,,

This idea puts fear into the hearts of infants, and they are incapable of fathoming it fully; thus then we call it deep.  We also say of it that there is “nothing at all to see”; meaning that—because things can never have started through some nature of their own—this is an object that can never be seen by the totally mistaken state of mind which imagines that things exist, or don’t exist, or else stand somewhere inbetween.
YANG NA RKYEN GYI DON LA DE LTAR RTOGS ZHES SBYAR RO,,
Which also means you could say that when they “realize causes,” what they realize is what we’ve just described.
Does the mind exist, during the
DE LA ‘DIR ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG NA BLO YOD MED DPYAD PAR BYA STE, GANG DAG BLO KHAS BLANGS NAS DE YANG SNANG BA DANG BCAS PA’O ZHES SMRA BA

While we’re on this subject, let’s examine the question of whether or not the mind exists at all with a realized being who is in the direct perception of emptiness.  Now suppose someone were to assert that “If we do accept that there exists a state of mind at this point, then it must be a state of mind which possesses the impression that things exist through some nature of their own.”
DE DAG NI DBU MA’I PHYOGS KYI DRI TZAM [f. 5a] YANG MI SNANG BAS SUN DBYUNG BA’I GNAS TZAM DU YANG MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR ‘BAD PAR MI BYED DO,,

A person who says something like this doesn’t have the least impression—not a whiff—of what the Middle Way means.  As such, it would be silly for me to even waste my time here destroying their wrong ideas.
MED PA’I PHYOGS DPYAD PAR BYA STE,
Instead, I would rather discuss the position that there is no mind during that state.
GNAS LUGS MNGON DU GYUR PA NA CHU LA CHU BZHAG DANG MAR LA MAR BZHAG GI TSUL DU DBYER MED PAS BLO CHOS DBYINGS SU GYUR PA’O ZHE NA,
Someone may begin with the following:

When we perceive the true nature of reality directly, the mind dissolves into ultimate reality and the two become the same thing, inseparable—it’s like pouring water into water, or mixing butter into butter.
DE LTAR NA CHOS DBYINGS KYANG BLOR ‘GYUR TE RGYU MTSAN MTSUNGS PAS SO,,
Well now, if that’s the case, then we can just as well say—for the very same reason—that ultimate reality here becomes the mind!
SBYOR LAM CHOS MCHOG GI DUS NA BLO YOD PA DE LA PHYI MA MA SKYES PA TZAM LA KHAS LEN NA, DE NI MED PAR DGAG PA TZAM YIN GYI, CHOS DBYINGS MTHONG BA’I DON DU MI RUNG NGO,,

Moreover, we all agree that there does exist some state of mind at the level called “highest thing in the universe,” during the stage of the path of preparation.  Are you saying then that ultimate reality is simply the fact that this state of mind leads to nothing right after it?  But that would simply be a normal absence of something—it wouldn’t be appropriate to say that this is what we see, when we see the realm of the ultimately real.
PHYI MA MA SKYES SHING SNGA MA GCIG PA LA ‘DOD NA YANG DON DAM BDEN PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, DNGOS PO GCIG PA RGYU ZAD PA’I RKYEN LAS SKYES PA’I PHYIR,

Even if you claim that there is just the state of mind that existed before, and the next one hasn’t arisen yet, that’s not ultimate reality.  And this is because the one thing has still arisen from a condition: the condition of the causes wearing out.
BLO SNGAR NAS YOD MA MYONG BA DE LTA BU’I DPYAD PA MI ‘JUG GO ZHE NA,
Someone may then argue: “You can’t examine this using normal logic, because we’re talking about a state of mind which is unprecedented.”
DE LTAR NA SO SKYE LA’ANG BLO MED PAS ‘PHAGS PA ‘BA’ ZHIG DMIGS KYIS BKAR BA LA DGOS PA MED DO,,
If that’s the case, then regular people must also go into a state of no-mind in each new moment.  There’s no reason to make a special case for realized beings.
SO SKYE LA GNYIS SU SNANG BA’I BLO YOD NA ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG NA YANG GNYIS SNANG DANG BRAL BA’I BLO CI’I PHYIR MI BZHAG

If regular people possess a state of mind which involves a discrepancy between the way things appear and the way things really are, then why shouldn’t we say there are beings in the direct perception of emptiness who have a state of mind that is free of this discrepancy?
,BLO TZAM LA GNYIS SNANG GI KHYAB PA GANG DU YANG SGRUB MI NUS TE, ‘BREL PA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,
There is no way you can say that just because someone has a mind, then that mind has to be involved in this discrepancy; there’s no connection.
DE LTA MIN NA MNYAM GZHAG NA GNYIS SNANG YOD PA’I THA SNYAD RIGS PAR ‘GYUR TE, BLO’I THA SNYAD SBYAR BA’I PHYIR RO,,
And if that’s not true, then it would be correct to say that the mind, during deep meditation on ultimate reality, did possess the discrepancy—since we do apply the word “mind” to it.
SNYING RJE’I SEMS DANG GNYIS SU MED BLO DANG, ZHES PA DANG, ‘DIR YANG DE LTAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
Our thinking here is expressed in the famous verse that includes the following phrase, as well as in the current work itself:
A state of mind beyond duality...
BLO YOD NA YUL YANG KHAS BLANG DGOS PAS YUL YUL CAN GYI SPROS PA MA ZHI BAR ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA,
Someone may then raise the following objection:

If there is a state of mind at this point, then we would have to say there is as well an object which it perceives; and then the mental elaborations of an object and a subject cannot have been put to rest.
MNYAM GZHAG GIS GZIGS PA’I DON NI YUL DANG YUL CAN GANG YANG MED PA’I PHYIR SPROS PA MA ZHI BAR GA LA ‘GYUR TE, DE TZAM GYIS YUL YUL CAN ‘GAG PAR NI MI RIGS TE,

How could you say that—just because there are no subjects with their objects which constitute the point of focus for a person in the direct perception of ultimate reality—this person has then failed to put to rest mental elaborations?  This alone would not be enough to disprove the existence of subjects with objects in general.

MIG SHES KYI NGOR SGRA MED PAS SGRA MED PAR [f. 5b] MI ‘GRUB PA BZHIN, MNYAM GZHAG DANG DON DAM BDEN PA YUL YUL CAN DANG RTOGS BYA RTOGS BYED DU SLOB DPON YAB SRAS KYIS GSUNGS SHING, DE LTAR THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS GZHAL BA’I PHYIR,

The fact that sound doesn’t appear to the consciousness of the eye doesn’t prove that sound doesn’t exist.  And so the masters—Father & Son—have said that the state of meditation of a realized being is the subject which is doing the perceiving; while ultimate reality is the object which is being perceived.  Moreover, this fact can be confirmed by a conventional type of accurate perception.

GANG DAG MNYAM GZHAG GIS MA GZIGS NA MED DGOS SO ZHES SMRA BA DANG, DON DAM PA’I TSAD MA DANG THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA DBANG GANG BTZAN DPYAD NAS THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA’I YUL LA GNOD PA BYED PA NI RIGS PA’I TSUL LAS ‘DAS PAR ‘OG NAS DPYAD PAR BYA’O,,

If you say that something not seen in the direct perception of emptiness cannot then exist; or that when the two come into conflict then the ultimate form of accurate perception takes precedence over the conventional form, and disproves the object of that latter perception; then you have gone beyond the bounds of logic itself.  I will examine this point further below.
GAL TE DER BLO KHAS BLANGS NA LAM LA MTSAN ‘DZIN DU ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA,
Someone may then come and argue:

If we do say that a state of mind exists during the direct perception of ultimate reality, then we’d also have to say that the path of a realized being holds that things have qualities in & of their own.
RIGS {%RIG?} NGOR BLO YOD PAR SMRAS NA DER ‘GYUR MOD, THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS DE LTAR BZHAG PAS GA LA ‘GYUR,

If we were saying that a mind existed which was presenting itself to the mind of the realized being during this direct perception, then you would admittedly be correct.  But that would have to be something confirmed by a conventional type of accurate perception; so how could it apply here?
DE LTA NA BLOS GANG DU GZUNG YANG MTSAN ‘DZIN DU ‘GYUR BAS LTA BA SKYONG LUGS RGYA’I MKHAN PO BZHIN DU ‘GYUR DGOS SO,,

If you persist in this idea—saying that anytime any state of mind holds an object, it must be holding that this object possesses qualities in & of itself—then the views we’re supposed to be maintaining must be those of the Chinese master.

LTA BA RGYA’I MKHAN PO LTAR ‘THAD NA NYAMS LEN YANG DE KHO NA LTAR ‘GYUR DGOS TE, MTSAN ‘DZIN RNAM PA KUN TU DGAG PA RIGS KYI SO SO SKYE BOS KYANG MTSAN ‘DZIN PA NYAMS LEN GYI MTHIL DU BYED PA NI RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MI RIGS SO,,

If the views of this master were correct, then a practice associated with the views would have to follow, accordingly.  In this case, it would be the right thing to do to attempt to put a stop to any & all perceptions where we hold that the characteristics of things belong to those things.  And in that case it would be completely wrong for normal people to utilize such perceptions at the very core of their practice.
DE LTA NA BLO DE LA DON SPYI JI LTAR ‘CHAR SNYAM NA, GZUNG RNAM MTHA’ DAG GIS DBEN PA NAM MKHA’ LTA BU’I DPES BSTAN PAR BYA’O,,

“How then,” you may ask, “would conceptualized objects ever appear to the mind?”  It is in this regard that such teachers would utilize the metaphor of the sky, claiming that it describes a state of mind devoid of all object aspects.
DNGOS POR SMRA BA GANG DAG GZUNG RNAM DANG ‘DZIN RNAM GNYIS SU ‘DOD PA DAG GIS ‘DZIN RNAM DE LA YANG THUN MONG MA YIN PA’I DON SPYI JI LTAR ‘CHAR YANG BSAM PAR BYA’O,,

But if you do put it this way, you’re also going to have to give some consideration to the Functionalist groups, who divide things into two: object aspects and subject aspects.  How then would their specific conceptualized objects ever appear to the subject aspects?
MYONG TZAM PAS SO ZHES PA NI MING GI THA SNYAD TZAM YIN NO, ,DE LTA NA DER ‘DZIN RNAM YOD PAR ‘GYUR TE, BLO KHAS BLANGS NAS GZUNG RNAM MTHA’ DAG GIS DBEN PA’I PHYIR CE NA,

That’s all just words that they use; after all, “it’s all just experience.”  And if that’s the way it is, then you can still have a subject aspect: once you accept that this is all the mind, then you’re also saying that it’s devoid of all object aspects.
SKYON MED DE, BLTOS CHOS KYI RNAM PAS DBEN PA YIN GYI, CHOS NYID KYI RNAM PA NI DER DGAG PAR [f. 6a] MI BYA’O,,

And yet there’s no such issue here; we can say that this direct experience of ultimate reality is devoid of any object which depends upon causes, but this wouldn’t preclude saying that its object was suchness.
‘BYUNG BA CHE LA SOGS BSHAD PA ZHES PA’I SKABS SU YUL GYI RNAM LDAN KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR BSGYUR BYA DANG SGYUR BYED BSGYUR BA’I RNAM PA GSUM YOD MED KYANG DPYAD DO,,

Later on, in this very text of Master Nagarjuna, there comes a section where he talks about “the great elements and so on which were described.”  At this point, the idea of the mind possessing an object aspect is accepted; and so if you’re going to accept the ideas you’ve expressed here, you’d better give some careful thought to the question of whether or not there exist the three aspects of something which changes; something which makes it change; and the changing itself.

GZHAN YANG LAM BDEN ‘DUS BYAS SU BZHAG CING, DE’I MTSAN GZHIR ‘PHAGS LAM YAN LAG BRGYAD BZHAG PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE DAG LA RJES THOB KYIS KHYAB PA GANG DU YANG MA GSUNGS SHING MNYAM GZHAG LAM MIN PAR YANG MA GSUNGS SO,,

Moreover, the truth of the path is described as a product of causes & conditions; and the classical example of this truth is described as the path of a realized being, with its eight different components.  Nowhere is it said that these must relate to the aftermath period of the path of seeing; and nowhere is it said that the period within the meditative experience cannot itself be a path.
SPANG BYA SPONG TSUL SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN ‘BYED SOGS KYIS ‘KHRUL PAS ‘KHRUL PA SPONG BAR DPE’I SGO NAS BZHAG PA NI SO SO SKYE BO’I SKABS SU DANG,

Moreover, Master Bhavaviveka describes a way in which undesirable qualities are eliminated by people who are still at the point where they have not yet seen emptiness directly.  He uses an example in which a mistaken state of mind is used to eliminate a mistake.

SPANG GNYEN DON LA GRUB PA ‘GOG PA YIN GYI, SA BON SPONG BA LA BDAG MED MNGON SUM DU MTHONG DGOS PAR ‘JUG ‘GREL SOGS KUN TU GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR DANG BDEN PA MNGON PAR RTOGS PA SKAD CIG MA GCIG TU GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,

We deny that problems and their antidotes could exist in reality.  But the great books—such as Entering the Middle Way, and its various commentaries—all agree that to eliminate negative seeds we need to see, directly, the fact that nothing is itself.  And they agree that the realization of this reality is something that changes from instant to instant.
THA SNYAD PA’I BLO’I DUS LA DPAGS NAS DPER BZHAD DO {%BZHAG GO}, ,ZHES PA LA YANG NGES BYED MI SNANG BAS SHIN TU MI GSAL BA’I TSIG DON LA ‘BAD PA BYED PAR MI RIGS SO,,

Moreover, there’s no definite interpretation you can give to statements like “The example is given with consideration to the period when the discursive state of mind is operating.”  It’s inappropriate to expend a lot of effort trying to resolve what obscure statements like this are trying to say.
MDOR NA, DON GANG LA ‘DZIN YANG MNYAM GZHAG NA BLO MED PA’I THA SNYAD SBYAR BAR MI BYA STE, SLOB DPON YAB SRAS RJES ‘BRANG DANG BCAS PAS BLO YOD PA’I THA SNYAD SBYAR BA’I PHYIR,

In summary, we would advise you never to use the expression, “No state of mind is present during deep meditation”—no matter what you take this to mean.  Because the masters here—the Father and his spiritual Son—and all those who have carried on their tradition through the centuries would all say, instead, that “there is a state of mind at this point.”
DE DAG DON DAM LA DPYOD PA’I RIGS PA YIN PAS DE LTA BUS DPYAD PAR MI BYA ZHE NA, DE LTA NA BLO MED PA’I PHYOGS KYANG MI BZHAG GO

You could state that “All these are a kind of reasoning where we are examining the ultimate; you can’t look at them in any normal way.”  That may well be the case, but even then no one would take the position that at this point there’s no state of mind at all.
,DON ‘DI NI SHIN TU DKA’ BAS DE LTAR DPYAD PA TZAM YIN GYI, DGAG PA LHUR BLANGS PA MA YIN TE, BDAG BLO MI GSAL BAS RTOGS PAR DKA’ BA’I PHYIR RO,,

These are tough points.  I’m just giving my own analysis, and I don’t mean to deny other people’s opinions out of hand.  For my own less than brilliant mind, these things are something quite difficult to resolve.
Refuting the extreme view that nothing exists
GNYIS PA, MED LTA DGAG PA BSHAD ZIN DRAN PA LA SBYAR BA DANG, YOD LTA DGAG PA LA MNYAN PAR GDAMS PA’O,,

This brings us to our second point from above: advice that we rely on an understanding of the profound.  We’ll cover this in two points—helping the reader recall the way in which the extreme view that nothing exists at all has already been refuted; and then advice that we should listen now to how the extreme view that everything exists as it seems is in its turn refuted.
DANG PO NI, RANG SDE NA RE, CHOS THAMS [f. 6b] CAD STONG NYID DU MI ‘THAD DE, SGRUB BYED MED CING GNOD BYED YOD PAS SO,,

Here is the first.  Now there are certain of our own Buddhist schools which say that it cannot be correct to assert that every existing thing in the universe is empty.  They would say that—first of all—there is no way to prove that this idea is correct; and secondly, there are ways to prove that it is wrong.
DANG PO NI, STONG NYID DU SGRUB PA’I ‘THAD PA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR DANG,
About there being no proofs for this idea, they would say that it’s in fact impossible to prove anything as correct, if it’s the case that everything is empty.
RIGS PAS GNOD DE, MNGON SUM GYIS DMIGS PAR MI ‘GYUR BAR THAL, MED PA’I PHYIR, BONG BU’I RVA BZHIN

They would also say that logic itself would disprove the idea that everything is empty—since in that case nothing could be perceived by any direct perception; since nothing would exist at all.  Everything would be, for example, just like the antlers on a rabbit’s head.
DES NA YOD DE, MNGON SUM GYIS DMIGS PA’I PHYIR DANG,
And so, they would say, it’s rather the case that all these things exist—simply because we can perceive them, directly.
LUNG GIS KYANG GNOD DE, MDO LAS, RTEN ‘BREL TSE GSUM PA GSUNGS PA DANG, CHOS MNGON PA LAS KYANG, PHUNG KHAMS SKYE MCHED KYI RANG SPYI’I MTSAN NYID GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR CE NA, LAN NI,

They would also say that the idea that everything is empty is disproved, by scriptural authority.  Sutra, for example, describes a chain of dependence which stretches across three lifetimes.  And the teachings on higher knowledge describe the particular & general natures of the five parts to a person; the twelve doors of sense; and the 18 categories.  The next verse of the root text offers a response to these assertions.
,MED NYID RNAM PAR LDOG ZIN GYIS,

‘JIG RTEN DANG ‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PA’I DGE RTZA THAMS CAD SUN ‘BYIN PA LA ZHUGS PAS DMYAL BA LA SOGS PA’I SDUG BSNGAL THAMS CAD BSKYED PA’I RGYU YIN PA DANG, DGE BA SNGAR YOD ‘GRIB PA’I RGYU YIN PAS NYES PA KUN ‘BYUNG BA’I GNAS LAS ‘BRAS LA SKUR BA ‘DEBS PA’I MED PA NYID DU LTA BA ‘DI NI KHYOD KYIS LOG ZIN PA NYID KYIS RE SHIG ‘GOG PAR MI BYED DO,,

The idea that nothing at all exists amounts to a denial of karma & its consequences.  As such it is a concept which is indeed the source of every fault: it leads us to a point where we rip out all the virtue we’ve ever gathered—both virtue of the world, and virtue beyond the world.

Thus it is a force which gives birth to each & every form of pain, from the hell realms on up.  It also raises obstacles to whatever good seeds we ever had from before.  And it’s a viewpoint that you yourselves have already disproven; and so, to start with, it’s not something I need to refute here.
YANG NA CHOS MNGON PA’I MDO LAS LOG ZIN PAS DGAG PA RE SHIG MI BYED DO ZHES PA’O,,
One can also read these lines as saying, “This idea has already been disproven in the sutras on higher knowledge; and so—to start with—I will not refute it here.”
DE LTA NA, YOD LTA YANG DGAG MI RIGS PAR ‘GYUR TE, DGE SLONG DAG ,BDEN PA DAM PA NI GCIG STE, MI SLU BA’I CHOS CAN MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA’O, ZHES PAS BKAG ZIN PAS SO ZHE NA,
Someone may raise the following objection:

Well then, neither should we disprove here the other view—that things exist as they seem to.  For it too has long since been disproved by the Buddha: “O monks, there is only one ultimate truth: there is only one thing which will never deceive you, and that is nirvana.”

DE NI MI MTSUNGS TE, YOD LTA ‘GOG PA NI, NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD LAS, LAN MANG DU DANG, BAR MED PA DANG, GZHUNG GCIG TU YOD LTA ‘BA’ ZHIG ‘GOG PA’I GZHUNG MA GSUNGS LA, MED LTA ‘GOG PA DE LAS LOG PAR GSUNGS PAS CHES GSAL BA’I DE DAG LA YANG RIGS PA MI STON TO,,

These two cases, however, are not the same.  There are no references in the scriptures of the listener group where Lord Buddha denied—repeatedly, continuously, and in a dedicated presentation—the idea that things exist the way they seem to.  And yet it is extremely clear that in these same scriptures he denied the idea that nothing exists at all, in exactly the opposite ways.  Neither did he present specific proofs, in either case.
THEG PA CHEN PO’I SDE SNOD LAS, DE LTAR GSUNGS ZHES [f. 7a] MI BSAM STE, ‘DI NI NYAN THOS SDE PA RANG LA GRAGS PA’I LUNG LA BRTEN NAS DGAG PA MDZAD PA YIN PA’I PHYIR,

And don’t think to yourself that the fact that these views were explained in the teachings of the greater way would apply here.  In this text, Nagarjuna is refuting the ideas of the listeners by using the specific scriptures which they themselves espouse.
‘O NA NYE BA’I GDUL BYA DE DAG LA BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS YOD LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA RGYAS PAR MI STON CE NA,

“Well then,” one may ask, “wouldn’t the Conqueror have devoted considerable time to teaching these close students the reasoning which would allow them to disprove the idea that things could exist the way they appear?”
DE DAG NI RGYUD SMIN PA YIN PAS, ‘BAD PA CHEN POS BSTAN MI DGOS LA, CHOS KYI BDAG MED RDZOGS PAR BSGOM PA MED PAS SO,,

It was not necessary for him to make much effort to impress these ideas upon them, as their minds were already ripe.  Moreover, they weren’t meditating on the full form of the lack of a self-nature to things.
‘O NA NYE BA’I GDUL BYA THEG PA CHEN PO PA LA YANG MTSUNGS SHE NA, SKYON MED DE, SHES BYA SHES PA LHUR LEN PA DANG, CHOS KYI BDAG MED RGYAS PAR SGOM PA’I PHYIR RO,,

To which someone may object, “Well then, wouldn’t the case have been the same for his close disciples who were practitioners of the greater way?  Were they not instructed in these ways?”  There’s no such problem though.  These kinds of disciples exert themselves in learning everything that there is to know.  And they were meditating, extensively, on the lack of a self-nature to things.
This brings us to the second point from above: the advice that we should listen now to how the extreme view that everything exists as it seems is in its turn refuted.
RIGS PA GANG GIS YOD NYID KYANG,
LDOG PAR ‘GYUR BA MNYAN PAR GYIS,
We use to deny as well
That things could be as they seem.

‘OG NAS ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA YI, JI LTAR BYIS PAS RNAM BRTAGS BZHIN, ZHES SOGS KYIS RIGS PA GANG GIS YOD PAR BLTA BA NYID KYANG RTEN ‘BREL GYI GTAN TSIGS SOGS KYIS LDOG PAR ‘GYUR BA BSHAD KYI MNYAN PAR GYIS ZHES GDAMS PA’O,,

This verse is advice to us, that we should listen then to explanations which use proofs (different kinds of reasoning)—such as the one based on dependence—to deny this idea that things could be as they seem to be.  These explanations are presented here in the Sixty Verses in verses such as the one which includes the line about “the way that infants imagine things to be.”  We will be covering these verses later on.
KYANG GI SGRA BRJOD PAR MI RIGS TE, MED LTA ‘GOG PA’I ‘BAD PA MI BYED PAR BSTAN PAS SO ZHE NA,
Someone may make the following objection:
There’s no point for Nagarjuna to say “as well” here in this verse, since he has just explained why it’s unnecessary to make any great effort to disprove the mistaken idea that nothing exists.
SKYON MED DE, YOD LTA YANG MDO LAS LDOG ZIN MOD, DE LTA NA YANG SNGAR GYI ‘GAL BA DE DAG MED CES PA’O,,

And yet there’s no such problem.  What the verse is saying is that—while it is true that the idea that things could exist the way they seem has already been refuted in the sutras—none of the objections that we raised in that earlier case apply here.
GNYIS PA YOD MTHA’ ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA LA, SKABS SU BABS PA’I THAL BA DANG, ZHAR BYUNG NGO,,

This brings us to our second major division from above: the reasoning that we use to  refute the extreme view that things could exist the way they appear.  We will begin with a proof by absurdity which is relevant to the current discussion, and then cover some incidental points.
DANG PO NI, RIGS PA DE YANG GANG ZHE NA, ,‘DI LTAR,
Here is the first.  “Just what,” you may ask, “is the reasoning we’re going to use to prove that things cannot exist the way they appear?”  The next verse is our reply:
JI LTAR BYIS PAS RNAM BRTAGS BZHIN,
DNGOS PO GAL TE BDEN GYUR NA,
DE DNGOS MED PAS RNAM THAR DU,
GANG GIS MI ‘DOD RGYU CI ZHIG
Suppose that things were real, in the way
That infants imagine them to be.
That nothing about them was left,
BYIS PA LA DA LTAR SNANG BA ‘DI DAG JI LTAR SNANG BA LTAR MI BDEN TE,
The fact is that nothing which is appearing right now to infants is real, in the way it seems to them to be.
GAL TE, JI LTAR BYIS PAS RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA BZHIN DNGOS PO ‘DI DAG GAL TE BDEN PAR GYUR NA,
Because just suppose that all these things were real, in the way that these infants imagine them to be.  If that were the case, then the following absurd statement would hold true:
BYIS PA DE DAG CHOS CAN,

PHUNG [f. 7b] PO’I DNGOS PO GTAN MED PAR PHYIS SKYE BA MI LEN PA’I RNAM PAR THAR PA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB PA’I BDAG NYID DU NYAN THOS SDE PA KHYOD RGYU MTSAN GANG GIS MI ‘DOD DE ‘DOD RIGS PAR THAL,

(2) It would then be alright to agree (and why—for what reason—would you followers of the listener group not agree) that these children were already people who had achieved freedom, or nirvana, where they would never again have to take rebirth—itself a state where nothing at all about them, their body or mind, was left!
MI ‘DOD PA LA RGYU CI ZHIG YOD DE, CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PA’I PHYIR TE, BDEN PA MTHONG BAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR,
(3) Because there’s not the single slightest reason why you wouldn’t agree—since, according to you, they would have already seen the truth!
DPER NA, DGRA BCOM PA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS NAS PHYIS MI SKYE BA BZHIN NO,,
(4) It would be like the case, for example, where an enemy destroyer had reached nirvana, and no longer took rebirth!
DE LTAR THAL BA LAS, BYIS PAS THAR PA MA THOB PA’I PHYIR, SNANG BA ‘DI DAG MI BDEN PAS, YOD PA’I MTHAR MA GRUB BO,,

And yet rather than things being the way this absurd statement proposes, the fact is that these infants have not achieved freedom.  The way that things appear to them is not real; and thus we can say that, in being the extreme of existence, the things that appear to them don’t even exist.
ZHANG THANG SAG PA ‘DI DAG KUN RDZOB SPYOD PAS RANG RGYUD DU MDZAD KYANG THAL LDOG GAM RANG GRAGS KYI GTAN TSIGS SO,,

Shang Tangsakpa takes this argument to be a case where the mind is exploring deceptive reality; and thus considers the reasoning here to constitute an “independent” type of logical statement.  In fact though this is the type of reasoning where absurdity blocks a mistaken idea; or, you could say, where the reason given is common knowledge to the person you’re talking to, themselves.
‘KHOR BA THOG MA MED PA NAS BDEN PA MTHONG NA, DE TZAM MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB PAR THAL BA ‘PHEN PA YIN GYI, MTHONG LAM NAS MYANG ‘DAS ‘JOG PA MIN TE ‘OG TU DPYOD DO,,

The idea being implied by this logical statement is that—if what normal people have been seeing for time with no beginning is real—then they would have to have achieved nirvana long since, with no more effort than that.  The statement here though is not meant to imply that anyone who has reached the path of seeing has thereby reached nirvana; we’ll look into this question more, further on.
LUNG LAS, BYIS PAS BDEN PA MTHONG BA LA GNOD BYED STON PA NI, DBANG PO DRUG BSTEN PA LA BRTEN GYIS, BRTAGS NAS TSAD MA MA YIN PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

When scriptures present arguments which call into question the idea that infants could have seen the truth, what they are saying is that any investigation that they’ve made into reality by using the method of relying upon their six senses is in fact not an accurate perception.
LUNG ‘DI DAG SHES BYED DU BYAS NAS, GNYIS SNANG GI BLO LA TSAD MA MIN PAS KHYAB PAR ‘DOD PO NI SMRA BA THAMS CAD RDZUN ZHES PA DANG CHOS MTSUNGS TE,

People who use scriptural references like this as proof for the idea that there is no state of mind involved in the discrepancy which is also an accurate perception are just the same as those who say that anything someone could ever say would be a falsehood.
DE LTAR GO BA’I RANG GI BLO TSAD MAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,
And that’s because they automatically assume that their understanding of these matters is an accurate perception!
DE MI ‘DOD NA, DE GNYIS LAS ‘THAD MI ‘THAD KYI KHYAD PAR JI LTAR ‘THAD DE, DES NA LUNG ‘DI DAG GIS NI DBANG PO DE KHO NA NYID DPYOD PA’I TSAD MA MIN TE,

And if these people didn’t assume that their understanding was an accurate perception, then how could they say that there was any difference between the validity of their own perceptions and the validity of the perceptions they are claiming are all invalid?
GZHAN DU ‘PHAGS LAM LA ‘BAD PA DON MED PAR THAL BA ‘PHANGS PA YIN GYI, DE ‘DRA MIN NA TSAD MA BZHI’I RNAM GZHAG BYED PA MI RIGS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And if their viewpoint were correct, then it would necessarily imply that it is meaningless to make any efforts in achieving the path of a realized being.  And if things weren’t this way, then the entire exercise of defining four types of accurate perception would itself be a mistake.
DA NI THAL ‘GYUR DANG RANG RGYUD DU SMRA BA’I DBU MA PA’I KHYAD PAR BSHAD PAR BYA STE,
At this point, I shall indulge in a slight digression, and explain the ideas which distinguish the Consequence group from the Independent group, amongst the proponents of the Middle Way School.
DE LA BSHAD PA’I RNAM GRANGS DANG ‘THAD PHYOGS [f. 8a] NGOS BZUNG BA’O,,
First I’ll enumerate the differences that are described, and then identify which of these are actually correct.
A list of ten proposed differences
Here is the first of these two steps: the concepts which the two groups discuss.  There are ten distinctions between the beliefs of these two—
SPYIR RANG RGYUD KYI DAM BCA’ KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(1) The first difference between the two groups concerns whether or not they accept, in general terms, the idea of an assertion which is “independent.”
DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(2) The next distinction is whether or not they accept the idea of an independent assertion within the context of examining the concept of suchness.
DNGOS PO STOBS ZHUGS KYI TSAD MA KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(3) Do they or do they not accept the idea of an accurate perception engendered by the very nature of an entity?
CHOS CAN LA MTHUN SNANG YOD MED DU SMRA BA DANG,
(4) Do they or do they not profess that the person who initiates an argument, and their opponent, can ever be perceiving the object under consideration in a compatible way?
RANG LUGS KYI KHAS LEN YOD MED DANG,
(5) Do they or do they not have a position which they themselves support?
YONGS GCOD KYI DAM BCA’ YOD MED DANG,
(6) Do they or do they not have a position which depends on exclusion?
RANG LUGS MI SGRUB PAR GZHAN GYI PHYOGS ‘GOG PA TZAM DU KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(7) Do they or do they not accept the idea of simply refuting an opponent’s position, without establishing ones own?
THAL ‘GYUR GYI DAM BCA’ TZAM YOD MED DANG,
(8) Do they or do they not even accept an assertion which is a logical proof based on demonstrating an absurdity?
SANGS RGYAS LA RANG RGYUD KYI YE SHES KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(9) Do they or do they not accept the idea that a Buddha can possess wisdom within their mindstream?
RANG RIG KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG BCU’O,,
(10) Do they or do they not accept the idea of apperception: the mind’s ability to perceive itself, within a single instant?
DE LA PHYI MA GNYIS NI, SBA BA LONG MED KYI DBU MA THAL RANG GI KHYAD ‘JOG PA DANG CHOS MTSUNGS SO,,

This brings us to the second point: identifying which of these distinctions are correct.  The final two of the ten distinctions listed are equivalent to the “hidden” and “insufficient time” distinctions sometimes made between the Consequence and Independent groups.
KHAS LEN YOD MED KYANG BEM RIG GI KHYAD DU ‘JOG NA MDZES PA TZAM MO,,
Saying there is some distinction between the two groups concerning matter & mind—whether or not they actually take different positions in this regard or not—is just window dressing.

DRUG PA DANG BDUN PA GNYIS KYANG MI ‘THAD DE, KUN RDZOB DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU YONGS GCOD KYI DAM BCA’ DANG, RANG LUGS THAL ‘GYUR BAS KYANG KHAS LEN LA, RIGS {%RIG} NGOR YONGS GCOD RANG RGYUD PAS KYANG KHAS MI LEN TE,

The sixth and seventh distinctions proposed here are also mistaken.  The idea of a position which depends on exclusion—when we are talking about an examination relating to deceptive reality—is something that members of the Consequence group would also say fits their own school; whereas not even the members of the Independent group would agree to the idea of this kind of exclusion presenting itself to the mind.

SLOB DPON CHEN PO LEGS LDAN ‘BYED KYIS, GZUGS KYI SKYE BA MED DO SNYAM DU DPYOD NA SHER PHYIN LA SPYOD KYI, GZUGS KYI SKYE BA MED PA YOD DO SNYAM NA SHER PHYIN LA MI SPYOD DE, RIGS {%RIG} NGOR SKYE BA ‘GOG PA YIN GYI, SKYE MED MI SGRUB PAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR, DES NA ‘THAD PHYOGS NI DANG PO LTAR YIN LA,

According to the great master Bhavaviveka, the mind is exploring the perfection of wisdom when we examine the concept that physical form never starts; whereas the mind is not exploring this perfection when we examine the concept that an absence of starting to physical form is something that itself exists.  This is because he has stated that—although this kind of starting is denied within the mind at this point—the absence of such starting is not itself established.  Therefore the position we would say is correct here would relate to the former.
DE YANG CHOS CAN LA MTHUN SNANG YOD MED YIN TE, RANG RGYUD KYI RTAGS YOD MED NI, MTHAR RGOL PHYI RGOL GYI MTHUN SNANG DU GZHI CHOS CAN GRUB MA GRUB LA RAG LAS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And as far as the question of whether the person who initiates an argument, and their opponent, can ever be perceiving the object under consideration in the same way, we would point out that—in the final analysis—the entire question of whether an “independent” proof exists or not itself depends on this question: of whether there even exists a basis of the argument—an object under consideration—which can appear in the same way to both the proponent and the opponent.
DNGOS PO STOBS ZHUGS ZHES PA YANG DNGOS PO RANG MTSAN PA KHAS LEN PA LA ZER NA YANG MI ‘THAD DE, SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN ‘BYED KYIS KYANG BKAG PA’I PHYIR,

Now in general we do use that expression, “logical conclusions engendered by the very nature of an entity,” and some people might claim that this implies that we accept an entity which exists in & of itself.  This though is mistaken—even Master Bhavaviveka would deny something like that.
THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA’I MTHUN [f. 8b] SNANG DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU MI RUNG LA, RIGS NGOR CHOS CAN MED PA SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN ‘BYED KYIS KYANG KHAS BLANGS PA’O ZHE NA,
One may then make another claim:

It’s incorrect to say that—in a case where we are investigating the suchness of things—the debaters in question could be seeing a thing in the same way, using nominal forms of accurate perception.  And even Master Bhavaviveka would agree that—to the minds of these thinkers—there was no object under consideration.
RANG RGYUD KYI RTAGS KHAS LEN PA DANG, RIGS NGOR CHOS CAN MED PAR ‘DOD PA LEGS LDAN ‘BYED KYI NANG ‘GAL DU ZLA BA GRAGS PAS MDZAD DE,

Master Chandrakirti points out that Master Bhavaviveka is contradicting himself when he accepts the idea of reasoning which is inherently effective, and then at the same time says that the subject under consideration here cannot be entertained by a state of mind acting in logical mode.

TSIG GSAL GYI STONG THUN DU ‘DIR SKYE BA BKAG PA BSGRUB BYA’I CHOS SU ‘DOD PA’I TSE DE KHO NAR RTEN CHOS CAN PHYIN CI LOG TZAM GYI BDAG GI DNGOS PO RNYED PA NYAMS PAR ‘GYUR BAR RTOG GE PA ‘DIS RANG NYID KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS SO,,
He expresses this point in his interlude on emptiness known as A Clarification of the Verses:

When we take the position here that denying the growth of things is the quality we seek to prove, then this logician has—on his own accord—accepted precisely, with nothing more than this, that the idea that the basis of the quality (the subject under consideration) can be perceived to be a self-existing entity, and thus simply mistaken, has been compromised.

MDO SDE PA DANG GRANGS CAN RTZOD PA NA, RTAG MI RTAG GANG GIS KYANG KHYAD PAR MA BYAS PA’I SGRA LA MTHUN SNANG YOD PA BZHIN DU, DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS POR SMRA BA LA YANG BDEN STONG GANG GIS KYANG KHYAD PAR MA BYAS PA’I SNANG TZAM LA MTHUN SNANG YOD PAS MTHUN SNANG MED PAR MA GRUB BO ZHE NA,
One may return with the following argument:

When a member of the Sutrist School debates a follower of the Numerist School, they both see the subject under consideration—sound—in the same way, without qualifying it in different ways, as being permanent or impermanent.  Similarly, when a member of the Middle Way School debates someone belonging to the Functionalist group, they see the subject under consideration in the same way—without qualifying it as existing in truth, or as being empty of true existence.  You are wrong, thus, when you say that the two parties cannot see such things in the same way.
‘DI’I LAN LA, KHA CIG TSIG GI CHA CUNG ZAD BZUNG NAS, DBU MA PA LA KHAS LEN MED PAS LAN ‘DEBS PA NI BDEN GNYIS KYI RNAM DBYE LA RMONGS PA YIN PAS DOR BAR BYA’O,,

In response to this argument, some people—grasping to bits of general expressions used to refer to those of the Middle Way—reply that the reason why the two parties do not see things in the same way is that members of this school are beyond taking any philosophical position at all.  This idea reflects a fundamental ignorance about the division of things into two realities, and as such should be discarded.
DES NA MDO SDE PA DANG DE GNYIS KA LA GANG GIS KYANG KHYAD PAR MA BYAS PA’I SGRA RANG MTSAN PA GNYIS KAS ‘DOD PAS MTHUN SNANG YOD LA, DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA GNYIS LA DE LTA BU MED DE,

As such, we can say that the Sutrist and the others in the example here can be seeing the subject under consideration in the same way—since both of them do accept the concept of sound which exists in & of itself, without any such distinction being made about it.  The case with the follower of the Middle Way and the Functionalist, however, wouldn’t be the same.
DBU MA PAS NI RANG MTSAN RTAGS KYI DGAG BYAR BYED LA, DNGOS POR SMRA BA NI RANG MTSAN BLO YUL DU MA SHAR BA’I GZUGS SOGS KYI THUN MONG MIN PA’I NGO BO BLO YUL DU MI ‘CHAR BAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR,

And that’s because the member of the Middle Way School would say that a thing which existed in & of itself is precisely what we seek to deny with the reasoning we present; whereas the Functionalist would say that an object which existed in & of itself could never appear to the mind without there being some kind of unique essence of form or the rest appearing to the mind.

DES NA RANG MTSAN DANG DES STONG PA GNYIS KA BLO YUL DU SHAR BA LA MA BLTOS PA’I GZUGS SOGS TZAM BLO YUL DU ‘CHAR BA DBU MA PAS KYANG BDEN PA GNYIS KAR DU MI ‘DOD, DNGOS POR SMRA BAS KYANG MI ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR,

As such, the member of the Middle Way would never accept—with regard to either of the two realities—the idea of form or the like appearing to the mind in a general format which did not depend on both the thing in & of itself, and the emptiness of such a thing, appearing to the mind.  Neither would the Functionalist accept this.

SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PA DANG PHYOGS GLANG GNYIS [f. 9a] KA RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS YIN NA TSUL SGRUB BYED KYI TSAD MA’I RTZA BA BLOS SGRO MA BTAGS PAR YOD PA’I DE KHO NA NYID ‘DZIN PA LA RAG LAS PAR BZHED PA GNYIS KA MTHUN KYANG, ZLA BA GRAGS PAS DE LTA BU MI SRID PA’I PHYIR, RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS MI BZHED PA YIN NO,,

Master Chandrakirti and Master Dignaga are the same in asserting that—if something were an independently effective syllogism—then the very root of the accurate perception which confirmed its three necessary elements is that it would have to depend on a perception of suchness that existed without any false elaboration by the mind.  Chandrakirti though would say that such a thing was impossible; and for this reason would deny the idea of an independently effective syllogism.
KHA CIG DBU MA PA YIN NA RANG GI RGYUD KYI RJES SU DPAG PA BYA BAR MI RIGS ZHES PA’I TSIG LA BRTEN NAS DBU MA RANG RGYUD PAS DBU MA PA’I GO MI CHOD PAR ‘DOD PA NI MI RIGS TE,

Some thinkers say that the followers of the Independent group of the Middle Way School don’t even qualify as members of this school; they take this position because of that reference from scripture where it says “If somebody were a member of the Middle Way School, they would never try to draw conclusions by using arguments that were independently effective.”
DE NI RANG RGYUD MI RIGS PAR BSTAN GYI, DBU MA PA DANG, RANG RGYUD KHAS LEN PA ‘GAL BAR STON PA NI MA YIN TE,

What this line is expressing though is simply that the idea of an independently effective syllogism is mistaken; it is not meant to say that it’s a contradiction for someone to be a follower of the Middle Way School and at the same time accept this form of reasoning.
DGE SLONG CHANG ‘THUNG MI RIGS PAR BSTAN PAS, CHANG SDOM PA’I GTONG RGYUR ‘GYUR BA NI MA YIN NO,,
The scriptures teach, for example, that it is a mistake for a monk to drink alcohol; but it’s not the case that a monk who drinks alcohol thereby relinquishes their vows altogether.
DES NI DNGOS PO BDEN PAR KHAS BLANGS PAS SO ZHE NA,
Someone may respond to this with—
But the person who accepts this form of logic cannot belong to the Middle Way!  Because they are, in effect, accepting the idea that a functional thing can exist in truth!
DE LTA NA GRANGS CAN PA SANGS RGYAS PAR THAL, PHUNG PO BDAG MED DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,
Well, if you look at it that way, then maybe we should say that the Numerists are Buddhists!
Because they take the position that parts of a person have no self-nature.
DE MA GRUB CES ZER NA DE YANG MA GRUB BO, ,DNGOS PO RIGS PAS GRUB PAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR CE NA,
The debater might come back with:
So if you say my point isn’t proven for that first reason, here’s another!
They can’t be followers of the Middle Way, because they accept the idea of logic that can engender an accurate perception by the very nature of an entity.
DES KYANG PHUNG PO BYAS PAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR, BYAS PA YIN NA BDAG MED YIN PAS KHYAB KYANG BYAS PA KHAS BLANGS PA LA BDAG MED KHAS BLANGS PAS MA KHYAB PO ZHE NA,

Are you saying this about Numerists because they agree that the parts of a person are made, and if anything is made it cannot possess a self-nature?  But isn’t it true that someone can agree that a thing is made, and not agree that it lacks any nature of its own?
DE NI ‘DIR YANG MTSUNGS PAS DNGOS PO BDEN PA BA KHAS MA BLANGS SHING THAMS CAD BDEN MED DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR, DBU MA PA MA YIN PAR GA LA ‘GYUR,

Our answer is that the case here is just the same.  How could you deny that a person belonged to the Middle Way School when they refuse the idea of a working thing that could exist in truth—and accept the idea that there’s nothing at all that could exist in truth?
DE SKAD SMRA BA DE NI KHYAB BYA KHAS BLANGS NA KHYAB BYED KHAS BLANGS DGOS PA DANG, BLANGS PA’I KHYAD PAR MA PHYED PAR ZAD PAS,

Saying this kind of thing reflects a failure to distinguish between (1) the fact that—if you agree to an individual case—you should agree to the principle that governs all such cases; and (2) the fact that someone has actually agreed to a case.  It’s as simple as that.
GRUB MTHA’ SMRA BA THAMS CAD ‘CHOL BAR ‘GYUR TE, DON SMRA GNYIS KYIS KYANG BYAS PA THAMS CAD BDEN MED SGYU MA LTA BUR KHAS BLANGS [f. 9b] PAR ‘GYUR TE, RTEN ‘BREL DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,

And if you continue with this line of thinking, then you’re going to make a jumble of all the schools of philosophy there are.  We’d have to say, for example, that the two schools which accept the existence of outer objects also accept that nothing in the world which is made could exist in truth—that they also accept that all made things exist in the manner of an illusion; all because they already accept the concept of dependence.
things don’t exist the way they appear

Which brings us to the second step in our presentation of the reasoning that we use to  refute the extreme view that things could exist the way they appear.  This is where we cover incidental points on this topic.
How those who have not overcome
GNYIS SU LTA BAS MI GROL BAR BSTAN PA DANG, GNYIS MED RTOGS PAS GROL BAR BSTAN PA’O,, DANG PO NI,

These incidental points themselves come in two parts: demonstrating that a person can never reach liberation as long as there is still a discrepancy between what they see and what’s really there; and then demonstrating that—when a person comes to a realization where there is no longer any such discrepancy—they can then reach liberation.  The first of these is expressed in the following lines of Arya Nagarjuna’s root text:
,YOD PAS RNAM PAR MI GROL TE,

DNGOS PO LA RANG BZHIN YOD PAR BLTA BAS KYANG SRID PA ‘KHOR BA LAS RNAM PAR MI GROL TE, DE NI TSE RABS KUN TU BDE ‘GRO’I ‘BRAS BU DANG TSOR BA BDE BA’I ‘BRAS BU CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR {%,?} LAS ‘BRAS MED PAR BLTA BAS KYANG SRID PA ‘KHOR BA ‘DI LAS GROL BAR ‘GYUR BA MIN TE, NYES PA THAMS CAD KYI ‘BYUNG GNAS SU GYUR PA NGAN ‘GRO’I ‘BRAS BU DANG TSOR BA SDUG BSNGAL GYI ‘BRAS BU CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR,

And when we do look at things as if they existed through some nature of their own, we can never reach liberation from this existence—this cycle of pain.  The only results that they can lead us to are higher rebirths in all our lives to come; and sensations of pleasure.  And yet when, on the other hand, we look at these things as if the law of actions and their consequences didn’t exist, we can never escape from this same cycle of pain, this existence.  And that’s because this viewpoint is the source of every problem we could ever have: the results it brings us are a birth in the realms of misery, and sensations of pain.
DES NA LTA BA ‘DI GNYIS NI ‘KHOR BA’I RGYU YIN PAS MI GTZANG BAS MI GTZANG BA DAG PAR MI ‘GYUR BA BZHIN DU GROL BAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,
As such, these two views are the very cause of the cycle of pain.  Trying to use them to free ourselves from this cycle is like trying to use a pile of feces to clean a pile of feces off the floor.
As the String of Jewels puts it,
Travel to higher births of pain;
Travel to lower births of pain.

This brings us to our second point from above: demonstrating that—when a person comes to a realization where there is no longer any such discrepancy between what they see and what’s really there—they can then reach liberation.
,DNGOS DANG DNGOS MED YONGS SHES PAS,
,BDAG NYID CHEN PO RNAM PAR GROL,
Things and the absence of things.
GAL TE LTA BA DE GNYIS KYIS MI GROL NA GANG GIS GROL BAR ‘GYUR ZHE NA, YOD MED DNGOS ‘GAL YIN PAS DE LTA NA GROL BA MI SRID SNYAM DU BSAM PA’O,,

So you say that a person cannot achieve liberation through either one of those viewpoints.  And yet existing and not existing are opposites that cover every possibility—if neither one holds true, then wouldn’t liberation be an impossibility?
DNGOS PO LA MA BRTEN PAR DNGOS PO MED PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, DNGOS PO GZHAN DU GYUR PA’I BZHIG PA LA DNGOS MED DU ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR,

When we say though that people “should not rely upon things,” we are not saying that no thing exists at all.  Because what we refer to here as “the absence of things” is the destruction left over when a thing changes into something else.
DNGOS MED LA MA BRTEN PAR DNGOS PO MI ‘GRUB STE, DNGOS MIN MA BKAG PAR DNGOS PO MI ‘GRUB PA’I PHYIR,

And it’s not that when we say “people should not rely upon the absence of things” that things come to exist.  Because you cannot say a thing exists without blocking the possibility that it was something that couldn’t exist.

DES NA DNGOS PO DANG DNGOS PO MED PA GNYIS PHAN TSUN BLTOS PAS RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID DU MNGON SUM DU YONGS SU SHES PAS DMIGS PA MED PA’I YE [f. 10a] SHES KYI RTEN YIN PAS NA BDAG NYID CHEN PO ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS RNAM PAR GROL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As such, we can say that things and the absence of things rely upon each other.  Thus they are empty of any nature of their own; and when we understand this fully, that is the basis of the wisdom which no longer sees anything existing independently.  And when they possess this basis, then “great beings”—which is a reference to realized beings—achieve liberation.
RIN PHRENG DU, GNYIS LA MI BRTEN THAR PAR ‘GYUR ZHES PA’I DON TO,,
This is the point that the String of Precious Jewels is making when it continues with:
in favor of the two extreme views
GNYIS PA LA, MTHA’ GNYIS KYI SGRUB BYED DGAG PA LA LUNG GI SGRUB BYED MI ‘THAD PA DANG, DE DAG LA MYANG ‘DAS MI ‘THAD PA’O,,

This brings us to our second major topic from above—refuting arguments in favor of the two extreme views.  We’ll proceed in two steps: demonstrating how it is incorrect to say that there are scriptural references which support these two views; and then showing how nirvana could never be correct if these two views are.
DANG PO LA, BYIS PA LA MA NGES PA DANG, ‘PHAGS PA LA BSTAN PA MA GRUB PA’O,,

As far as the first step, we will again cover the point in two parts: showing that these arguments lead to indefinite conclusions when presented to an infant, and then showing that they fail altogether when presented to a realized being.

DANG PO NI, DNGOS PO DANG DNGOS MED YOD DE, ‘KHOR BA DANG MYANG ‘DAS YOD PA’I PHYIR, KHYAB PA YOD DE, NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA’I DNGOS PO ‘KHOR BA YIN LA, DE RGYUN CHAD PA’I DNGOS MED MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA YIN PAS ‘KHOR ‘DAS MED PAR YANG MA GRUB STE, DE MED NA BLANG DOR BYA BA’I PHYIR STON PAR MI RIGS PA LA, BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR CE NA,
Here is the first.  Now someone may come and make the following argument:
Things and the absence of things do indeed exist,
Because the cycle of pain, and nirvana, do exist.
And the one does follow from the other,

Because “things”—as represented by the five parts to a person that we’ve taken on—are the cycle of pain; whereas “the absence of things”—as represented by the discontinuation of these parts—is nirvana.  And as such, you cannot say that neither the cycle, nor nirvana, exists.
For if they did not exist, then it would be incorrect to teach about them, in order that disciples could reach the one and abandon the other—whereas Lord Buddha did describe them.
‘PHAGS PA LA BSTAN PA’I PHYIR ZER NA MA GRUB STE,
Now suppose you continue this argument with:
Because he described them to realized beings.
In that case, we would have to say, “We disagree.”
‘PHAGS PAR MA GYUR PA ‘PHAGS PAR ‘GYUR BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR TU DE GNYIS BSTAN DGOS,  DE GNYIS STON PA LA DE’I GONG DU ‘PHAGS PA DGOS PAS PHAN TSUN BRTAN PA’I PHYIR RANG BZHIN MED PAR GRUB PO,,

And that’s because Lord Buddha would have had to teach about these two in order to make realized beings out of people who were not realized beings.  And to teach the two, there would have had to be realized beings before he taught them.  These two prerequisites being interdependent in fact proves that these things can have no nature of their own.
BYIS PA LA BSTAN NA KHYAB PA MA NGES TE,
And if you say that these arguments were presented to infants, then we’d have to say that the arguments were inconclusive.  As the next lines of the root text put it:
Nirvāṇaṃ caiva lokaṃ ca manyante’tattva darśinaḥ…
Nirvanan chaiva lokan cha manyantetattva darshinah…
To see the way things are
DE KHO NA NYID MA MTHONG BA’I BYIS PA RNAMS NI, ‘JIG RTEN ‘KHOR BA RANG MTSAN PA SPANG BYA DANG, DE RGYUN CHAD PA’I MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA BLANGS BYAR RLOM SEMS SHING MNGON PAR ZHEN TE,

Let’s consider “those who have yet to see the way things really are”—that is, let’s consider the infants.  These people have delusions—and strong beliefs—about the world, meaning the cycle of life, as being a thing in & of itself that we must eliminate within ourselves.  And they have the same type of thoughts about the discontinuation of this world: about nirvana, as a thing which exists in & of itself, and which we need to attain, inside of us.
DE’I PHYIR ‘KHOR BA TZAM LA ‘DOR ‘DOD SKYES PA NA YANG ‘KHOR BA RANG MTSAN PA MED PAR BSTAN PA YID LA ‘BAB CING
