As such, even beginning to feel that we want to abandon the cycle itself requires that we feel comfortable with teachings that Lord Buddha gave where he said that there was no such thing as a cycle of pain that could exist in & of itself.
DE MED NA DE RGYUN CHAD PA’I MYANG ‘DAS KYANG MED PAR RTOGS NUS PAS ‘KHOR BA RANG [f. 10b] BZHIN MED PA NYID MYANG ‘DAS SU RTOGS NUS PAS

If we come to understand that there is no such cycle, then we’ll be able to realize that there is no nirvana either, where we shut off this kind of cycle—and then we’ll be able to realize, as well, that the very fact that the cycle of pain has no nature of its own is nirvana.
BYIS PA LA BSTAN YANG DRANG DON DU GSUNGS PAS KHYAB PA MA NGES SO ZHES PA’O,,

As such, even when Lord Buddha did make to infants the statements you describe, he was only speaking figuratively.  And so we can say that the arguments you make based on these statements are inconclusive.
DNGOS PO LA MNGON PAR ZHEN PA ‘GA’ SHIG {%ZHIG} GI ZHEN PA LDOG PA’I DON DU BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS ‘KHOR ‘DAS RANG MTSAN PA GZHAN NGO KHO NAR ZHAL GYIS BZHES NAS GSUNGS PA YIN NO,,

The fact is that Lord Buddha did talk about a cycle of pain, and a nirvana where we escape it, in a way where these two seemed to exist in & of themselves; he did this in order to overcome the feelings of certain students who had a strong belief that things existed in this way.  He was accepting such terms only in the perceptions of those to whom he was giving these teachings.
GANG DAG MDO SDE LAS GANG ZAG DANG CHOS BDAG MA GSUNGS SO ZHES SMRA BA PO DE DAG GIS NI SANGS RGYAS KYI GSUNG LA SGRA JI BZHIN PA’I KHYAB PA KHAS LEN DGOS PA YIN NO,,

Those who make the assertion that “Lord Buddha never spoke about the lack of a self-nature to people, or a lack of a self-nature to things, in his sutras” have to take teachings that he gave—such as these—as being literal.
GNYIS PA LA ‘PHAGS PAS MA GZIGS PA DANG, DE’I ‘THAD PA GNYIS SO,,

This brings us to the part where we show that arguments based on these statements in scripture fail altogether, when presented to a realized being.  First we describe how none of these things is seen by a realized being; and then secondly how this is in fact correct.
The first point is presented in the following lines of the root text:
Naiva lokaṃ na nirvāṇaṃ manyante tattva darśinaḥ.
Naiva lokan na nirvanam manyante tattva darshinah.
DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS NI ‘JIG RTEN SPANG BYA DANG MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA BLANG BYAR RLOM SEMS SHING ZHEN PA MED LA RTOG PAR MI MDZAD DO,,

Let’s consider realized beings: those people who are directly seeing suchness—the way things really are.  They have no delusions about what is the world—what is to be abandoned; or what is nirvana—what we need to achieve.  That is, they have no belief in these things as having their own nature: they are not entertaining these kinds of deluded ideas about the cycle & nirvana.
DE DAG ‘PHAGS PA LA BSTAN PA MA YIN NA, ‘PHAGS PA’I BDEN PA JI LTAR ‘GYUR ZHE NA,
One may return with the following question:

If the Buddha’s statements about the cycle of pain and the nirvana where we escape from it were not directed at these higher, realized beings, then why do we refer to the four truths as the four “higher” truths—a reference to these same beings?
SKYON MED DE, GANG ZHIG RTOGS NA ‘PHAGS PAR ‘GYUR BAS NA ‘PHAGS PAR BYED PA’I BDEN PA ‘PHAGS PA’I BDEN PA’AM YANG NA ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS BSTAN PA’I BDEN PA ‘PHAGS PA’I BDEN PA YIN GYI,

But there’s no such problem.  We call the four truths the four “higher” truths because they are truths that make you into one of these higher, realized beings: they are what you have to realize to become such a being.  We can also say they are “higher” truths because they are taught by these higher, realized ones.
DE LTA MA YIN PAR ‘PHAGS PA KHO NA LA GRUB NA ‘PHAGS PA’I THA SNYAD BRGYAD KYANG MI RIGS PAR ‘GYUR LA, ‘JIG RTEN NA YANG JI LTAR BSTAN PA LTAR GNAS PA LA ‘PHAGS PA’I THA SNYAD DU GRAGS SO,,

If this were not the case—and if something were spoken of as “higher” only if it had been seen to be true by these higher, realized beings—then there would be no such thing as the eight higher expressions; and the expression “high words” would never be used in the everyday world to refer to words which described things in the way they truly were.
SDUG BSNGAL YANG MI RTAG SOGS JI LTAR ‘PHAGS PAS BSTAN PA DE LTA DE LTAR GNAS KYI, GTZANG BDE SOGS SU KUN RDZOB TU MI GNAS SO,,

The truth of suffering moreover does indeed exist as realized beings describe it in the aspects of impermanence and so on; whereas supposed aspects such as being clean or happiness do not exist even in a deceptive way.
DE LTAR YANG ‘GREL PAR, DE LA PHYIN CI LOG NI BDE [f. 11a] BA LA SOGS PA NYID DU ‘DZIN PA GANG YIN PA DE KUN RDZOB TU YANG BDAG NYID DER DNGOS PO DE RNAM PAR MI GNAS PA NYID KYI PHYIR RO,,
It is to this point that the commentary states:

And that is true because those things which comprise the complete opposites that people hold to—that things could actually be happiness or the like—do not exist even in a deceptive way as composites of these supposed qualities.
PHYIN CI MA LOG PA NI SDUG BSNGAL BA LA SOGS PA NYID DU ‘DZIN PA STE, DNGOS PO DE KUN RDZOB TU BDAG NYID DER YOD PA NYID KYI PHYIR RO ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

Not holding to things in an entirely mistaken way then would be considering those things to be—as they really are—painful and the rest.  And that’s because things really do exist, at least in a deceptive way, as composites of these other qualities.
‘DIS NI GANG DAG ‘KHRUL NGOR YOD PA KUN RDZOB TU YOD PA’I DON LDOG TU BYAS SHING SGRA BSHAD ‘JUG GIS KHYAD MA PHYED PAR KUN RDZOB TU YOD NA YOD ‘GAL DU ‘DOD PA’I NGAN RTOG KYANG BSAL BA YIN TE,

This also serves to dispel the deluded idea where people believe that it is a contradiction to say that something can exist in a deceptive way and yet still exist.  This idea itself stems from the belief that an object existing to the senses of a mistaken perception is what it means to exist in a deceptive way; and reflects a failure to distinguish between the explanation of a term and its apparent application.
DE LTA NA GTZANG BDE RTAG BDAG KYANG KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR THAL, ‘KHRUL NGOR YOD PA’I PHYIR RTAGS KHYAB KHAS BLANGS, ‘DOD NA LUNG ‘DIS BSAL LO,,
As such, we would present you with the statement—
Are you saying that things being clean, pleasant, permanent, and themselves is something that exists in a deceptive way?
Because they do exist to the senses of a mistaken perception.
But the one doesn’t prove the other.
And yet you have already accepted that it does.
Well then, I accept your statement.
But you can’t accept it, for it is disproven by the citation we have just presented to you.
that the realized do not see
Here is the second part, where we describe how it is in fact correct to say that none of the things we’ve been discussing is seen by a realized being.
Nirvāṇaṃ ca bhavaś caiva dvayam etan na vidyate
Nirvanan cha bhavash chaiva dvayam etan na vidyate
And the nirvana where we go beyond it—
Are not things that could exist.

‘KHOR BA DANG MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB NA ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG GIS GZIGS PAR RIGS NA YANG SRID PA DANG MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA GNYIS PO ‘DI NI RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN PA’I PHYIR GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DE RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN PA GZIGS PA NI DE KHO NA GZIGS PA MA YIN TE, RAB RIB CAN LA SOGS PAS KYANG DE KHO NA NYID MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Now even suppose that it was correct to say that—if the cycle of pain, and the nirvana where we escape this cycle, existed in & of themselves—then they could be perceived by a realized being during that deep meditation upon ultimate reality.

The fact though is that these two—the life of suffering and the nirvana where we go beyond it—are not things that could exist through any nature of their own.  As such, they are similar to the reflection of something that we see in a mirror.
To see then that they are not things which exist through any nature of their own is not to see that they exist in & of themselves.

And that’s true because a person who thought they saw something there—but only because they had a serious problem with cataracts—would then have to be a person who was seeing the way things really are.
GNYIS PO DE DAG LA MYANG ‘DAS MI ‘THAD PA LA RANG GI MYANG ‘DAS NGOS BZUNG BAS GZHAN LA MYANG ‘DAS ‘THOB PA MI ‘THAD PA DANG, RANG LA ‘THAD PA’O,,

We will now cover why—of the two we just mentioned, the cycle and escape from it—the particular escape or nirvana described is incorrect.  To do this, we’ll first identify what nirvana is, according to our own viewpoint; use this to describe why achieving nirvana the way those others describe it must be incorrect; and then cover why nirvana as we describe it would be correct.
DANG PO LA MDOR BSTAN DANG, RGYAS BSHAD DO,,
We’ll convey the first point in a brief presentation, followed by a more detailed explanation.
DANG PO NI, MYANG ‘DAS ZHES BYA BA CI YANG YOD PA MA YIN NA ‘PHAGS PAS MYANG ‘DAS THOB PAR RNAM PAR BZHAG PA DE NYID JI LTAR ‘GYUR ZHE NA,
As for the first of those, someone may begin with the following question:
If what we call “nirvana” is actually nothing at all, then how is it that you would describe the process of attaining it?
,SRID PA YONGS SU SHES PA NYID,
,MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS {%NGAN ‘DAS} ZHES BYA [f. 11b] BAR BRJOD,
SRID PA RANG BZHIN MED PAR MNGON SUM DU YONGS SU SHES PA NYID LA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB CES BYA BAR BRJOD PA YIN PAS THA SNYAD DU MED PA MA GRUB CING DON DAM DU KHYAB PA MA GRUB BO,,

When we have understood, completely (or directly) that the cycle of existence has no nature of its own—then that itself is what we call achieving nirvana, or going beyond all grief.  As such, we can say that nirvana is something that cannot be established as not existing in a nominal sense; and then neither is it something that must then exist in an ultimate sense.
Here secondly is the more expanded explanation of our own beliefs on nirvana.
,DNGOS PO BYUNG BA BZHIG PA LA,
,DE BZHIN DAM PA RNAMS KYIS KYANG,
DNGOS PO MI RTAG PA NI RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA MED KYI, DNGOS PO SNGAR BYUNG ZHING SKYES PA BZHIG PA LA JI LTAR ‘GOG PA STE MI RTAG PAR RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA

The fact that functional things are changing is not something that exists in & of itself; rather, the way in which a functional entity occurred in the past—started—and then later ends, or comes to a stop, is an event that we label a “changing nature.”
BZHIN DU MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS KYANG RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA MED KYI, ‘KHOR BA RANG BZHIN MED PA MYANG ‘DAS YIN PAS DE BLO YUL DU ‘CHAR BA ‘KHOR BA BLO YUL DU ‘CHAR BA LA BLTOS PA’I PHYIR,

In the same way, achieving nirvana—going beyond grief—is not something that could exist in & of itself; rather, that fact that the cycle of pain has no nature of its own is itself nirvana.  As such, forming a mental image of nirvana is something that relies upon forming a mental image of the cycle.
DPE DE BZHIN DU ‘PHAGS PA DAM PA RNAMS KYIS KYANG SGYU MA BYAS PA LTA BU’I PHUNG PO SKYE MED KYI ‘GOG PA BZHED DO,,

In the same way as with the example just described, the holy ones—which is to say, realized beings—also take the position that parts of a person (which resemble something created by a magician) are a kind of stopping, in the sense of never having started.
‘DI NGOS BZUNG BA NI, RANG BZHIN MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA YIN LA, LAM GYIS THOB PA’I MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA GLO BUR DRI BRAL GYI ‘GOG PA YIN NO,,

Just to confirm the identification here, we are referring at this point to what we call an innate or “natural” nirvana.  When we reach nirvana through practicing the path, that is a stopping or cessation which is an “adventitious”—a manufactured—freedom from impurities.

MTHONG LAM THOB NAS MYANG ‘DAS THOB PAR ‘DZOG PA YANG ‘GREL PA ‘DI’I LUGS SU MI GSAL TE, MDO LAS, BDAG GI SKYE BA NI ZAD DO, ,BYA BA NI BYAS SO ZHES PA NI YANG DGRA BCOM GYI SKABS KHO NAR SNANG BA’I PHYIR DANG,

This commentary by the way is not attempting to present reaching the path of seeing as the point at which we complete the attainment of nirvana.  When sutra mentions expressions such as “My rebirths are finally ended; I have done all I needed to do,” we see those descriptions only with reference to the point where one has reached the state of an enemy destroyer.
GAL TE CHOS SHES MJUG THOGS SU ZHES SOGS KYI ‘GREL PA’I {%BA’I} RDZOGS MTSAMS SU RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I DON DE MTSAN NYID GCIG PA JI LTA BA BZHIN

Remember the verse which includes the line, “If, after the knowledge of things”; this is explained as meaning that the import of things occurring in dependence—considered in its final form—is “that one definitive thing”: the way things really are.

MTHONG BA DE NYID RIM GYIS GOMS PAR BYAS PAS MA RIG PA MA LUS PAR ‘GAGS PAS RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I RANG BZHIN LA DMIGS PA’I YE SHES LA GNAS PA NI MTHONG BA’I CHOS LA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA [f. 12a] DANG BYA BA BYAS PA NYID DU RNAM PAR BZHAG GI ,RNAM PA GZHAN DU NI MA YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

What’s being said thus is that, first we see this truth; and then, in stages, we habituate ourselves to it.  This process then puts a stop to each & every form of misunderstanding how things really are.  And then we are residing in the wisdom where we see the nature of things: how they occur in dependence.  This is what we refer to as “nirvana in the nature of what we have seen,” or having done all that we need to do; we are not however speaking of something else.

DE MA RIG PA MA LUS PAR ‘GAG PA DGRA BCOM PA’I GNAS SKABS MA YIN PA LA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR, ‘JUG PAR ‘JIG LTA RGYUN ZHUGS KYIS SPONG BAR BSHAD PAS NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA MTHONG LAM NAS ZAD PAR SPANGS SO SNYAM NA,
The following thought may occur to some of our readers—

What you have described cannot be possible in any situation except at the point where one has become an enemy destroyer.  As such, when it states in Entering the Middle Way that one who has entered the stream has eliminated the view of destruction, what it’s saying is that we have eliminated, in its entirety, misunderstanding related to negative thoughts, when we reach the path of seeing.
SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PAS DBU MA PHUNG PO LNGA PAR THA SNYAD PHAL CHER MNGON PA SDE BDUN DANG MTHUN PAR MDZAD PAS ‘JIG LTA LA MTHONG SPANGS KYIS KHYAB TU CHUG KYANG

Master Chandrakirti, in his work on the Middle Way entitled The Five Heaps, utilizes wording which is for the most part in keeping with the Seven Works on Higher Knowledge.  We can thus allow that the view of destruction might be considered, in this context, to invariably be something eliminated by the path of seeing.
DER SGOM SPANG GIS BSDUS PA’I NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR ZHAR LA NYAN THOS ‘PHAGS PAS CHOS KYI BDAG MED RTOGS KYANG SHES SGRIB MA SPANGS PAR ‘DOD PA ‘DI YANG DPYAD PAR BYA STE,

We do though see there mention of a form of misunderstanding, involved with negative emotions, which is included into those problems which are eliminated by the path of habituation.  This would imply a belief that realized beings on the listener track do perceive the lack of a self-nature to things, but have not yet eliminated obstacles to knowledge—which is something we would have to look into further.

THEG CHEN MTHONG SPANGS KYIS BSDUS PA’I SHES SGRIB DE DAG CHOS KYI GNAS LUGS MNGON SUM GYIS GSAR DU RTOGS TZAM GYIS SPONG NGAM, ‘ON TE GOMS PAR BYED DGOS PHYI MA MI RIGS TE, SGOM SPANGS SU ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR, DANG PO LTAR NA, NYAN THOS ‘PHAGS PAS MA SPANGS PA NYAMS SO,,

That is, a question arises of whether obstacles to knowledge taken in by problems eliminated, on the greater way, by the path of seeing are eliminated simply through the direct perception of the way that things exist; or, rather, is a process required here where we habituate ourselves to the realization.  The latter position would though have to be mistaken, since these obstacles would then have to be problems eliminated by the path of habituation.  And the former position would call into question the position that realized beings on the listener track had not eliminated the obstacles.
GNYIS PA GZHAN GYI {%GYI LUGS} LA MYANG ‘DAS ‘THOB PA MI ‘THAD PA LA, MDOR BSTAN PA DANG, RGYAS BSHAD DO, ,DANG PO NI,

With this, we have reached our second point from above, which is why achieving nirvana the way that others describe it must be incorrect.  We will cover this point in a summary presentation, and then an expanded explanation.  Here is the first.
,‘DUS BYAS YONGS SU SHES PAS MIN,
It is not when we reach
PHYED DANG POS THAL BA BKOD NAS PHYED PHYI MAS LHAG MED MI ‘THAD PA DANG, LHAG BCAS MI ‘THAD PA GNYIS KYIS GSAL BA STON PA’O,,

The first half of this verse presents the absurd consequence of the opponent’s position; whereas the second half presents the resulting position of our statement of consequence by indicating that the opponent’s idea on nirvana without remainder is incorrect; and that their idea on nirvana with remainder is incorrect as well.
PHUNG PO MA LUS PA RNAM PAR ‘JIG CING ZAD PA LAS LHAG MED KYI ‘GOG PA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PAR ‘GYUR BAR THAL,
Are you saying then that a cessation where the parts to the person have been completely destroyed and finished represents nirvana without remainder?
PHUNG PO YOD KYANG NYON [f. 12b] MONGS ZAD PA LHAG BCAS SU THAL,
And are you saying that the cessation where we still possess the parts to a person—but where the negative emotions have been finished off—represents nirvana where something still remains?
LAS NYON MONGS RANG MTSAN PA’I RGYU RKYEN ZAD PAS PHUNG PO SLAR MI SKYE BAS MYANG ‘DAS SU ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR,

Because, according to you, nirvana consists of that point where the parts to a person can no longer arise, since their causes & conditions have been finished off; that is, causes & conditions which, according to you, consist of karma and negative emotions that exist in & of themselves.
‘DUS BYAS RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE MED DU YONGS SU SHES PAS MYANG ‘DAS SU ‘GYUR BA MIN PAR THAL,
And isn’t it necessarily the case that it does not represent nirvana when we reach the total knowledge of how produced objects cannot arise through some nature of their own?
For the same reason as before.
PHYI MA SHIN TU ‘DOD PAS DE LA LHAG BCAS MI ‘THAD PA’I THAL BA ‘PHEN PA YIN NO,,
Where the opponent would agree to the latter enthusiastically, a new absurd consequence arises where it could not be correct to say that that was a nirvana where something was left over.

‘DOD PA’I PHYIR SKYON MED CE NA, LHAG MED KYI MYANG ‘DAS DE NI SU LA MNGON SUM DU ‘GYUR TE, MNGON SUM DU BYED PA PO MI ‘THAD PAS, NGAS MYANG ‘DAS MNGON SUM DU BYAS SO ZHES PA’I THA SNYAD MI ‘THAD PAR THAL LO,,

And suppose you say that there is no problem, since you agree.  But then who is it that brings about this nirvana where nothing is left over?  It would be incorrect to say that anyone did bring it about.  Because it would be incorrect to say that the sentence even existed: “Oh! I have brought about my nirvana!”
LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS NA NI PHUNG PO MA LUS PA ‘GAG PA MED PAS MNGON DU BYA RGYU MED PA’I PHYIR BYED PA MI ‘THAD,

If we are talking about the point at which something is still left over, then it is not the case that each & every part of the person has been stopped.  And in that case it would be incorrect to say that there was nothing still to be brought about.
LHAG MED KYI GNAS SKABS NA BYED PA PO MI ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR SU LA YANG MNGON DU MI ‘GYUR RO,,

Since at the point where we have reached nirvana with nothing left over it would be incorrect to say that there was any longer someone doing the achieving, then there would be no one at all who was bringing the nirvana about.
KHO BO CAG LA NYES PA MED DE, ‘PHAGS PA SH’A RI’I BU LA SOGS PAS RANG BZHIN SKYE MED KYI ‘GOG PA DE MNGON SUM DU BYAS PA’I PHYIR,
With our own position though, there are no such problems; this is because we say that people like Shariputra brought about a cessation with a nature of never starting.
GZHAN YANG ‘GOG PA MNGON SUM DU MI ‘THAD DE, DGAG GZHI PHUNG PO MNGON SUM DU RTOGS NAS ‘GOG PA SHUGS LA RTOGS PAR MI ‘THAD DE, GNAS SKABS DER PHUNG PO KHYOD MI ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR,

And anyway there would be a problem with referring to a cessation as being brought about, or manifested; since it would be incorrect to speak about the parts of a person—the very thing that we had ceased—as being perceived manifestly, even as we were (by implication) perceiving their cessation.  And that in turn is because you in any case would disagree to there being any parts to the person present at that point.
DNGOS SU RTOGS PAR MI ‘THAD DE, MNGON SUM GYI SHES PA RANG MTSAN GYI DNGOS YUL CAN DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Direct perception in this case would be incorrect, since you assert that direct knowledge is something which requires an object of perception which is an actual manifestation, as opposed to a concept.

THAL BA PHYI MA LA BSAL BA STON PA NI, LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS NA, BDAG GIR {%GI} SKYE BA ZAD CING BZHIG GO SNYAM PA’I SHES PA GANG YIN PA DE YANG JI LTAR ‘GYUR TE MI RUNG BAR THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA’I PHYIR,

Let’s move on to presenting the position resulting from our latter statement of an absurd consequence.  How then—at the point where we reach a nirvana where something is still left over—could one think to themselves, “I have put an end to my rebirths; I have destroyed them”?  Wouldn’t that be illogical?  Because don’t those births occur in & of themselves?
And if you agree to the idea, then you contradict sutra.
DBU MA PA SKABS DER YANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE MED DU KHAS LEN PAS, MDO DANG ‘GAL BA MED DO,,
Those of us who belong to the Middle Way assert that—at that point as well—nothing can start in & of itself.  And so we do not contradict sutra.
[f. 13a] BZHIG CES PA DE JI LTA BU ZHES PA’I ‘GYUR LTAR NA, MDO’I TSIG SNA LA BZUNG NGO,,

One may ask where we got the unusual spelling for the Tibetan translation of the word “destroyed” here.  We are following what we believe to be the original translation of Arya Nagarjuna’s verse at this point.
GNYIS PA LA, LHAG BCAS MI ‘THAD PA DANG, LHAG MED MI ‘THAD PA GNYIS,

This brings us to our second point from above, which is a more expanded explanation of why achieving nirvana the way that those others describe it must be incorrect.  We cover this in two parts: explaining why their description of nirvana where something is still left over is incorrect; and then explaining why their description of nirvana where nothing is left over is incorrect.
DANG PO NI SKYE BA ZAD DO ZHES PA NI, MA ‘ONGS PA’I SKYE BAR NYING MTSAMS MI SBYOR BA LA DGONGS PA YIN GYI, DA LTAR GYI PHUNG PO MI SKYE BA LA BRJOD PA MA YIN NO ZHE NA,
Now suppose, on the first point, that someone says—

When they say here that “our births are finished,” what they have in mind is cases where we cross the line into a new birth in the future; they are not referring to some manner in which the present parts to ourselves fail to arise.
DE LTA YIN NA, GNAS SKABS DE NA LHAG BCAS KYANG MI ‘THAD DE,
And yet if that were the case, it would also be incorrect to say that we could achieve nirvana with something left over, at that point.  As the root text puts it—
If the parts to a person
Then even if we had finished off
MDO LAS, SDUG BSNGAL ‘DI MA LUS PAR SPANGS ZHES DA LTAR GYI PHUNG PO MI SKYE BA LA BSAMS NAS MA LUS PAR SPANGS PA NAS NUB PA’I BAR DU GSUNGS LA,

Sutra though makes that statement that “this suffering has been eliminated, in its entirety” with reference to the way in which the present parts to ourselves do not arise.  And thus we see statements about “having eliminated everything, on up to the time we reach the final end.”
MA ‘ONGS PA’I SKYE BA’I DBANG DU MDZAD NAS ‘DI LAS SRID PA GZHAN MI SHES SO ZHES GSUNGS PAS, MA ‘ONGS PA’I PHUNG PO KHO NA LA SKYE BA ZAD PA’I SGRA SBYOR BAR MI ‘THAD DO,,

And then we see the statement that “they will see no other existences,” with reference to future rebirths.  As such, it is incorrect to interpret the words “our births are finished” as referring only to the future parts to ourselves.
GAL TE DE YI TSE PHUNG PO RANG MTSAN PA MA ‘GAGS PAR YOD NA NYON MONGS ZAD PAR SPANGS KYANG MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB PAR MI ‘GYUR TE,

If it were the case that—at that point—there were parts to a person that existed in & of themselves and had yet to be stopped, then even if we had finished off the last of our negative emotions, we would still not have attained nirvana: “going beyond grief.”
And that’s because we see statements like the following:
LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS MYANG ‘DAS MTSAN NYID PA MIN PAR ‘DOD NA BDAG GI SKYE BA ZAD DO ZHES SOGS KYIS
,MNGON DU BYAS NAS BSHAD PA YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS PA ‘DI JI LTAR DRANG,

If you hold the position that—at the point where we still have something remaining—we cannot yet have attained a genuine form of nirvana, then how can we refer to the following lines when we say things like “our births are finished”?
SH’A RI’I BUS, RANG NYID KYIS MYANG ‘DAS MNGON DU BYAS NAS GROGS PO GZHAN LA RJES SU BZLAS PA BSHAD PAS SO,,
That is, Shariputra himself said that he had repeated this sutra to other friends, after he himself had brought about his own nirvana.
DE NI NYON MONGS LOG PA MNGON DU BYAS KYI, PHUNG PO LOG PA MA YIN NO ZHE NA,
Shariputra was here only referring to the fact that he had brought about a state where he had stopped all his negative emotions; he was not saying that he had stopped all the parts to himself.
MI ‘THAD DE, RJES BZLAS KYI MDO LAS, SDUG BSNGAL [f. 13b] ‘DI SPANGS PA ZHES GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, SKABS ‘DIR SPYI MING BYE BRAG LA SBYOR BA YANG MI ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR,

And yet that is not the case, for the Sutra Repeated After itself has a line that says “I had eliminated all this suffering”; and it would further be incorrect to say that this refers only to a case where the general term is used to apply but to a specific instance.

RJES BZLAS KYI MDO LAS, JI SKAD BSHAD, ‘DI NYID LA ‘GREL PA ‘DIR GSAL GYI, SNGAR ‘PHAGS PA LA RTA THUL GYIS SMRAS PA’I SHO LO KA DE LA YE MI GSAL BA’I PHYIR DANG, DE DUS SH’A RI’I BUS MTHONG LAM THOB PA YIN GYI, MYANG ‘DAS NI PHYIS KUN TU RGYU SEN RINGS LA STON PAS CHOS GSUNGS PA’I DUS SU THOB PAR BSHAD PA’I PHYIR YANG LHAG BCAS KYI MYANG ‘DAS MTHONG LAM NAS ‘DZIN PAR MI GSAL LO,,

It is clear from the commentary that “the words themselves were stated” in the Sutra Repeated After.  We have no such clarity about what was said—in those lines we quoted earlier—by the realized one to Ashvajit.  Moreover, at that point Shariputra had only attained the path of seeing; it is explained that he achieved nirvana later, at the point where the Teacher was teaching the Dharma to the wandering ascetic named Dirghanaka.  It is not though clearly indicated here that we are to consider nirvana with something remaining as something that starts from the path of seeing.
Here secondly is our explanation of why the other thinkers’ description of nirvana where nothing is left over is incorrect.
Have come to a stop for them
GANG GI TSE ‘DI NI PHUNG PO DE’ANG ‘GAGS PAR GYUR PA DE’I TSE NA GROL BA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB PAR ‘GYUR BA ZHIG TU ‘DOD NA YANG,
Now suppose someone asserts that an individual has attained liberation—meaning nirvana—when those parts to a person as well have come to a stop for them here in this life.

PHUNG PO MA ‘ONGS PA RNAMS RGYUN BCAD PA DE YANG KHYED KYI LUGS LA MI SRID DE, LHAG BCAS KYI DUS NA PHUNG PO RANG MTSAN PA YOD PAS DER ‘DZIN YOD LA, DES NYON MONGS DANG LAS BSKYED NAS YANG PHUNG PO LEN PA’I PHYIR,

Even if this is your position, in your own system it would be impossible to say that the flow of future parts to a person had been cut off.  And that’s because parts to a person which exist in & of themselves would still exist at the point of nirvana where something was left over; and then the person would hold to them.  Due to this, the person would still give rise to karma and to negative emotions; and thus they would again take on the parts to a person.
MA ‘ONGS PA’I SKYE BA LA BLTOS NAS KYANG BZHIG, SHES PA DE JI LTAR ‘GYUR TE MI RUNG NGO,,
Even with reference to a future birth, things would have been destroyed; and so how could any awareness arise anyway?  It would be wrong to say it did.
GSUM PA RANG LA ‘THAD PA LA ‘DUS BYAS ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG GIS MI GZIGS PA’I RGYU MTSAN DANG, DE NYID GOMS PA BYA BA BYAS SO ZHES PA’I THA SNYAD KYI YUL DU BSTAN PA’O,,

This brings us to the third section we promised above, which is an explanation of why nirvana as we describe it would be correct.  We proceed in two parts: explaining the reason why produced things cannot be seen by a realized being in their deep meditation upon emptiness; and demonstrating how accustoming oneself to the true nature of things is what the expression “they have done what they had to do” refers to.
DANG PO NI, DE LTAR DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BA LA GROL BA MI SRID PAR BSTAN NAS STONG PA NYID DU SMRA BA LA SRID PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR,

Here is the first.  The following verse then is for the purpose of demonstrating how liberation is not something which is possible where one is asserting that functional things do have a nature of their own; and how it is possible where we are asserting that these things are empty—
Utpādo vā nirodho vā na kaścid upalabhyate.
Utpado va nirodho va na kashchid upalabhyate.
,MA RIG RKYEN CAN BYUNG BA LA,
,YANG DAG YE SHES KYIS GZIGS NA,

‘DU BYED LA SOGS PA BCU GCIG LA MA RIG PA DNGOS PO DANG RGYUD CI RIGS PAR RKYEN DU YOD PAS NA MA RIG [f. 14a] RKYEN CAN TE DE LAS BYUNG BA LA YANG DAG PA’I ‘PHAGS PA’I YE SHES KYIS GZIGS PA’I NGO NA ‘DUS BYAS THOG MAR SKYE BA DANG MTHAR ‘GAG PA YANG RUNG STE SPROS PA ‘GA’ YANG DMIGS PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

Fresh karma and the rest of the eleven links have misunderstanding as the factor that gives rise to them, either directly or indirectly.  As such, we can refer to them as “having misunderstanding as their factor,” or as the thing which they have come from.  And yet the fact is that neither the initial arising of a produced thing, nor its eventual stopping—these examples of a mental construction—can ever be something that presents itself as something to be seen by the pure wisdom of a realized being.
DE NI ‘DU BYED LA SOGS PA NI MA RIG PAS BRTAGS PA YIN PAS BLO ‘KHRUL PA LA SNANG GI ,‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG GIS GZIGS PA LA MA YIN TE,

What this means is that fresh karma and the rest of those links—as things which are only imputed to exist by misunderstanding—are something that makes its appearance to a mistaken state of mind.  It is not something that presents itself to the sight of a realized being who is in that deep meditation upon emptiness.
RAB RIB CAN LA SNANG BA DE, RAB RIB MED PAS BLTAS NA MI SNANG BA BZHIN NO,,

It’s similar to where something appears to exist to the vision of a person who has a serious problem with cataracts; when someone without cataracts looks in the same direction, they don’t see the thing in question at all.
GANG DAG ‘PHAGS PA’I YE SHES KYIS YOD PAR MA GZIGS PA DANG, YOD PA MA YIN PAR GZIGS PA GCIG TU ‘KHRUL NAS

Now it is possible that a person might misunderstand the difference between something which the wisdom of a realized being does not see as existing, and something which this wisdom sees does not exist—thinking that the two amount to the same thing.
RTEN ‘BREL YOD PA MA YIN TE, ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG GIS MA GZIGS PA’I PHYIR, CES SMRA BA NI

And then they might say something like “Dependence is not something that could ever exist, since it is not something which is ever seen by a realized being in the state of deep meditation upon emptiness.”
DBU MA PA’I LTA BA ‘DI YANG DAG PA YIN TE, BLUN POS MA GO BA’I PHYIR CES PA DANG MTSUNGS SO,,
This would be the equivalent of saying something like “The viewpoints of those who follow the Middle Way School are perfectly correct, since they are misunderstood by fools.”
LTA BA YANG DAG YIN NA BLUN POS GO BAR ‘GAL LO ZHE NA,
If a viewpoint is really pure, then wouldn’t it be a contradiction to say that a fool understood it?
RTEN ‘BREL YOD NA YANG MNYAM GZHAG GIS GZIGS GA LA DGOS, RANG BZHIN YIN NA GZIGS DGOS PA YIN GYI BLTOS CHOS YIN NA DES GZIGS PAR ‘GAL BA’I PHYIR,

Why would we have to say that—if something existed in dependence—it would have to be seen while a person is in that deep meditation?  If something were the nature of things, then it would have to be seen; but if it were something that relied on something else, it would be a contradiction to say that it was seen.
RIGS PA LTAR SNANG ‘DI LTA BU LA BRTEN NAS DBU MA PA LA KHAS LEN MED CES ZER NA KHO BOS KYANG RNAM RIG PA LA KHAS LAN MED CES SMRA BAR BYA’O, ,DES DNGOS PO RANG MTSAN KHAS BLANGS PAS SO ZHE NA,

People have used faulty logic like that to make the claim that followers of the Middle Way take no position at all; our reply is to assert that it is the Mentalists who take no position.  And that’s because they agree to the idea that functional things have an existence in & of themselves.
DBU MA PAS KYANG RTEN ‘BREL KHAS BLANGS SO,,
The fact though is that those of the Middle Way accept the idea of dependence.
DE ‘KHRUL NGO KHO NAR KHAS LEN GYI, RANG LUGS LA YOD PA MA YIN TE, BLO MA ‘KHRUL PA ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG YIN PAS DES MA GZIGS PAS SO ZHE NA,

But they accept dependence as something that can make its appearance only to a mistaken state of mind; in their own system then, dependence is something that has no existence.  And that’s because it cannot be observed by a truly unmistaken state of mind: the deep meditation of a realized being.
‘O NA RNAM RIG PA LA YANG LKOG GYUR RANG MTSAN YOD PA MA YIN PAR THAL, BLO MA ‘KHRUL BA MNGON SUM YIN PAS DES MA GZIGS PA’I PHYIR,

Well then, the Mentalists must say that an abstruse object which exists in & of itself is not something that could ever exist; for direct perception is the unmistaken state of mind, and abstruse objects cannot be observed by this type of perception.
LKOG GYUR YOD KYANG [f. 14b] MNGON SUM GYIS MI ‘JAL ZHE NA, SNGA MA LA YANG MTSUNGS SO,,
One may reply with the claim, “Abstruse objects do in fact exist, but they are never something that is considered by a direct perception.”  This amounts to the same thing as the previous idea.
‘DOD NA LKOG GYUR KHEGS PAS KHYAB BYA BDAG MED KHEGS PAR ‘GYUR LA, DES MA KHYAB PA MI SRID PAS SHES BYA MTHA’ DAG KHEGS PAS GANG YANG KHAS BLANG DU MED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And if you agree to that position, then you are denying the existence of abstruse objects.  Which then means that you are denying the existence of the fact that nothing is itself, since this fact is itself one of the abstruse objects in the world.  And since there is nothing in the world that they do not subsume, you would be denying the existence of the entirety of all knowable things.  And then, if you think about it, you would be left with nothing that you could ever accept.
refers to the true nature of things
GNYIS PA LA, DNGOS DANG, RTOGS BYA CHOS DBYINGS LA RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA MED PAR BSTAN PA, GZHAN GYIS BRTAGS PA BYA BA BYAS PA’I THA SNYAD KYI YUL DU MI RUNG BA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

This brings us to the second part here: demonstrating how accustoming oneself to the true nature of things is what the expression “they have done what they had to do” refers to.  We cover this in three sections: (1) the actual demonstration; (2) showing how that thing which we realize—the realm of all things—cannot be possessed of dissimilarities; and (3) explaining how what others imagine cannot be what the expression “they have done what they had to do” refers to.  The first section starts with the following verse of the root text:
Dṛṣṭe dharme ca nirvāṇaṃ kṛta kṛtyaṃ tad eva ca.
Dirshte dharme cha nirvanan kirta kirtyan tad eva cha.
,DE NYID MTHONG CHOS MYA NGAN LAS,
,‘DAS SHING BYA BA BYAS PA’ANG YIN,
It also means that we have
Done what we had to do.

RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I SKYE BA DANG ‘GAG PA MI DMIGS PA’I LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS DE NYID MTHONG BA’I CHOS TSE ‘DI NYID LA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA THOB PA DANG NYON MONGS PA SPONG BA SOGS KYIS BYA BA BYAS PA’ANG YIN NO,,

Let’s consider that point in time where we have achieved nirvana in which we still have something left over—a state where we cannot perceive things starting & stopping, in dependence.  That in itself is the achievement of nirvana as something “seen”: meaning something we experience in this present life.  It also represents, for example, the elimination of things involved with negative emotions.  And with this, we have “done what we had to do,” as well.
‘ANG GI SGRA NI BYA BA BYAS PA’I MJUG THOGS SU BYUNG BA’I SKYE BA ZAD PA SOGS SDUD DO,,
The word “also” here in the root text subsumes other items which occur subsequent to doing what we had to do, such as finishing off our future rebirths.

‘GREL PAR ‘PHAGS PA SH’A RI’I BUS MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA MNGON SUM DU BYAS NAS MDO ‘DI BSHAD DO ZHES GANG GSUNGS PA ‘DI NYID MTHONG BA’I CHOS LA MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PAR RIGS PAR BYA LA, GANG YANG SKYE BA ZAD DO ZHES SOGS BSHAD DO,,

Remember how it is stated, in the commentary, that “Shariputra explained this sutra once he had brought about his own nirvana.”  This statement is something which we have to understand as referring to the state of nirvana occurring as something he saw in this very life.  And only then do they speak of a state where we have finished off our births.
‘DIS KYANG RJES BZLAS KYI MDO GANG YIN SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR GSAL LO,,
This then clarifies the reference we saw earlier from the Sutra Repeated After.
Which brings us to our second section, where we show that thing which we realize—the realm of all things—cannot be possessed of dissimilarities.
,GAL TE CHOS SHES MJUG THOGS SU,
,‘DI LA BYE BRAG YOD NA NI,
,DNGOS PO SHIN TU PHRA BA LA’ANG,
,GANG GIS SKYE BAR RNAM BRTAGS PA,
,RNAM PAR MI MKHAS DE YIS NI,
,RKYEN LAS BYUNG BA’I DON MA MTHONG,
Those who truly have no wisdom—
For things to arise from factors.
GAL TE MTHONG LAM SDUG BSNGAL LA CHOS BZOD DES CHOS TE, RTEN ‘BREL GYI GNAS LUGS STONG PA NYID MNGON SUM DU SHES PAS DE’I MJUG THOGS SU RTOGS BYA CHOS DBYINGS LA RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA MED DE,

Suppose then that through the path of seeing—specifically, through the mastery of things relating to the truth of suffering—we perceive, directly, emptiness: the ultimate manner in which dependence exists.  Subsequent to this point, the way of all things which is what we realize exhibits no differentiations.
GAL TE YE SHES PHYI MA ‘DI LA MI RTAG [f. 15a] PA RANG MTSAN PA SOGS DON DAM BDEN PA RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA SO SOR BYE BRAG TU YONGS SU BCAD PAR BYA BA YOD NA NI

And suppose that—for this subsequent state of wisdom—there were some sort of differentiation going on, between different individual details, various aspects, of ultimate reality: an aspect of impermanence that existed in & of itself, or any of the rest.

DNGOS PO SHIN TU PHRA BA RTEN ‘BYUNG GI GNAS LUGS LA’ANG NYAN THOS SDE PA GANG GIS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BAR RNAM PAR BRTAGS SHING KHAS BLANGS NA RAGS PA SA LA SOGS PA LA LTA SMOS KYANG CI DGOS,

If those who belong to the listener group were to imagine, or accept, that even extremely subtle entities such as the true nature of dependence have, through some nature of their own, a starting point; then there’s no need to mention how they’d think about more coarse entities such as the element of earth, or the like.
DES NA GRUB MTHA’ ‘DZIN PA’I NYAN THOS RNAM PAR MI MKHAS PA DE DAG CHOS CAN,
As such, let us consider those who truly have no wisdom: those listeners who hold to that particular school of thought.
KHYED LTAR NA MTHONG LAM PA DE YIS NI RKYEN LAS BYUNG BA’I DON RTEN ‘BYUNG SPROS BRAL RO GCIG PA DE MA MTHONG BAR THAL,

Isn’t it true that—according to them—this person on the path of seeing would have failed to see what it means for things to arise from factors, this “single taste” of how things that arise in dependence are free of all mental elaborations of self-existence?
CHOS NYID LA RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BAR SO SO RIM CAN DU BCAD DU YOD PA’I PHYIR,
Because isn’t it the case that they would have separated ultimate reality into different aspects, one by one?
DES NA RTEN ‘BYUNG GI CHOS NYID STONG PA NYID RANG BZHIN MED PA DE LA RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA’I DBYE BA MED PAS BDEN PA MNGON PAR RTOGS PA NI SKAD CIG MA GCIG TU ZAD DO,,

As such we can say that there are no different aspects to the real nature of things that occur in dependence; to their emptiness, to their lack of any nature of their own.  And we can say then, in turn, that the realization of the truth is completed, in essence, in a single second of time.
‘O NA SKAD CIG MA BCU DRUG TU BZHAG PA JI LTA BU ZHE NA,
With this, someone may pose the following question:
If that’s the case, then what about that presentation of sixteen different seconds of time?
DE NI LDOG PA’I SGO NAS BZHAG PA YIN TE, BDEN PA DE DANG DE’I STONG NYID RTOGS PA DE’I CHA NAS SDUG BSNGAL SHES PA DANG KUN ‘BYUNG SHES PA SOGS DANG, DE DAG KYANG SHES BZOD DU LDOG PAS ‘BYED PA’O,,

These sixteen though are established as the opposites of absences; we speak of  things like “knowing suffering” and “knowing the source of suffering” from the viewpoint of grasping the emptiness of whichever one of the four truths involved.  And these are further divided into stages of knowing and mastery, again by a process of double negation.
DE LTA BU’I THA SNYAD MI BZHED PA YANG MA YIN TE, SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PAS DBU MA PHUNG PO LNGA PAR BSHAD PA’I PHYIR,
And it’s not as if our school does not accept this type of terminology; we see explanations of it in Master Chandrakirti’s Five Heaps.
NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD KHA CIG LAS SKAD CIG MA GCIG TU BSTAN LA, GZHAN LAS SKAD CIG MA BCO LNGAR BSTAN PA MI ‘GAL TE,
And it is no contradiction that we see some collections of the scriptures of the listeners which present this process as occurring in a single instant, while others describe it as fifteen seconds.
RGYUD LA BSKYED RIM DANG SPROS PA LA DGA’ BA’I NGOR THA SNYAD SNA TSOGS KYIS BSTAN PA TZAM DU ZAD PA’I PHYIR,

These relate to how these realizations are triggered in a stream of moments of consciousness, and are also simply meant to satisfy the predilections of those students who are attracted to more detail, by giving them more terms to work with.
GAL TE DE LTA NA BDEN PA BZHI LA DMIGS NAS RNAM PA MI RTAG SOGS BCU DRUG GI RNAM PA CAN DU BSHAD PA JI LTA BU ZHE NA,
If that is the case, then what about the explanation that we focus upon the four different truths in sixteen different aspects, such as impermanence and the rest?
DE DAG NI TSOGS SBYOR GYI GNAS SKABS SU BSGOM PAR BYA BA RGYUD SMIN PAR BYED PA’I LAM TZAM YIN GYI, GROL LAM MA YIN TE, DE LA NGES PAR CHOS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS DGOS PA’I PHYIR,

Those are simply references to what we meditate upon at the point of the paths of accumulation and preparation; as paths to mature our mindstream.  They do not constitute the path of liberation, for that state of mind must invariably realize how things have no nature of their own.
THOS CHUNG GANG DAG BYAMS CHOS SU YANG NYAN THOS [f. 15b] LA YANG CHOS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA YOD PAR BSTAN TO ZHES SMRA BA
Now there are those of little learning who say that even the Five Books of Maitreya teach that there are listeners who realize how things have no nature of their own.
DE DAG NI SHING RTA CHEN PO RNAMS KYI GZHUNG LUGS RGYA MTSO LTA BU’I RNAM DBYE LA ‘DRIS SHING MKHAS PAR MA BYAS PA’I GZU LUMS ‘BA’ ZHIG YIN TE,

This though is just a tale concocted by some persons who have failed to familiarize themselves with, and master, all the details within the scriptural tradition of the great innovators—a tradition which is as vast as the sea.

BYAMS CHOS RJES ‘BRANGS DANG BCAS PA’I GZHUNG GANG DU YANG GROL BA TZAM DANG THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA’I LAM GNYIS SU BYAS PA’I GROL LAM DU MI RTAG SOGS RNAM PA BCU DRUG ‘BA’ ZHIG BSTAN GYI, RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS DGOS PA GANG YANG MA BSTAN PA’I PHYIR DANG,

And that’s because—in the major classics of the Five Books of Maitreya, and in the works that follow them—the sixteen aspects of impermanence and so on are taught only with the path of liberation, where a division is made between the two paths of simple liberation and omniscience.  There is no indication there at all that one must realize how nothing has any nature of its own.
KLU SGRUB YAB SRAS KYI DGONGS PA DPAL LDAN ZLA BA GRAGS PAS BKRAL BA’I GZHUNG RNAMS SU DE DAG RGYUD SMIN BYED KYI LAM TZAM DU GSUNGS KYI, GROL LAM DU GANG DU YANG MA GSUNGS PAS

As for the thinking of Arya Nagarjuna and his spiritual son, the great books in which the glorious Chandrakirti makes his commentary refer to those sixteen only as paths which function to ripen our mental stream; he says nothing about them being paths of liberation.
CHEN PO DE DAG GI LUGS LEGS PAR DKRUGS NAS BSHAD PAS DAM PA’I CHOS LEGS PAR SPANGS PA’I LAS KYI SGRIB PA BSAGS PA YIN NO,,

And so all those other thinkers are doing here is taking the systems of these great beings and perfectly confusing all of them; they are working hard to stock up for themselves those unique mental obstacles that are created by the karma of abandoning the holy Dharma.
GSUM PA LA GZHAN PHYOGS NYES PA DANG BCAS PA DANG, RANG PHYOGS LA NYES PA MED PA’O,,

With this we have reached our third section from above: explaining how what others imagine cannot be what the expression “they have done what they had to do” refers to.  We proceed in two steps: demonstrating how the position that others take here has problems with it; and then showing how our own position is free of any such faults.
DANG PO LA THOG MA YOD PAR THAL BA DANG, ‘DOD PA LA BSAL BA DGOD PA’O,,
The first step itself will come in two parts: presenting an explanation of why there would have to be beginning; and then presenting a necessary consequence of that thinking.
The first of these is presented in the next verse of the root text:
,NYON MONGS ZAD PA’I DGE SLONG GI
,DE’I RTZOM RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS KYIS,
,GANG MA BSHAD PA RGYU CI ZHIG
If they have put a final stop to
,GAL TE YE SHES KYIS NYON MONGS PA ZAD PAR BYAS PA’I DON DAM PA’I DGE SLONG GI NYON MONGS PA ZAD PAS
Suppose we have an “ultimate monastic” who has managed to use their wisdom to eliminate within themselves everything related to the negative emotions.
LAS MA BSAGS PA DE’I DBANG GIS GAL TE ‘KHOR BA PHUNG PO RANG MTSAN PA ‘JUG RUNG DU SONG NAS LDOG CING ZAD PAR KHYOD SEMS NA THA MA YOD PAR THAL LA,

If—due to the fact that they were no longer collecting karma—they have put a final stop to, or finished, the cycle of pain (in the sense of still being able to enter into parts of a person that existed definitively), then it would have to be the case that their mind had a final end to it.
DE ‘DOD NA THA MA THOG MA LA BLTOS PAS ‘KHOR BA DE’I THOG MA’I RTZOM PA YOD NA
And if you agree to that idea, then since endings rely on beginnings, there would have to be an outset or first beginning to that cycle of suffering.

GSUNGS DGOS PAS RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS THOG MA GANG MA BSHAD PA LA RGYU CI ZHIG YOD DE MI MKHYEN PAS MIN TE, KUN MKHYEN DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR, MI STON PA’I RGYU GZHAN YANG MED PAS MED PA KHO NAS MA BSTAN PAR RIGS SO,,

And if there were such a beginning, it would have to have been described in scripture.  Why then haven’t the totally enlightened ones ever mentioned any such start to things?  It’s not as if they wouldn’t have known about it!  You do agree that a Buddha is omniscient, don’t you?  And so—since there would be no other compelling reason for them not to speak about it—then logically we would have to say that they didn’t describe such a first beginning simply because there is no such thing!
Which brings us to the second point, about that necessary consequence.
,[f. 16a] RTZOM PA YOD NA NGES PAR YANG,
,YANG NA NYES NYID DU ZHES GDON NO,
You could also read the second half of this verse as “You would be wrapped in certain error.”
GAL TE THOG MA’I RTZOM PA YOD PAR THAL BA ‘DOD DO ZHE NA,
Now suppose that someone comes and says,
You say that there would have to be an outset or first beginning to things; what if I agree that there is?
DE LTA NA NGES PAR YANG DE’I SNGON DU GZHAN MA SONG BAS RGYU MED PA DANG CHAD PAR BLTA BAR GYUR PA YONGS SU ‘DZIN CING KHAS LEN DGOS PA NYID DU ‘GYUR RO,,

If you were to agree to that, then most certainly there could not have been anything that happened before that.  And then you would be wrapped in one of those views which says that things can happen without a cause; or that things in general can have simply discontinued.  Which is to say, there is no way you could avoid the necessity of accepting such ideas.
GNYIS PA RANG PHYOGS LA NYES PA MED PA LA RTEN ‘BYUNG MTHA’ BRAL DU BSTAN PA DANG, RANG BZHIN YOD NA RTAG PAR THAL BA DANG, RANG BZHIN MED PA’I DPE BSTAN PA’O,,

Which brings us to our second step from above—showing how our own position is free of any such faults.  We cover this in three points: (1) demonstrating that dependence is free of all extremes; (2) showing how—if things did have a nature of their own—then they would have to be unchanging; and (3) presenting an example of something which has no nature of its own.
The first of these is covered in the following verse—
,DE LA SNGON DANG THA MA CI,

RTEN ‘BREL SMRA BA LA NYES PA ‘DI MED DE DNGOS PO BLTOS CHOS SU SMRA BA DE LTAR NA, RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR GANG ‘BYUNG BA, DE LA NI RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES PA’I PHYIR SNGON THOG MA DANG THA MA CI LTAR ‘GYUR TE, GANG YANG KHAS BLANG MI DGOS SO,,

Those of us who profess the principle of dependence incur no such faults.  According to those who assert that entities exist in reliance, anything which occurs in a dependent relationship cannot have started through any nature of its own.  And how could such entities then ever have any first beginning, or final end?  In our system, we avoid having to accept either extreme.
Which brings us to that second point, of showing how—if things did have a nature of their own—then they would have to be unchanging.
,SNGON SKYES PA NI JI LTAR NA,
They could come to a stop?
‘DI NI DE KHO NA LTAR NGES PAR KHAS BLANG DGOS TE, GZHAN DU NA THOG MA YOD PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU MA ZAD RTAG PAR YANG ‘GYUR TE,
We must certainly come to accept then that these points are as we made them above; otherwise, things would not only have a first beginning, they would also have to be unchanging.
‘DI LTAR, GAL TE SNGON RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYES PA NI RGYU MTSAN JI LTAR PHYI NAS SLAR YANG LDOG PAR ‘GYUR BAR RTAG PAR THAL, RANG BZHIN GZHAN DU ‘GYUR BA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR,

Which is to say, if things had—earlier on—come to a start through some nature of their own, then how—for what reason—could we say that, later on, they could ever come to a stop?  They would have to be unchanging, because it would be impossible for their nature ever to waver.
GSUM PA LA, DPE’I SGO NAS MDOR BSTAN PA DANG, DNGOS BSHAD PA DANG, DON BSHAD PA’O,,

Which brings us to that third part—presenting an example of something which has no nature of its own.  This we cover, with our example, in three steps: a brief introduction; the actual point; and then a clarification of what the example refers to.
,DE LA SNGON DANG THA MA CI,
,RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES PA’I PHYIR,
As for the first, we have in effect already explained this point in lines above—
It cannot have started through any nature of its own.
,SNGON DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ BRAL BA,
,‘GRO BA SGYU MA BZHIN DU SNANG,

RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES PAS SNGON DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ DANG BRAL BA SKAD CIG KYANG MI SDOD PAR ‘GRO BAS ‘GRO BA RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA ‘DI DAG SGYU MA BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN MED BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SNANG [f. 16b] ZHING BSLU BAR BYED PA’I BDAG NYID CAN NO,,

Since beings do not start through any nature of their own, we can say that they are without any first beginning or final ending; which is to say, they continue on without pausing even for a second.  And that means that these beings—occurring as they do in a dependent relationship—are entities which are like a magical illusion: even though they have no nature of their own, they appear to.  And thus they deceive us.
SGYU MA SHES PAS SGYU MA’I RTA GLANG SOGS LA SNGON MTHA’ DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ RTOGS {%RTOG?} PAR MI RIGS PA BZHIN DU ‘DI LA YANG MI RIGS SO,,

It would be inappropriate—once we realize that they are actually a magical illusion—to think that a magical horse or cow or the like had a first beginning or a final end; and it would be just as wrong here in our current case.
Which brings us to the actual point:
,SGYU MA SHES PA DER MI RMONGS,
,SGYU MA MI SHES YONGS SU SRED,
Are free then of that ignorance.
RKANG PA DANG PO GSUM RNAL ‘BYOR PA MKHAS PA’I DPE, BZHI PA NI, BYIS PA’I DPE’O,,

The first three lines [in the Tibetan translation, or the first section in the English] present our example as it is perceived by a wise one: a deep practitioner.  And then the fourth line [second section in the English] presents the example as seen by an infant.
LTAD MO MI MKHAS PA’I RANG BZHIN CAN DAG SGYU MA’I NA CHUNG DE DAG LA SHA KHRAG DANG BCAS PA’I NA CHUNG DU ZHEN NA DUS GANG GI TSE NA CHUNG ‘DI DAG BYUNG ZHING SKYES PAR GYUR,

Onlookers who possess a nature of not being wise ones look at the image of a young maiden which is actually an illusion, and take it to be a real, flesh-and-blood maiden.  When that happens, maidens like this have “come up,” or started.
GANG GI TSE RNAM PAR ‘JIG CING ‘CHI BAR ‘GYUR SNYAM DU MNGON PAR ZHEN PA DE BZHIN DU
When they think of her reaching her final destruction—death—they have extreme attachment.

SGYU MA’I RANG BZHIN SHES PA’I SKYES BU DAG SGYU MA MTHONG BA’I SKABS DER DE LTAR MI RMONGS SHING MNGON PAR MI ZHEN LA, SGYU MA’I RANG BZHIN MI SHES PA’I LTAD MO BDAG YONGS SU SRED CING ZHEN PAR BYED DO,,

Just so, those people who understand the illusory self-nature see the illusion.  Then—at moments like those—they are free of that ignorance, and do not have extreme attachment.  Those spectators who don’t understand that the self-nature is an illusion will be filled with clinging; that is, they become attached.
Here third is our clarification of what the example refers to—
,DNGOS PO {%Tengy=SRID PA} SMIG RGYU DANG ‘DRA BAR,
,BLO YIS MTHONG BAR GYUR BA NI,
PHYED DANG POS GNAS LUGS RTOGS PA’I BLO DANG PHYED PHYI MAS PHAN YON BSTAN TO,,
The first portion of this verse presents the state of mind which realizes the way things really are; and the second portion presents its benefits.

RNAL ‘BYOR PA DNGOS PO ‘DUS BYAS MA LUS PA SGYU MA DANG SMIG RGYU DANG ‘DRA BAR BLO MNYAM GZHAG SO SOR RANG RIG PA’I YE SHES KYIS MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BAR GYUR PA SNGON GYI MTHAR BLTA BA’AM PHYI MA’I MTHAR BLTA BA’I BRTAG {%RTAG} CHAD KYI LTA BAS RGYUD YONGS SU SMIN CING ZIN PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

Deep practitioners have used their mind—that wisdom which comprehends the various objects in their deep meditation—to see, directly, that all entities (meaning here produced things) are like an illusion, or like a mirage in the desert.  As such, their mindstreams are free of any corruption, in the form of being influenced by seeing some first beginning or seeing some final end to things.  Which is to say, their minds are free of the viewpoints that things are unchanging, or that they have stopped altogether.
MNYAM GZHAG GI RTOGS BYA DE NYID SGYU MA LTA BUR STON PA YIN GYI, MNYAM GZHAG GI NGOR SGYU MA LTA BUR STON PA NI MA YIN NO,,

The point being made here, by the way, is that the very thing we realize in our deep meditation is itself like an illusion; it is not to say that this object appears to our mind, in that same meditation, as being like an illusion.
MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA SGYU MA LTA BUR GO BA NI THA SNYAD PA’I BLO YIN GYI, MNYAM GZHAG PA MA YIN NO,,
The understanding that nirvana is like an illusion is itself a conventional state of mind; it is not the mind as we sit in that deep meditation.
GSUM PA MTHA’ GNYIS KYI NGO BO DGAG PA LA
With this, we have reached a third major section which we promised earlier in the work.  This is where we refute the substance of the two extreme views.
‘THAD PA DGOD PA DANG, LUNG ‘GAL SPANG BA’O,,
Here first we will present the correct idea, and then deny that this idea contradicts scripture.
DANG PO LA, SKABS ‘GOD PA DANG, ‘THAD PA DNGOS DANG, [f. 17a] MJUG BSDU BA’O,,
We’ll cover the first of those in three parts: (1) setting the context; then (2) actually presenting the correct idea; and finally (3) offering a concluding summary.
The first of the three steps relates to the following verse of the root text—
,‘GRO BA RNAM PAR MI SHES SO,,
RKANG PA PHYED DANG GSUM GYIS MI MKHAS PA’I GANG ZAG BSTAN NAS PHYED DANG GNYIS KYIS NYES DMIGS BSTAN TO,,

The first two and a half lines in the Tibetan here [the first section in the English] present what it is to be a person who has no nature of being wise; and then the next line and a half [second section in the English] relate the problems of being like this.

MI MKHAS PA GANG DAG GIS NI SNANG TZAM GYIS ‘DUS BYAS LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA DE DAG GIS NI RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA THOG MA DANG DBUS DANG THA MA DANG BRAL BA ‘KHOR LO LTA BU’I ‘GRO BA STE ‘JUG TSUL RNAM PAR MI SHES SHING MI RTOGS TE, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR,

Those who have no nature of being wise imagine—simply because of the way things appear—that produced things have a starting and an ending, through some definition of their own.  People like this have no understanding at all of the workings of all those entities which occur in a dependent relationship: of how they operate.  They cannot grasp how much like a wheel these things are, devoid of any kind of starting point, or middle point, or ending point.  And all this because they cannot see how—with things that exist in & of themselves—the very events of starting & stopping are impossible.
GNYIS PA LA, SPYI’I DON DANG, YAN LAG GI DON TO,,
We will treat the second step in two parts: an overview, and then ancillary points.
DANG PO LA, BDEN PA GNYIS KYI MTSAN NYID DANG, DBYE BA DANG, GRANGS NGES DANG, RNAM GZHAG GTAN LA PHAB PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

We’ll cover the first in four sections: (1) presentations of the definitions of the two realities; (2) their divisions; (3) why their number is fixed at two; and then (4) their more complete descriptions.
KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA GNYIS LAS RIM PA BZHIN DU THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA’I GZHAL BYA DANG, MNYAM GZHAG SO SO RANG RIG PA’I YE SHES KYI GZHAL BYA’O,,

Of these two realities—deceptive and ultimate—the first refers to that object which is considered by a conventional form of accurate perception.  The second then refers to that object which is considered by that wisdom which comprehends the various objects in the deep meditation of a realized being.
GNYIS PA DBYE BA LA KUN RDZOB DANG, DON DAM BDEN PA’I BDEN PA GNYIS SO,,
As for the divisions of the two realities, we first have the division into the two of deceptive reality, and ultimate reality.
DANG PO LA, YANG DAG PA DANG LOG PA’I KUN RDZOB GNYIS SO,,
Deceptive reality itself can be divided into a further two: correct, and mistaken.
DANG PO NI, THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA BZHI’I GZHAL BYA RNAMS SO,,
The first of these consists of all those objects which are considered by the four different forms of the conventional type of accurate perception.
DE YANG GNOD PA MED PA’I DBANG PO DRUG GI YUL DANG, YUL CAN NO,,
We can also describe the correct form of deceptive reality as the objects and subjects involved with the six powers of sense, when they are free of any defect.
GNYIS PA NI, GNOD BCAS KYI DBANG PO YUL YUL CAN RNAMS TE, RMI LAM GYI RTA GLANG SOGS NI PHYI DON RDZUN PA’O,,

And then secondly, the mistaken form of deceptive reality consists of these same subjects & objects involved with the sense powers, when they are possessed of some defect.  Outer objects which are deceptive would be things like a horse or cow that we perceive in a dream.
SHA KHRAG DANG BCAS PA’I RTA GLANG NI PHYI DON BDEN PA STE, BSAM NGO LA BLTOS PA’I YIN GYI, DON DU NA THAMS CAD RDZUN PA’O,,
A flesh-and-blood horse or cow would be an example of an outer object which is true.  We say it is “true” only with reference to our perceptions, since in the end all of these are deceptive.
PHUNG PO LA GTZANG BDE RTAG BDAG BZHI NI KUN RDZOB TU YANG TSAD MA’I GZHAL BYA MA YIN PAS GZHI MA GRUB PA KHO NA’O,,

The perception that the parts to us could be clean; pleasure; lasting; or possessed of any kind of self-nature is—even in terms of deceptive reality—something that could never be considered by any form of accurate perception.  As such, parts like that simply could never exist.
MI RTAG SDUG BSNGAL STONG BDAG MED BZHI NI THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA’I GZHAL BYA’O [f. 17b],,

The facts that these things are impermanent; that they are suffering; that they are empty, and that they cannot be themselves are all objects which in fact can be considered by a conventional form of accurate perception.

GANG DAG DE DAG KUN RDZOB TU YOD MED MTSUNGS PAR ‘DOD PA NI, ‘KHRUL NGO KHO NAR YOD PA KUN RDZOB TU YOD PA’I DON DU BSAMS NAS GZHAN NGO KHO NAR KHAS LEN DGOS PA’I KUN RDZOB DANG, RANG LUGS LA KHAS LEN PA’I KUN RDZOB KYI KHYAD PAR MA PHYED PA YIN TE,

Now there are those who assert that it’s all the same to say that these things exist in a deceptive way, and that they don’t exist in a deceptive way.   They would assert that what it means to exist in a deceptive way is that the object in question is presenting itself to a mistaken state of mind.  And so they fail to make the distinction between forms of deceptive reality which must be accepted only with reference to how the object in question appears to another’s perceptions; and forms of deceptive reality which are accepted in our own system.
DE LTAR YIN PAR YANG SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PAS DE LTAR SONG SONG NAS SGYU MA TZAM ZHIG LUS PA YIN NO, ZHES PA DANG,
At this point, someone may express the following view—
Remember though that Master Chandrakirti has spoken about “going, and going deeper, until all that’s left is a mere illusion.”
‘GA’ ZHIG TU SGRA TZAM ZHIG LUS YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS PAS BRDA TZAM BTAGS PA TZAM GYI KUN RDZOB NI GANG DU YANG MA BKAG CING KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,

He has also spoken about how “we are left with only the names,” meaning that he does not at all deny the possibility of deceptive reality where things exist only in names, only called what they are.  In fact, he accepts it.

GTZANG BDE RTAG BDAG DANG DNGOS PO RANG MTSAN PA SOGS NI, LTA BAS {%LTA BA} MGO BAS {%MA GO BA’I} GANG ZAG ‘GA’ ZHIG GZHUG PA’I THABS SU GZHAN NGO KHO NAR KHAS BLANGS PA MA GTOGS RNAM PA KUN TU BKAG PA’I PHYIR,

And when he mentions things like objects which are clean; pleasure; lasting; or possessed of any kind of self-nature—or when he talks about entities which exist in & of themselves, or anything of the like—he is simply doing so as a skillful means of engaging other people who do not yet understand the correct viewpoint.  That is, he accepts certain ideas only in front of other people; whereas in truth he personally denies them completely.
RANG LUGS LA KUN RDZOB TZAM YOD KYANG KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MED DO ZHE NA,
And so the fact is that—in the system which we ourselves accept—we can say that, although the concept of deception itself does exist, there is no such thing as a “deceptive reality.”

DE LTAR YANG GTAN NAS MA YIN TE, GNOD PA MED PA’I DBANG PO DRUG GI BZUNG YUL GYI GZUGS SGRA SOGS DE, DBU MA PA RANG LUGS KYI KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN LA, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I NGOR DON DAM BDEN PA DANG, ‘PHAGS PA’I RJES THOB NA BDEN SNANG YOD KYANG BDEN PA’O SNYAM PA MED PAS KUN RDZOB TZAM DU RNAM PAR BZHAG PA’O,,

And yet that’s not the way it is at all.  According to the system that those of the Middle Way do accept for themselves, things like visible forms and sounds—those objects which are perceived by the six sense organs where they are free of any kind of corruption—are indeed deceptive reality.  That is, we can accept that, to the perceptions of those of the world, things do appear as ultimate reality; and that—to the state of mind of a realized being once they have come out of their deep meditation on how nothing is itself—things do appear as if they were real.  These latter practitioners never though think that what they are seeing then is reality; they consider it nothing more than deception.
‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS KYANG BDEN GNYIS KYI RNAM DBYE BYED PA NA DE DAG KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR KHAS LEN PA YIN TE, KLU SGRUB BZHIN,
Realized beings then do accept the division of things into two realities; and thus they do accept the concept of a deceptive reality—just the same way that Arya Nagarjuna does.
DE LTA NA, ‘PHAGS PA’ANG BDEN ‘DZIN CAN DU ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA,
Well, if that’s the way it is, then even realized beings must be people who still take things as being real.

RAB RIB CAN LA SKRA SHAD ‘DZAG PAR RTOG PA’I GANG ZAG GI MIG LA SKRA SHAD SNANG GA LA DGOS, KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR RTOGS PA’I PHYIR RDZUN PA SGYU MA LTA BUR RTOGS PA YIN GYI, BDEN PAR KHAS BLANGS MI DGOS SO,,

Consider then a person who has a scratch on the surface of their eye, and who thus thinks they see a hair lying on the surface of their kitchen sink.  How could you say then that a hair was appearing to their eyes?  A person can perceive that things are deceptive—that they are like an illusion—because they have understood what deceptive reality is; but that doesn’t mean they have to take it as real.
JI SKAD SMRA BA DES NI KUN RDZOB BDEN PA LA BDEN PA’I KHYAB PA KHAS BLANGS PAS, PHYIN CI LOG TU SMRAS SO,,
Those who make statements like those we’ve described above think that—if something is deceptive reality—then it has to be real.  And so what they are saying is all wrong.
BLO DE DAG GI YUL GYI MTSAN GZHI THUN MONG PA {%BA} KHAS BLANGS PAS, DON CHOS KHAS [f. 18a] BLANGS SO ZHE NA,
Well then, since the states of mind you’re describing accept the existence of a common referent, you must be accepting here the concept of an actual referent out there.
DE DAG KYANG THA SNYAD TZAM YIN GYI, DE LTA MIN NA TSIG GSAL DU ‘JIG RTEN PA’I DON DAM PA DE ‘PHAGS PA’I KUN RDZOB CES BZHAG PA YANG MI RIGS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Those referents though exist only in name.  If that were not the case, then it would be incorrect for A Clarification of the Verses to describe what the world believes to be ultimately real as what realized beings understand as deceptive.

THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA BZHI’I GZHAL BYA YANG BYIS PA RNAMS KYIS BDEN PAR ZHEN YANG BDEN GNYIS KYI RNAM DBYE LA MKHAS PA’I SO SO SKYE BO DANG, ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS RDZUN PAR GZIGS PAS RDZUN PAR GNAS PA’I PHYIR GZHI MA GRUB PA’I SKYON MED LA,

When we speak of the objects which are held under consideration by the four forms of the conventional type of accurate perception, these are things that infants grasp to as real; whereas both people who have yet to see emptiness directly—but who are well versed in the division into two realities—and realized beings see that these objects are deceptive.  And because they do exist, as deceptive, then we avoid the problem of saying that they have no existence at all.
GANG DAG DBU MA PA LA KHAS LEN YE MED PA’I SHES BYED DU KLU SGRUB KYIS DE LTAR SGRUB BO ZHES SMRA BA RNAMS KYIS GRUB MTHA’I RNAM DBYE MA BYAS NA MDZES SO,,

Yes there are those who point to statements such as where Arya Nagarjuna says “that’s the way they are” and take them as evidence that those of the Middle Way take no position at all.  In my opinion though it would be better if such people stayed out of the business of trying to distinguish between the different schools of Buddhism.
KHA CIG ,DNGOS KUN YANG DAG RDZUN PA MTHONG BA YI, DNGOS RNYED NGO BO GNYIS NI ‘DZIN PAR ‘GYUR, ZHES PA’I GZHUNG GI DON MA RTOGS PAR
There are other people who fail to grasp what the following lines of scripture are trying to say—
PHYI DANG NANG GI DNGOS PO ‘DI DAG ‘PHAGS PAS DON DAM BDEN PAR GZIGS BYIS PAS SPROS PAR GZIGS SHING, DE GNYIS ‘PHAGS PA DBANG BTZAN PAS ‘DI DAG NI DBU MA’I DON DAM BDEN PA’O ZHES SMRA BA
Now some other people, at this point, would make this further statement—

Realized beings perceive all of these entities—whether they be outside of a person or within them—as being ultimate reality.  Infants though see them as false elaborations.  Of the two opinions, those of the realized beings must take precedence.  Thus we can speak here, with the two, of an ultimate reality for the Middle Way school.
DES NI ‘PHAGS PA’I GANG ZAG SMAD DE, MDO LAS,
,KUN RDZOB DE LA DON DAM DU SMRA BA,
,DE DAG NOR BA’I BLO LDAN SHES PAR BYA,
ZHES PA’I NYES PA ‘PHAGS PA LA ‘GEL BA’I PHYIR,

Persons who say things like this, though, are in the end defaming people who have reached the state of a realized being; they are loading faults onto these beings that they in fact are free of.  As sutra puts it,

DES NA GZHUNG DE’I DON NI ‘PHAGS PAS DE DAG RANG BZHIN MED PAR RNYED LA, BYIS PAS DE LAS LOG PAR RNYED PAS ‘PHAGS PAS RNYED PA’I RANG BZHIN MED PA DON DAM BDEN PA YIN LA, PHYI NANG KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN GYI, BYIS PAS RNYED PA’I KHYAD CHOS RANG MTSAN NI KUN RDZOB TU YANG MI SRID DO ZHES PA’O,,

And so the point of that other text is to say that realized beings discover how things have no nature of their own; whereas infants “discover” the opposite.  The lack of a self-nature to things that realized beings discover then is ultimate reality; whereas those outer & inner objects are deceptive reality.  And what the text is saying, further, is that the particular characteristic “discovered” by the infants—the supposed quality of things where they could exist in & of themselves—is an impossibility, even with the deceptive side of things.
‘GA’ YANG MTHONG BA MED PA NI DE KHO NA MTHONG BA’O ZHES GSUNGS PAS RANG BZHIN MED PA RNYED PA MI ‘THAD DO ZHE NA,
Someone else may continue here with the following:

We do see that line which says that “not seeing anything at all is what it means to see the real nature of things.”  As such, it would be incorrect to talk about “discovering” that things have no nature of their own.
DE NI RANG BZHIN MED PA RTOGS NA MIG DAG PA LA SKRA SHAD BZHIN DU SNANG BA MTHA’ DAG NUB CING MA MTHONG BA’I SGO NAS RTOGS PA DANG,

What this line is actually saying though is that—when we realize that nothing has any nature of its own—it’s like that hair on the sink for someone whose eyes are perfectly fine.  That is, the appearance of the hair has faded away into nothing; we don’t see the hair at all.  And it’s the same process here, for that realization.

BUM PA YOD NA DMIGS SU [f. 18b] RUNG BA LAS, BUM PA MA DMIGS PA LAS BUM MED RTOGS PAR ‘JOG PA YIN GYI, RANG BZHIN MED PA YONGS GCOD DU RTOGS RGYU MED PAS RTOGS TSUL STON PA YIN GYI, CI YANG MA MTHONG BA DE DAG DE KHO NA MTHONG ZHES ‘JOG PA NI MIN TE,

If a water pitcher were present in front of us, then we would see it; and the way we establish the realization that there is no water pitcher there is that no such pitcher is observable.  When we perceive that nothing has any nature of its own, it’s not as though there is something that could be present that we deny is there—that’s not the way it would work.  But it’s not as though we’re saying that—when we don’t see anything at all somewhere—we see suchness there.
DE LTA NA MO GSHAM GYI BU LA YANG DE KHO NA MTHONG BA’I THA SNYAD CI’I PHYIR MI ‘DOGS,

Because—if that were the case—then we could call it “seeing the way things really are” when for example we think about the daughter or son of a woman who is physically incapable of having children anyway.
Which brings us to our third section from above; that is, why the number of realities is fixed at two.
TSAD MA DE LA THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA DANG DON DAM PA’I TSAD MA GNYIS SU NGES PAS DE’I YUL DE LA BDEN PA GNYIS SU NGES PA YIN NO,,

The types of accurate perception are fixed at two, no more and no less; these are the conventional form of accurate perception, and the ultimate form of accurate perception.  As such, the objects of these two forms of perception—that is, the types of reality—are also fixed at two.
More detail on the two types of reality
And now for our fourth section here: the more complete descriptions of the two kinds of reality.

GZHI DANG LAM DANG ‘BRAS BU JI LTAR ‘GYUR RNAMS KYIS SHES PAR BYA STE, DE YANG SNANG TZAM ‘DI CHOS CAN RANG BZHIN MED DE, RTEN ‘BREL YIN PA’I PHYIR CES PA’I THAL SBYOR ‘DI LA BDEN PA GNYIS KA TSANG STE, RTAGS SU BZUNG BA KUN RDZOB DANG, CHOS SU BZUNG BA DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA’O,,
These descriptions are something which can be understood from the three points of the original condition; the path; and the result of the path here.  Which is to say—
Consider all that simply appears before us.
It has no nature of its own;
Because it is based upon a dependent relationship.

Both of the two types of reality are complete in this one syllogism of necessity.  The term that we have put forth as the reason—“it is based upon a dependent relationship”—represents deceptive reality; whereas the term we have put forth as the quality we wish to prove—“no nature of its own”—represents ultimate reality.
DE LA RTEN ‘BREL RTOGS PA’I BLO RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA’I THABS SU ‘GYUR BA YIN TE, BSGRUB BYA RTOGS PA’I BLO RTAGS RTOGS PA LAS SKYE DGOS PA’I PHYIR,

This argument serves as a method for the state of mind which realizes the fact of dependent relationship to go further and realize how things have no nature of their own.  And this is because the state of mind which realizes the truth of a statement arises from a realization of the reason presented.
BLO DANG PO DE GOMS PAR BYAS PAS LAM GYI SKABS SU BSOD NAMS KYI TSOGS SU ‘GYUR LA PHYI MA GOMS PAS YE SHES KYI TSOGS SU ‘GYUR BA YIN LA, RGYAS PAR NA PHA ROL TU PHYIN PA DRUG GO

When we have accustomed ourselves to the first state of mind, then in the context of the spiritual path, it becomes the accumulation of merit.  And when we have accustomed ourselves to the latter, it becomes the accumulation of wisdom.  To describe this in more detail, we can turn to the six perfections.

,RTEN ‘BREL GYIS BSDUS PA’I SHES BYA JI SNYED PA LA SGRIB PA’I NYON MONGS PA CAN MA YIN PA’I MI SHES PA RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PAS SEL BAR BYED PA BLO DE NYID SANGS RGYAS KYI SAR THABS GOMS PAS ‘GYUR BAR BYED PA’I PHYIR,

We use the realization that things have no nature of their own to clear away that form of not knowing things which is not involved with negative emotions—a state of mind which blocks us from seeing the total number of knowable things subsumed by dependence.  This state of mind comes about at the level of a Buddha, when we have accustomed ourselves to the method side of things.
DE GNYIS THABS DANG THABS BYUNG YIN TE, DBU MA LA ‘JUG PAR THA SNYAD BDEN PA THABS SU GYUR PA DANG, DON DAM BDEN PA THABS BYUNG GYUR PA STE, ZHES DANG,
These two then represent the method, and what results from employing the method.  Entering the Middle Way puts it this way:
Conventional reality represents a method; whereas ultimate reality represents what results from employing that method.
KUN RDZOB DE NYID GSHOG YANGS
NGANG PA’I RGYAL PO DE NI
MDUN DU BDAR NAS DGE BA’I RLUNG GI
RGYAL BA’I YON TAN RGYA MTSO’I PHA ROL
On vast wide-spreading wings of both
The king goose flies on at the
Of the other geese, all beings, spurred
Reaching to the farthest shore of the ocean
THA SNYAD KYI SKABS SU GZHAN NGO’AM ‘KHRUL NGO ZHES TSIG TU MA BRJOD PAR RNAM GZHAG MI SHES PA DE DAG GIS NI BDEN PA GNYIS PO TSA REG DANG GRANG REG BZHIN DU KHAS BLANGS PA

These people don’t understand the usage where—when we are referring to the conventional—we add the wording “to the perceptions of these others,” or “to perceptions which are mistaken”; rather, they take the position that the two realities are opposed, like the touch of something very hot and the touch of something very cold.
THABS DANG THABS BYUNG DU BZHAG MI NUS SHING, DON DAM GYI RNAM GZHAG MI NUS TE, DON DAM GYI RNAM GZHAG BYED NA KUN RDZOB YOD PA MA YIN PAR MO GSHAM GYI BU BZHIN DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,

As such, they are unable to lay out the concepts of method and that which results from  employing the method; which means they are unable then to describe what is ultimate.  They would say that—if you can make a presentation of the ultimate—then necessarily the deceptive could not exist at all; they would take the position that deceptive reality would be like that child of a barren woman.
LUGS DES NI TSIG TU GANG LTAR BRJOD KYANG STONG PA’I DON YE MED DU GZUNG BAS ‘PHAGS PA’I BDEN BZHI MI ‘THAD PAR THAL BA LA ‘DOD THOG BYED DGOS PA YIN NO,,

However people who hold to this position choose to express it in words, the fact is that they believe that what the word “emptiness” refers to is “nothing at all.”  This then means that they would end up having to agree to the necessity that the four higher truths were mistaken.
,‘PHAGS PA’I BDEN PA BZHI PO RNAMS,
ZHES RANG LA BDEN BZHI MI ‘THAD PA’I NYES PA MED PAR BSTAN LA,
The Realized One, Nagarjuna, composed the following verse to show how he himself was free of this problem, of believing that the four truths were mistaken—
That all these things are empty,
ZHES BDEN GNYIS TSAD MA GCIG GI NGOR ‘TSOG TU MI RUNG YANG, GZHI GCIG GI STENG DU ‘TSOG TU RUNG STE, GZUGS SGRA BZHIN,

What this is actually saying is that—although it would be inappropriate to say that the two realities could both present themselves at the same time to a single accurate perception—it is entirely appropriate for the two realities to apply to a single object or basis at the same time.
DES BLO LA MA BLTOS PA’I DGE CHOS KHAS LEN PAR YANG YE MI ‘GYUR TE, KUN RDZOB NI THAG KHRA LA SBRUL DU BTAGS PA BZHIN DU RTOG PA’I ‘DZIN STANGS BSKAM PO MING TZAM YIN ZHING,

What this is also indicating is that we could never accept that something was a virtue independent of the state of mind involved.  When we say something is “deceptive,” what we mean is that the way the mind holds to it is hollow, something that exists in name only: in the same way that the mind might think of a coil of checkered rope as being a real snake.

RANG GI GDAGS GZHI DANG, DE NYID DANG GZHAN GANG YANG MA GRUB PAS, MI BLUN PO LA BA LANG DU BTAGS PA NA RVA RING THUNG GI DPYAD PA MI ‘JUG PA BZHIN DU, RGYU ‘BRAS DE NYID DANG GZHAN GYI DPYAD PA MI ‘JUG PA YIN NO,,

The thing that we are giving the name “snake” here is actually no more that than anything else; once somebody has referred to an animal as a “cow,” fools wouldn’t think of measuring its horns to see how short or long they might be.  Neither would they think to examine whether cause & effect were just that, or something else too.

YANG DE TZAM LA ‘KHRUL NAS DPYAD PA BYAS PA NA KUN RDZOB MED PAR ‘GYUR SNYAM DU MI BSAM STE, RIGS NGOR MA GRUB PA YIN GYI, KUN RDZOB KYI THUN MONG MIN PA’I GO BA NI SPROS PA MTHA’ DAG BKAG RJES SU RNYED PA’I PHYIR TE, RTEN ‘BYUNG SGYU MAR GO BA NI, BDEN PA’I SPROS PA KHEGS PA LA [f. 19b] BLTOS PA’I PHYIR,

We can also say that—if we make an error just on this much but then continue our examination—we could avoid thinking that there was no such thing as deceptive reality.  That is, we could say that a deceptive object fails to stand up in the face of proper reasoning; but the fact is that, once we have managed to block all elaborations of things existing in & of themselves, we gain a truly unique understanding of this deceptive reality.  And that’s because really understanding how dependence resembles an illusion relies upon the ability to block all these elaborations of things existing in reality.
KHA CIG DPYAD NAS RNYED PA’I STONG PA NYID LA BLOS BYAS KYI STONG PA ZHES PA DANG, GZHAN DAG HA CANG DPYAD PA SKYON YIN ZHES SMRA BA DE DAG GIS NI STONG PA NYID KYI GO BA RGYANG RING DU SPANGS TE,
