Some people say that the emptiness which you come to through a process of analysis should be called “emptiness concocted by the mind.”  Others have said that “It’s a problem when you over-analyze all this.”  But in fact, thinkers who say things like this are rejecting a proper understanding of emptiness, pushing it farther & farther from them.
DPYAD NAS RNYED PA NI SNGAR STONG PA MA YIN PA STONG PAR GSAR DU RNYED PA MA YIN TE

That is, you should understand that when we use a process of analysis to come to an understanding of emptiness, it’s not as if we are taking something that was not emptiness and then making it into emptiness, fresh.
DE LTA NA BUM PA BZOS PA BZHIN DU GNAS LUGS MA YIN PA RNYED PAS BLO PHYIN CI LOG TU ‘GYUR ZHING STONG NYID SHES MTHONG GIS BYAS PAR ‘GYUR LA,

If that’s the way it was—if we could just make emptiness the way we make a water pitcher out of some clay—then any time we determined that something was not the way things really are, we would have to be mistaken.  Emptiness would be something that our knowing, our seeing, had produced.
DGAG BYA SNGAR YOD BKAG NA YANG, BUM PA BSHIG BYED KYI THO BA BZHIN DU, STONG NYID DNGOS PO’I BSHIG BYED DU ‘GYUR DGOS SO,,

Even in the case where what we are denying is something that previously existed, and was then stopped, the whole process would be similar to using a hammer as something to smash a ceramic water pitcher with.  That is, emptiness would have to turn into an instrument which smashed all existing entities.

DES NA RTEN ‘BYUNG LA BLOS GZUNG BA’I DRI MA MTHA’ DAG ‘KHRUD PA’I PHYIR TU {%DU} MTHA’ GZHAN DU SRID PA’I DOGS PA MTHA’ DAG DPYAD DGOS PAS JI SRID DOGS PA MA CHOD PAR {%BAR} DU YANG DANG YANG DU DPYAD DGOS PA CI TZAM DU DPYAD PA DE TZAM DU NGES PA RNYED PAR ‘GYUR BAS

As such, we need to look into each & every one of our suspicions that other approaches might be possible, as we engage in laundering away each & every impurity that might come up in the way we think about the concept of dependence.  Until such time as we investigate and thus eliminate all the possible questions that arise in our mind, we have to continue this exercise of investigation.  And the more we investigate this concept, the more we ascertain the truth of the matter.
YOD PA SGRUB MI DGOS, MED PA SGRUB MI NUS ZHES PA’I TSIG RIGS LA BRTEN NAS, TSAD MA’I DGAG SGRUB SPANG BAR MI BYA STE,

I advise you not to rely upon statements like “If it were really there, you wouldn’t have to prove it; if it weren’t really there, it’s not something that you could prove.”  That is, I advise you not to abandon the process of disproving or proving ideas by using the process of accurate perception.
DE NI DGAG SGRUB DON LA YOD PA ‘GOG PA YIN GYI, TSAD MA’I DGAG SGRUB ‘GAG PA MA YIN TE, DE LTA NA RIGS PA’I BSTAN BCOS BRTZAMS PAS CI BYA,

If you approach disproving or proving things the way they describe it there, you’re going to end up denying something which is, in fact, actually here.  It is not that what we’re denying is the process itself of using accurate perception to establish that something either doesn’t or does exist; if that were the case, then why would so many masters have expended such effort to compose the great classics on logical thinking?
YANG KHA CIG SNANG TZAM YANG DGAG PAR BYA’O ZHES SMRA BA NI LTA BA DE NYID KYIS NGAN ‘GRO’I RGYU BYED PAS THAR ‘DOD RNAMS KYIS RNAM PA KUN TU SPANG BAR BYA STE,

We also see some people who come along with the claim that the simple appearance of things is also something we should deny.  This is exactly the viewpoint that can transport you to the lower realms of suffering; and so I would advise those of you who are striving to stop your pain to reject it wholeheartedly.
DGAG MI NUS, DGAG MI DGOS, BKAG NA SKYON YOD PA’I PHYIR,

Our own position is that this simple appearance is not something you could ever successfully deny; not something that you would ever have to deny; and in fact something that—if you did deny it—you would run into a lot of trouble.
SNANG BA ‘GOG BYED KYI TSAD MA MED NA, ‘GEGS BYED MED PAS DGAG MI NUS PA’I PHYOGS KHAS BLANGS PAR ‘GYUR LA,

There is no accurate form of perception which would allow us to disprove the existence of this simple appearance to things.  And we personally support the idea that—if there is nothing that could disprove an idea—then you could not in fact disprove it.
YOD NA DE NYID KYANG DGAG BYAR ‘GYUR TE, DE YANG SNANG TZAM LAS MA ‘DAS PA’I PHYIR,

And if there were something that could disprove a particular idea, then it too would become one of those things that you are attempting to disprove; since, after all, there is no way to deny that it too would be…simply…appearing!
DES NA SNANG BA ‘GOG PAR KHAS BLANGS SHING, ‘GOG BYED KYANG ‘GOG PAR KHAS BLANGS PAS RANG TSIG DANG ‘GAL BAR ‘GYUR LA,

And then you would have reached a point where you were accepting both that the simple appearance of things is something which we should deny; and what we use to deny it is as well something we should deny—your words would be contradicting exactly what you’re using those words to deny.
[f. 20a] BKAG PA LA DGOS PA YANG MED DE, BDEN PA’I SPROS PA BCAD PAS DE GOMS PA NA RANG ‘GAGS SU ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR,

Nor would there be any point to all these denials anyway; if you are able to use your logic to refuse elaborations that things could exist in truth, and if you habituate yourself to this conclusion, all the necessary denials make their appearance of their own accord.
BKAG NA SKYON YOD DE, BSOD NAMS KYI TSOGS BSAG PAR MI NUS PA’I PHYIR,
Denying things in the way you hope to though would be a great problem, since in that case we would forever be incapable of assembling the accumulation of merit.
LAM GYI DGAG BYA DANG RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA’I KHYAD MI PHYED PA’I DBU MA PA DE LA PHYAG ‘TSAL LO,,
I have to take my hat off to you “Middle Wayers” who make no distinction at all between what the path puts a stop to, and what the ultimate reasoning puts a stop to.
DES NA BDEN PA DGAG DGOS DGAG NUS BKAG NA YON TAN YOD DE, BDEN PAR GZUNG BAS NYES PA THAMS CAD BSKYED PA’I PHYIR DANG,
And so what we do need to stop, and what would be very helpful to stop, is some thing that could truly exist; after all, every problem in the world comes from grasping on to this kind of existence.
YOD NA RIGS PAS DMIGS SU RUNG BA LAS RIGS PAS BRTAG MI BZOD PA’I PHYIR,
If this kind of reality did exist, then we should be able to use reasoning to observe it—whereas, in actuality, it is not something that can stand up to reasoning.
DE MED PAR RTOGS PA LAS ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BA BZLOG PA’I PHYIR, BDEN ZHEN DGAG BYA YIN GYI, BDEN PA DGAG BYA MIN TE, YE MED YIN PA’I PHYIR CES SMRA BA
Now some people have said it like this—

When we talk about something that we have to put a stop to, we’re talking about the tendency of grasping to things as real—because realizing that it doesn’t exist is described as the thing that prevents the very root of the cycle of pain.  It isn’t though that things being real could ever be what we have to put a stop to, since that never existed in the first place.
DES KYANG YE MED PA DES MED DU RTOGS PA TSAD MA’I DGAG SGRUB KYI DON DU MA GO BAR ZAD DE, BDEN ZHEN ‘GOG PA LA DE’I ZHEN YUL YE MED DU RTOGS DGOS PAS SO,,

People like this have simply failed to understand that something which was never there in the first place is exactly what we either deny or establish when we talk about using accurate perception to come to an understanding that something doesn’t exist.  That is, when we undertake to stop our tendency to grasp to things as real, we have to do so by coming to the realization that what this tendency thinks is there was never there in the first place.
DES NA CHOS THAMS CAD RTOG PAS BTAGS PA TZAM DU RANG LUGS LA KHAS BLANGS NA RTEN ‘BYUNG YOD PAR MI RUNG LA,

And so then we see people who say that—if what our own system believes is that every object in the universe exists through nothing more than labels applied by our imagination—it would be wrong to say that things existed through dependent relationships.
RTEN ‘BYUNG YOD PAR KHAS BLANGS PA NA MTHAR LTUNG DU ‘GYUR PAS {%BAS}, YOD PAR BZHAG TU MI RUNG ZHES SMRA BA

They would then say that, if after that we accepted that things did exist in these types of relationships, we would have fallen into an extreme view—and could no longer establish what it is that did exist.

DE NI RANG NYID MNGON PAR RTOGS PA’I RGYAN NAS BSHAD PA’I LOG RTOG BCU DRUG LA GNAS BZHIN DU SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN ‘BYED LA SOGS PA’I SHING RTA CHEN PO RNAMS LA SMOD PA NI BDAG NYID MA RUNGS PAR BYED PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU ZAD DO,,

People who think this way would themselves be living inside of the sixteen wrong views described in the Jewel of Realizations; and, as such, they would be insulting great innovators such as Master Bhavaviveka.  And then we could say that they were, in the end, simply hurting themselves.
GNYIS PA YAN LAG GI DON LA, SKYE BA’I MTHA’ DGAG PA DANG, ‘JIG PA’I MTHA’ DGAG PA’O,,
Here secondly are the ancillary points we promised above; we will cover them with, first, a denial of the extreme of starting; and secondly a denial of the extreme of ending.
DANG PO NI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA KHAS BLANGS PA DANG RTEN ‘BYUNG JI LTAR ‘GAL ZHE NA
As for the first, one may ask how it is that a belief that things could start through some nature of their own stands in contradiction to the concept of dependence:
Tat tat prāpya yad utpannaṃ notpannaṃ tat svabhāvataḥ,
Yat svabhāvena notpannam utpannaṃ nāma tat katham.
Tat tat prapya yad utpannan notpannan tat svabhavatah,
Yat svabhavena notpannam utpannan nama tat katham.
DE DANG DE RTEN GANG ‘BYUNG DE,
RANG GI NGO BOR SKYES MA YIN,
RANG GI NGO BOR GANG MA SKYES,
DE NI SKYE ZHES JI SKAD BYA,
RGYU DANG RKYEN DE DANG DE LA BRTEN NAS GANG ‘BYUNG BA DE NI RANG GI NGO BOR RANG [f. 20b] BZHIN GYIS SKYES PA MA YIN NO,,
Anything which occurs in dependence on any particular thing—referring to any particular cause or contributing factor—cannot have started in & of itself: through any nature of its own.
CI’I PHYIR CE NA, RGYU’I SNGAR YOD NA RGYU LA MI LTOS LA, SKYE BA’I SNGAR MED NA SKYES PA’I DUS NA YANG GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU BCOS MAR ‘GYUR GYI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID DU GRUB PAR GA LA ‘GYUR,

And why is that?  If something were present even before its cause, then it wouldn’t be dependent upon that cause.  And if it didn’t exist at all before it started, then at the point when it did start, it would have to be an artificial construction—similar to the reflection of an image in a mirror.  And then how on earth could we say that it somehow existed through some nature of its own?
RANG GI NGO BOR RANG BZHIN GYIS MA SKYES KYANG SKYE BA TZAM NI YOD DE, GZUGS SKYES SO ZHES PA’I THA SNYAD MTHONG BA’I PHYIR,
Even if it didn’t start in & of itself—through some nature of its own—we could say that it had simply started; after all, we do see people use the phrase, “That physical thing just started.”
DE YOD NA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA YANG YOD DE, BTAGS PA THAMS CAD RDZAS KYI RTEN CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,
One might respond to this with—

Well, if that could be the case, then we could also say that things can start through some nature of their own; after all, any time we label something something, at the bottom there’s something substantial there, to take the name.
RANG GI DNGOS POR RANG BZHIN GYIS GANG MA SKYES PA DE NI RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYES SO ZHES JI SKAD BRJOD PAR BYA STE, GZHAN GYI NGO BOR SKYE BA DUS NAM YANG MI SRID PA’I PHYIR,

And yet how could you ever say that something which had not yet started—by nature, and in & of itself—suddenly then started, all on its own?  Because isn’t it an impossibility, at any moment in time, that it could start, as something now with a different essence?

RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA MED NA SKYE BA TZAM MED DO ZHES SMRA BA DES NI GONG ‘OG LEGS PAR MA BRTAGS TE, DON BSDU BA’I SKABS SU YANG RIGS PAS DPYAD PA’I SKYE BA MED CES PA DANG ZAD MTHA’ ‘GOG PA’I SKABS SU YANG ZAD PA RANG BZHIN PA MED CES GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,

Someone may object here, saying “Well, if something could never start though any nature of its own, then it could never just start.”  When you make this kind of statement, you are failing to follow the flow of the argument here carefully.  After all, in the verses which follow closely below—where we summarize the points we’ve made—we mention how, upon logical analysis, “there can be no starting” of things.  And then in the lines just before that—where we deny the extreme of ending—we show how “there can be no nature” of coming to an end.
With this we have reached our second point: denying the extreme of ending—
,RGYU ZAD NYID LAS ZHI BA NI,
,ZAD CES BYA BAR DMIGS PA STE,
,RANG BZHIN GYIS NI GANG MA ZAD,
,DE LA ZAD CES CI SKAD BRJOD,
Through any nature of its own
DNGOS PO RNAMS GNAS PA NI GNAS BYED KYI RKYEN LA RAG LAS TE GNAS PA’I RKYEN MED NA ‘JIG PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR,
When working things stay for some time, this depends upon certain factors which allow them to stay.  If there are no such factors, then the entity in question ends.
DES NA GNAS BYED KYI RGYU RAS SNUM SOGS ZAD CING ‘GAGS PA NYID LAS BYUNG BA’I MAR ME’I ‘OD ZAD CING ‘GAGS PA’I ZHI BA NI ZAD PA DANG ‘GAGS PA ZHES BYA BAR DMIGS PA STE,

And because of that—for this reason—we observe what we call the wearing out, or the ending, of things.  The light of a butter lamp comes to a rest—from the simple wearing out, and ending, of the cloth wick and lamp oil which provided the cause which sustained it.
ZAD PA RGYU LA BLTOS PA’I RANG BZHIN GYIS GANG MA ZAD PA DE LA ZAD PAR RANG BZHIN PAR JI SKAD BRJOD PAR BYA STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS MA ZAD PA DE NI NGO BO GZHAN GANG GIS ZAD PAR RNAM PAR BZHAG PAR BYA,

How then could you ever say that something which could never have worn out through any nature of its own—something which, rather, wore out because of its dependence upon a cause—had some nature of wearing out?  How could you ever say that something which could never wear out through any nature of its own had, instead, worn out because of some separate nature?
GSUM PA MJUG BSDU BA NI,
Which brings us to our third point: the concluding summary.
Na hyatrotpadyate kiṃcin nāpi kiṃcin nirudhyate.
Na hyatrotpadyate kinchin napi kinchin nirudhyate.
,DE LTAR CI YANG SKYE BA MED,

DE [f. 21a] LTAR RIGS PAS RNAM PAR DPYAD PA NA CI YANG RANG DANG GZHAN GYI NGO BOS SKYE BA MED LA, RANG DANG GZHAN GYI NGO BOS CI YANG ‘GAG PAR YANG MI ‘GYUR TE, RNAL ‘BYOR PAS CI YANG DMIGS PA MED DO ZHES PA’I DON TO,,

And so when we have examined the question in this way, with logical reasoning, we can say that there is no starting to things at all—at least, the kind of starting which occurs through some essential nature of the object itself, or of some other object.  Neither is it the case that things can stop, in any way at all, through some essential nature of themselves, or something else.  And this in fact is what deep practitioners mean, when they say that “there is nothing at all to see.”
GNYIS PA LUNG ‘GAL SPANG BA LA, SKYE ‘JIG GSUNGS PA DRANG DON DU BSTAN, SKYE ‘JIG LA BRTEN NAS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS TSUL, MNGON ZHEN CAN GYIS MI RTOGS PAR BSTAN, MOS PA RNAMS KYIS RTOGS TSUL LO,,

This brings us to our second part from above, which is our denial that our description of the two realities contradicts scripture.  We proceed in four steps: (1) demonstrating how statements about starting & ending were only figurative; (2) how to reach the realization that things have no nature of their own, by using starting & ending; (3) a description of how those who still cling to things cannot have this realization; and (4) a discussion of how those with the right ideas can indeed come to realization.
DANG PO NI, GAL TE DE LTAR SKYE ‘JIG GNYIS MI SRID NA BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS,
,DE DAG NYE BAR ZHI BA BDE,
For the first, one may begin with the following objection—
If it is indeed the case that the pair of starting & ending are impossibilities, what about the following lines, from scripture?
ZHES SKYE ‘JIG MED NA MYANG ‘DAS THOB PA’I THABS SU GSUNG MI RIGS PA LAS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR YOD DO ZHE NA,

If there are no starting & ending at all, it would have been inappropriate for Lord Buddha to describe them as a means of attaining nirvana.  And yet he did, in these words for example, do exactly that.
SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB NAS GSUNGS PA MA YIN GYI, ‘JIG RTEN DAM PA MA YIN PA’I LAM DU ‘GRO BA ‘DI DE KHO NA NYID LA SBYOR BAR ‘DOD PAS

Lord Buddha was not though saying here that starting & ending existed through any essential nature of their own.  Rather, he was simply hoping to take those of the world who were travelling on a path which was not the highest one, and lead them to the concept of suchness.
SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA’I LAM ‘DI BSTAN PAS DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS NUS PA’I PHYIR, DE KHO NA RTOGS PA’I THABS SU DGOS PA’I DON DU BSTAN PA’O,,

And he was hoping that, when he taught people like this about a path based on starting & ending, they would be able to come to the realization of suchness.  And so he taught about this path simply as a means to an end: as a way of helping people to grasp the concept of suchness.

SKYE ‘JIG STON PA’I MDO DRANG DON YIN YANG SGRA JI BZHIN PA YIN PAS RANG LUGS LA SKYE ‘JIG KHAS LEN TE DE KHAS LEN PA DANG STONG PA GZHI GCIG LA ‘DU BA’I PHYIR, DE LTAR MIN NA RTEN ‘BREL LA BDEN PAS KHYAB PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

The sutras which teach about starting & ending have to be interpreted, but on the face of it they are also literal.  As such, in our own system we accept the concepts of starting and ending, but we would say that these two concepts that we do accept can also be present, together with emptiness itself, within a single base entity.  If this were not the case, then the concept of dependent relationship itself would have to exist in truth.
GNYIS PA LA DNGOS DANG PHAN YON NO,,

With this, we have reached our second point here: how to reach the realization that things have no nature of their own, by using starting & ending.  We will proceed in two steps: the actual presentation, and then the benefits of this particular methodology.
DANG PO NI, SKYE ‘JIG BSTAN PA LA DGOS PA CI YOD CE NA,
As for the first, one may begin by asking what the “end” or purpose was for Lord Buddha to teach starting & ending—
,‘JIG PA SHES PAS MI RTAG SHES,

BYIS PA BUD MED LA CHAGS PA LDOG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR TU BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS SKYE [f. 21b] ‘JIG BSTAN, DE LTAR SKYE BA SHES PAS ‘JIG PA YANG SHES PAR ‘GYUR TE, ‘JIG PA NI SKYE BA’I RTZA BA CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR,

The conquering Buddha taught starting and ending to help infants of the world put a stop to their feelings of desire.  With this we can also understand ending, through an understanding of starting.  And that’s because ending has starting as its very root.
‘JIG PA SHES PAS DE DON GCIG PA’I MI RTAG PA SHES PAR ‘GYUR LA, KHAMS GSUM MI RTAG PA’I ME RAB TU ‘BAR BA’I NANG DU ‘DUG PAR SHES PAS DE LAS ‘DA’ BAR ‘DOD CING,

When we do understand ending, we come to understand impermanence, which is synonymous with it.  And then we will realize that we are living here, in the three realms of existence, wrapped in the blazing fire of impermanence.  And with that, we will be inspired to try to get beyond this state.
DE KHO NA NYID LA ‘JUG PA SHES PAS DAM PA’I CHOS MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA DANG THA MI DAD PA’I SPROS BRAL STONG PA NYID GSUNGS PA RTOGS SHING KHONG DU CHUD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Once we know how to engage in the very nature of things, we can realize—we can grasp, completely—the highest of all things: emptiness (that freedom from elaborations of self-existence) which was stated to be inseparable from nirvana itself.
Which brings us to those benefits we talked about—
,SHES PAR GYUR PA DE DAG NI,
,LTAR GYUR SRID PA’I RGYA MTSO BRGAL,
JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I RIM GYIS DE KHO NA NYID TSOL BA LHUR BYED PA’I BLO MCHOG DANG LDAN PA GANG DAG RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG ‘JIG PA RNAM PAR SPANGS PA

There are those then—individuals of great intelligence—who have made serious efforts to reach suchness in the stages we have suggested so far.  They have given up, completely, the idea that anything which occurs through a relationship of dependence could exhibit starting & stopping that existed through any nature of their own.
RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BAS GNAS MI THOGS PAR SHES PAR GYUR PA
As such, they now understand how their life cannot be touched by the mistaken viewpoints which then imply that things would have to remain forever unchanging, or stop altogether.
DE DAG NI RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BAR GYUR PA NYID SRID PA’I RGYA MTSO YIN PAS NA LTA BAR GYUR PA’I SRID PA’I RGYA MTSO LAS STONG NYID RTOGS PA’I GRUS NGES PAR BRGAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

People like this then have used the ship of realizing emptiness in order to cross over—completely, and with certainty—the ocean of this suffering life: an ocean which consists of how we view things.  And that’s because the ocean of pain actually consists of viewing things as either being unchanging, or stopping altogether.
And now we have reached our third point: a description of how those who still cling to things cannot have the realization we’ve just spoken of—
Bhāvābhāva viparyāsa doṣa kleśa vaśaṃ gatāḥ.
Bhavabhava viparyasa dosha klesha vashan gatah.
,SO SO’I SKYE BO DNGOS BDAG CAN,
,YOD DANG MED PAR PHYIN CI LOG
,NYES PAS NYON MONGS DBANG GYUR RNAMS,
LAS JI LTA BA DANG NYON MONGS JI LTA BA BZHIN SKYE GNAS SO SOR ‘GRO BAS NA SO SO’I SKYE BO PHUNG PO DANG THA MI DAD PAR BDAG TU ‘DZIN PAS DNGOS BDAG CAN NAM,

Individual ordinary people are people who pass on to their individual types of rebirth, according to the dictates of their karma, and their negative emotions.  We can also refer to them as “those who keep to a real self,” since they hold to themselves as being inseparable from the parts that make them up.
YANG NA DNGOS PO NI CHOS BDAG YIN PAS DE SO SKYE’I BDAG TU LDAN PAS DNGOS BDAG CAN NAM,

We can also say that people like this are individuals who keep to a real self in that they possess the nature of an ordinary person, where all the things of reality are—for them— the self-nature of things.
YANG NA DNGOS PO LA MNGON PAR ZHEN PA RNAMS NI DNGOS BDAG CAN,
We could also say that we refer to these types of people as ones who keep to a real self because they still cling to the idea that things exist in the way they think.
STONG PA NYID DU LTA BAS ‘JIGS PA RNAMS DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA DANG MED PA RANG MTSAN PAR ‘DZIN PA’I PHYIN CI LOG GI KUN RTOG GIS BSKYED PA’I NYES PAS

Those who are frightened by viewing things as emptiness are overcome by the problems that come when we imagine, wrongly, how things exist; that is, when we hold things to either to exist through some nature of their own, or to not exist, in & of themselves.
CHAGS SDANG LA [f. 22a] SOGS PA NYON MONGS PA’I GZHAN DBANG DU GYUR PA RNAMS NGES PAR SEMS SKYE MED DU MA SHES PAR RANG GI SEMS KYI ‘DZIN PAS BSLUS NAS ‘KHOR BAR ‘KHOR BAR ‘GYUR RO ZHES PA’I DON TO,,

And because of all this, people like this fall under another power: that of everything involved with negative emotions such as ignorant desire, and anger.  These individuals, with all certainty, have failed to grasp how their own mind has no nature of starting.  And as such, they are deceived by how they themselves hold to their own mind—which in turn then causes them to cycle around in this cycle of pain.  This is the point being made here.
BZHI PA MOS PA RNAMS KYIS RTOGS TSUL LA, MDZAD PA MTHAR PHYIN PA RNAMS KYIS RTOGS TSUL DANG, SLOB DPON RANG NYID KYIS GZIGS TSUL DANG, DE’I ‘THAD PA’O,,

With that we come to our fourth and final point: a discussion of how those with the right ideas can indeed come to realization.  We’ll cover this section in three steps: (1) how it is that those who have brought their deeds to their final end understand things; (2) how the Master himself sees things; and (3) how that particular sight is indeed correct.
The next verse covers that first step—
Anityaṃ moṣa dharmāṇaṃ muktaṃ śūnyam anātmakam,
Viviktam iti paśyanti bhāvaṃ bhava vicakṣaṇāḥ.
Anityam mosha dharmanam muktan shunyam anatmakam,
Viviktam iti pashyanti bhavam bhava vichakshanah.
,DNGOS LA MKHAS PA RNAMS KYIS NI,
,DNGOS PO MI RTAG BSLU BA’I CHOS,
,GSOG DANG STONG PA BDAG MED PA,
,RNAM PAR DBEN ZHES BYA BAR MTHONG,
See things as what we call
STONG PA NYID LA G-YANG SA LTA BUR MI SEMS SHING CHOS RNAMS KYI DON DAM PA DANG, MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PAR ‘GRO BA’I LAM DU RTOGS PA’I DNGOS PO LA MKHAS PA RNAMS KYIS

Let’s consider then those persons who do not think of emptiness as though it were some great chasm that they might fall of into.  Rather, they are masters of all things: masters in the realization of the ultimate nature of all entities, who also see this nature as the path for traveling to nirvana.
NI DNGOS PO RNAM PAR DBEN ZHING RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG NGO ZHES BYA BAR MTHONG NGO,,
These are people who see things as what we call “totally devoid”; that is, empty of any nature of their own.

DE’I ‘THAD PA NI, KHYAD PAR LNGA STE, DNGOS PO SKAD CIG RE RE LA ‘JIG PA’I NGANG TSUL CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR MI RTAG PA, SGYU MA BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN MED PA RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SNANG BAS BSLU BA’I CHOS {%,} YUN RING DU MI GNAS SHING NYAM CHUNG BA NYID KYIS GSOG DANG, CHOS BDAG GI RANG BZHIN DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR STONG PA, GANG ZAG GI BDAG DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR BDAG MED PA’O,,
And why is this the case?  It’s because entities are possessed of five different features:
1) They are impermanent, in the sense that they exhibit a nature of ending in every millisecond of their existence.
2) They are things which tend to deceive us, in that they are like an illusion: they have no nature of their own, but they appear to have one.
3) They are hollow, in that they cannot remain in existence for any long period of time, and are also extremely fragile;
4) They are empty, in that they lack any nature of things that belongs to them; and
5) They lack any nature of their own, for they are devoid of any self-nature of the individual.
Here secondly we cover how the Master himself sees things—
Saṃmoha nagaraṃ ghoraṃ jagan māyeva dṛśyate.
Sammoha nagaran ghoran jagan mayeva dirshyate.
,GNAS MED DMIGS PA YOD MA YIN,
,RTZA BA MED CING GNAS PA MED,
,MA RIG RGYU LAS SHIN TU BYUNG,
,THOG MA DBUS MTHA’ RNAM PAR SPANGS,
,CHU SHING BZHIN DU SNYING PO MED,
,RMONGS PA’I GRONG KHYER MI ZAD PA’I,
,‘GRO BA SGYU MA BZHIN DU SNANG,
And so they are not sustained.
They are like shoots of bamboo,
It is all a city of the ignorant,
SNOD BCUD KYIS BSDUS PA’I, ‘GRO BA ‘DI SLOB DPON GYIS RJES THOB LA SGYU MA BZHIN DU SNANG ZHING GZIGS PA YIN NO,,

The types of births here, subsumed by both the vessel of the world, and its contents, appear—to the subsequent wisdom of Master Nagarjuna himself, he sees them as—in the same way that a magical illusion does.
JI LTAR SGYU MA LTA BU YIN ZHE NA, ‘THAD PA BZHI STON PA NI ‘GAL RKYEN GYI SGO NAS
“In what way,” one may ask, “are these things like an illusion?”  We can express how seeing them in this way is correct, in four different ways, according to what might work against them.
GNAS SAM RTEN [f. 22b] BDEN PA MED CING DMIGS PA BDEN PA BA YANG YOD PA MA YIN PAS SA BON GYI TSUL GYIS RTZA BA MED CING MI GNAS PAS RKYEN GSUM GYI TSUL GYIS GNAS PA MED PA’O,,
1) They have no “place,” or basis, which is real.
2) Neither do they have any object of focus which is something that really exists.
3) As such, they have no root—in the sense of a seed; they cannot stay in this way.
4) And so they are not things which are sustained through these three necessary factors.
‘GRO BA RANG BZHIN MED NA SNA TSOGS SU JI LTAR SNANG ZHE NA,
One might next ask the following question:
If the types of beings have no nature of their own, how is it then that they appear in such variety?
MED KYANG SNANG BA’I RGYU’I KHYAD PAR NI MA RIG PA’I RGYU LAS SHIN TU ‘BYUNG BAS SNANG BA’O, ,DES NI SNANG BA MI ‘GOG PAR BSTAN PA’O,,
The fact though is that they have no such nature; but they do appear to, because of the feature of their cause: they pour forth from their cause, of misunderstanding.
GRUB PA RANG BZHIN MED PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR THOG MAR RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG DBUS SU GNAS PA DANG, MTHA’ MAR ‘JIG PA RNAMS SPANGS SHING DE DANG BRAL LO ZHES PA’I DON TO,,

The fact that things’ having come into existence has no nature of its own is expressed in the following words of the root text: they have “left behind”—meaning they are devoid of—any starting (through any nature of their own); any such staying, in the middle of the process; and any ending, at the finish.
CHU SHING BZHIN DU SNYING PO CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, DRI ZA’I GRONG KHYER DANG ‘DRA BAR BDEN PAR SNANG YANG RNAM PAR DPYAD NA DE LTAR MED PA’I PHYIR YANG MA RIG PA’I RGYU LAS BYUNG BA’O,,

These things have, further, arisen from the cause of misunderstanding.  And this is because—first of all—they are like shoots of bamboo: they have not the slightest essence inside.  Moreover, they “resemble the city of the craving spirits,” meaning that they appear from a distance to be real, but when you look closer they are not that way at all.
‘GRO BA’I KHYAD PAR NI RMONGS PA’I GRONG KHYER LUS NGAG GI ‘JUG PA RANG NYID LA GNOD BYED LAS LDOG DKA’ BAS NA MI ZAD PA’I ‘GRO BA DE LTAR SNANG ZHING GZIGS SO,,

There is also a detail here of how beings move through these types of birth.  This city of the ignorant, where people work to hurt no one but themselves in how they act and speak, is something very difficult to put a stop to.  As such, they move here without an end.  This then is how these things appear to the Master; and how he sees them.
Scripture on the sight of The Arya
GSUM PA LA, LUNG DANG RIGS PA GNYIS SO, ,DANG PO NI,

Which brings us to our third step here: how that particular sight of The Arya is indeed correct.  We’ll present this part through citations from scripture, and then move on to the related logic.  Here is the first—
Brahmādyair asya lokasya yat satyaṃ saṃprakāśitam,
Tad āryāṇāṃ mṛṣetyuktaṃ kiṃ na śeṣam ataḥ param.
Brahmadyair asya lokasya yat satyan samprakashitam,
Tad aryanam mirshetyuktan kin na shesham atah param.
,BDEN PA RAB TU GANG SNANG BA,
,DE LAS GZHAN LTA CI ZHIG LUS,
To Pure One and the like—
And what else could be left over?
‘JIG RTEN NA DBANG PO LAS ‘DAS PA’I DON MTHONG BA LA MCHOG TU GRAGS PA TSANGS PA LA SOGS PA LA PHYI NANG GI ‘JIG RTEN ‘DI LA NI BDEN PAR RAB TU GANG SNANG BA

There are certain beings in the everyday world—Pure One and the like—who are widely celebrated as being able to perceive objects that are far beyond the normal senses.  But the fact is that both the outer and inner parts of this world appear to them as perfectly real.
DE NI BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA GCIG PU BDEN PA DAM PA YIN  GYI ‘DUS BYAS RDZUN PA BSLU BA’I CHOS CAN NO ZHES ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS LA RDZUN PA YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS NA,

The Conqueror though has stated that these same things—to realized beings—are nothing but a lie.  That is, he said that only nirvana, and nirvana alone, is ultimately true.  Produced entities, on the other hand, are nothing but things that mislead us.
DE LAS GZHAN SGYU MA LTA BUR MI ‘GYUR BA LTA CI ZHIG ‘DUS {%LUS } TE YOD PA MIN PA’O,,
And so what else could be left over, which were not like an illusion?  There wouldn’t be anything!
Reasoning on the sight of The Arya
Here secondly is the related logic on the sight of The Arya—
,‘JIG RTEN MA RIG LDONGS GYUR PA,
,MKHAS PA SRED PA DANG BRAL BA,
,DAM PA RNAMS LTA JI LTAR MNYAM,
By the strong current of desire.
Wise ones are free of desire;
TSANGS PA LA SOGS PA’I ‘JIG RTEN [f. 23a] PA BLO’I MIG MA RIG PA’I RAB RIB KYIS LDONGS SHING KHEGS PAR GYUR PA PHYIN CI LOG GI SRED PA’I CHU BO’I RGYUN GYI RJES SU ‘BRANGS PA’I SO SO’I SKYE BO DANG

Let’s consider first the mental eyes of Pure One and the like—those of the world.  These eyes are blinded, and blocked, by the cataracts of misunderstanding; these ordinary beings are swept along by the strong current of the river of desire, in itself mistaken.
MKHAS PA BLO’I MIG DAG PA ‘DI PA’I CHOS KYI BDUD RTZI’I KHU BAS NGOMS PA SRED PA DANG BRAL BA’I DAM PA RNAMS LTA BA JI LTAR MNYAM ZHING MTSUNGS PAR ‘GYUR,

And then on the other hand we have the wise ones, whose eyes are perfectly clear; holy ones who have drunk their full of the deathless nectar of this particular presentation of the spiritual teachings; and are thus free of desire.  How could we ever say that the viewpoints of the first group were in any way the same, or equal to, those of the second—of those holy ones who are free of all such desire?
DE LTAR NA ‘PHAGS PA BYIS PAR THAL BA DANG, BYIS PA ‘PHAGS PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,
In that case, realized beings would have to be infants; and infants realized beings.
GNYIS PA PHUNG SOGS BSTAN PA DRANG DON YIN PA LA, DE KHO NA NYID BSTAN PA’I RIM PA DANG, PHUNG SOGS DGONGS PAS GSUNGS PA, SKYE MED NGES DON YIN PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

This brings us at last to the second major topic of the entire text: establishing that statements about the parts of a person and so on were figurative.  We will cover this in three different parts: an explanation of the stages by which we teach suchness; showing how statements about the parts of a person and so forth were made with another point in mind; and then finally a demonstration that what was really being referred to was the way in which nothing starts at all.
DANG PO LA, RIM PA DNGOS DANG, DE LAS ‘DAS PA’I NYES DMIGS, DE’I GNYEN PO’O,,
We will present the first in three steps of its own: the actual treatment of the stages; the problems that arise when we fail to follow those stages; and then the antidote for those problems.
The first step is described in the following verse of the root text—
Sarvam astīti vaktavyam ādau tattva gaveṣiṇām,
Sarvam astiti vaktavyam adau tattva gaveshinam,
,DE NYID TSOL LA THOG MAR NI,
,THAMS CAD YOD CES BRJOD PAR BYA,
,DON RNAMS RTOGS SHING CHAGS MED LA,
And who are free of attachment,
GAL TE THAMS CAD RDZUN PA YIN NA BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS DON DAM PA KHO NA BSTAN PAR BYA BA MA YIN NAM, RDZUN PA BSTAN PA CI BYA ZHE NA,
Someone may come with the following question:
Suppose then that all these things really are deceptive.  Isn’t it though the case that the Conqueror teaches only that which is ultimate?  Why would he have taught something that was deceptive?
RDZUN PA YANG DGOS PA YOD NA BSTAN PAR BYA LA, BDEN YANG DGOS PA MED NA BSTAN PAR MI BYA BAS,

The fact though is that the deceptive is also something that should be taught, if there is a special purpose for doing so.  And it is also the case that the truth is not something that should be taught, if there is no special purpose for that.

DE KHO NA NYID KYI RTOGS PA TSOL BA’I SLOB MA LA BLA MA ‘GRO BA’I DON BSGRUB PA LA MKHAS SHING PHAN PAR ‘DOD PAS THOG MA KHO NAR NI PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED THAMS CAD YOD DO ZHES BRJOD PAR BYA’O,,

And so what we have here are sages who are masters at accomplishing the goals of living beings: teachers for those students who seek to reach a realization of suchness.  Out of nothing less than a desire to help these students, such teachers will (though only at the beginning) make statements about how all these things—the parts to a person; the categories of existence; and the doors of sense—do in fact exist.
BRAM ZE THAMS CAD CES BYA BA NI PHUNG PO LNGA DANG, SKYE MCHED BCU GNYIS DANG KHAMS BCO BRGYAD KYI BAR DAG GO ZHES GSUNGS SO,,
Lord Buddha did, after all, make that statement which goes:
O Brahmins, when I say “everything,” what I’m referring to is everything from the five parts to the person, to the twelve doors of sense, on up to the eighteen categories of existence.

YOD PA YANG RING PO LA BRTEN NAS THUNG NGUR ‘DOGS PA BZHIN DU GZUGS SOGS LA BRTEN NAS PHUNG POR ‘DOGS PA DANG, MAR ME LAS ‘OD ‘BYUNG BA BZHIN DU RGYU LA BLTOS NAS ‘BRAS BU RNAM PAR BZHAG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA’O,,

The way in which entities are established is that we call something “parts to a person” based on the presence of the physical form that makes up the first part; this is the same as when we call something “short” in comparison to something which is “long.”  Or sometimes we establish something which is a result based upon its cause, as when we talk about “the light that is coming from a lamp.”  These things do not though have any existence in & of themselves.
‘BRAS BU RE RE LA YANG RKYEN DU MA CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR [f. 23b] DANG, RKYEN RE RE LA YANG MTHA’ MED PA SKYE BA NA ‘BAD PA DU MAS SGRUB DGOS SHING ‘JIG PA NA ‘BAD PA MED PAR RANG GI NGANG GIS ‘JIG PAR

All the separate results there are in the universe have multiple factors that make them occur.  And each one of these factors can bear limitless results; we just have to make it happen, by putting forth many efforts.  But when these things come to an end, they tend to end all of their own accord—we need not put forth any effort for that to occur.

DON RNAMS RTOGS SHING ‘KHOR BA LA CHAGS PA ‘DOR BAR ‘DOD PA BDAG LA CHAGS PA LA SOGS PAS CHAGS PA MED PAR GYUR PA’I GANG ZAG LA DUS PHYIS NI RNAM PAR DBEN PA ZAB MO STONG PA NYID BSTAN PAR BYA’I, SNGA ROL TU MA YIN NO,,

Those who understand these things, and who seek to rid themselves of any attachment to the cycle of pain—those people who are free of attachment (in the form of attachment to some supposed self)—are candidates to whom, at some later point in time, the profound concept of emptiness, or sheer absence, can be taught.  This should not though be done before that point.
This brings us to our second step here, on the problems that arise when we fail to follow the proper stages for teaching emptiness—
Ye na kurvanti puṇyāni hatās te puruṣādhamāḥ.
Ye na kurvanti punyani hatas te purushadhamah.
,RNAM PAR DBEN DON MI SHES LA,
,GANG DAG BSOD NAMS MI BYED PA,
,SKYES BU THA SHAL DE DAG BRLAG

,‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS BSOD NAMS DANG BSOD NAMS MA YIN PA’I LAS DAG MI BYA BAR RIGS NA DE KHO NA NYID MA RTOGS PA RNAMS KYIS DANG POR RNAM PAR DBEN PA STONG PA NYID KYI DON MI SHES LA, BAR DU STONG PA NYID KYI SGRA THOS PA TZAM GYIS STONG PA NYID LA JI LTA BA BZHIN DU ‘JUG PAR BYED CING

Realized beings understand what they shouldn’t be doing, as far as actions which are merit and those which are not.  Thus they have a special way of dealing with those who have not yet realized suchness—who at first lack an understanding of the meaning of that sheer absence, emptiness.  They wait until later on, acquainting these people with simply getting used to hearing expressions having to do with emptiness, introducing them in an appropriate way to the void.
GANG DAG STONG PA’O ZHES LAS ‘BRAS YAL BAR DOR NAS BSOD NAMS DGE BA’I LAS MI BYED PA’I SKYES BU THA SHAL DE DAG BRLAG PAR ‘GYUR TE GCIG TU MI DGE BA LA ‘JUG PAS SKYES BU THA SHAL LO,,

They proceed in this way because those worst of the worst among people who—the minute you talk about emptiness—give up on the idea of karma & its consequences, and stop trying to perform good deeds, merit, ruin their life.  We call them the “worst of the worst” because then the only kinds of actions they are left doing are the non-virtuous ones.
With that we have reached our third step here: a description of the antidote for the problems that arise when we fail to follow the appropriate stages for teaching emptiness—
Gatayaś ca samākhyātāḥ saphalatvaṃ ca karmaṇām,
Tat svabhāva parijñānam anutpādaś ca deśitaḥ
Gatayash cha samakhyatah sapalatvan cha karmanam,
Tat svabhava parijnanam anutpadash cha deshitah.
,‘GRO BA DAG KYANG YANG DAG BSHAD,
,DE YI RANG BZHIN YONGS SHES DANG,
,SKYE BA MED PA DAG KYANG BSTAN,
And he also taught these two,
Where there is no more arising.

JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I NYES PA DE YONGS SU SPANG BAR BZHED NAS, BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS DANG POR RGYU DGE MI DGE’I LAS RNAMS DANG ‘BRAS BU RNAM SMIN BDE SDUG DANG BCAS PA NYID DANG ‘BRAS BU LA LONGS SPYOD PA’I ‘GRO BA DAG KYANG YANG DAG PAR YOD DO ZHES BSHAD LA,

Deigning to avoid, completely, the potential problems we’ve just described, the Conqueror first taught about this one thing; causes—that is, virtuous and non-virtuous types of karma—along with their inevitable effects: the karmic ripenings of pleasure and pain.  And he explained as well how, truly, there do exist the corresponding types of beings who experience these results.
DE’I RJES SU LAS ‘BRAS DE’I RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID DU YONGS SU SHES PA’I LAM BDEN DANG, DES THOB PA’I RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA MED PA’I ‘GOG BDEN DAG KYANG BSTAN TO,,

After all that, the Conqueror also described the truth of the path, where we come to a complete understanding of emptiness: the very nature of these karmas & their effects.  And then he also taught us a second of these two truths: the truth that we thus attain, of the end of suffering, where there is no more birth, or arising—at least, through any quality of its own.
RKANG PA DANG PO GNYIS KYIS SDUG KUN DANG PHYI MA GNYIS KYIS ‘GOG [f. 24a] LAM BSTAN TO,,

The first two parts of the verse here then are indicating the truths of suffering and the source of suffering; whereas the latter two parts refer to the truths of the end of suffering, and the path to that end.

DES NA DE KHO NA NYID STON PA RNAMS KYIS RIM PA LA MKHAS PAR BYA STE, PHAN YON CHE BAS SNYAM PA DANG, PHAN ‘DOD LTAR SNANG GIS DANG POR STONG NYID BSTAN NA RANG BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’I SDOM LDAN DU KHAS ‘CHE NA RTZA LTUNG ‘BYUNG LA,

Given all this, we can say that those of you who are teaching people about emptiness should gain some fluency in applying these stages we’ve been talking about.  Be careful about teaching someone emptiness straight off, because you think of this particular instruction as being so beneficial to people; or even because you think you want to help them but you actually have other intentions.  Remember that—if you have already taken your bodhisattva vows—you commit a root downfall when you share emptiness this way.

GZHAN YANG BRLAG PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR, SHING RTA CHEN PO RNAMS KYIS GO RIMS LOG PAR STON PA RNAMS KUN TU BKAG LA, PHAN YON TSOGS LAM LAS KYANG MTHONG LAM CHE STE, DANG POR SKYE MI SRID PA’I PHYIR DANG, PHAR PHYIN DRUG YANG DANG POR SHER PHYIN ‘BYUNG RIGS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And so—since otherwise we would also ruin ourselves—the great innovators have always taken care to object, strenuously, to those who have taught emptiness in the wrong order.  For example, as far as benefit, the path of seeing far outweighs the path of accumulation; but it is impossible to give rise to the former without first giving rise to the latter.  And if the six perfections were presented according to the same priority, then we would have seen them list the perfection of wisdom in first position.

STONG NYID LA SKRAG PA YANG LAS ‘BRAS LA YID CHES NAS DE’I RJES SU SKRAG PA ‘BYUNG BA YIN GYI, DANG POR BSTAN KYANG BLO KHAM PHYOGS PAS MI SKRAG CING LAS ‘BRAS RI BONG RVA’I GNYER MA BGRANG BA BZHIN DU GO NAS

And when we say that people are frightened by emptiness, that fright tends to occur after one has gained faith in the principles of karma & its consequences.  If we teach the emptiness first, then people’s thoughts would tend to head that way; and the fear would never come up.  They would start to think of observing the laws of karma & its consequences as being of as much use as counting the divisions on the antlers atop the head of a rabbit.
DGA’ BA PHAL CHER SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE, MI DGE BA SPONG BA’I SDUG BSNGAL BYA MI DGOS PAR GO BA’I PHYIR,

And in that case people would mostly feel at ease, rather than feeling frightened; they would start to get the idea that they no longer had to go through the pains required by working hard to give up our non-virtues.
GNYIS PA PHUNG SOGS GSUNGS PA DGOS PA CAN YIN PA LA DNGOS DANG SHES BYED DO,,

This brings us to our second more general part from above: showing how statements about the parts of a person and so forth were made with another point in mind.  We proceed with that explanation itself, followed by support for it.
The first of these is presented in the next verse—
Mametyaham iti proktaṃ yathā kāryavaśāj Jinaiḥ,
Mametyaham iti proktan yatha karyavashaj Jinaih,
,DGONGS PA’I DBANG GIS RGYAL BA RNAMS,
,NGA DANG NGA YI ZHES GSUNGS LTAR,
,PHUNG PO KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED RNAMS,
,DE BZHIN DGONGS PA’I DBANG GIS GSUNGS,
‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA MTHA’ DAG ZAD PAR SPANGS KYANG, DGONGS PA’I DBANG GIS RGYAL BA YANG DAG PAR RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS RNAMS GDUL BYAS SKYE MED RTOGS PA’I THABS SU NGA DANG NGA YI ZHES GSUNGS PA

Even though they had eliminated within themselves each & every trace of the view of destruction, the Victors—those perfectly and fully enlightened Buddhas—did indeed describe a “me” and a “mine,” but only because they had something else in mind.  That is, they did so only as a method for helping disciples to realize how nothing ever starts.
LTAR, PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED RNAMS THA SNYAD TZAM DU YOD PA LA DGONGS NAS DPE DE BZHIN DU DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PA’I THABS SU DGONGS PA’I DBANG GIS GSUNGS PA YIN NO,,

In the same way, only because they had something else in mind, the Victors described the parts to a person, and the categories of existence, and the doors of sense.  What they had in mind was for us to understand how all of these things existed only nominally, in a metaphorical way of speaking.  It was all spoken as a means for helping us realize suchness.
Logical support for saying there was
GNYIS PA LA, RIGS PA DANG, LUNG NGO,
We’ll present our support for saying that the Victors had something else in mind first with reasoning, and then with scriptural support.
The first of these is found in this next verse—
Taj jñāne vigamaṃ yāti nanu mithyā vikalpitam.
Taj jnane vigaman yati nanu mithya vikalpitam.
,‘BYUNG BA CHE LA SOGS BSHAD PA,
,LOG PAR RNAM BRTAGS MA YIN NAM,
The great elements and so on

RGYU’I GZUGS ‘BYUNG BA CHEN PO BZHI DANG ‘BRAS BU’I GZUGS BCU GCIG LA SOGS PA MDO LAS BSHAD PA NI MA RIG PA’I RANG BZHIN GYI RNAM PAR SHES PA LA RNAM PA GTAD NAS RNAM PA SHAR BA TZAM MA GTOGS YOD PAR BZHAG MI NUS PAS RNAM PAR SHES PA’I KHONGS SU ‘DU LA,

Let’s consider causal form—the four great elements;  and resultant form—their eleven products and so on, as those were described in the sutras.  These present themselves to our awareness—which has a nature of misunderstanding—and thus appear to it.  But because there is no other way that we would be able to establish them as existing, we consider them to be subsumed by this consciousness itself.
RNAM PAR SHES PA DE RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR SHES PAS NI ‘BYUNG BA SOGS LA BDEN PAR ZHEN PA’ANG ‘BRAL BAR ‘GYUR NA,
Once we understand that this consciousness doesn’t start through any nature of its own, then we are free as well of any belief that the elements and so on are real.
DE DAG LOG PA YANG DAG PA MA YIN PAR RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA MA YIN NAM DE YIN PAR THAL LO,,
And so wouldn’t we realize that these things are wrong, in the sense of not being as true as they seemed?  Of course we would!
MDOR NA ‘BYUNG SOGS CHEN PO RANG BZHIN MED DE, DE BRTEN NAS SKYES PA’I PHYIR CES PA’O,,
To put it briefly, what this verse is saying that the great elements and such don’t exist through any nature of their own—for they start through the process of dependence.
RNAM PA SHAR BA MA GTOGS PHYI DON YOD PAR BZHAG MI NUS TE, MO GSHAM GYI BU LA SOGS PA YANG YOD PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,
Beyond appearing to be that way, we cannot say that any of these things exist as outer objects.  If they did, then we would have to say that things like the child of a barren woman also existed.
SHES PA’I ‘DZIN RNAM YOD DAM MED, DANG PO LTAR NA, GZUNG RNAM YANG KHAS BLANGS PAS NANG DU PHYOGS PA DANG PHYIR PHYOGS PA’I CHA GNYIS KHAS BLANGS PAS
Now suppose someone comes and raises the following issue:

So does our awareness possess an aspect of being what grasps its object, or not?  If it does, then we would also have to accept that there was an aspect here of something which is grasped.  And then we would have to accept the idea of one part of awareness that focused inwardly, and another part which focused outwardly.
RANG RIG KHAS BLANGS LA, PHYI MA LTAR NA GZUNG RNAM MI ‘THAD DO ZHE NA,

And in that case, we would have accepted the concept of apperception: the ability of the mind to focus upon itself, in a single moment.  But if on the other hand we say that awareness does not possess an aspect of being what grasps its object, then the idea of there being an aspect where something is grasped would also be called into question.

SHES PAS YUL RIG PA GRUB PA RIG PA TZAM GRUB ZIN PAS RIG PA GRUB PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR TU RANG GI {%GIS?} RIG GAM GZHAN GYIS RIG DPYOD PAR MI RIGS TE, DE LTAR NA SHES PA BEM POR ‘GYUR TE, SGRON MES BUM PA GSAL DGOS PA BZHIN,

When we know an object with our awareness, then this knowing itself is already established!  It’s not necessary that we go from further from there, and in order to establish that there was a knowing, examine the question of whether the knowing is done through a process of the mind being known by itself or through a process of the mind  being known by something other than itself.  In such a case then awareness itself would become a physical thing—something that had to be illuminated, in the way that a lamp illuminates a water pitcher.
Scriptural support for saying there was
This then brings us to our second point here: the scriptural support.
,RGYAL BA RNAMS KYIS GANG GSUNGS PA,
,DE TSE LHAG MA LOG MIN ZHES,
,MKHAS PA SU ZHIG RTOG PAR BYED,
As the only thing which is true;
What person could there ever be
Were not things which were wrong?
LUNG LAS KYANG, BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS DGE SLONG DAG BDEN PA DAM PA ‘DI NI GCIG STE ‘DI LTA STE, MI BSLU BA’I CHOS CAN MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA’O ZHES GSUNGS PAS
We see too the following words from scripture—
And the Conqueror said, “O monks, there is only one truth which is ultimate, and that is the one thing which cannot deceive us: nirvana.”
MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA KHO NA BDEN PA GCIG PUR RGYAL BA RNAMS KYIS [f. 25a] GSUNGS PA
And so it is that the Victors have described nirvana as being the only thing which is true: the thing which is ultimate truth alone.
DE’I TSE, DE LAS LHAG MA PHUNG PO LA SOGS PA RNAMS LOG PA RDZUN PA’I DON CAN MA YIN NO, ZHES BDEN GNYIS KYI RNAM DBYE LA MKHAS PA SU ZHIG RTOG PAR BYED DE MI RIGS SO,,

That being the case, what person could there ever be who was wise in the division of things into the two truths, and who nonetheless would say something like “The rest of things—those other than nirvana, referring to parts to the person and so on—are though not things which lie to us; and are not things which are wrong.”  It would be a mistake for them ever to think this way.
GSUM PA SKYE MED GSUNGS PA NGES DON YIN PA LA,
We have now reached the third part promised earlier: a demonstration that what was really being referred to was the way in which nothing starts at all.
MA RIG PA LA SNANG BAS RANG BZHIN MED PA DANG, MA RIG PA’I RJES SU ‘GRO LDOG BYED PAS RANG BZHIN MED PA DANG, SKYE ‘JIG GNAS GSUM RGYU LA BLTOS PAS RANG BZHIN MED PA’O,,

We proceed in three sections: demonstrating that (1) things have no nature of their own, because they make their appearance to misunderstanding; (2) again they have no nature of their own, for the reason that they appear in the presence of misunderstanding, and disappear in its absence; and (3) the three of starting, ending, and staying have no nature of their own, since they rely upon their causes.
The first of these is expressed in the following verse—
Mano vispanditaṃ yāvat tāvan mārasya gocaraḥ.
Mano vispanditan yavat tavan marasya gocharah.
,JI SRID YID KYI RNAM G-YO BA,
,DE SRID BDUD KYI SPYOD YUL TE,
If it’s as we’ve described it,

JI SRID TSUL BZHIN MA YIN PA’I YID BYED KYIS YID KYI RNAM PAR G-YO BA YUL LA ‘JUG PA DE SRID DU ‘PHAGS PA’I SHES RAB KYI DBANG PO’I SROG GI BAR CHAD BYED PA SOGS KHYAD PAR DRUG DANG LDAN PA MA RIG PA’I BDUD KYI SPYOD YUL TE, GZHAN DBANG DU GYUR PA’O,,

So long as the misled state of mind—a state of mind where we are considering things in a mistaken way—is the one engaging in objects, it will create an obstacle to the very life force of the power of wisdom that belongs to a realized being.  This is but one of six different problems that arise at that point, as our mind becomes a playground for the very demons, and we fall under their power.
SKYE MED MNGON DU GYUR PA DE LTA YIN NA SKYE MED MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA ‘DI LA JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I NYES PA MED PAR CI’I PHYIR MI ‘THAD, BDUD KYI YUL DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR,

If on the other hand the direct appearance of the fact that nothing starts on its own is as we’ve described it, then who could ever deny that this—the state of realization where we see, directly, the way that nothing starts—possesses none of those problems which we’ve described here?  And that’s because one is freed then from the entire sphere of influence of the demons.
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS LAS, DANG PO MA RIG PA’I RJES SU BYED PAR BSTAN PA NI,

Which brings us to the second of our three sections here: demonstrating that things have no nature of their own, for the reason that they appear in the presence of misunderstanding, and disappear in its absence.  We proceed in two steps, beginning with a demonstration of how things follow upon misunderstanding.
Avidyā pratyayaṃ yasmāt Sambuddho lokam abravīt,
Tasmāl loko vikalpo’yam iti kiṃ nopapadyate.
Avidya pratyayan yasmat Sambuddho lokam abravit,
Tasmal loko vikalpoyam iti kin nopapadyate.
‘JIG RTEN MA RIG RKYEN CAN DU,
GANG PHYIR SANGS RGYAS RNAMS GSUNG BA,
RNAM RTOG YIN ZHES CIS MI ‘THAD,
Why then would it ever be
‘JIG RTEN NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA GANG LA MA RIG PA RKYEN DU YOD PAS MA RIG PA’I RKYEN CAN DU GRUB BO,,
Any time the world—referring to the five parts to the person that we have taken on at our birth—has misunderstanding as a contributing factor, then we can say that it is rooted in misunderstanding.

GANG GI PHYIR NA RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS KYIS MA RIG PA’I RKYEN GYIS ‘DU BYED, ‘DU BYED KYI RKYEN GYIS RNAM PAR SHES PA ZHES GSUNGS PA DE’I PHYIR NA ‘JIG RTEN ‘DI RNAM PAR RTOG PAS BTAGS PA TZAM YIN NO ZHES CIS MI ‘THAD DE,

The completely enlightened ones, the Buddhas, have stated that misunderstanding acts as the trigger for fresh karma; and fresh karma acts as the trigger for the continuation of our consciousness.  Why then would it ever be incorrect to say that this entire world is nothing more than a product of our imagination?
,GANG GI SA BON RDZUN PA DE’I,
,SKYE BA BDEN PA GA LA ZHIG
It’s just as the String of Precious Jewels describes it:
If the seed of something were false,
Then how could its birth be true?
GNYIS PA MA RIG PA LOG NA LDOG PA NI,
Here then is our second step, where we show how—when misunderstanding is stopped—all the rest comes to a stop as well.
Tat kathaṃ nāma na spaṣṭam ajñāna parikalpitam.
Tat kathan nama na spashtam ajnana parikalpitam.
,MI SHES PA LA KUN BRTAGS PAR,
SNANG BA NYE BA NA MUN PA BZHIN DU RIG PA’I YE SHES BYUNG BAS MA RIG PA ‘GAG PAR ‘GYUR BA NA
When wisdom—which does understand things—rises, then misunderstanding comes to a stop; just the way that darkness behaves as dawn approaches.
‘DU BYED LA SOGS PA GANG ZHIG ‘GAG PAR ‘GYUR BA DE MI SHES PA GTI MUG PA LAS KUN BRTAGS PAR JI LTA BUR NA GSAL BAR RTOGS PAR MI ‘GYUR TE,

Why then wouldn’t those elements of fresh karma and the rest come to a stop—why wouldn’t we see them cleared away—when all the mistaken imaginations of failing to understand things, these forms of darkness, were brought to light?
RAB RIB MED NA SKRA SHAD LDOG PAR MTHONG BA’I PHYIR RO,,
After all, we can see that—when a cataract is removed from our eyes—we stop seeing hairs sticking to our white porcelain sink.
No starting, no ending, no staying
With this we arrive at our third section from above: demonstrating that the three of starting, ending, and staying have no nature of their own, since they rely upon their causes.
Hetutaḥ sambhavo yasya sthitir na pratyayair vinā,
Hetutah sambhavo yasya sthitir na pratyayair vina,
,RKYEN MED PAR NI GNAS PA MED,
,DE NI YOD CES CI LTAR RTOGS,
Cannot remain, in the absence of
How then could you ever come
‘DUS BYAS GANG ZHIG SKYE BA RGYU DANG BCAS PA LA RAG LAS NAS ‘BYUNG BAS SKYE BA RGYU LA BLTOS CING GNAS BYED KYI RKYEN MED PAR YANG GNAS PA MED PAS GNAS PA’ANG RKYEN LA RAG LAS LA,

When any produced thing arises, it occurs in conjunction with—or reliant upon—a cause.  Thus we can say that the arising of things relies upon their cause, and that—in the absence of the necessary factors to sustain it—those things cannot remain.  As such, the remaining of things also relies upon specific factors.
GNAS PA’I RKYEN ZAD NAS MED PA’I PHYIR YANG ‘JIG PAR ‘GYUR BAS ‘JIG PA GNAS RGYU ZAD PA’I RKYEN LA RAG LAS NAS ‘BYUNG BA

When the necessary factors for something to remain have worn out, then because they are no longer present, that thing will go further and come to an end.  As such, ending is something which occurs dependent upon its own factors—represented by the wearing out of the causes for it to remain.
DE NI RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD CES CI LTAR RTOGS TE, RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD NA SLAR GZHAN DU ‘GYUR BA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR RO,,

How then could you ever come to some “realization” that these things existed through some nature of their own?  If a thing ever could exist through such a nature, then it would be totally impossible for it to change into something else.
GSUM PA PHUNG PO LA ZHEN PA’I NYES DMIGS LA, SKABS DGOD PA DANG, NYES DMIGS DNGOS SO,,

This brings us to the third topic from the very beginning of our work: the problems of attachment to the parts of a person.  We proceed in two sections: a presentation of some background; and then a description of the actual problems.
DANG PO LA, GZHAN SDE RANG BZHIN YOD PAR SMRA BA DE TZAM YA MTSAN MED PA DANG, RANG SDE RANG BZHIN YOD PAR SMRA BA CHES MI RIGS PA DANG, DE’I ‘THAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first topic we will cover in three steps: (1) explaining why it is nothing very strange when other groups assert that things have some nature of their own; (2) why it would be inappropriate in the extreme for our own group to say that things had some nature of their own; and (3) demonstrating how that truly is the case.  The first of these is presented in the next verse of the root text—
,GAL TE YOD PAR SMRA BA RNAMS,
,DNGOS MCHOG GZUNG NAS GNAS PA RNAMS,
,LAM DE NYID LA GNAS PA STE,
,DE LA NGO MTSAR CUNG ZAD MED,
Stay in this kind of viewpoint
GAL TE GRANGS CAN PA YON TAN GSUM DANG BYE BRAG PA RDUL PHRAN RTAG PAR YOD PAR SMRA BA RNAMS NI DNGOS PO MCHOG BDEN PAR [f. 26a] GZUNG NAS GNAS PA RNAMS NI

Suppose then that people from the Numerist school of thought—who believe in the existence of three unchanging qualities; and again people from the Detailer school of thought—who believe in unchanging, partless particles as constituents of all matter—stay in this kind of viewpoint where they hold things to be ultimate, or real.
RANG GI RTZA BA’I GRUB MTHA’I LAM DE NYID LA MI ‘GAL BAS GNAS PA STE DE LA NGO MTSAR CUNG ZAD KYANG MED DE,

In a way then they are simply remaining on their very own path—in the fundamentals of their own school of thought—since this idea in no way contradicts that path.  And so there’s not the slightest thing amazing about it: about their accepting this concept.
‘JIG RTEN NA MI SRID PA’I DON DMIGS NA YA MTSAN GYI RGYU YIN GYI, SRID PA NI MA YIN TE, DE NI LUGS DANG MTHUN PA’I PHYIR,

If we were talking about ideas that were completely unknown in the history of the world, that would make these ideas something strange.  But since they have been known here, people are just following a system they’re familiar with.
This brings us to our second step from above, which is why it would be inappropriate in the extreme for our own group to say that things had some nature of their own.
,SANGS RGYAS LAM LA BRTEN NAS NI,
,KUN LA MI RTAG SMRA BA RNAMS,
,RTZOD PAS DNGOS RNAMS MCHOG GZUNG NAS,
,GNAS PA YANG NI DE RMAD DO,,

SANGS RGYAS KYI LAM RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA KHAS LEN PA LA BRTEN NAS NI DNGOS PO KUN LA MI RTAG PA’O ZHES SMRA BA’I BYE BRAG SMRA BA DANG, MDO SDE PA DANG, RNAM RIG PA RNAMS NI CHOS THAMS CAD STONG PAR SMRA BA’I DBU MA PA LA RTZOD PAS

Let’s move on to those schools of thought which accept the path of the Buddha, in the sense of the concept that all things occur in a dependent relationship.  These schools also assert, since they rely on this position, that all functioning things are changing; and they include the members of the Detailists; the Sutrists; and the Mentalists.  Those latter though do dispute the thinking of those who belong to the Middle Way, since they profess that every existing thing is empty.
DNGOS PO RNAMS MCHOG BDEN PAR GZUNG NAS GNAS PA GANG YIN PA DE NGO MTSAR RMAD DU BYUNG NGO ZHES BRDA’I MING TSIG STE PHYAG ‘TSAL BAR MI ‘OS PA LA PHYAG ‘TSAL LO ZHES BRJOD PA BZHIN NO,,

And since they do engage in this dispute, we can say that they stay, keeping to the idea that things are “supreme”—which in this case means “real.”  And these then we can call “amazing,” which is meant to carry a connotation of disparagement.  It would be like saying “let’s bow to them” about a person who was not worthy of being bowed to.
With this we have reached the third part here, where we demonstrate how—truly—that is the case.
,RNAM PAR DPYAD NA MI DMIGS NA,
RTEN ‘BYUNG KHAS LEN PA SANGS RGYAS KYI LAM LA BRTEN NAS NI GZUGS ‘DI’AM TSOR BA DE’O ZHES GANG DU RIGS PAS RNAM PAR DPYAD NA RANG BZHIN CUNG ZAD KYANG MI DMIGS SO,,

When those who accept the concept of dependence—who rely upon the path of the Buddha—take this heap of physical form or that heap of feelings, and really examine any of them with logical thinking, then not the slightest self-nature can be observed in any of them.
RANG BZHIN MI DMIGS NA GZHAN LA BSTAN PAR MI NUS SO,,
And if a self-nature cannot be observed, then no one would ever be able to show it to another person.
BSTAN PAR MI NUS PA DE NI RTZOD PAS GZUGS ‘DI’AM TSOR BA DE BDEN ZHES SAM, RANG PHYOGS ‘DI’AM GZHAN PHYOGS ‘DI BDEN ZHES MKHAS PA SU ZHIG SMRA BAR ‘GYUR TE MI RIGS SO,,

And then suppose you take this something which could never be shown to anyone and argue about it—suppose you say that this heap of form or that heap of feelings was real.  What wise person would ever talk this way, deciding that this side or that side was correct on the matter?  It wouldn’t make any sense!
Which brings us to our second point from before, on a description of the actual problems of attachment to the parts of a person.

DNGOS POR SMRA BA THAR LAM LAS GROL BAR LTA BA’I CHUS KHYER BAR BSTAN, LTA BA DE NYID DON MIN PA’I RGYUR BSTAN, DNGOS ZHEN YOD NAS NYON MONGS SPONG MI NUS PAR BSTAN, YUL GYI GZEB [f. 26b] LA THOGS PA DANG MI THOGS PA’I DBYE BA BSTAN PA’O,,

This topic we will cover in four steps: (1) showing how those who assert that things which perform a function do so in & of themselves have been carried off on the mighty current of a viewpoint which “liberates” them from the real path to freedom; (2) demonstrating how that viewpoint serves as a cause for something we never wanted; (3) describing how—so long as one has this craving towards the reality of things—they will never be able to eliminate their negative emotions; and (4) detailing the two possibilities here, of getting stuck in the middle of objects, or not.
DANG PO LA, GZHAN SDE LTA BAS PHROGS PAR BSTAN, RANG SDE LTA BAS PHROGS PAR BSTAN, STONG PAR SMRA BA DE LAS LDOG PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

The first step will have three parts of its own: (1) showing how other groups have been stolen away by their mistaken views; (2) showing how some of our own groups have also been stolen away by mistaken views; and (3) showing how those who profess the principle of emptiness are the complete opposite.
The first part here is expressed in the next verse of the root text—
,GANG DAG GIS NI MA BRTEN PAR,
,DE DAG KYE MA RTAG MI RTAG
,LA SOGS LTA BAS PHROGS PA YIN,
GRANGS CAN SOGS GANG DAG GIS RGYU RKYEN LA MA BRTEN PAR BDAG GAM RTAG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG ‘JIG RTEN PHUNG PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR MNGON PAR ZHEN PA DE DAG LA NI

Let’s consider first the Numerists, and other such groups: those who refuse to rely upon ideas of causes & conditions, and who instead have a strong attraction to the idea that the self—or an unchanging thing—could exist through some nature of its own; or that the world (here a reference to the parts to a person) could exist through the same sort of nature.
MI ‘GYUR NA RTAG PAR SMRA BA DANG ‘GYUR NA CHAD PAR SMRA BAR ‘GYUR BAS

When people like this hold that the world could never change, what they are really saying is that nothing in the world could ever change; when they hold that the world could ever change, what they are really saying is that nothing in the world could exist at all.
RJES SU BRTZE BAS NA KYE MA RTAG PA DANG MI RTAG PA DANG {%DANG RTAG} MI RTAG GNYIS YIN PA DANG MA YIN PA LA SOGS PA’I LTA BAS PHROGS NAS DE’I GZHAN DBANG DU GYUR PA YIN NO,,

Out of sheer love for them then we have to cry out “My goodness!  You have been stolen off by viewpoints such as saying that things are either unchanging, or changing, or both unchanging & changing, or neither unchanging nor changing!  You have completely lost yourself to their power!”
YANG NA RANG SDE GANG DAG PHUNG PO LNGA GZUGS BRNYAN LTAR RANG BZHIN MED PA LA BDAG TU MING ‘DOGS KYI, SEMS KYI RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA BDAG TU ‘JOG PA DE DAG LTA BA’I CHU BOS KHYER TE,

Or we could put it this way, as referring to how some members of our own group have chosen to refer to the five parts of a person—which, after all, are similar to a reflection in a mirror in that they have no nature of their own—as being the “self.”  Or else those who assert that the mind (which they see as something that exists through some nature of its own) is the “self.”  All of these people have been swept away on the mighty current of wrong views.
SEMS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DE ‘GYUR NA CHAD PAR ‘GYUR MI ‘GYUR NA RTAG PAR ‘GYUR ZHES SBYAR TE, SNGA MA MDZES SAM BLA MA GSUNGS,

At this point you could also say it as someone has fallen into the extreme of holding that nothing exists at all, when they say that the mind exists through some nature of its own and can change.  And then when you say that the mind exists and cannot change, you have fallen into the extreme of holding that nothing can ever change.  My own Lama once said though that he thought expressing this idea as we did above might be more elegant.
Which brings us to the second part: showing how some of our own groups have also been stolen away by mistaken views.
Teṣām api kathaṃ na syur doṣās te śāśvatādayaḥ.
Tesham api kathan na syur doshas te shashvatadayah.
GANG DAG BRTEN NAS DNGOS PO RNAMS,
DE NYID DU NI GRUB ‘DOD PA,
DE DAG LA YANG RTAG SOGS SKYON,
GANG DAG DNGOS PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS ‘BYUNG BAR KHAS LEN BZHIN DU YANG DE KHO NA NYID DU GRUB PAR ‘DOD PA DE DAG LA YANG RTAG PAR LTA BA LA SOGS KYIS {%KYI} SKYON DE DAG JI LTAR ‘BYUNG BAR MI ‘GYUR TE,

The problems that come up with these others—seeing things as unchanging, or the like—don’t occur with those who, even as they accept the idea that things have come about through a process of dependence, at the same time hold that these entities still happen inside suchness.
RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I DNGOS PO KHAS BLANGS BAR ‘GYUR NA CHAD PA DANG, MI ‘GYUR NA RTAG PAR LTA BAR ‘GYUR RO,,
If you accept that things exist through some nature of their own, you’re a nihilist; while if you don’t, you’re of the viewpoint that things are unchanging.
Which then takes us to our third part: showing how those who profess the principle of emptiness are the complete opposite.
Nāpi tathyaṃ na cātathyaṃ hriyante te na dṛṣṭibhiḥ.
Napi tathyan na chatathyan hriyante te na dirshtibhih.
,GANG DAG BRTEN NAS DNGOS PO RNAMS,
,CHU YI ZLA BA LTA BUR NI,
,YANG DAG MA YIN LOG MIN PAR,
,DBU MA PA GANG DAG BRTEN NAS BYUNG BA’I DNGOS PO RNAMS CHU YI NANG GI ZLA BA’I GZUGS BRNYAN LTA BUR NI YANG DAG PA BDEN PAR GRUB PA YANG MA YIN LA, LOG PA GTAN MED KYANG MA YIN PAR SNANG LA

These of the Middle Way though understand those entities which occur through a process of dependence, and so resemble a reflection of the moon in a body of water.  That is, these things do not appear to them to exist purely, or in truth; but at the same time neither do they see them as having stopped: as things that do not exist at all.
RANG BZHIN MED PAR ‘DOD PA DE DAG RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BAS MI ‘PHROGS TE, DNGOS PO LA RANG BZHIN CUNG ZAD KYANG KHAS MA BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,
Those who believe that things have no nature of their own then are never stolen away by those viewpoints that things would either never change, or have already stopped altogether.
BRTEN NAS SKYES PA RNAMS NI YOD PA RANG BZHIN PA DANG MED PA RANG BZHIN PA SPANGS TE, GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU KHAS BLANG BAR BYA STE,

What we need to learn to accept is that things which arise in dependence neither exist, in some way that is natural to them; but nor do they not exist, in the sense of being devoid of any nature at all.
,KHYIM GYI DON DU KA BA SOGS,
Master Aryadeva put it this way—
To set up a plank of wood or such
To hold up the roof of their house.
ZHES KA BA LA SOGS RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD NA YANG, DE DAG GI DON DU ‘BAD PA BYED MI DGOS PAR ‘GYUR, MED PA RANG BZHIN PA YIN NA YANG DE DAG GI DON DU ‘BAD PA DON MED PA’I THAL BA ‘PHEN PA YIN GYI,

What this is saying is that—if it were the case that things like the supports which hold up a house existed through some nature of their own—then there would be no need to exert the effort to set them up.  But if, on the other hand, they didn’t exist—through some nature of their own—then that would imply that it would be meaningless to take the trouble to set them up.
YOD NA MI DGOS, MED NA MI NUS ZHES PA TZAM NI MA YIN NO,,
All we could say to ourselves then would be—
If they were here, we wouldn’t need them.
If they were not, we couldn’t need them.
GNYIS PA LA, DNGOS DANG, DE LDOG TSUL LO,,

And so we have reached the second step from above: demonstrating how that other viewpoint serves as a cause for something we never wanted.  Here in turn there are two parts: the actual presentation, and then how to prevent this disaster from happening.
The first of these comes in the following verse of the root text—
Rāga dveṣodbhavas tīvraḥ kaṣṭo dṛṣṭi parigrahaḥ,
Vivādās tat samutthāś ca bhāvābhyupagame sati.
Raga dveshodbhavas tivrah kashto dirshti parigrahah,
Vivadas tat samutthash cha bhavabhyupagame sati.
,DNGOS POR KHAS LEN YOD NA NI,
If we hold to a view
DNGOS PO BDEN PAR KHAS LEN PA YOD NA NI, NGES PAR RANG PHYOGS LA CHAGS PA’I ‘DOD CHAGS DANG, GZHAN PHYOGS LA RGYAB KYIS PHYOGS PA’I ZHE SDANG ‘BYUNG BA’I RGYUR GYUR PA’I LTA BA RNAMS SMIN,

If we hold to a view where we accept things as real, it will certainly mature into a view that serves as a cause for attachment to arise within our heart: where we grasp to our own version of things.  And it will mature as well into a view which serves as a cause for aversion to rise in that same heart: where we labor to oppose the views of others.
BSRAN PAR DKA’ BA BSKYED PAS MI BZAD PA ‘DA’ BAR DKA’ BA NYID KYIS MA RUNGS PA ‘DZIN LA DE LAS RANG PHYOGS BRTAN PAR ‘DOD, GZHAN PHYOGS BSAL BAR ‘DOD PA’I RTZOD PA ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And then we’ll start to feel that we can no longer stand it; that things have become unbearable, that we won’t be able to get through it.  That is, we will hold it all as a great tragedy, and then from that our attachment to our own version of things becomes ever more rigid.  From this then springs conflict, where we hope to stop the way that others think altogether.
GNYIS PA LA, MDOR BSTAN DANG, RGYAS BSHAD DO,,
Which brings us to how we prevent this disaster from happening.  We’ll start with an introduction, and then move on to a more detailed explanation.
The first is reflected in the next verse—
Sa hetuḥ sarva dṛṣṭīnāṃ kleśotpattir na taṃ vinā,
Tasmāt tasmin parijñāte dṛṣṭi kleśa parikṣayaḥ.
Sa hetuh sarva dirshtinan kleshotpattir na tan vina,
Tasmat tasmin parijnate dirshti klesha parikshayah.
,DE NI LTA BA KUN GYI RGYU,
,DE MED NYON MONGS MI SKYED DE,
,DE PHYIR DE NI YONGS SHES NA,
For all sorts of wrong views;
If we no longer possessed it,
If we come to a complete

DNGOS POR ‘DZIN PA DE NI SNGON MTHA’ DANG PHYI MTHA’ LTA BA SOGS LTA BA KUN GYI RGYU YIN LA LTA BA LA BRTEN NAS RANG GI LTA BA LA CHAGS SHING NGA RGYAL BA DANG, GZHAN GYI LA SDANG BA DANG, THAMS CAD DU GTI MUG ‘BYUNG NGO,,

This one grasping on to entities serves as a cause for all sorts of wrong views about the first beginning of things, and the final end—and the like.  And due to those views, we start becoming attached to our own viewpoints, and start to develop pride as well.  We begin to feel aversion towards the views of others; while dark ignorance infects every bit of it.
RJES ‘GRO BSTAN NAS, LDOG PA STON PA NI
Having explained the problems that follow on certain ways of looking at things, we turn to a description of how stopping these views then puts an end to the same problems.
DNGOS POR ‘DZIN PA DE MED NA CHAGS SDANG LA SOGS PA’I NYON MONGS PA MI SKYE STE DE’I PHYIR DNGOS PO DE NI RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID DU YONGS SU SHES NA

If we no longer possessed this tendency of holding to things as real, the corresponding negative emotions of attachment and aversion and the like simply wouldn’t occur.  As such, we need to come to a complete understanding of how the true nature of these things is that they are simply empty.
RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA NYON MONGS PA YONGS SU ‘BYANG ZHING DAG PAR ‘GYUR BAS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA’I THABS LA ‘BAD PAR BYA’O,,

Once we have reached such an understanding, we will be cleaned completely—totally purified—of viewpoints related to the negative emotions: viewpoints which necessitate either that things are unchanging, or stopped altogether.  As such, we should all be doing our best to master the various methods of coming to a realization that nothing has any nature of its own.
GNYIS PA LA, SHES BYA’I GNAS TSUL DANG, BLOS RTOGS TSUL LO,,
And this takes us to our more detailed explanation of the same point.  Here we’ll first describe the way of all things, and then move on to how we can come to a realization of that way.
DANG PO LA BRTEN NAS SKYES PA DANG, RANG BZHIN MED PA MI ‘GAL BA DANG, ‘GAL BAR GZUNG BAS NYES PA KUN ‘BYUNG BAR BSTAN PA’O,,

As for the first part, we’ll proceed in two steps: (1) showing how the idea that things arise in dependence, and the idea that nothing has any nature of its own, in no way contradict each other; and (2) a demonstration that—when we do think of these two ideas as opposed to each other—it brings about all the problems we ever face.
The former of these last two points is covered in the next verse of the root text—
Pratītya jātaṃ cājātam āha tattva vidāṃ varaḥ.
Pratitya jatan chajatam aha tattva vidan varah.
,BRTEN NAS SKYES PA MA SKYES PAR,
,THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA MCHOG GIS GSUNGS,
How is it that we reach
They do not start at all;
The one who knows all things.
RKANG PA DANG POS DRI BA, GNYIS PAS LAN, GSUM PAS RTEN ‘BYUNG GI RANG BZHIN, BZHI PAS DE GSUNG PA PO BSTAN TO,,

(1) The first section of the root text here poses a question, and (2) the second presents an answer.  (3) The third presents the nature of dependence, while (4) the fourth clarifies who it was that described this nature.
RANG BZHIN MED PAR SHES PAS NYON MONGS SPONG NA RANG BZHIN MED PA DE GANG GIS SHES PAR ‘GYUR SNYAM NA,
(1) One might ask themselves the following question—

People in the form or formless realms are the opposite: when they bring unattractive objects to mind, they lose manifest forms of desire.  Realized beings, though, who see beings as though they were illusions, devoid of any nature of their own, come to attain nirvana.

And just what is that like?  There is a point where we come to a complete realization of things and the lack of things—which is to say, when we no longer perceive any essence to entities, or to the lack of those entities.  And this is when, from the bottom of our hearts, we realize emptiness in all those things fully; when we know it perfectly.
Which brings us, secondly, to those other benefits—

Suppose we have, within us, that opportunity or cause for the birth of emotions like desire and the rest; that is, suppose we have the habit of holding to things as being real.  If we are residents of the desire realm, this will lead to feelings of desire arising in our hearts.

Suppose though that we meditate on the impermanence of things, and free ourselves of desire.  Which is to say, we will have destroyed that thing which dark ignorance sustains.

And think then of those great beings, those realized beings, who have realized that things have no nature of their own; who have seen what cannot be real. One may ask: How do we describe the ocean of suffering life?  It is a place which is constantly embroiled with the great water serpent of the negative emotions of desire and the like; a terrible and never-ending place, where the serpent breeds even more of himself.

And who can cross safely over this dreadful sea?  It can be crossed by any of those deep practitioners who, earlier—while they were on the paths of accumulation and preparation—have managed to have the thought that all the things there are, are completely devoid of any nature of their own.

These are great beings who have taken the thoughts—thoughts which are constantly jumping around, like a monkey—and stopped them from this jumping. When they do come to these thoughts that nothing has any nature of its own, we can say that they have had that realization of the entire accumulation of things which is like an illusion. ,GANG DAG GI BLO YOD MED LAS,
