,ZAB MO [f. 4b] DMIGS MED RNAM PAR RTOGS,
Those whose minds have gone beyond
The idea that things could exist or not,
And who no longer dwell there,
Understand that the meaning of a cause
That there is nothing at all to see.
KHO NA RE, BU MA SKYES PA DE BU SKYES PA’I SGRA DON DU MI ‘THAD PA LTAR, RANG BZHIN GYIS [f. 2b] MA SKYES PA DE RTEN ‘BREL GYI SGRA DON DU ‘GAL LO ZHE NA,
One may begin with the following claim—

It would be wrong to describe the fact that a child had not been born as “a child was born.”  Just so, it would be a contradiction to say that the literal meaning of the term “dependence” was “nothing started through any nature of its own.”
DE KHO NA NYID MA RTOGS PA’I BYIS PA LA LTOS TE ‘GAL BAR RTOG NA NI ‘GAL DU CHUG ,KHO BO CAG LA MI GNOD DE, DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA’I BLO LA LTOS NA NI MI RIGS TE,

Well, we suppose that—if you perceived something as a contradiction relative to the perceptions of an infant who has not yet realized suchness—you could in a way call it a “contradiction.”  But that wouldn’t hurt our own position in any way; it would be wrong to say the same thing relative to the perceptions of someone who had seen suchness.

DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA’I SH’A RI’I BU LA SOGS PA’I GANG ZAG GI MNYAM GZHAG DE DAG CHOS CAN, KHYOD KYI NGOR RANG BZHIN MED PA DANG RTEN ‘BREL MI ‘GAL BAR THAL, KHYOD DE NYID MA RTOGS PA’I PHYI MA’I {%BYIS PA’I?} YUL MA YIN PA DANG, MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI BLOS DMIGS PA MED PA’I RKYEN {%?} RTEN ‘BREL RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG PAR MNGON SUM GYIS RTOGS PA YIN PA’I PHYIR,
We could put this in the form of a logical argument:
Consider the deep meditative states of individuals—such as Shariputra—in which they see suchness.
To their perceptions, there is no contradiction between saying that things have no nature of their own, and saying that they occur in a dependent relationship;

Because these things could never be an object that an infant—someone who had not yet realized suchness—would ever perceive; whereas that element which the state of mind which holds to extremes cannot perceive is, indeed, realized by that state of mind which perceives, directly, that dependence is empty of any nature of its own.
DER THAL, YOD PA DANG MED PA DANG DE GNYIS KYI DBUS KYI MTHA’ GANG LA YANG MI GNAS PAR DNGOS PO MTHA’ DAG RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG PAR RTOGS PA’I PHYIR,
And that certainly is the case,

Because when we can keep ourselves from falling into any of the various extremes—thinking that things do exist, or thinking that things do not exist, or thinking that things are somewhere between the two—then we are able to come to the realization that every existing entity is empty of any nature of its own.
GNYIS PA LA MED LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA BSHAD ZIN DRAN PA LA SBYOR BA, YOD LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA MNYAN PAR GDAMS PA’O,,

With this we have reached our second point from above, which is advice to listen to teachings on the profound.  We’ll present this in two sections: (1) reminding our reader of the process of reasoning, which we’ve already presented, for denying the view that nothing exists; and then (2) presenting our advice to listen to the reasoning we use to deny the view that everything exists the way it seems to.
DANG PO NI, RE SHIG {%ZHIG} SOGS RKANG PA GNYIS LA,
The first of these points is covered in the two lines [of the Tibetan, five in the English] which begin with “To start with”—
,MED NYID RNAM PAR LDOG ZIN GYIS,

KHO NA RE, RTEN ‘BREL RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR MI RIGS TE, MNGON SUM LA SOGS PAS GNOD PA’I PHYIR DANG, LUNG GI GNOD BYED CHOS MNGON PA’I MDO LAS RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA TSE GSUM PA DANG, PHUNG KHAMS SKYE MCHED KYI RANG DANG SPYI’I MTSAN NYID GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR CE NA,
Someone may come with the following claim—
It is a mistake to say that dependence cannot exist through any nature of its own;
Because, first of all, this idea is drawn into question by our own direct perceptions, and the like.

Moreover, the idea is also drawn into question by scripture: the sutras on higher knowledge include those statements about how the process of dependent relationship requires three lifetimes for completion; while at the same time scripture talks about both the individual (“own self”) and overall defining characteristics of the parts to the person; the categories of existence; and the doors of sense.

MGON PO KLU SGRUB CHOS CAN, SKABS ‘DIR NYAN THOS SDE PA’I NGOR YON TAN ‘GRIB CING, NYES PA KUN GYI ‘BYUNG GNAS MED LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA RGYAS PAR MI STON PA’I RGYU MTSAN YOD DE, NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD RANG LAS MED LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA RGYAS PAR GSUNGS SHING, DE LA BRTEN NAS NYAN THOS DE DAG GIS [f. 3a] KYANG MED LTA BKAG PA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS ‘DIR MA BSHAD PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider then our protector, Nagarjuna.

There is a reason why, at this point in the text, he does not present—to those who belong to the listener group—any detailed presentation of the reasoning needed to deny that view that nothing could exist (a view which blocks the development of all good qualities, and serves as a source for every fault);

Because this reason is that the logic for denying the view that nothing could exist is something which has already been described, at length, in the body of scriptures belonging to these listeners themselves; and because of that, these listeners already deny the view that nothing could exist.
GNYIS PA NI, RIGS SOGS GNYIS LA,

Here next is that second section, where we present our advice to listen to the reasoning we use to deny the view that everything exists the way it seems to.  This is covered in the two lines [of the Tibetan, three lines in the English] that refer to “reasoning”—
RIGS PA GANG GIS YOD NYID KYANG,
LDOG PAR ‘GYUR BA MNYAN PAR GYIS,
We use to deny as well
That things could be as they seem.

RIGS PA GANG GIS YOD LTA ‘GOG PA LA NYAN THOS SDE PAS MNYAN PAR BYA BAR RIGS TE, RANG GI SDE SNOD LAS YOD LTA ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA GSUNGS KYANG, BAR MA CHAD PA DANG, RGYUN RING BA DANG, GZHUNG GCIG TU RGYAS PAR MA GSUNGS PA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS NYAN THOS SDE PA RNAMS YOD PAR BLTA BA LA ZHEN PA’I PHYIR,
It is appropriate that those of the listener group should listen to the reasoning which is used to deny the view that things exist the way they seem,

Because—even though the reasoning which denies this view has been described in their own collection of scriptures—those who belong to the listener group are still attracted to the idea that things exist as they seem.  And the reason for this is that those teachings (1) were not spoken in an uninterrupted flow; and they (2) were not spoken for any very long period of time; and they (3) were not described in any great detail within any one major teaching.
GSUM PA NI, JI LTAR SOGS BZHI LA,

Which brings us to our third part from before: a presentation of the reasoning used to disprove the extreme that things could exist.  This point is covered in the four lines [in the Tibetan, five lines in the English] which start with “Suppose that things”—
JI LTAR BYIS PAS RNAM BRTAGS BZHIN,
DNGOS PO GAL TE BDEN GYUR NA,
DE DNGOS MED PAS RNAM THAR DU,
GANG GIS MI ‘DOD RGYU CI ZHIG
Suppose that things were real, in the way
That infants imagine them to be.
That nothing about them was left,

DNGOS SMRA BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD KYI LUGS LA BYIS PA SO SO SKYE BO THAMS CAD PHUNG PO’I DNGOS PO PHYIS LEN PA MED PA’I MYANG ‘DAS THOB ZIN PA’I BDAG NYID DU RGYU MTSAN CIS MI ‘DOD NAS ‘DOD RIGS PAR THAL, KHYOD KYI LUGS LA BYIS PA RNAMS KYI DNGOS PO BDEN PAR BTAGS PA BZHIN DU DE DNGOS PO’I DE KHO NA NYID DU GRUB PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider those who assert that things which perform a function have some existence of their own.

Why—for what reason—wouldn’t they agree, in their system, that each & every infant (every ordinary person, who had not seen emptiness directly) was a special being who had already attained nirvana; a state where, after that, they would no longer have to take on those entities which are parts of a person?
Because it would certainly make sense for them to do so!

Because, according to their system, these same infants would be functioning things that we could label as being real; which means that they would have to be examples of the very suchness of functioning things.
so long as we hold the extremes
GNYIS PA LA, MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI LTA BA SRID PA LAS GROL BAR MI BSTAN, MTHA’ BRAL RTOGS PA GROL BAR BSTAN, RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O,,

With that we have reached our second more general section from above, which is describing how the state of wisdom we use to realize this point constitutes the path to free ourselves from this world of pain.  Here again we have three parts: (1) how we don’t say that you can ever be freed from this life of pain, if you keep to the view which holds to the extremes; (2) how you can be freed if you grasp the view that is free of the extremes; and (3) refuting objections to these positions.
DANG PO NI, YOD SOGS GNYIS LA RIM PA BZHIN,
Let’s proceed in two steps to treat the two lines here [seven in the English], which include “as if they existed”—
,YOD PAS RNAM PAR MI GROL TE,
DNGOS PO BDEN ‘DZIN GYI BLO CHOS CAN, KHYOD LA BRTEN NAS SRID PA LAS GROL MI NUS TE, SRID PA’I RGYU’I GTZO BO YIN PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider that state of mind where we take things to be real.
If we continue to rely upon such thinking, then there is no way that we will ever be free;
Because that way of thinking is, in fact, the principal cause of the life of pain.
RGYU ‘BRAS LA SKUR ‘DEBS KYI LTA BA CHOS CAN, BSAL BA SNGA MA LA, KHYOD NYES PA KUN GYI ‘BYUNG GNAS YIN PA’I PHYIR,
And let’s consider that state of mind where we discount the way that cause & effect functions.
(And then insert here the same assertion as in that last one);
Because that way of thinking is the actual source of each & every problem in the universe.
GNYIS PA NI, DNGOS SOGS GNYIS LA,

Which brings us to the second part, on how you can be freed if you grasp the view that is free of the extremes.  This point is covered in the two lines [four in the English] that include, “things and”—
,DNGOS DANG DNGOS MED YONGS SHES PAS,
,BDAG NYID CHEN PO RNAM PAR GROL,
Things and the absence of things.

DNGOS PO DNGOS MED RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG PAR RTOGS PA’I YE SHES CHOS CAN, KHYOD LA BRTEN NAS BDAG NYID CHEN PO ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS SRID PA LAS GROL BAR ‘GYUR TE, KHYOD SRID [f. 3b] PA’I RGYU’I DNGOS GNYEN YIN PA’I PHYIR,
Let us consider that wisdom with which we realize that things, and the absence of things, are empty of any nature of their own;
When they rely upon this wisdom, great beings—referring to the realized beings—are freed from this life of suffering,
Because this is the direct antidote to the very cause of suffering life.
are equally devoid of any nature
GSUM PA NI, DE SOGS RKANG PA BZHI LA,
This brings us to our third part, where we refute objections to these positions.  This is expressed in the four lines [in the Tibetan, eight in the English] which include “the way”—
Nirvāṇaṃ caiva lokaṃ ca manyante’tattva darśinaḥ,
Naiva lokaṃ na nirvāṇaṃ manyante tattva darśinaḥ.
Nirvanan chaiva lokan cha manyantetattva darshinah,
Naiva lokan na nirvanam manyante tattva darshinah.
To see the way things are
RIM PA BZHIN, RTEN ‘BREL RANG BZHIN MED KYANG SRID PA RANG MTSAN SPANG BYA DANG, MYANG ‘DAS RANG MTSAN PA THOB BYAR BSTAN PA LA DGOS PA YOD DE,

What these lines are indicating are the successive ideas that even though the principle of dependent relationship has no nature of its own, there was a purpose for teaching that this suffering life, in & of itself, was something we had to eliminate; and that nirvana, in itself, was something we had to achieve.
SRID PA DANG MYANG ‘DAS RANG MTSAN SPANG BLANG DU ZHEN PA LDOG PA’I PHYIR TU DE LTAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
The point of saying that this is the case was to stop people’s deep, mistaken belief that this suffering life, and nirvana, did in fact exist in & of themselves.
DE LTAR BSTAN NAS ZHEN PA LDOG NUS TE, ‘KHOR BA TZAM LA ‘DOR ‘DOD SKYES PA NA ‘KHOR BA RANG MTSAN PA LA ‘DOR ‘DOD BDE BLAG TU SKYE BA’I PHYIR RO,,

And the fact is that teaching them this way does have the capacity to put a stop to that deep, mistaken belief; because if we are able to raise a desire in ourselves to discard the cycle of pain as a normal entity, we can easily continue on to raising a desire in ourselves to discard a cycle of pain which exists in & of itself.
DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG LA LTOS TE ‘KHOR ‘DAS SPANG BLANG DU BSTAN PA MIN PAR THAL, BLO DE’I NGOR DE GNYIS SPANG BLANG THA DAD DU MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR,

But it is not the case that what we are indicating here is that the cycle of suffering, and nirvana, are—respectively—something that we seek to give up, and something that we seek to take up, all relative to that deep meditation in which we see suchness.  And that’s because these two cannot exist, to the perceptions of that state of mind, as things to give up or take up which are distinct from each other.
DER THAL, SRID PA DANG MYANG ‘DAS RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR,
And that certainly is the case, because neither this suffering life nor nirvana is a thing which exists through any nature of its own.
GSUM PA NI, SRID SOGS DRUG LA,

Which takes us to our third step from before: explaining how—by accustoming ourselves to this wisdom—we achieve the result.  This is presented in the six [eight] lines [of the Tibetan, sixteen in the English] which start by talking about the “life of suffering.”
Nirvāṇaṃ ca bhavaś caiva dvayam etan na vidyate
Nirvanan cha bhavash chaiva dvayam etan na vidyate
,SRID PA YONGS SU SHES PA NYID,
,MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS {%NGAN ‘DAS} ZHES BYA [f. 11b] BAR BRJOD,
,DNGOS PO BYUNG BA BZHIG PA LA,
,DE BZHIN DAM PA RNAMS KYIS KYANG,
And the nirvana where we go beyond it—
Are not things that could exist.

RTEN ‘BREL RANG BZHIN MED PA LA MYANG ‘DAS THOB RUNG BAR THAL, SRID PA RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA’I BLO GOMS PAR BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS GLO BUR GYI DRI MA DANG BRAL BA’I ‘GOG PA DE MYANG ‘DAS YIN PA’I PHYIR,
It is so certainly the case that nirvana can be achieved, even in a situation where dependence has no nature of its own;

Because it actually represents nirvana when we achieve a cessation where we are free of adventitious, or manufactured, impurities, because we have been accustoming our thoughts to the realization that this suffering life itself has no nature of its own.

DE ‘DRA’I MYANG ‘DAS DE SNANG LA RANG BZHIN MED PA SGYU MA DANG MTSUNGS PA YIN TE, DNGOS PO SNGAR SKYES PA DE PHYIS RGYU’I DNGOS PO ‘CHAR BA LA LTOS PA MA GTOGS RANG DBANG DU ‘CHAR RGYU MED PA’I PHYIR,
This type of nirvana does appear, but in a way where it has no nature of its own; and so is like a magical illusion.
And that’s because an entity which has already arisen can only do so by relying on the later appearance of its cause; there is no such thing as a case where it could appear all on its own.
GNYIS PA RGYAS BSHAD LA, ‘BRAS BU THOB TSUL, GZHI GTAN LA DBAB PA, LAM LA ‘JUG TSUL LO,,

With this we have reached our second general section from above: a more extensive explanation of the actual text which the author has committed to compose.  Here we will first describe how it is that we attain the result; then present the foundation nature of things; and then finally describe how it is that we engage in the path.
DANG PO LA, NYAN THOS SDE PA’I LUGS LA MYANG ‘DAS THOB PA MI ‘THAD PAR BSTAN PA, RANG LUGS ‘THAD PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

We’ll cover the first in two additional steps of (1) demonstrating how it would be impossible to say we had attained nirvana, in the system of the listener group; and (2) showing how our own position on the question is correct.
DANG PO LA, MYANG ‘DAS SPYIR BSTAN, BYE BRAG TU DGAG PA’O,,
Still further, with the first of these last two, we will give a general presentation on nirvana, and then our refutation, in greater detail.
DANG PO LA, MYANG [f. 4a] ‘DAS MNGON DU BYAS PA MI ‘THAD PAR THAL BA, ZAD MI SHES MI ‘THAD PAR THAL BA’O,,

And for the first of these last two we will first demonstrate (1) how it would have to be incorrect to say that someone had brought about their nirvana; and then (2) just how it would also have to be incorrect to say that someone had reached the knowledge of the end.

For the first of these, let’s focus just on the first three lines [in the Tibetan, first seven in the English] of the next verse—the ones that mention “completely”; and then we’ll go on to the fourth [in the Tibetan, eighth in the English].
,‘DUS BYAS YONGS SU SHES PAS MIN,
It is not when we reach

SDUG BSNGAL RANG MTSAN ZHIG STE RGYUN CHAD PA LA BRTEN NAS MYANG ‘DAS THOB PAR THAL BA DANG, ‘DUS BYAS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA LA BRTEN NAS MYANG ‘DAS MI THOB PAR THAL, LAS NYON DANG SDUG BSNGAL RANG MTSAN GNYEN PO’I STOBS KYIS BCOM PA’I STOBS KYIS MYANG ‘DAS THOB PA’I PHYIR,

And so you must be saying that we achieve nirvana through the destruction of suffering which exists in & of itself; or you must be saying that it is not the case that we achieve nirvana by relying upon the realization that products of causes have no nature of their own.

Because, according to you, we achieve nirvana through a process where karma & the negative emotions—and suffering itself—which all exist in & of themselves are destroyed by the power of their antidote.
‘DOD NA, MYANG ‘DAS MNGON DU BYAS PA MI ‘THAD PAR THAL, PHUNG PO ZHIG PA’I DUS DER MNGON DU BYED PA PO’I GANG ZAG MED, GANG ZAG YOD DUS PHUNG PO ZHIG PA MI ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR,
And suppose you agree to all that.  But wouldn’t it then be incorrect to say that someone had brought about their nirvana?

Because—at that point when the parts to the person had been destroyed—wouldn’t there be no person left; no one left to be the one who had brought about their nirvana?  And wouldn’t it be incorrect to talk about the parts to a person having been destroyed, at a point in time when the person was still present?
GNYIS PA NI, ZHIG SOGS GCIG LA

Which brings us to our second point here: how it would also have to be incorrect to say that someone had reached the knowledge of the end.  This idea is covered in the single line [of the Tibetan, two lines of the English] of this verse which mention “destroyed.”
DGRA BCOM THOB TSE BDAG GI SKYE BA ZAD DO SNYAM PA’I ZAD PA SHES PA MI ‘THAD PAR THAL, DGRA BCOM PA’I DUS NA PHUNG PO RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA YOD PA’I PHYIR,
And then wouldn’t it be wrong for us—at the point where we had achieved the state of an enemy destroyer—to have that knowledge of the end where we say, “I have finished off all my births”?
Because wouldn’t the parts to us—even during that time when we were an enemy destroyer—arise or be born, in a process that existed in & of itself?
ZHIG CES ZHES PA LTAR NA, SKYE BA ZAD DO ZHES PA’I MDO’I DON MI ‘THAD PAR THAL, RTAGS SNGA MA’O,,
And then when it says “destroyed” here, wouldn’t it be incorrect to say that the point of sutra at that juncture was to say that we had finished off our births?
For the same reason that we just listed.
GNYIS PA LA LHAG BCAS DANG, LHAG MED KYI MYANG ‘DAS DGAG PA’O,,

In the second part then, we continue our refutation—in greater detail.  Here there are two steps: (1) refuting the idea of a nirvana where something is still left over; and then (2) refuting the idea of one where nothing is left over.
DANG PO NI, GAL TE SOGS GNYIS LA,
The first of these is presented in the root text with the two lines here [six in the English] that start with “If”—
If the parts to a person
Then even if we had finished off
NYON MONGS ZAD PA’I LHAG BCAS KYI MYANG ‘DAS MED PAR THAL, PHUNG PO RANG GI MTSAN NYID MA ‘GAGS PAR YOD PA’I PHYIR,
And so isn’t it the case that there is no such thing as a nirvana where something is still left over—where we have eliminated our negative emotions?
Because isn’t it the case that parts to a person which exist in & of themselves have not stopped, but are—rather—still present?
KHYAB PAR THAL, JI SRID PHUNG POR ‘DZIN PA YOD PA, DE SRID DU NGAR ‘DZIN SKYE BA’I PHYIR RO,,
And isn’t it the case that one certainly does imply the other?
To the parts to a person,
GNYIS PA NI, GANG SOGS GNYIS LA,
Which brings us to our second point, refuting the idea of a nirvana where nothing is left over.  This we find in the two lines [four in the English] which mention “when” at this point.
Have come to a stop for them
PHUNG PO MA LUS ‘GAGS PA’I LHAG MED KYI MYANG ‘DAS MED PAR THAL, LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS SU PHUNG PO RANG MTSAN YOD LA, DE YOD NA DE LA DMIGS NAS NYON MONGS [f. 4b] SKYE BA’I PHYIR RO,,
And so can’t we say then that there is no such thing as a nirvana where there is nothing left at all; where we have put a stop to each & every one of the parts to a person?

Because isn’t it the case that—during the period when we are in that nirvana where something is still left over—don’t we have parts to us that exist in & of themselves?  And isn’t it true that, so long as we do have such parts, we will experience negative emotions arising, which are focused on those parts?
RANG LUGS LA MYANG ‘DAS THOB PA ‘THAD PA LA, RANG BZHIN MED PA’I LTA BA GOMS PAR BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS MYANG ‘DAS THOB PAR ‘THAD PA DANG, ‘GOG PA DE SGYU MA LTA BUR BSTAN PA’O,,

Which brings us to our second additional step from before: showing how our own position on the attainment of nirvana is correct.  We’ll cover this in two parts of (1) demonstrating how it would be impossible to say we had attained nirvana, in the system of the listener group; and (2) showing how our own position on the question is correct.
DANG PO LA, MYANG ‘DAS MNGON DU BYAS PA’I DUS, CHOS NYID RTOGS PA’I YE SHES LA NGO BOS BYAS PA’I DBYE BA MED PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

And we’ll cover the first of these parts in two sections of its own: (1) describing when it is that we bring about nirvana; and (2) demonstrating how there are no essential divisions to the wisdom with which we realize the real nature of all things.
DANG PO NI, MA SOGS DRUG LA,
The first of these points is presented in the six lines [of the Tibetan, thirteen in the English] that talk about “misunderstanding”—
Utpādo vā nirodho vā na kaścid upalabhyate.
Dṛṣṭe dharme ca nirvāṇaṃ kṛta kṛtyaṃ tad eva ca.
Utpado va nirodho va na kashchid upalabhyate.
Dirshte dharme cha nirvanan kirta kirtyan tad eva cha.
,MA RIG RKYEN CAN BYUNG BA LA,
,YANG DAG YE SHES KYIS GZIGS NA,
,DE NYID MTHONG CHOS MYA NGAN LAS,
,‘DAS SHING BYA BA BYAS PA’ANG YIN,
It also means that we have
Done what we had to do.
‘DU BYED SOGS CHOS CAN, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED DE, DE YOD NA ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG YE SHES KYIS GZIGS DGOS PA LAS MA GZIGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,
Let’s consider fresh karma and the rest.
They do not arise through any nature of their own,
Because—if they did—then that would have to be something which can be observed by that deep meditation of a realized being, whereas no such observation occurs.
DES MA DMIGS PAR THAL, MA RIG PA’I RKYEN STOBS LAS BYUNG BA YIN PA’I PHYIR,
And it is in fact correct to say that no such observation by that state of meditation occurs here,
Because that would have occurred through the power of the factor of misunderstanding.
And then we can say the following about the last two lines [in the Tibetan; last four lines in the English] here:

RANG BZHIN MED PA LA MYANG ‘DAS MNGON SUM DU BYAS PA ‘THAD PAR THAL, RANG BZHIN MED RTOGS GOMS PAR BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS NYON MONGS MA LUS PA ZAD PA’I LHAG BCAS KYI GNAS SKABS DER, MTHONG CHOS TSE DE LA MYANG ‘DAS THOB PA DANG TSANGS DANG SPYOD STOBS LA SOGS PA’I BYA BA BYAS PA’I PHYIR,
It certainly is correct to say that a person can bring about their nirvana, in a case where nothing has any nature of its own;

Because the following is true, when we are talking about that point in time where—because they have been accustoming themselves to the realization that nothing has any nature of its own—a person has reached a nirvana where something is still left over, and come to the end of each & every negative emotion.  That is, at this point they have attained nirvana as something experienced in this very life; and they have done those things that they needed to do, as far as their keeping a pure way of life; and undertaking the necessary activities; and practicing the powers and so on.
‘ANG SGRAS BDAG GIS {%GI} SKYE BA ZAD PA DANG, ‘DI LAS SRID PA GZHAN MI SHES PA LTA BU’O,,

When the root text lines mention here that “it also means,” it refers to things like knowing that I have finished off my births; and knowing that I will experience no other lifetimes here in the world of pain.
GNYIS PA NI, GAL TE SOGS DRUG LA,

Which brings us to that second section: demonstrating how there are no essential divisions to the wisdom with which we realize the real nature of all things.  This is found in the six lines [of the Tibetan, thirteen in the English] which begin with “suppose that”—
,GAL TE CHOS SHES MJUG THOGS SU,
,‘DI LA BYE BRAG YOD NA NI,
,DNGOS PO SHIN TU PHRA BA LA’ANG,
,GANG GIS SKYE BAR RNAM BRTAGS PA,
,RNAM PAR MI MKHAS DE YIS NI,
,RKYEN LAS BYUNG BA’I DON MA MTHONG,
Those who truly have no wisdom—
For things to arise from factors.

DE KHO NA NYID LA MI MKHAS PA’I DNGOS SMRA BA’I LUGS MA MTHONG BA DES, RKYEN RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA RO GCIG PA’I DON MNGON DU MA MTHONG BAR THAL, DNGOS PO SHIN TU PHRA BA RTEN CING ‘BREL BAR ‘BYUNG BA’I RDUL PHRA RAB LA SOGS PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA RNAM PAR BTAGS PA’I PHYIR,

Let’s consider those who belong to schools of thought where they say that functioning things exist in & of themselves; that is, schools of thought for those who are not wise in the ways of suchness: those who cannot see.
They cannot have seen, directly, that “single taste” of factors, of things that occur in a dependent relationship.

And that’s because they fantasize that there is a way that extremely subtle entities—atomic particles or the like which occur in a process of dependent relationship—arise through some quality of their own.

KHYAB PAR THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA YOD NA CHOS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA SNGAR MA SHES GSAR DU SHES PA’I MJUG THOGS SU [f. 5a] MI RTAG PA LA SOGS PA’I DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA MTHONG LAM GYI SKABS DER, RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA SO SOR GCOD DGOS PA’I PHYIR,
And the reason we’ve given here certainly does imply our conclusion,

Because if there did exist such a thing as things starting through some quality of their own, then following upon our new understanding of what we did not understand before—about “things,” or ultimate reality; then at that point in time, upon the path where we see, see the ultimate truth about things like impermanence and the rest, we would have to perceive those things in different aspects: we would have to be breaking things into these dissimilar aspects.
YANG NA, DNGOS PO SMRA BA DE DAG GIS RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I DON PHYIN CI MA LOG PA MA MTHONG ZHES PA’O,,

You could also gloss these lines as describing how those that hold functioning things to exist in & of themselves have not yet seen the unmistaken meaning of how things occur in a dependent relationship.
GNYIS PA LA ‘GAG PA RDZAS GRUB DGAG ,SGYU MA LTA BU’I ‘GOG PA SGRUB PA’O,,

This brings us to our second point in this discussion on nirvana, which is showing how our own position on the question is correct.  Here we proceed in two steps of (1) denying that there could be such a thing as a cessation which existed in a substantial way; and (2) proving the idea of a cessation that is similar to a magical illusion.
DANG PO NI, NYON MONGS SOGS DRUG LA,
The first of these steps is discussed in the six lines [of the Tibetan, thirteen in the English] which mention “negative emotions”—
,NYON MONGS ZAD PA’I DGE SLONG GI
,DE’I RTZOM RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS KYIS,
,GANG MA BSHAD PA RGYU CI ZHIG
,[f. 16a] RTZOM PA YOD NA NGES PAR YANG,
If they have put a final stop to
DNGOS PO SMRA BA’I LUGS LA ‘KHOR BA LA THOG MA’I RTZOM PA YOD PAR THAL, NYON MONGS ZAD PAR SPANGS PA’I GONG NAS ‘KHOR BA RANG MTSAN RGYUN CHAD PA’I MYANG ‘DAS ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR,

Wouldn’t it be the case, then, that according to this system of those who say that functioning things could exist in & of themselves, there would have to exist an “outset” or first beginning to the cycle of pain?

Because wouldn’t it then be correct to say that there did exist a nirvana where we had cut off the flow of a cycle of pain that existed in & of itself, even before we had eliminated the negative emotions, down to their very last one?
‘DOD NA, CHOS CAN, {%’DOD NA,} DER THAL, DE YOD NA SANGS RGYAS KYIS GSUNG RIGS PA LAS MA GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
And suppose you agree that there were such an “outset.”
Wouldn’t it then have to be as we just said it?
But wouldn’t that be mistaken?  Because, if there were such a thing, wouldn’t it have been appropriate for the Buddha to have mentioned it?  Whereas, in fact, he never did.
GANG ZAG DE NGES PAR RGYU LA SKUR BA ‘DEBS PA’I LOG LTA CAN DU ‘GYUR LA {%’GYUR BAR THAL,} ‘KHOR BA LA THOG MA, {%no ,} YOD PAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,
And wouldn’t this person then become somebody who was surely entertaining wrong views, discounting the principles of causation?
Because wouldn’t they be accepting the mistaken idea that the cycle of pain did have a first beginning?
GNYIS PA LA, DPE DON SGO NAS MDOR BSTAN, RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI, RTEN SOGS DRUG LA,

Here then is our second step here, where we prove the idea of a cessation that is similar to a magical illusion.  This discussion covers two sections: a brief presentation using a metaphor and what it refers to; and then a more detailed presentation.
,DE LA SNGON DANG THA MA CI,
,SNGON SKYES PA NI JI LTAR NA,
,SNGON DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ BRAL BA,
,‘GRO BA SGYU MA BZHIN DU SNANG,
They could come to a stop?
‘KHOR BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD LA SNGON DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, RTEN ‘BREL YIN PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider then the cycle of pain.
Its first earlier parts and its later parts cannot exist through any nature of their own,
DE CHOS CAN, RTAG PAR THAL, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYES PA’I PHYIR,
And let’s consider that same cycle.
Shouldn’t it be an unchanging thing?
Because, after all, it has arisen (according to you) through some nature of its own.
KHYAB PAR THAL, SNGON SKYES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, SLAR DE LDOG TU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR,
And our reason here does indeed establish our assertion,
Because if the parts that started earlier existed through some nature of their own, then it would not make sense to say that—at some later point—they had stopped.
PHYI MA LA ‘KHOR ‘DAS THAMS CAD SNANG LA RANG BZHIN MED PA SGYU MA DANG MTSUNGS PAR THAL, SNGON DANG PHYI MTHA’I RANG BZHIN DANG BRAL BAR GNAS PA’I PHYIR,

As for the latter part of the root text here, we can say that it is the case that everything which appears in the world—whether it belongs to the cycle of pain or to what is beyond that circle—must be exactly the same as an illusion.
And that’s true because the earlier part and the later parts of this cycle are devoid of any nature of their own.
GNYIS PA LA, DPE BSHAD, DON BSHAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI, GANG SOGS BZHI LA,

Our more detailed presentation will proceed in two steps: an explanation of the metaphor, and then an explanation of what it refers to.  The first of these is found in the four lines [in the Tibetan, ten lines in the English] which include the words “those who”—
,SGYU MA SHES PA DER MI RMONGS,
,SGYU MA MI SHES YONGS SU SRED,
Are free then of that ignorance.

SGYU MA MKHAN CHOS CAN, SGYU MA’I RTA GLANG LA RTA GLANG TSAD MAR ZHEN [f. 5b] NAS DE’I SNGON DANG PHYI MTHA’ LA RMONGS PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, DE DAG SNGAGS DANG RDZAS LA SOGS ‘KHRUL RGYUS BSLAD PA TZAM LAS BYUNG BAR SHES PA’I PHYIR,

They might have a feeling that a horse and cow which are magical illusions are a real horse and a real cow, but it’s not as though they lack an understanding about how they first appeared, or how they are going to disappear.  That is, they understand that the perception they have of these two animals is only something occurring because their senses have been affected by conditions that create the deception; these might include, for example, special spells or powders.
SGYU MA’I LTAD MO BA DE DAG CHOS CAN, SGYU MA’I RTA GLANG GI SNGON DANG PHYI MTHA’ LA RMONGS PAR ‘GYUR TE, DE DAG RTA GLANG TSAD MAR ZHEN PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider next the onlookers who are watching the illusion.
They are ignorant about how these things have first made their appearance; or where they are going to afterwards.  And that’s because they are attached to thinking of the horse or cow as being real.
GNYIS PA NI SRID SOGS BRGYAD LA,
The second step here—explaining what the metaphor refers to—is covered in the eight lines [in the Tibetan, fourteen in the English] which mention “this life of suffering.”
,BLO YIS MTHONG BAR GYUR BA NI,
,‘GRO BA RNAM PAR MI SHES SO,,

DE DAG RTOGS PA’I ‘PHAGS PA CHOS CAN, SNGON DANG PHYI MA’I MTHAR RTOG PA’I MTHAR ‘DZIN GYIS LTA BAS RGYUD BSLAD PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, ‘GRO BA THAMS CAD SMIG RGYU SGYU MA DANG MTSUNGS PAR RANG BZHIN MED PAR MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA’I PHYIR,
Now let’s consider realized beings who have come to a realization about these things.
Their minds are never infected by any point of view which holds on to an extreme—where they imagine that there is some first beginning, or final end;
Because they see, directly, that each & every being there is, is just the same as a mirage, or an illusion: they have no nature of their own.
Let’s take a special look at the latter four lines [in the Tibetan, seven in the English] here.

NYAN THOS SDE BA DE DAG CHOS CAN, RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA YAN LAG BCU GNYIS KYI ‘KHOR LO SNGON GYI MTHA’ DANG PHYI MA’I MTHA’ RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA’I ‘KHOR TSUL JI LTA BA BZHIN MI SHES PAR THAL, ‘DUS BYAS THAMS CAD RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE ‘JIG BYED PAR RTOGS {%RTOG} PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider those who belong to the listener group.

They certainly do not understand, correctly, the wheel of life, with its twelve different links describing how things occur in a dependent relationship; that is, they certainly do not understand how the earlier parts and the later parts of this wheel spin in a circle, with no nature of their own.
And that’s because they still imagine that each & every produced entity there is goes about starting & stopping through some quality of its own.
GZHI GTAN LA DBAB PA LA,
This brings us to our second general section from above; that is, how we present the foundation nature of things.
‘DUS BYAS RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR BSTAN PA DANG, DE GZHAN LA JI LTAR ‘CHAD PA’I TSUL, DE RGYAL BA’I DGONGS PAR BSGRUB PA, ZHAR LA LTOS PA’I DBYE BA BSTAN PA’O,,

We’ll cover this point in four steps.  (1) First we’ll demonstrate how it is that produced things cannot exist through any nature of their own; (2) then describe how we explain this point with other things; (3) next prove how this is actually the true intent of the Victors; and (4) finally present, as an incidental point, the different divisions of the concept of reliance.
DANG PO LA SKYE ‘JIG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG ,SKYE ‘JIG GSUNGS PA’I DGOS PA, DON DE NYID NGES PAR BYA BA’O,,

We’ll treat the first of those three steps in three parts of its own: (1) denying that starting & stopping could occur through any nature of their own; (2) explaining the purpose why statements were made about starting & stopping; and (3) confirming certain points about this subject.
DANG PO LA RGYAS PAR BSHAD, DON BSDU BA’O, ,DANG PO LA SKYE BA DGAG ,‘JIG PA DGAG PA’O,,

We’ll cover the first of these in two steps: a more detailed explanation, and then a concluding summary.  For the first step, we’ll first present a denial of starting; and then move on to a denial of stopping.
DANG PO NI, DE SOGS BZHI LA,
Our denial that things start is found in the four lines [in the Tibetan, ten in the English] which start with “anything”—
Tat tat prāpya yad utpannaṃ notpannaṃ tat svabhāvataḥ,
Yat svabhāvena notpannam utpannaṃ nāma tat katham.
Tat tat prapya yad utpannan notpannan tat svabhavatah,
Yat svabhavena notpannam utpannan nama tat katham.
DE DANG DE RTEN GANG ‘BYUNG DE,
RANG GI NGO BOR SKYES MA YIN,
RANG GI NGO BOR GANG MA SKYES,
DE NI SKYE ZHES JI SKAD BYA,
‘DU BYED SOGS CHOS CAN, RANG GI NGO BO’I RANG BZHIN DU MA SKYES PAR THAL, RGYU DE DANG DE LA BRTEN NAS ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider then fresh karma, or any of the rest of those;
The fact is that they cannot have started through any essential nature of their own,
Because they each occur in dependence upon their individual causes.
‘DOD NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR THAL, RANG GI NGO BO DANG GZHAN [f. 6a] GYI NGO BO’I RANG BZHIN DU MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR,
Suppose you agree to that idea.
Can’t we say, then, that there is no such thing as something arising through any nature of its own?
Because isn’t it true that they exist neither as something with an essence of its own, nor as something with some other kind of essence?
GNYIS PA NI, RGYU SOGS BZHI LA,
This brings us to our second step from above: a denial of stopping.  This we find in the four lines [of the Tibetan, ten of the English] which mention “the cause”—
,RGYU ZAD NYID LAS ZHI BA NI,
,ZAD CES BYA BAR DMIGS PA STE,
,RANG BZHIN GYIS NI GANG MA ZAD,
,DE LA ZAD CES CI SKAD BRJOD,
Through any nature of its own
‘DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, ‘DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA DE ‘DU BYED SOGS KYI RGYU ZAD PA LAS,{%no ,} ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider the ending of fresh karma, and the rest.
It must not be something which occurs through any nature of its own,
Because that ending of things like fresh karma is something that comes about through the wearing out of its causes.
‘DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, RANG GI NGO BO DE GZHAN GYI NGO BO’I RANG BZHIN DU MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR,
And it must so be the case that the ending of things like fresh karma cannot be something which comes about through any nature of its own,
Because its own essence cannot exist as the nature of the essence of something else.
DON BSDU BA NI, DE SOGS GNYIS LA,
Na hyatrotpadyate kiṃcin nāpi kiṃcin nirudhyate.
Na hyatrotpadyate kinchin napi kinchin nirudhyate.
,DE LTAR CI YANG SKYE BA MED,
SKYE ‘GAG GNYIS KA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, DE GNYIS KA RGYU LA BRTEN NAS BYUNG BA’I PHYIR,
And so let’s consider starting & stopping.
The fact is that neither one of them can exist through any nature of its own;
Because both of them come about through dependence on their causes.
GNYIS PA NI, SKYE SOGS DRUG LA,

Which brings us to our second part from above: explaining the purpose why statements were made about starting & stopping.  This point comes in the root text in the six lines [in the Tibetan, fifteen in the English] that include “starting”—
,‘JIG PA SHES PAS MI RTAG SHES,
SKYE ‘JIG RANG BZHIN MED KYANG MDO LAS, SKYE ‘JIG GSUNGS PA LA DGOS PA YOD DE, DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA RTOGS PA’I PHYIR TU SKYE ‘JIG GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
Even though they have no nature of their own, still there was a specific purpose why the Buddha spoke of them—both starting & stopping.
And that’s because he mentioned them as a way for people to come to a realization of ultimate reality.
DE GSUNGS PA LA BRTEN NAS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR TE, ‘DUS BYAS SKYE BAR SHES NA DE LA BRTEN NAS DE DANG DON GCIG PA’I MI RTAG PA SHES PAR ‘GYUR LA,

And it is indeed the case that people can come to a realization of ultimate reality based on Lord Buddha’s having spoken of those things.  Once we understand how produced things arise, then based on that understanding we can grasp that impermanence which is synonymous with the arising.
DE SHES NA DE LA BRTEN NAS ‘KHOR BA ‘DOR ‘DOD DANG MYANG ‘DAS THOB ‘DOD KYI ‘JUG PA SHES SHING, DE SHES NA DE LA BRTEN NAS DAM PA’I CHOS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR,

And once we grasp that, we can grasp how it works that we want give up on the cycle of pain, and want to reach nirvana.  And once we grasp that, we can realize how ultimate reality is the highest of all existing things.
DON DE NYID NGES PAR BYA BA LA, RANG BZHIN MED PA RTOGS PA’I PHAN YON, MA RTOGS PA’I NYES DMIGS, ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS RIM PA JI LTAR GZIGS PA’I TSUL{%,} DE’I SHES BYED,

To perceive that very point with absolute certainty, we should at this juncture cover four steps: (1) the benefits of realizing how nothing has any nature of its own; (2) the problems of failing to have this realization; (3) the way in which realized beings see these things in specific stages; and (4) support for the same.
DANG PO NI, GANG ZAG {%DAG} BSTEN {%RTEN} SOGS BZHI LA,

Here is that first point, where we cover the benefits of realizing how nothing has any nature of its own.  This is covered in the four lines [of the Tibetan, eleven of the English] about “anything in dependence”—
,SHES PAR GYUR PA DE DAG NI,
,LTAR GYUR SRID PA’I RGYA MTSO BRGAL,

DE NYID GZIGS PA’I ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS CHOS CAN, MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI LTA BA’I STOBS KYIS BSKYED PA’I SRID PA’I RGYA MTSO LAS BSGRAL BAR ‘GYUR TE, RTEN CING ‘BREL ‘BYUNG SKYE ‘JIG GI RANG [f. 6b] BZHIN DANG BRAL BA MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider those realized beings, who have seen the way things really are.
They have crossed over the ocean of this suffering life, itself created through the power of the view which holds to those extremes;
For they have realized, directly, how the way that things arise in a dependent relationship is free from any automatic nature of starting & stopping.
GNYIS PA NI, SO SO SOGS BZHI LA,

Which brings us to our second point, the problems of failing to realize that things have no nature of their own.  This is covered in the next verse of the root text; the one which includes the words “individual, ordinary”—
Bhāvābhāva viparyāsa doṣa kleśa vaśaṃ gatāḥ.
Bhavabhava viparyasa dosha klesha vashan gatah.
,SO SO’I SKYE BO DNGOS BDAG CAN,
,YOD DANG MED PAR PHYIN CI LOG
,NYES PAS NYON MONGS DBANG GYUR RNAMS,

DNGOS PO RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA’I BDAG NYID CAN DU ZHEN PA’I SO SO SKYE BO RNAMS CHOS CAN, RANG GI SEMS KYIS BSLUS NAS ‘KHOR BAR ‘GYUR TE, CHAGS SOGS NYON MONGS PA’I,{% no ,} GZHAN DBANG DU GYUR PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider those individual, ordinary people who are so strongly attached to the idea that entities possess a nature which occurs of its own accord.
They are deceived by their own mind, and so continue to circle inside the cycle of pain;
Because they have fallen under the power of attachment and everything else involved with the negative emotions.
DER THAL, YOD PA DANG MED PAR LTA BA’I MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI LTA BA PHYIN CI LOG GI NYES PAS SEMS RGYUD BCINGS PA YIN PA’I PHYIR,
And this indeed must be the case,
Because the stream of their mind is chained by all the problems of that totally mistaken view which holds to the two extremes of things existing, or not existing.
GSUM PA LA, MDZAD PA MTHAR PHYIN PA’I ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS GZIGS TSUL, MGON PO KLU SGRUB NYID KYIS GZIGS PA’I TSUL,

Which then takes us to our third step from above; about the way in which realized beings see these things in specific stages.  We’ll cover this in two sections: (1) the way in which realized beings—those who have come to the final completion of all the deeds they had to do—see things; and then (2) how our protector, Nagarjuna, sees things himself.
DANG PO NI, DNGOS SOGS BZHI LA,
The first of these is covered in the root text, in the four lines [in the Tibetan, and eight lines of the English] which talk about “all things”—
Anityaṃ moṣa dharmāṇaṃ muktaṃ śūnyam anātmakam,
Viviktam iti paśyanti bhāvaṃ bhava vicakṣaṇāḥ.
Anityam mosha dharmanam muktan shunyam anatmakam,
Viviktam iti pashyanti bhavam bhava vichakshanah.
,DNGOS LA MKHAS PA RNAMS KYIS NI,
,DNGOS PO MI RTAG BSLU BA’I CHOS,
,GSOG DANG STONG PA BDAG MED PA,
,RNAM PAR DBEN ZHES BYA BAR MTHONG,
See things as what we call

DNGOS PO MI RTAG CING BSLU BA’I CHOS CAN ‘DI DAG CHOS CAN, MDZAD PA MTHAR PHYIN PA’I MKHAS PA ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS RANG BZHIN MTHA’ DAG GIS DBEN PAR MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA YIN TE, NYAMS CHUNG BA’I DON GYI GSOG LTA BU DANG, CHOS DANG GANG ZAG GI BDAG GIS STONG PAR MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider all these things that are impermanent, and things which deceive us.

Those beings who are wise ones, who have come to the end of everything they ever needed to accomplish—which is to say, those realized beings—see, directly, that these things are devoid of each & every kind of self-nature.
And that’s because they see, directly, that these things are hollow, similar to a piece of straw, feeble: empty of any nature where things or the person are themselves.
GNYIS PA NI, GNAS SOGS BRGYAD LA,
Which brings us to how our protector, Nagarjuna, sees things himself.  This is found in the eight lines [of the Tibetan, nineteen in the English] which mention a “place.”
Saṃmoha nagaraṃ ghoraṃ jagan māyeva dṛśyate.
Sammoha nagaran ghoran jagan mayeva dirshyate.
,GNAS MED DMIGS PA YOD MA YIN,
,RTZA BA MED CING GNAS PA MED,
,MA RIG RGYU LAS SHIN TU BYUNG,
,THOG MA DBUS MTHA’ RNAM PAR SPANGS,
,CHU SHING BZHIN DU SNYING PO MED,
,RMONGS PA’I GRONG KHYER MI ZAD PA’I,
,‘GRO BA SGYU MA BZHIN DU SNANG,
And so they are not sustained.
They are like shoots of bamboo,
It is all a city of the ignorant,
‘DU BYED SOGS ‘DI DAG CHOS CAN, RKYEN GSUM GYI DBANG GIS, BDEN PAR GNAS PA MED DE, GNAS BYED RKYEN GSUM GA BDEN PAR MED PA’I PHYIR,
Let’s consider these links of fresh karma, and the rest.
It is not the case that they remain in existence, in any real way, through the power of three different factors;
Because all three factors that would cause them to remain so lack any reality of their own.
BDAG RKYEN, DMIGS RKYEN, DE MA THAG RKYEN GSUM RIM PA BZHIN DU GNAS MED DMIGS MED RTZA BA GSUM GYIS BDAG MED DU STON TO,,

The three types of factors in question here—those we call a dominant factor; an object factor; and an immediately-subsequent factor—are described in the verse here as having no self-nature, where it speaks (respectively) about “having no place”; “having no object of focus”; and “having no root.”
RKANG PA GSUM PA LA DE CHOS CAN, RANG BZHIN MED BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SNANG BA’I RGYU MTSAN YOD DE, MA RIG PA’I RGYU’I STOBS LAS BDEN PAR SNANG BA’I PHYIR RO,,
And let’s consider the third line here [corresponding to lines 9-11 in the English]: “they pour forth from their cause, of misunderstanding.”
There is then a reason why—even though in actuality they have no self-nature—they appear to have a nature;
Because they do appear to exist, in reality; and that’s all due to the power of a certain cause: misunderstanding.
DE NAS RKANG PA GCIG LA, DE CHOS CAN, RANG BZHIN MED DE, THOG MTHA’ DBUS GSUM GYI [f. 7a] RANG BZHIN DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR,
And then as for the next single line [in the Tibetan, lines 12-13 in the English], let’s consider those same three factors.
They have no nature of their own;
Because they are without any nature of possessing the three of starting, middle, or finish.

YANG RKANG PA GNYIS LA, DE CHOS CAN, RANG BZHIN MED BZHIN DU MA RIG PA’I STOBS LAS RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PA SNANG BAR THAL, CHU SHING BZHIN DU SNYING PO CUNG ZAD MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, DRI ZA’I GRONG KHYER DANG ‘DRA BAR BDEN PAR MED BZHIN DU DER SNANG BA’I PHYIR RO,,
Now let’s look at the next two lines, the fifth & sixth lines [in the Tibetan; or lines 14-17 in the English]—
Let’s consider those same three factors, one more time.
Even though they have no nature of their own, they do appear—all because of the power of our misunderstanding—to have just such a nature;

Because, first of all, they are like shoot of bamboo, in that they lack even the slightest essence inside; and they resemble too the city of the craving spirits, since they have no true existence, but do appear to.

RKANG PA THA MA GNYIS LA, MGON PO KLU SGRUB CHOS CAN, ‘DU BYED RANG BZHIN MTHA’ DAG GIS DBEN PAR MNGON SUM DU MTHONG STE, RMONGS PA’I GRONG KHYER MI ZAD PA’I ‘GRO BA MTHA’ DAG SGYU MA DANG ‘DRA BAR MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I PHYIR,
And then finally, let’s take the final two lines here—
He has seen, directly, that fresh karma is devoid of every kind of a self-nature;
Because he has seen, directly, how the City of the Ignorant—filled with an endless number of suffering beings—is like a magical illusion.
BZHI PA LA LUNG GI SHES BYED DANG, RIGS PA’I SHES BYED DO,,

With this we have reached our fourth step from above, describing support for how realized beings see these things in specific stages.  We’ll start here with scriptural support, and then move on to supporting logic.
DANG PO NI, TSAD MAS {%TSANGS} SOGS BZHI LA,
The first of these is found in the four lines [in the Tibetan, eight lines in the English] which mention the Pure One—
Brahmādyair asya lokasya yat satyaṃ saṃprakāśitam,
Tad āryāṇāṃ mṛṣetyuktaṃ kiṃ na śeṣam ataḥ param.
Brahmadyair asya lokasya yat satyan samprakashitam,
Tad aryanam mirshetyuktan kin na shesam atah param.
,BDEN PA RAB TU GANG SNANG BA,
,DE LAS GZHAN LTA CI ZHIG LUS,
To Pure One and the like—
And what else could be left over?

‘DU BYED SGYU MA LTA BU LAS GZHAN PA’I CHOS CUNG ZAD KYANG ‘DUS {%LUS} PA MED PAR THAL, DBANG PO LAS ‘DAS DON MTHONG BA LA ‘JIG RTEN TSAD MAR GRAGS PA’I TSANGS PA SOGS LA BDEN PAR SNANG BA DE DAG ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS RDZUN PAR GZIGS ZHES PA SANGS RGYAS KYIS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
It is indeed the case that there is not the slightest factor in the universe left over, if you eliminate all those which are similar to a magical illusion,

Because—let us consider the perceptions of beings such as Pure One: perceptions which are considered, among those of the world, to be accurate, and which these beings use to see objects which are far beyond the normal powers of sense.  Things appear, to these perceptions, to exist in reality; whereas the Buddha stated that realized beings see that the perceptions themselves are nothing but a lie.
GNYIS PA NI, ‘JIGS {%’JIG} TSOGS {%SOGS} BZHI LA,
We have now reached the supporting logic for the stages in which realized beings see things.  This is presented in the four lines [of the Tibetan, nine in the English] that mention “the world”—
,‘JIG RTEN MA RIG LDONGS GYUR PA,
,MKHAS PA SRED PA DANG BRAL BA,
,DAM PA RNAMS LTA JI LTAR MNYAM,
By the strong current of desire.
Wise ones are free of desire;
