The translation of the work into Sanskrit was edited and finalized by the Indian master Mutita Shri, working with the master Tibetan translator Pa-tsab Nyima Drak.

The Middle Way philosophical school is classically divided into two groups: one higher and one lower.  The higher division, the Consequence group of the Middle Way School (Skt: Mādhyamika Prāsaṃgika) (Tib: dBu-ma thal-‘gyur-ba) is said to hold a position on emptiness which is perfectly correct.  The lower division, the Independent group of the Middle Way School (Skt: Mādhyamika Svātantrika) (Tib: dBu-ma rang-rgyud-pa), has many similar philosophical viewpoints, but is distinct from the higher group in a number of ways.

We have selected a number of authoritative Middle Way commentaries which list and explain these distinctions between the two groups.  We have compiled and translated excerpts from them here in order to help the reader understand some of the finer details of these philosophical systems, especially as they relate to comments on these ideas expressed by Gyaltsab Je in his work on Arya Nagarjuna’s Sixty Verses.

Classically, within the monastic tradition descended from Je Tsongkapa, there are eight philosophical positions which distinguish the Consequence group from the Independent.  There are however, different enumerated presentations of these distinctions; and as we see in his current work, Gyaltsab Je himself describes ten.  In this appendix, we present both the eight and the ten, and other helpful lists.  We have also included, interstitially, a number of detailed descriptions of some of the more difficult distinctions explained by trusted masters of the tradition.

We begin with a selection from a famed monastic textbook of Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) commonly referred to as An Overview of the Middle Way.  He begins his discussion by referring us to a section of Master Chandrakirti’s Autocommentary to “Entering the Middle Way” which is the famous starting point for the study of the differences between the groups.
THUN MONG MA YIN PAS {%PA’I} KHYAD CHOS BSTAN PA’I SGO NAS RTZA SHE’I DGONGS PA ‘GREL BA LA ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR,
Master Chandrakirti commented on the true intent of the foundational verses entitled Wisdom by describing certain unique features.
DE YANG YIN TE, ‘GREL PA LAS, LUGS ‘DI NI THUN MONG MIN PA’O ZHES MKHAS PA RNAMS KYI NGES PAR BYA’O, ,ZHES DANG,
This description begins at the point in the autocommentary where he says,
My goal is that wise ones among you should come to realize, “This is truly a unique system!”
Here is the full section of Master Chandrakirti referenced by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye:

YANG GANG DAG BYE BRAG TU SMRA BA RNAMS KYIS GANG DON DAM PAR SMRAS PA DE DBU MA PA RNAMS KYIS KUN RDZOB TU YIN NO SNYAM DU SEMS PA DE DAG GIS KYANG BSTAN BCOS KYI DON GYI DE NYID YONGS SU MA SHES PA DE KHO NA STE,

Some people are of the opinion that what the Detailist School describes as being ultimate reality is what the followers of the Middle Way School would describe as deceptive reality.  But those who think this way have simply misunderstood the real point of this classical commentary.
‘DI LTAR ‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PA’I CHOS NI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I CHOS DANG CHOS MTSUNGS PAR MI RIGS PA’I PHYIR TE, LUGS ‘DI NI THUN MONG MA YIN NO ZHES MKHAS PA RNAMS KYIS NGES PAR BYA’O,,

And this is because it is illogical to say that things which are beyond the world are equivalent to things of the world.  My goal is that wise ones among you should come to realize, “This is truly a unique system!”
Master Jayananda, an Indian sage who commented upon Master Chandrakirti’s root text and commentary, begins to clarify these lines for us:
JI LTAR ZHES BYA BA LA SOGS PA GSUNGS TE, ‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PA’I CHOS ZHES BYA BA NI, BYE BRAG TU SMRA BA DANG, MDO SDE PAS DON DAM PAR BRTAGS PA GANG YIN PA’O,,

This brings us to the part where Master Chandrakirti describes “how it is.”  When he speaks of “things which are beyond the world,” he is referring to what the followers of the Detailist School, and those of the Sutrist School, imagine to be ultimate reality.

‘JIG RTEN PA’I CHOS DANG CHOS MTSUNGS PAR MI RIGS PA’I PHYIR ZHES BYA BA NI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I CHOS RNAMS NI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I RJES SU ‘BRANGS NAS GRUB PA YIN GYI, MI RTAG PA NYID DANG, STONG PA NYID DANG, BDAG MED PA NYID DANG LA SOGS PA NI ‘JIG RTEN PA NYID LAS GRUB PA MA YIN NO,,

Here is what Master Chandrakirti means when he states that “it would be illogical to say that these things which are beyond the world are equivalent to things of the world.”  The expression “things of the world” refers to things which are established following the way this is done in the normal world.  But there are things which cannot be established using this same way of the world: things like the impermanence of things; emptiness; and the fact that things are not themselves.
DES NI ‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PA DANG ‘JIG RTEN PA DAG CHOS MTSUNGS PAR MI ‘GYUR PA’O, ,
We cannot say then that these two—things beyond the world, and things that are of the world—could ever be equivalent.
LUGS ‘DI NI THUN [f. 362b] MONG MA YIN PA’O ZHES BYA BA NI KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA’I RNAM GZHAG ‘DI THUN MONG MA YIN PA STE, GZHAN LA YOD PA MA YIN NO ZHES PA’O,,

When Master Chandrakirti says that “this is a truly unique system,” what he’s saying is that the way this school describes what is deceptive, and what is ultimate, is unique—meaning that it is not something that you could ever find among these other thinkers.

As we come to see in his work, the truly “unique system” of the Middle Way that Master Chandrakirti is referring to boils down to the system of the Consequence group within the Middle Way School.  To identify the details of this uniqueness even within this one school, let’s begin with the ten distinctions listed by Gyaltsab Je in our current text:
SPYIR RANG RGYUD KYI DAM BCA’ LAS {%KHAS} LEN MI LEN DANG,
(1) The first difference between the two groups concerns whether or not they accept, in general terms, the idea of an assertion which is “independent.”
DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(2) The next distinction is whether or not they accept the idea of an independent assertion within the context of examining the concept of suchness.
DNGOS PO STOBS ZHUGS KYI TSAD MKHAS {%TSAD MA KHAS} LEN MI LEN DANG,
(3) Do they or do they not accept the idea of an accurate perception engendered by the very nature of an entity?
CHOS CAN LA MTHUN SNANG YOD MED DU SMRA BA DANG,
(4) Do they or do they not profess that the person who initiates an argument, and their opponent, can ever be perceiving the object under consideration in a compatible way?
RANG LUGS KYI KHAS LEN YOD MED DANG,
(5) Do they or do they not have a position which they themselves support?
YONGS GCOD KYI DAM BCA’ YOD MED DANG,
(6) Do they or do they not have a position which depends on exclusion?
(7) RANG LUGS MI SGRUB PAR GZHAN GYI PHYOGS ‘GOG PA TZAM DU KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(7) Do they or do they not accept the idea of simply refuting an opponent’s position, without establishing ones own?
THAL ‘GYUR GYI DAM BCA’ TZAM YOD MED DANG,
(8) Do they or do they not even accept an assertion which is a logical proof based on demonstrating an absurdity?
SANGS RGYAS LA RANG RGYUD KYI YE SHES KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
(9) Do they or do they not accept the idea that a Buddha can possess wisdom within their mindstream?
RANG RIG KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG BCU’O,,
(10) Do they or do they not accept the idea of apperception: the mind’s ability to perceive itself, within a single instant?
Do the parties in a debate

The fourth distinction in the above list addresses whether or not two parties in a debate can ever be perceiving exactly the same object under consideration.  Gyaltsab Je, in the present work, mentions that this question is a criterion that we must use for establishing whether or not an independently effective reason (the first item in his list) can exist.  He then goes on to describe how some say that Master Bhavaviveka, hailed as the founder of the Independent Group, denies that there could be a common subject that can be discussed logically in the context of examining suchness; and how that is in direct contradiction to the idea that a reason could have some power of its own.

It would appear that the idea which is being attributed to Master Bhavaviveka has its roots in a famous debate that he put forth some 1500 years ago, where he tries to clarify the meaning of the opening lines of Arya Nagarjuna’s Wisdom.  Here first is a presentation of Master Chandrakirti’s famous refutation of Master Bhavaviveka’s arguments, as given by the great Mongol scholar Chujey Ngawang Pelden in his commentary upon the wording of Entering the Middle Way.  The focus of this discussion is the use of the expression “in an ultimate sense” as a qualifier in a proof that the sense powers cannot start on their own.
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, RANG RGYUD ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA DANG, RIGS PA DE PHA ROL POS KYANG DON GYIS KHAS BLANGS TSUL DANG, SKYON BRJOD DE RANG GI SBYOR BA LA MI MTSUNGS PA’I RGYU MTSAN NO,,

Our second point is divided into three parts: reasoning which denies the idea of an independently effective reason; a description of how this reasoning is, implicitly, already accepted by the opponent; and an explanation of why these same criticisms do not apply to our own logic.
DANG PO LA GNYIS, DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA DON MED PAR BSHAD PA, CHOS CAN SPYI TZAM ‘DZIN PA’I LAN DGAG PA’O,,

The first of those has two parts of its own: an explanation of why it was meaningless to apply the qualifier “ultimately”; and a refutation of the response that we can speak of a subject in a general way.
DANG PO NI, LEGS LDAN GYIS, DON DAM PAR NANG GI SKYE MCHED RNAMS BDAG LAS SKYE BA MED PAR NGES TE, YOD PA’I PHYIR, SHES PA YOD PA NYID BZHIN NO, ,ZHES BKOD PA LA,
Here is the first.  Master Bhavaviveka would posit the following argument:
Consider, in an ultimate sense, the inner doors of sense.
They certainly do not grow from themselves,
They are similar, for example, to how consciousness exists.
ZLA BA’I ZHABS KYIS, DE LA DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA LA DGOS PA MED DE, CHOS LA SBYAR NA YANG DGOS PA MED, CHOS CAN LA SBYAR NA YANG DGOS PA MED PA’I PHYIR,
And the esteemed Chandrakirti answers with this:
There is no need to add the qualifier “in an ultimate sense” to it;
Because, first of all, there is no need to apply it to the quality you are trying to prove.  And neither is there any need to apply it to the subject under consideration.
DANG PO GRUB STE, SNGA RGOL LA LTOS NA YANG DGOS PA MED, PHYI RGOL LA LTOS NAS KYANG DGOS PA MED, ‘JIG RTEN PA LA LTOS NAS KYANG [f. 43a] DGOS PA MED PA’I PHYIR,
I disagree that there is no need to apply the phrase “in an ultimate sense” to the quality we’re trying to prove.
And yet there is no need,

Because, first of all, there is no need for it relative to the person presenting the argument.  Neither is there any need relative to the person to whom the argument is being presented.  And finally, even in terms of the everyday world, there is no need.
DANG PO GRUB STE, SNGA RGOL DBU MA PAS BDAG SKYE KUN RDZOB TU YANG KHAS MA BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,
I disagree that—relative to the person presenting the argument—there is no need to add the expression “in an ultimate sense.”
And yet there is no need,

Because where the person presenting the argument is a member of the Middle Way School, the idea of something growing from itself would never be accepted, even if we were just speaking of it happening in a deceptive way, and not an ultimate way.
GNYIS PA GRUB STE, BDEN PA GNYIS LAS NYAMS PA’I MU STEGS NI BDEN PA GNYIS CHAR ‘GOG PAR RIGS PA’I PHYIR,
Well then I disagree to the second part of your reason.  I disagree that—relative to the person to whom the argument is being presented—there is no need to add the expression “in an ultimate sense.”
And yet even in this second context there is no need for it;

Because in a case where the opponent is a follower of a non-Buddhist school and has failed even to grasp the concept of two realities—deceptive & ultimate—it is appropriate to make our refutation from the point of view of both of those realities at once.
GSUM PA GRUB STE, ‘JIG RTEN PAS NI RGYU LAS ‘BRAS BU ‘BYUNG BA TZAM ZHIG ‘DOD KYI, BDAG DANG GZHAN GANG LAS SKYE ZHES MI DPYOD PA’I PHYIR,
Then I disagree to the third part of your reason.  I disagree that—even in terms of the everyday world—there is no need to add the expression “in an ultimate sense.”
And yet there is no need to add “in an ultimate sense” even in this third context;

Because people in the everyday world simply accept a scenario where results come from causes; they don’t dig deeper into it, to see whether those results came from causes that were the results themselves, or from causes that were something other than those results.
RTZA RTAGS GNYIS PA GRUB STE, DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR CHOS CAN LA SBYOR NA, SNGA RGOL LA LTOS TE CHOS CAN MA GRUB PA’I SKYON DU ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR,

Well then, I disagree with the reason you’ve given in the second case above; that is, I disagree that—in a case where the opponent is a follower of a non-Buddhist school and has failed even to grasp the concept of two realities, deceptive & ultimate—then it is appropriate to make our refutation from the point of view of both of those realities at once.
And yet this second reason we’ve given is correct;

Because if you do decide to apply the qualification “in an ultimate sense” to the subject under consideration here, you will incur the fault that the subject under consideration will no longer be valid, with respect to the opponent.
GAL TE KUN RDZOB PA’I MIG SOGS RTZOD GZHIR BZUNG NAS DON DAM PAR SKYE BA ‘GOG PAS SKYON MED DO ZHE NA,
Someone may object to this last, asserting:

The thing that we agree to debate about in this case is the eye or other sense power—something which is a deceptive object; and what we are denying about it is that it could ever grow, in an ultimate sense.  As such, there’s no problem.
DE YANG MI RIGS TE, DE SKAD DU MA SMRAS PA’I PHYIR DANG, SMRAS NA’ANG PHYI RGOL LA CHOS CAN MA GRUB PA’I SKYON DU ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR TE,

But you are mistaken in saying this, since nobody here has spoken of the eye or such in this way.  And even if they had, you would still incur that fault that the subject under consideration would be invalid for the opponent.
GRANGS CAN GYIS MIG SOGS DBU MA PAS ‘DOD PA LTAR GYI DON DAM DU ‘DOD KYI, KUN RDZOB TU MI ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR RO,

Because the fact is that the Numerists hold that the eye and so on do exist in the way that the followers of the Middle Way describe as “ultimate”—and would not say that these things exist in a deceptive manner.
Why we cannot speak of a subject
Which brings us to the second part of our presentation, where we offer a refutation of the response that we can speak of a subject in a general way.

LEGS LDAN NA RE, DPER NA SANGS RGYAS PAS BYE BRAG PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR SGRUB PA NA, ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR GYI SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG BA {%PA} LA MI ‘GRUB, NAM MKHA’I YON TAN GYI SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA SANGS RGYAS PA LA MI ‘GRUB PO,,
Master Bhavaviveka would make the following claim:

It’s similar, for example, to the case where someone from a Buddhist school is proving, to a member of the Detailer school, that sound is impermanent.  If they take, as the subject under consideration, sound as a product of the elements, then this subject will not be acceptable to the Detailer.  If they take as this subject sound as a quality of space, then it will not be acceptable to the Buddhist.

DE BZHIN DU BYE BRAG PAS GSAL BYED PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR DAM ‘CHA’ BA NA, BYAS BA’I SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA GSAL BYED BA {%PA} LA MI ‘GRUB, SNGAR YOD RKYEN GYIS GSAL BA’I SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG BA {%PA} LA MI ‘GRUB BO,,

And let’s consider a similar case, where a Detailer is asserting to one of the Manifestors that sound is impermanent.  If they consider sound as something made, then the subject under consideration will not be valid to the Manifestor.  But if they consider sound from the point of view of something which is already present in the cause, and then later becomes manifest, then this subject won’t be valid for the Detailer.

DE BZHIN DU SANGS RGYAS PAS BYE BRAG PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR SGRUB PA NA, ‘JIG PA PHYIS ‘BYUNG GI RGYU DON [f. 43b] GZHAN LA MI LTOS PA’I MI RTAG PA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG PA LA MI ‘GRUB, DE LA LTOS PA’I MI RTAG PA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA SANGS RGYAS PA LA MI ‘GRUB BO,

For yet another case, suppose a Buddhist is undertaking to prove to a Detailer that sound is impermanent.  If they take, as part of the subject under their consideration, a kind of impermanence where the later destruction of the sound depends on no separate, later factor, then this subject will not be acceptable to the Detailer.  And yet if they take, as part of this subject, a kind of impermanence where that later destruction does depend on a separate, later factor, then the subject under consideration will be unacceptable to the Buddhist.
DE’I PHYIR RGOL BA SO SO’I ‘DOD PA THUN MONG MA YIN PAS KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR, SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I SPYI TZAM ZHIG CHOS DANG CHOS CAN DANG DPER BZUNG DGOS SO,,

We can conclude then that we must select—as the quality we are attempting to prove; and as our subject under consideration; and as our parallel example—a general form of things which appears the same way to both the proponent and the opponent in an argument; we should never qualify any of these in a way which is unique to the beliefs of either debater.
DE BZHIN DU DBU MA PAS MIG SOGS BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA MED PAR GRANGS CAN PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA LA SGRUB PA NA,

Still another example is offered when a member of the Middle Way School seeks to prove, to either a Numerist or a Functionalist, that things like the sense power of the eye arise neither from themselves, nor from other things.
BDEN PAR GRUB PA’I MIG SOGS CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA DBU MA PA LA MI ‘GRUB, BRDZUN PAR GRUB PA’I MIG SOGS CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA DNGOS SMRA BA LA MI ‘GRUB PAS NA,

If they take, as their subject under consideration, an eye or other sense power which exists in truth, then the subject would not be valid for the follower of the Middle Way.  And yet if they took as their subject an eye or such which existed in a deceptive way, it would not be valid for the Functionalist.
BDEN BRDZUN GANG GIS KYANG KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I MIG SOGS TZAM PO CHOS CAN DU BZUNG DGOS TE,

As such, they should take—as the subject of their debate—the simple eye, or whatever, itself: the one which appears in the same way to both the proponent of the Middle Way and to the Functionalist; without specifying whether they are talking about an eye which exists either in truth or in a deceptive manner.
DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA GNYIS KYIS KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS DPYOD PA’I GZHI YIN PAS GNYIS KA’I MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB DGOS PA’I PHYIR, ZHES ZER RO,,

This then would be correct; for what we need here is a single object which both the follower of the Middle Way and the Functionalist can examine, to see whether or not it possesses a specific characteristic: we need a subject under consideration which appears the same to both parties.
MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I DON YANG PHYI RGOL LA TSAD MA JI LTA BA ZHIG GIS GRUB PA’I TSAD MA DE ‘DRA BA ZHIG GIS SNGA RGOL LA YANG GRUB BA’O,,

Now what does it mean when we say that “the object must appear the same to the two parties”?  It means that the perception of the object which is considered accurate by the opponent must also be accepted as accurate by the proponent.
DE DGAG PA LA GNYIS, DON MI ‘THAD PA DANG, DPE BKOD PA DANG MI ‘DRA’O,,

We will refute Master Bhavaviveka’s idea here in two steps.  First, we’ll demonstrate that his points are incorrect.  Secondly, we’ll demonstrate that his examples of different schools debating each other don’t apply to the current debate.
DANG PO NI, SKABS ‘DIR SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA’I MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I CHOS CAN BZHAG TU MI RUNG STE,
Here is the first, in classic debate form:
It is, in the current context, incorrect to posit a subject under consideration which could appear in the same way to both the proponent and the opponent.

CHOS CAN MIG SOGS DE PHYI RGOL DNGOS SGRA {%SMRA} BA’I LUGS LA YUL GYI RANG BZHIN LA MA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MA’I RNYED DON DANG, SNGA RGOL DBU MA PA’I LUGS LA YUL GYI RANG BZHIN LA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MA’I RNYED DON YIN PA’I PHYIR,

And that’s because where we take the subject under consideration as a sense power such as the eye, we’d be talking about something that—in the beliefs of the opponent, the Functionalist—would be an object observed by an accurate perception which was unmistaken about the nature of this object.  This same sense power though—in the beliefs of the proponent, the follower of the Middle Way—would be an object observed by an accurate perception which was mistaken about the nature of this object.

KHYAB [f. 44a] STE, SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG BA YIN NA, PHYI RGOL GYI LUGS LA TSAD MA JI LTA BU ZHIG GIS GRUB PA’I TSAD MA DE ‘DRA BA ZHIG GIS SNGA RGOL GYI LUGS LA YANG GRUB DGOS PA’I PHYIR TE, MTHUN SNANG BA’I DON DE LTAR LAM RIM LAS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO, ,
That doesn’t prove that it would be incorrect, in the current context, to posit a subject under consideration which could appear in the same way to both the proponent & the opponent.

And yet it does.  If the subject under consideration here did appear in the same way to both the proponent & the opponent, then the version of accurate perception accepted in the system of the opponent as one with which we could establish things would also have to be accepted as the same kind of accurate perception in the system of the proponent.
And that certainly is the case, because this is how the literature on the steps of the path to enlightenment describes what it is for an object to appear the same way to both parties.
GZHAN YANG, RGOL BA GNYIS KA’I LUGS LA BDEN GNYIS KYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM CHOS CAN DU BZUNG DU MI RUNG STE,

We can, moreover, assert that it would be mistaken to take, as the subject we are considering in this debate, a power of the eye or whatever which could—in the systems of both parties—be discussed without regard to any distinction relating to the two realities.
DE GNYIS KA’I LUGS LA BDEN GNYIS KYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR TE,

And that’s true because a general form of the eye or whatever which could be discussed—in the systems of both parties—without regard to any distinction relating to the two realities is simply not something which could be considered by the mind at all.

SNGA RGOL DBU MA PA’I LUGS LA BDEN GNYIS KYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU RUNG YANG, PHYI RGOL DNGOS SMRA BA’I LUGS LA BDEN GNYIS KYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR,

And that in turn is true because—although it is possible to consider, in the system of the proponent, the follower of the Middle Way, a general form of the power of the eye or the like without regard to any distinction relating to the two realities—it is not possible to consider, in the system of the opponent, the Functionalist, any general form of the eye or such without regard to any such distinction between the two realities.
RTAGS PHYI MA GRUB STE, DNGOS SMRA BA’I LUGS LA, DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR TE,

And the latter reason we have given here holds true, because it would not be correct—in the Functionalist system—to take into consideration a general form of the eye or the rest, without regard to the distinction of existing in an ultimate way.
DE’I LUGS LA RANG MTSAN GYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR TE,
And that’s true because—in their system—it would not be correct to say that the mind could consider the eye or such in a general way, without regard to the distinction of existing in an ultimate way.
DE’I LUGS LA MIG SOGS LA TSAD MAR SONG NA MIG SOGS KYI RANG MTSAN LA TSAD MAR SONG BAS KHYAB PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s true because—in that system—whenever any state of mind is an accurate perception towards the eye or such, then it must always be because it has constituted an accurate perception towards the eye and so forth as a specific expression.
GZHAN YANG RGOL BA GNYIS KA’I LUGS LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I CHOS CAN MED DE, RGOL BA GNYIS KA’I LUGS LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I CHOS CAN SGRUB BYED KYI TSAD MA MED PA’I PHYIR TE,
Beyond all this, we can say that there can be no subject under consideration which appears, according to the systems of the two debaters, in the same way to both parties.
CHOS CAN SGRUB BYED TSAD MA DE SNGA RGOL DBU MA BAS {%PAS} YUL GYI RANG BZHIN LA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MAR ‘DOD, PHYI RGOL DNGOS SMRA [f. 44b] BAS DE LA MA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s because the accurate perception which establishes the existence of the subject under consideration is—according to the proponent, the follower of the Middle Way—an accurate perception which is mistaken about the nature of its object; whereas the opponent, the Functionalist, would assert that it is an accurate perception which is unmistaken about this nature.
‘DI NI DON THOB KYI DBANG DU BYAS PA’I BSHAD PA’O,,
This last section represents necessary conclusions we can draw from what we know about the positions of these masters and schools.
TSIG GSAL LAS, [,DE’I PHYIR JI LTAR ‘DIR CHOS DANG CHOS CAN SPYI TZAM ZHIG ‘DZIN PA DE BZHIN DU, ‘DIR YANG KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I CHOS CAN TZAM ZHIG ‘DZIN PAR ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA,]
A Clarification of the Verses includes the following extended section:
Now suppose you say the following:

And so, what we see there is that what’s being considered is simply the general form of both the quality they’re trying to prove, and the subject under consideration—which they are saying possesses that quality.  We can do the same here, considering the simple subject of consideration without regard to those distinctions.

DE NI DE LTAR MA YIN TE, ‘DI LTAR GANG GI TSE ‘DIR SKYE BA BKAG BA BSGRUB PAR BYA BA’I CHOS SU ‘DOD PA DE’I TSE, DE KHO NAR DE’I RTEN CHOS CAN PHYIN CI LOG TZAM GYIS BDAG GI NGO BO RNYED PA NI NYAMS PAR GYUR PAR ‘DIS RANG NYID KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA NYID DO,,

But that’s not the way it is; and here’s why.  Suppose we have a case where we’ve accepted—as the quality we are trying to prove about a particular subject that we have under consideration—the absence of the starting of a thing.  We entirely accept that, with nothing more than that, the tendency of a state of mind which is nothing but mistaken to see some self-nature in the subject under consideration—that which acts as the basis of this quality—is undermined.

PHYIN CI LOG DANG PHYIN CI MA LOG PA DAG NI THA DAD PA YIN NO, ZHES PA NAS, [DE’I PHYIR, GANG GI TSE RAB RIB CAN GYIS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA LTAR PHYIN CI LOG GIS YOD PA MA YIN PA YOD PA NYID DU ‘DZIN PA DE’I TSE NI YOD PAR GYUR PA’I DON CHA TZAM YANG DMIGS PAR GA LA ‘GYUR,

After all, a state of mind which is entirely mistaken is completely separate from one which is not mistaken in any way.  We can for example look at a case where a person with cataracts on their eyes believes that there is a strand of hair lying on a white porcelain sink; they are certain that there is something there, when in fact there is nothing—they’re just seeing a line on the eyeball itself.  We could never say, in this instance, that there was present there even a tiny percentage of any actual object—any actual hair there.

GANG GI TSE RAB RIB CAN MA YIN PAS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA LTAR PHYIN CI MA LOG PAS YANG DAG PA MA YIN PA SGRO MI ‘DOGS PA DE’I TSE NA YANG GANG GIS NA DE’I TSE NA KUN RDZOB TU ‘GYUR BA YOD PA MA YIN PAR GYUR PA’I DON CHA TZAM YANG DMIGS PA GA LA YOD,

And suppose another person comes along who has no cataracts on their eyes.  They have none of this tendency for seeing a false object; one which simply isn’t there—the hair or whatever it may be.  And this is because their state of mind is one which is not mistaken.  We could never say, again, that there was present there even a tiny percentage of any object which did not exist in a deceptive manner.
DE NYID KYI PHYIR SLOB DPON GYI ZHAL SNGA NAS KYANG,
,GAL TE MNGON SUM LA SOGS PA’I,
,SGRUB PAR MA BZLOG PAR BYA NA DE,
,MED PHYIR NGA LA KLAN KA MED,
And this is why the Master himself has said,
I have no debate with you,
Could be seen, in & of themselves,
By a perception that was direct,

GANG GI PHYIR DE LTAR PHYIN CI LOG PA DANG PHYIN CI MA LOG PA DAG THA DAD PA DE’I PHYIR, PHYIN CI MA LOG PA’I GNAS SKABS NA PHYIN CI LOG YOD PA MA YIN PA’I PHYIR NA, GANG ZHIG CHOS CAN NYID DU ‘GYUR BA’I MIG KUN RDZOB PA GA LA YOD,

Now suppose it really is the case that a state of mind which is entirely mistaken is completely separate from one which is not mistaken in any way.  This means that—in an instance where the mind was not mistaken—there could not be present a state of mind which was mistaken.  How then could we have a sense power of the eye which was deceptive, and which was supplying this very subject to be considered?
DE’I PHYIR GZHI MA GRUB PA’I PHYOGS KYI SKYON DANG GZHI MA GRUB PA’I GTAN TSIGS KYI SKYON LDOG PA MED PAS ‘DI LAN MA YIN PA NYID DO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA’I

As such, your proposed solution is no solution at all—for you cannot escape the defect of your subject here where it simply cannot exist; and neither then can you escape the same defect with your syllogism itself.

TSIG DON NI, LEGS BSHAD SNYING PO LTAR NA, RGOL BA GNYIS KA’I LUGS LA BDEN GNYIS KYI KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS TZAM PO CHOS CAN DU GZUNG DU MI RUNG STE, LEGS LDAN KHYED RANG LTAR NA DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR DOR NAS MIG SOGS TZAM YUL DU BYED PA’I TSAD MA MED PA’I PHYIR TE,
Here’s the point that Master Chandrakirti is making here.  We can start our explanation from that found in the Essence of Eloquence:

What that work says is that it would be incorrect to consider, as our subject under consideration, just a simple form of the power of the eye or such, without regard to distinctions—held in the system of either party—between the two realities.
MIG SOGS DE RANG BZHIN LA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MA’I RNYED DON MA YIN PAR LEGS LDAN RANG NYID KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR,

And that’s because Master Bhavaviveka himself accepts the idea that the eye, or whichever sense power it may be, cannot be something which is perceived by an accurate perception which is mistaken about the nature of its object.

KHYAB STE, DE LTA NA YUL GYI RANG BZHIN LA ‘KHRUL BA’I SHES PA’I RNYED DON DANG DE LA MA ‘KHRUL BA’I SHES PA’I RNYED DON GNYIS DNGOS ‘GAL YIN PAS NA MIG SOGS DE YUL GYI RANG MTSAN LA MA ‘KHRUL BA’I SHES PA’I RNYED DON DU ‘GYUR LA, DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS TZAM PO ‘JAL MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR,

Just because Master Bhavaviveka accepts that idea doesn’t prove that it would be incorrect to consider, as our subject under consideration, just a simple form of the power of the eye or such, without regard to distinctions—held in the system of either party—between the two realities.

And yet it does prove that; after all, it would be a direct contradiction for one thing to be both an object which is perceived by a state of mind that is mistaken about the nature of its object; and at the same time be an object which is perceived by a state of mind that is not mistaken about the nature of its object.  As such, the eye power—or whatever it may be—would be an object which is perceived by a state of mind which is not mistaken about the actual expression of this object; and given that, it would be incorrect to say that this state of mind were considering just a general form of the eye or whatever, without regard to any distinction of existing in an ultimate sense.

MIG SOGS KYI RANG MTSAN SNANG BA LA LTOS TE MA ‘KHRUL BA’I TSAD MAS NI MIG SOGS DON DAM PAR YOD PAR ‘JAL DGOS KYI DON DAM PA’I KHYAD PAR DOR BA’I MIG SOGS TZAM PO ‘JAL MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR, RTAGS SNGA MA LEGS LDAN RANG GI KHAS BLANGS KYIS [f. 45a] GRUB STE,

Relative to the appearance of the actual expression of the eye or such, an accurate perception which was not mistaken would have to be considering an eye or such as something that existed in an ultimate sense; but it would be wrong to say that it was considering just the general form of the eye and the like, without regard to the distinction of it being ultimate.  As such, the first part of the reason given here is validated by Master Bhavaviveka’s own position.
LEGS BSHAD SNYING PO LAS, YOD PA GANG YIN RANG GI NGO BOS YOD PAR ‘DOD PA’I LUGS LA RANG MTSAN SNANG BA LA LTOS TE ‘KHRUL BAR SONG NA, DES RANG GI GZHAL BYA RNYED PAR ‘JOG MI NUS PAS,
As the Essence of Eloquence puts it—

When we are talking about any system which accepts that anything which actually exists, exists through some essence of its own, then once we have said that a state of mind is mistaken relative to the actual expression of that object as it appears to this mind, we cannot say that this state of mind has perceived the object—has taken this object as what it considers.
RTOG PA DANG RTOG MED KYI TSAD MA GANG YIN KYANG TSAD MAR SONG SA SNANG YUL DANG ZHEN YUL RANG MTSAN LA MA ‘KHRUL BA ZHIG DGOS SO,,

Whether we are talking about an accurate perception which employs images or does not, the measure of whether it is an accurate perception or not must then be considered to be the question of whether or not it is mistaken towards the actual expression of the object that appears to it, and that it thinks it sees.
DE’I TSE THA SNYAD DU MING DU BTAGS PA TZAM MIN PA’I DON RANG GI GNAS TSUL GYI NGO BO’AM RANG BZHIN LA TSAD MAR ‘GRO DGOS SHING RANG GIS KHAS LEN PA YANG YIN NO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,

At this point, the state of mind must constitute an accurate perception towards the essence, or nature, of the actual way in which its object exists—and not towards something which is no more than nominal: a product of a naming process.  And this is in fact the position that they take here.
GNYIS PA GRUB STE, DE NYID LAS, DE ‘DRA BA’I TSAD MAS RNYED PA’I DON YIN NA SHES BYA PHYIN CI LOG YIN PAR ‘GAL BAS RTAGS PHYI MA ‘GRUB BO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,
The second part of the reason also holds true; for the same work states—

The latter part of the reason also holds true, for it would be a contradiction to say that if something were the object that this type of accurate perception perceives, then it would at the same time be something perceived in a mistaken way.
KHYAB STE, SHES BYA PHYIN CI LOG NI RANG MTSAN SNANG BA LA LTOS TE ‘KHRUL BA’I SHES PAS RNYED PA’I DON YIN PA’I PHYIR RO, ,
I disagree that if something were this kind of object, then it would at the same time have to be perceived in a mistaken way.

And yet it would have to be, because when something is an object which is perceived in a mistaken way, it is something perceived by a state of mind which is mistaken, relative to the actual expression of the object appearing to it.
DES NA RGOL BA GNYIS KAR MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA’I CHOS CAN MED PAS RANG RGYUD KYI SBYOR BA’I CHOS CAN MA GRUB BA’I SKYON LDOG TU MED DO,,

Given all this, we can say that—because there is no subject under consideration which appears in the same way to both debaters—there is an irrefutable problem with the idea of an independently effective logical statement, that the object under consideration cannot be valid.

Here is further commentary on the same subject by Kedrup Je Gelek Pel Sangpo (1385-1438), who is considered one of the two greatest disciples of Je Tsongkapa (the other being our author, Gyaltsab Je, himself).  In his classic work Interlude on Emptiness, Kedrup Je offers another possibility of how the logical statement being discussed could have been put forth by Master Bhavaviveka, and then explains a refutation of it by Master Chandrakirti.

RTZA SHES LAS, BDAG LAS MA YIN GZHAN LAS MIN, CES SOGS GSUNGS PA’I RJES SU ‘BRANGS NAS DBU MA SNANG BA SOGS RANG RGYUD PA’I GZHUNG LAS KYANG MTHA’ BZHI SKYE ‘GOG GI RIGS PA BSHAD PA LA RDO RJE GZIGS {%GZEGS} MA’I GTAN TSIGS ZHES GRAGS PAS,

The Root Text on Wisdom famously begins with the lines that start with “Nothing grows from itself…”  Taking after these concepts, scriptures of the Independent group of the Middle Way School—works such as Light on the Middle Way—further present what is called the “Proof which Denies that Things Can Grow in Any of Four Different Extreme Ways.”  This is widely referred to as the “Proof of the Sliver of Diamond.”
DE LA RANG RGYUD PA’I THUN MONG MA YIN PA CUNG ZAD BSHAD NA,
Given all this, I will offer just a brief explanation of the unique beliefs of this Independent group.

MYU GU CHOS CAN, BDEN PA’I SKYE BA MED DE, DON DAM PAR BDAG DANG GZHAN DANG GNYI GA DANG RGYU MED GANG LAS KYANG MI SKYE BA’I PHYIR, CES PA’DI RTZA SHE’I, BDAG LAS MA YIN GZHAN LAS MIN, CES SOGS KYI TSIG DON DU RANG RGYUD PA DAG ‘CHANG {%’CHAD} LA,

Followers of the Independent group of the Middle Way express the proof as follows, as a way to explain the wording of the Root Text on Wisdom, where this text itself says that “Nothing grows from itself, / Nothing grows from something else,” and so on:
It lacks any growth which occurs in truth;
Because it grows, in an ultimate sense, neither from itself; from something else; from both itself and something else; nor without any cause at all.
TSIG GSAL LAS RTAGS SBYOR DE LTAR ‘GOD PA GZHUNG DE’I TSIG DON YIN PA BKAG PA YIN GYI,
The Clarification of the Verses denies that stating the proof this way correctly represents the meaning of the words of Arya Nagarjuna’s lines here.
SPYIR BDEN PA’I SKYE BA MED DE, BDAG GZHAN GNYI GA RGYU MED LAS MI SKYE BA’I PHYIR, ZHES PA’I RTAGS ‘GOD DU MI RUNG BAR ZLA BA GRAGS PA YANG MI BZHED DO,,

It is not though the case that Master Chandrakirti would say that the logic here could not be expressed as “There is no true growing, because there is no growth either from itself, from something else, from both, or without any cause at all.”

‘ON KYANG BDAG SKYE SOGS GSUM THA SNYAD DU YANG MI SRID PAR THAL RANG GNYI GA MTHUN YANG, GZHAN SKYE THAL ‘GYUR BA THA SNYAD DU YANG MI SRID PAR ‘DOD CING, RANG RGYUD PA THA SNYAD DU GZHAN SKYE KHAS LEN PAS,

We would have to say however that both the Independent group of the Middle Way School and the Consequence group within the same school would agree that the three of the possibilities mentioned—that something could grow from itself, and so on—are flatly impossible.  It’s the possibility that things could grow from something else that the two groups disagree on: the followers of the Consequence group would say that—even nominally speaking—it’s impossible for something to grow from something other than itself; whereas the followers of the Independent group would assert that, nominally speaking, the growth of things does occur because of something other than themselves.
GZHAN SKYE ‘GOG PA LA NGES PAR DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR SBYOR GYI THA SNYAD DU YANG GZHAN SKYE MED PA RANG RGYUD PA’I GZHUNG GANG LAS KYANG MA BSHAD CING,

These latter thinkers would say that—when we deny that things could come from something other than themselves—we must always add the qualification “in an ultimate sense.”  You will never find, though—in any scripture of the Independent school—a statement that things could never grow, in a nominal sense, from something other than themselves.
ZHI ‘TSO YAB SRAS DANG ‘PHAGS SENG SOGS RGYU ‘BRAS RDZAS GZHAN BZHED PAR DE DAG GI GZHUNG LAS SHIN TU GSAL LO,,

And the fact that Master Shantarakshita and his spiritual son—as well as the Realized One and the Lion, among others—believe that causes and their results are substantially different from each other is something that is extremely clear, in the scriptures they have composed.

DE’I PHYIR YANG THAL RANG LA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB BA THA SNYAD DU’ANG ‘DOD MI ‘DOD KYI KHYAD PAR YOD PAR BLA {%BLO} MIG PHRAG DOG GI DUG CHUS MA BSLANG {%BSLAD} PA DAG GIS GSAL BAR RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As such, there is a vast difference between the Consequence and Independent groups, about whether—even in a nominal sense—things can exist through some nature of their own.  This is something that thinkers with minds whose eyes have never been infected by the venom of jealousy can easily come to realize.

As we’ve seen, the question of whether we need to add the phrase “in an ultimate sense” to Arya Nagarjuna’s famous denial that things could grow from something else has been hotly debated for centuries.  As we were translating this section, a member of our Mixed Nuts Translation Team at the Sedona College of International Management made an observation so insightful that we thought we would add it here; it may help our readers immensely in “cracking” this difficult concept.  Translator Bets Greer observed:

The reason that Master Bhavaviveka wants to add the qualification “in an ultimate sense” to Nagarjuna’s sentence “Things don’t grow from something else” is that he hopes the listener will realize that we’re talking about things growing without the participation of karmic seeds opening up in our mind to make us see them grow.  But what Master B doesn’t realize is that a person who doesn’t have the seeds to understand that already won’t have the seeds to understand the clarification either!

By the time that Kedrup Tenpa Dargye and his contemporaries are writing textbooks for the monasteries founded a century before them by Je Tsongkapa and Gyaltsab Je and their generation, the following list of “primary” and “ancillary” distinctions has developed.
GRUB MTHA’ ‘OG MA RNAMS DANG THUN MONG MA YIN PA’I KHYAD CHOS KYI GTZO BO LA DU MA YOD DE, RTZA BA’I DAM BCA’ BRGYAD, ‘PHROS PA YAN LAG LTA BU’I DAM BCA’ DANG BCAS PA YOD PA’I PHYIR,

There are many principal distinctions that separate this school [the Consequence group of the Middle Way] from the lower systems.  These can be presented in terms of eight primary positions, and then ancillary positions that branch off from them.
which set the Consequence Group apart
DANG PO LA BRGYAD YOD DE, RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA GZHIR BYAS PA’I SGO NAS, GZHIR BYAS PA
Here is the first group, of eight; please keep in mind that—in the end—they all trace their roots to the idea that nothing exists through any nature of its own.
‘PHAGS PA LA STONG NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS MYONG DANG,
Of these eight positions, the first four are all assertions that something is the case:
(1) A realized being is someone who has experienced the direct realization of emptiness.
(2) The tendency to see things as real is an obstacle to nirvana.
ZHIG PA DNGOS POR YOD PA DANG BCAS PA’I SGRUB PA’I DAM BCA’ BZHI DANG,
(4) The process of an object ending is a functioning thing.
The second four positions are all denials that something could be the case:
(5) There is no such thing as foundation consciousness.
(6) There is no such thing as apperception: the ability of the mind to see itself, within a single instant.
RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS MED PA DANG,
(7) There is no such thing as an “independent” reason, where the reason has an innate power to prove something.
GZHAN SKYE MI ‘DOD PA DANG BCAS PA’I DGAG PA’I DAM BCA’ BZHI DANG BCAS PA’I BRGYAD YOD PA’I PHYIR,
(8) There is no such thing as something growing from something else.
which set the Consequence group apart
‘PHROS PA YAN LAG LTA BU LA DU MA YOD DE,
There are a great number of ancillary positions, which branch off from the eight.  Here are some examples:
TSUR MTHONG GI [f. 114b] RGYUD LA RNAL ‘BYOR MNGON SUM YOD PA DANG,
(1) There can exist a yogic direct perception within the mind of someone who believes that things are coming towards them.
MYANG ‘DAS GNYIS KYI NANG NAS DANG POR LHAG MED MYANG ‘DAS MNGON DU BYED PA DANG,
(2) Of the two types of nirvana, the one which we achieve first is nirvana “without anything left over.”
‘GOG BDEN LA DON DAM BDEN PAS KHYAB PA DANG,
(3) All forms of the truth of the end of pain are ultimate reality.
STONG NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG YE SHES KHYAD PAR BA ZHIG THUN MONG MA YIN PA’I ‘GOG SNYOMS SU ‘DOD PA DANG,

(4) The belief that there does exist a special form of the wisdom we possess during deep meditation in which we are perceiving emptiness directly; and that this wisdom is a unique type of cessation meditation.
YANG DAG KUN RDZOB MI BZHED PA DANG,
(5) The denial that any “correct” form of the deceptive could exist.
SGRIB GNYIS LAM GANG GI GNAS SKABS SU SPONG TSUL THUN MONG MA YIN PA DANG,
(6) A unique position on the question of which stages of the path we are on, when we rid ourselves of the two types of obstacles.
STONG NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I SLOB PA’I MNYAM GZHAG YE SHES LA GZHI SHES KYIS KHYAB PA DANG,
(7) All types of the wisdom possessed by a person who has not yet achieved nirvana, as they are in deep meditation where they are perceiving emptiness directly, constitute “foundation wisdom.”
SLOB PA’I RGYUD KYI GNYIS SNANG CAN GYI SHES PA LA ZAG BCAS KYIS KHYAB PA DANG,
(8) All forms of awareness which are possessed by a person who has not yet achieved nirvana, and which are still involved with the discrepancy, are necessarily impure.
DE YIN NA RANG GI SNANG BA LA TSAD MA YIN DGOS PA DANG,
(9) All of these types of impure perceptions are still accurate, with regard to what is appearing to them.
RANG GI GZHAL BYA LA ‘KHRUL PA’I TSAD MA YOD PA DANG,
(10) There do exist accurate perceptions which are mistaken about the object they are considering.
GZHI GRUB NA LKOG GYUR DANG, MNGON GYUR GNYIS KA YIN DGOS PA DANG,
(11) If something exists, it must exist both on the level of something which is beyond normal perception, and something which is obvious to normal perception.
BCAD SHES LA TSAD MAS KHYAB PA SOGS DU MA YOD PA’I PHYIR,
(12) Recollection is a form of accurate perception.
RTZA BA’I DAM BCA’ BRGYAD PO KHAS LEN PA DE, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA KHAS LEN PA LA THUG PA YIN TE,
In conclusion, we can say that whether or not you accept the eight primary positions listed here all comes down to whether or not you accept the idea that nothing can exist in & of itself.

Crucial to grasping the unique differences between the Consequence and Independent groups within the Middle Way School is a clear understanding of the seventh primary position in the list of the differences between the two schools found above: the concept of an “independently effective” reason, from which in fact the latter school takes its name.  We begin with a very helpful piece from Kedrup Tenpa Dargye that can help us get there; it’s excerpted from another of his textbooks: A Dialectic Analysis of the Middle Way.
SLOB DPON ‘PHAGS SENG GNYIS THAL ‘GYUR BA YIN ZER NA,
Some people claim that Masters Vimuktisena and Haribhadra belong to the Consequence group, within the Middle Way School.
‘O NA, SLOB DPON SENG BZANG GIS RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS DANG RANG RIG MI BZHED CING, PHYI DON BZHED PAR THAL, DAM BCA’ ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR,
And we answer them as follows:

Well then, I suppose these two masters deny the idea of a logical statement with components that have some inherent power to prove something; and that they also deny the idea of apperception.  And on top of that, I suppose they agree to the idea that there do exist outer objects!
‘DOD NA, SLOB DPON GYIS RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS BZHED PAR THAL, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB PA’I RTAGS YANG DAG BZHED PA’I PHYIR,
Well then, I agree: These two masters do deny those two concepts, and accept the third.
Suppose you do agree.  So Master Haribhadra accepts the idea of a logical statement with components that have some inherent power to prove something, right?
Because he accepts the idea of a good reason which exists from its own side!
DER THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GTAN TSIGS YANG DAG BZHED PA’I PHYIR,
No he wouldn’t accept the idea of a good reason which exists from its own side.
But of course he would, because he would accept the idea of a good reason which existed in & of itself.
DER THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA BZHED PA’I PHYIR TE,
No he wouldn’t accept the idea of a good reason which existed in & of itself!
And yet he would, because he accepts the idea that there are things which exist in & of themselves!
DON DAM PAR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA ZHES DGAG BYA LA DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR ‘GREL CHUNG NGU YANG YANG SMOS PA’I PHYIR DANG,

And that’s true because, in his briefer commentary, he feels that he has to add the word “ultimately” to his description of what it is we deny: he repeatedly uses the phrase, “something that could exist ultimately from its own side.”
YANG DAG KUN RDZOB BZHED PAS KYANG GRUB PA’I PHYIR,
This point is also made because he accepts the idea that there could exist a “correct” form of the deceptive.
GZHAN YANG, DE GNYIS LA SNGAR BSHAD PA’I KHYAD PAR DE DAG YOD PAR THAL,
And there’s yet another reason why the characterizations we’ve just made of these two masters are true!
THAL ‘GYUR BAS THAL ‘GYUR TZAM GYI {%GYIS} DGAG BYA BDEN GRUB KHEGS PA DANG, BDAG MED DU SGRUB NUS PAR ‘DOD,

Those who belong to the Consequence Group believe that a statement of absurdity—a statement that points out the absurd consequence of another person’s position—is sufficient to disprove the idea that we deny: the idea of an object which could exist in truth.  And they also believe that it is enough to prove the opposite idea: that nothing could have any nature of its own.
RANG RGYUD PAS DE LTAR MI NUS PAR RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS YANG DAG GI DGAG SGRUB DE DAG BYED DGOS PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR TE,

Those who belong to the Independent Group, on the other hand, believe that a statement of absurdity is not sufficient for these purposes—and that, in order to deny the one idea and establish the other, we would have to use a good reason of the kind that has some independent or inherent power to prove its point.
THAL RANG GI KHYAD PAR NGES PAR KHAS [f. 67b] LEN DGOS PA’I PHYIR,
And that in turn is true because we must all agree, in the end, that there is some difference between the Consequence Group and the Independent Group!
KHYAD PAR DBU MA’I LTA BA KHAS LEN BZHIN DU RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS KHAS LEN PA ‘GAL [f. 80b] ‘DUR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR TE,

And this difference has in fact been stated in authoritative sources as following: It would be a contradiction of terms if someone were, on the one hand, to say that they accepted the viewpoint of the middle way; and at the same time agreed to the idea of a reason with components that had some inherent power to prove something.
DBU MA’I LTA BA KHAS LEN BZHIN DU YANG RANG RGYUD KYI SBYOR BA’I DAG {%NGAG} BRJOD PA GANG YIN PA DE NI CHOS SHIN TU NYES PA DU MA’I GNAS SU RTOGS TE ZHES GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR,

And that’s true, finally, because it has been stated—by these same sources—that we should “understand that accepting, on the one hand, the viewpoint of the middle way; and on the other hand trying to utilize some kind of ‘independent’ reasoning, is a teaching which is the source of countless faults.”
Gyaltsab Je gives yet another pertinent list in an important piece called A Record of Teachings [by Je Tsongkapa] on Eight Great Difficult Points in the “Foundational Verses on the Middle Way”:

SLOB DPON ‘PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS MDZAD PA’I RTZA BSHES {%BA SHES} RAB LA ‘GREL PA GRAGS CHE BA BRGYAD DU YOD CING, DE’I NANG NAS KYANG DGONGS PA PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR ‘GREL PA {%BA} NI SLOB DPON SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS DANG, SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PA GNYIS KYIS MDZAD PA ‘DI GNYIS YIN LA,

There are eight famous commentaries on the work of that realized being, Master Nagarjuna, entitled Wisdom: Foundational Verses.  Two of these explain the master’s true thought in an unerring way—these are the commentaries composed by Master Buddhapalita, and by Master Chandrakirti.
DE LA YANG ‘GREL BYED GZHAN DANG MI MTHUN PA’I KHYAD PAR PHRA MO MTHA’ YAS KYANG GNAD DU CHE BA BRGYAD YIN GSUNG STE,

There are virtually infinite subtle & unique features that separate the thinking of these two masters from that of other commentators; but there are eight ideas which are considered especially crucial.  Four of these positions are expressed in terms of assertions—about things we do accept; and four involve things we don’t accept.
GZHI’I SKABS SU THA SNYAD DU YANG KUN GZHI DANG RANG MTSAN KHAS MI LEN CING, PHYI DON KHAS LEN PA DANG,

Our first three distinctions relate to the period in our spiritual evolution when we are not yet travelling a spiritual path; that is, they relate to our original condition.  Here we do not accept, even nominally, that there are such things as (1) foundation consciousness, or (2) manifestations of an archetype.  We do accept though (3) outer objects.
LAM GYI SKABS SU, DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PA’I THABS SU RANG RGYUD DANG RANG RIG KHAS MI LEN CING,
Relative to the period spent on the path, we accept neither (4) independent forms of reasoning that can act as a means of attaining the realization of suchness; nor (5) apperception.
(6) SGRIB GNYIS KYI ‘JOG TSUL DANG, NYAN RANG LA CHOS RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA KHAS LEN PA’I TSUL DANG,

We do have (6) a special way of defining the two types of obstacles; and (7) a special way of accepting the idea that listeners and self-made buddhas do in fact realize how nothing has any nature of its own.
‘BRAS BU’I SKABS SU SANGS RGYAS KYIS JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PA’I TSUL TE, KHAS LEN PA’I DAM BCA’ BZHI DANG, MI LEN PA’I PHYOGS BZHI’O,,

As for the period in our spiritual evolution when we have already reached the final goal, we do describe (8) a way in which enlightened beings do perceive, individually, each & every object which ever exists.

Three centuries after the first writers of the monastic textbooks—people like Kedrup Tenpa Dargye—we see a pretty standard list of unique features developing.  Here is a concise one by the esteemed scholar Welmang Konchok Gyeltsen (1764-1853) from a commentary on the steps of the path.
Here are the eight unique features of the Consequence Group, within the Middle Way School.
TSOGS DRUG LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I KUN GZHI’I RNAM SHES, RANG RIG ‘GOG LUGS THUN MONG MA YIN PA, RANG RGYUD KYI SBYOR BAS PHYI RGOL LA LTA BA SKYED PAR KHAS MI LEN PA GSUM DANG,

Three of the positions they take are in the form of denying certain beliefs.  They have unique ways of denying (1) a foundation consciousness which is distinct from the collection of six consciousnesses, and (2) apperception.  And they deny (3) that by using a logical statement with components that have some inherent power you can inspire an opponent to a correct view of reality.
SHES PA KHAS LEN PA BZHIN DU PHYI DON YANG KHAS LEN PA DANG,
(4) They accept the idea of outer objects of awareness, in the same way that they accept awareness itself.
NYAN RANG LA STONG NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PAR KHAS LEN PA DANG,
(5) They accept the idea that listeners and self-made buddhas can perceive emptiness directly.
CHOS KYI BDAB {%BDAG} ‘DZIN NYEN {%NYON} MONGS SU ‘JOG PA DANG,
(6) They classify the tendency to believe in some self-nature to things, as opposed to a self-nature of people, as a negative emotion.
ZHIG PA DNGOS POR ‘DOD PA DANG,
(7) They believe that the process of something coming to an end is itself a functioning thing.
DE’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS DUS GSUM GYI ‘JOG TSUL THUN MONG MA YIN PA DGOS PA’O,
(8) And they believe that, for this reason, a unique way of explaining the past, present, and future is required.

III. Arya Nagarjuna’s dedication of the virtue created by this composition

We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one.  It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri (“gold calligraphy,” perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition).

We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there.  We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur.

In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like “my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna”—and then in time the book would actually be credited to him.  We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers’ opinions, and have not included those particular titles.  We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition.

The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work.  We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order.

The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more—and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years.

In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in.  We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact.  The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume.

We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works.  In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur.  These categories may perhaps be polished in time, but for now are very indicative of topics that The Arya considered important; which is the purpose of the exercise for our present volume.
